explanation.pattern: Compute the weighted average revenue, subtract cost, and divide by the cost.

items.stem: A tank holds 80 liters of salt solution that is 15% salt by volume. Water is evaporated until the solution is 20% salt, with no salt lost. Then 20 liters of a 35% salt solution are mixed in. What percent salt is the final mixture?

steps: Salt in the tank: 0.15 × 80 = 12 L. At 20% salt the volume is 12/0.20 = 60 L.
Adding 20 L of 35% solution adds 7 L of salt: 12 + 7 = 19 L of salt in 60 + 20 = 80 L.
Concentration: 19/80 = 23.75%.
explanation.why: The salt amount stays at 12 L during evaporation, which is what fixes the 60 L volume; using 80 L would give the wrong denominator.
explanation.pattern: Track the amount of salt, not the percent, through each stage.

items.stem: In a survey, 60% of respondents were older than 30. Of those older than 30, 35% preferred brand X; of those 30 or younger, 55% preferred brand X. If 215 respondents in all preferred brand X, how many respondents 30 or younger preferred brand X?

steps: Fraction preferring X overall: 0.60 × 0.35 + 0.40 × 0.55 = 0.21 + 0.22 = 0.43 of all respondents.
So there were 215/0.43 = 500 respondents.
Respondents 30 or younger who preferred X: 500 × 0.40 × 0.55 = 110.
explanation.why: The 215 is a count of everyone who preferred X, so it must be turned into a total of 500 before the younger subgroup's share is found.
explanation.pattern: Convert nested percents to one fraction of the whole, find the total, then take the subgroup.

items.stem: A bag contains \(6\) red marbles, \(4\) blue marbles, and \(10\) green marbles. One marble is selected at random. What is the probability that it is blue?

choices.slip: Divided 4 by 40 (doubled the total).
Divided by 16, the number of marbles that are not green, instead of all 20.
This is the probability of not choosing blue.

steps: Total marbles: \(6 + 4 + 10 = 20\).
explanation.why: 4 of the 20 marbles are blue, which is 1 out of every 5.
explanation.pattern: Probability = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, using all the items.

items.stem:
The table shows how 110 students in two grades prefer to take a class.
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{} & \text{Online} & \text{In person} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Grade 9} & 24 & 36 & 60 \\ \hline \text{Grade 10} & 30 & 20 & 50 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 54 & 56 & 110 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
If a grade 10 student is selected at random, what is the probability that the student prefers online? (Express your answer as a decimal or fraction, not as a percent.)

steps: Given grade 10, only the grade 10 row counts: 50 students.
Of those, 30 prefer online.
explanation.why: The condition 'a grade 10 student' shrinks the group to 50, and 30 of them prefer online: 0.6.
explanation.pattern: For 'given' probability, the denominator is only the group named in the condition.

items.stem:
The table shows the number of club events attended last year by the members of three clubs.
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Club} & \text{0 to 1} & \text{2 to 3} & \text{4 or more} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{A} & 14 & 9 & 7 & 30 \\ \hline \text{B} & 5 & 12 & 13 & 30 \\ \hline \text{C} & 11 & 16 & 13 & 40 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
One member who is not in club B will be selected at random. What is the probability that this member attended at least 2 events? (Express your answer as a decimal or fraction, not as a percent.)

steps: 'Not in club B' means clubs A and C: \(30 + 40 = 70\) members.
At least 2 events: club A \(9 + 7 = 16\), club C \(16 + 13 = 29\), so \(45\) members.
explanation.why: The condition removes club B entirely, leaving 70 members, 45 of whom went to 2 or more events.
explanation.pattern: A 'not in' condition is a 'given' condition: rebuild the denominator from every group that is left, then count across columns.

items.stem: In a class of \(40\) students, \(\frac{3}{8}\) of the students play an instrument, and \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the students who play an instrument also sing in the choir. If a choir member is selected at random, the probability that the student plays an instrument is \(\frac{5}{8}\). How many students in the class sing in the choir but do not play an instrument?

steps: Instrument players: \(\frac{3}{8}(40) = 15\). Players in the choir: \(\frac{2}{3}(15) = 10\).
Let \(c\) be the number of choir members: \(P(\text{plays} \mid \text{choir}) = \frac{10}{c} = \frac{5}{8}\), so \(c = 16\).
Choir members who don't play: \(16 - 10 = 6\).
explanation.why: The choir has 16 students; 10 of them play an instrument (10/16 = 5/8), so the other 6 don't.
explanation.pattern: Turn each fraction into a count step by step, and use the conditional probability to find the unknown group size.

items.stem: A company surveyed its 120 employees about how they commute: by bus, by bike, or by train. Of the employees, 70 work full-time and the rest work part-time. A total of 38 employees take the bus, and 22 of those work full-time. A total of 41 employees take the train, and 15 of those work part-time. One of the employees who does not take the bus is selected at random. What is the probability that the selected employee works full-time?

choices.slip: This divides 48 by all 70 full-time employees, but the group is the 82 employees who do not take the bus.
This divides 48 by all 120 employees, ignoring that the selection is only from employees who do not take the bus.
This is the probability that a bus rider (22 of 38) is full-time, the wrong group.

steps: Employees who do not take the bus: \(120 - 38 = 82\).
Full-time employees who take the bus: 22, so full-time employees who do not: \(70 - 22 = 48\).
Probability: \(\frac{48}{82} = \frac{24}{41}\).
explanation.why: The group is the 82 non-bus employees, so 82 is the denominator; the train details are extra.
explanation.pattern: Conditional probability: restrict to the stated group first, then count the favorable members inside it.

items.stem: A box contains 8 blue beads and some red beads. Two beads are drawn at random from the box without replacement. The probability that both beads are blue is \(\frac{14}{33}\). How many red beads are in the box?

steps: With \(r\) red beads there are \(8 + r\) beads. \(P(\text{both blue}) = \frac{8}{8+r} \cdot \frac{7}{7+r}\).
explanation.pattern: Without replacement, both the numerator and the total shrink by 1 on the second draw; set up an equation in the unknown count.

items.stem: Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent. The probability that \(A\) occurs is 0.3, and the probability that at least one of \(A\) and \(B\) occurs is 0.58. What is the probability that \(B\) occurs?

steps: Independence gives \(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)P(B)\).
explanation.why: Subtracting only P(A) from 0.58 gives 0.28, which wrongly assumes A and B never occur together.
explanation.pattern: For independent events, the union rule has a product term: P(A) + P(B) - P(A)P(B).

items.stem: A factory has three independent sensors that each monitor a machine. When a fault occurs, sensor A detects it with probability 0.8, sensor B with probability 0.75, and sensor C with probability 0.6. When a fault occurs, what is the probability that exactly one of the three sensors detects it? (Express the answer as a decimal or fraction.)

explanation.why: Exactly one means one sensor detects and the other two both miss, added over the three possible sensors.
explanation.pattern: Independent events: multiply along each case, then add the disjoint cases.

items.stem: In a survey of residents, 60% own a car. Of the residents who own a car, 30% also own a bike. Of the residents who do not own a car, 70% own a bike. One resident who owns a bike is selected at random. What is the probability that the selected resident owns a car?

choices.slip: This is the probability that a car owner owns a bike, the reverse conditional.
This compares bike owners with a car (18) to bike owners without a car (28), instead of to all 46 bike owners.
This is the probability that a randomly selected resident owns a bike (46%), not the conditional.

steps: Suppose there are 100 residents. Car and bike: \(60 \times 0.30 = 18\). No car and bike: \(40 \times 0.70 = 28\).
Bike owners: \(18 + 28 = 46\).
Probability of a car given a bike: \(18/46 = 9/23\).
explanation.why: The denominator is all bike owners (46), not all car owners.
explanation.pattern: Reverse a conditional by building the two-way counts from a convenient total.

items.stem: A bag contains 5 red marbles, 4 blue marbles, and 3 green marbles. Two marbles are selected at random from the bag without replacement. What is the probability that the two marbles are different colors?

choices.slip: This is the probability for selections with replacement (1 - 50/144); the marbles are not replaced.
This is the probability that the two marbles are the same color.
This is the probability of two marbles of the same color when the first is replaced (50/144), the wrong event and the wrong method.

steps: Pairs from 12 marbles: \(\binom{12}{2} = 66\).
Same-color pairs: \(\binom{5}{2} + \binom{4}{2} + \binom{3}{2} = 10 + 6 + 3 = 19\).
Different colors: \(1 - 19/66 = 47/66\).
explanation.why: It is easier to count same-color pairs and subtract from 1.
explanation.pattern: For 'not the same', use the complement of the same-color probability.

items.stem: Of 200 students at a school, 120 take Spanish, 90 take French, and 30 take both languages. One student is selected at random from the students who take exactly one of the two languages. What is the probability that the selected student takes Spanish?

choices.slip: This divides the Spanish-only students (90) by all Spanish students (120), a different group.
This divides all Spanish students (120) by the students taking at least one language (180).
This divides the Spanish-only students (90) by all 200 students.

steps: Spanish only: \(120 - 30 = 90\). French only: \(90 - 30 = 60\).
Students taking exactly one language: \(90 + 60 = 150\).
Probability: \(90/150 = 3/5\).
explanation.why: The group is the 150 students taking exactly one language, and favorable outcomes exclude those taking both.
explanation.pattern: Remove the overlap from each category before forming a conditional probability on 'exactly one'.

items.stem:
A streaming service recorded whether subscribers on two plans renewed. Some entries are missing, as shown.
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{} & \text{Renewed} & \text{Did not renew} \\ \hline \text{Basic} & 36 & ? \\ \hline \text{Premium} & 30 & ? \\ \hline \end{array}\)
In all, 162 subscribers are included, and 60% of the Basic subscribers renewed. A subscriber who did not renew is chosen at random. What is the probability that the subscriber is on the Premium plan? (Express your answer as a decimal or fraction, not as a percent.)

steps: Basic subscribers who renewed are 60% of the Basic total, so the Basic total is \(36 \div 0.60 = 60\), and 24 Basic subscribers did not renew.
Premium subscribers who did not renew: \(162 - 36 - 24 - 30 = 72\).
Among the \(24 + 72 = 96\) who did not renew, 72 are Premium: \(\frac{72}{96} = \frac{3}{4}\).
explanation.why: The conditional is restricted to the 'did not renew' column, whose entries come from two different constraints.
explanation.pattern: Fill the table using the given percent and total, then divide within the column named by the condition.

items.stem: A lab runs two independent tests on a sample. Test 1 is positive with probability 0.10 (that is, 10%) and Test 2 is positive with probability 20%. Given that at least one of the tests is positive, what is the probability that both tests are positive?

choices.slip: This is P(both) = 0.02, the unconditional probability.
Divided by 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30, adding the probabilities without subtracting the overlap.
Divided by P(exactly one positive) = 0.26 instead of P(at least one) = 0.28.

steps: Conditional probability: \(\frac{0.02}{0.28} = \frac{1}{14}\).
explanation.why: 'Given at least one' shrinks the sample space to 28% of outcomes, so the denominator is the union, not the overlap.
explanation.pattern: P(A | at least one) = P(A and the condition) / P(condition), and the condition's probability needs the complement rule.

items.stem: In a survey, 40% of respondents were under 30 years old. Of the respondents under 30, 70% use a certain app, and of the respondents 30 or older, 20% use the app. Exactly 1200 respondents use the app. How many respondents who are 30 or older do not use the app?

steps: Let \(N\) be the number of respondents. App users: \(0.40 \times 0.70N + 0.60 \times 0.20N = 0.28N + 0.12N = 0.40N\).
Respondents 30 or older: \(0.60 \times 3000 = 1800\). Those who do not use the app: \(0.80 \times 1800 = 1440\).
explanation.why: The total is hidden: it must be recovered from the number of app users before the target group can be counted.
explanation.pattern: In percent-tree problems, express the known count with the total as a variable, solve for the total, then follow the branch.

items.stem: A bag contains only red and green marbles. Two marbles are drawn one at a time with replacement. The probability that the two marbles are the same color is 0.52, and a red marble is less likely than a green marble on any single draw. If three marbles are drawn one at a time with replacement, what is the probability that all three are red?

choices.slip: Found p = 0.4 but cubed too few times: this is P(both red) in two draws.
Multiplied the same-color probability 0.52 by 0.4.
Took the other root, p = 0.6, which is the probability of green.

steps: The solutions are \(p = 0.4\) and \(p = 0.6\). Red is less likely, so \(p = 0.4\).
explanation.why: The quadratic has two roots, and the condition about red being less likely selects one of them.
explanation.pattern: When a probability condition gives a quadratic, use the stated inequality to pick the root, then use independence.

items.stem: An inspector tests units one at a time. Each unit independently has a 25% chance of being defective. What is the smallest number of units she must test so that the probability of finding at least one defective unit is at least 90%?

choices.slip: Divided 90% by 25% to get 3.6 and rounded up, as if probabilities added.
Solved \(0.75^n = 0.10\) to get 8.004 and rounded down; 8 tests give only 89.99%.
Added an unnecessary extra test: 9 tests already give 92.5%, and the question asks for the smallest.

steps: The probability of at least one defective unit in \(n\) tests is \(1 - 0.75^n\), so we need \(0.75^n \le 0.10\).
For \(n = 8\), \(0.75^8 \approx 0.1001 > 0.10\), so the probability is only about 89.99%, just under 90%.
For \(n = 9\), \(0.75^9 \approx 0.0751\), so the probability is about 92.5%. The smallest number is 9.
explanation.why: The threshold is missed by a hair at 8 tests, so rounding the logarithm instead of checking the boundary gives the wrong answer.
explanation.pattern: Use the complement for 'at least one', then test the integer just below and at the bound.

items.stem: A bag holds only red and blue marbles in the ratio 3 to 5. Then 4 red marbles are removed and 8 blue marbles are added, and the probability of drawing a red marble is now \(\frac{1}{4}\). Two marbles are then drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?

choices.slip: Used the original counts, 15 red out of 40, ignoring the removal and addition.
Used 10/44 for the second draw, removing the red marble but not the total.
Treated the draws as independent (with replacement): \(\frac14 \times \frac14\).

steps: Let the original bag have \(3k\) red and \(5k\) blue marbles. Then \(\dfrac{3k - 4}{8k + 4} = \dfrac14\), so \(12k - 16 = 8k + 4\) and \(k = 5\).
Now there are \(15 - 4 = 11\) red and \(25 + 8 = 33\) blue marbles: 44 in all.
explanation.why: After the first red marble is drawn, both the red count and the total fall by one, so the second fraction is 10/43, not 11/44 or 10/44.
explanation.pattern: Use the ratio and the given probability to find the actual counts, then multiply successive probabilities, reducing both parts of the second fraction.

items.stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Given that at least one of the dice shows a 6, what is the probability that the sum of the two dice is at least 9?

choices.slip: Found P(sum at least 9) = 10/36 and ignored the condition.
Divided by all 36 outcomes instead of the 11 allowed by the condition.
Counted the 7 favorable outcomes over the 12 that result from counting (6, 6) twice.

steps: Outcomes with at least one 6: \(36 - 25 = 11\).
explanation.why: The condition shrinks the sample space from 36 to 11 outcomes, and the pair (6, 6) must be counted only once.
explanation.pattern: Conditional probability: count outcomes meeting both conditions over outcomes meeting the given condition.

items.stem: A circular dartboard has an outer radius of 10 centimeters. A dart lands at a random point on the board. The probability that it lands in the central bullseye is 0.09. A scoring ring surrounds the bullseye and extends out to a distance of 6 centimeters from the center. What is the probability that the dart lands in this ring (outside the bullseye and within 6 centimeters of the center)?

choices.slip: Found the probability for the whole disk of radius 6 and did not subtract the bullseye.
Used a ratio of radii: \((6 - 3) \div 10\).
Doubled the bullseye probability because the radius doubles, forgetting that area grows with the square.

steps: Probability is proportional to area. The bullseye has \(\pi r^2 = 0.09 \times \pi (10)^2\), so \(r = 3\) cm.
The region within 6 cm has probability \(6^2 \div 10^2 = 0.36\).
Subtract the bullseye: \(0.36 - 0.09 = 0.27\).
explanation.why: Radii scale probability by their squares. Radius 6 is twice radius 3, so its region is four times the bullseye, not twice.
explanation.pattern: For a random point on a disk, probability equals area ratio; subtract nested regions.

items.stem: Of 60 students, 28 take art, 24 take band, and 19 take chess. Also, 9 take both art and band, 7 take both art and chess, 6 take both band and chess, and 3 take all three. (Each pair count includes the students who take all three.) A student is chosen at random from those who take at least one of the three subjects. What is the probability that the student takes exactly two of the subjects?

steps: At least one subject: \(28 + 24 + 19 - 9 - 7 - 6 + 3 = 52\).
explanation.why: The pair counts include the students taking all three, so each must be reduced by 3, and the denominator is the 52 who take at least one subject, not all 60 students.
explanation.pattern: Use inclusion-exclusion for the union, remove the triple overlap from each pair, and condition on the union.

items.stem: A point is chosen at random inside a rectangle that is 14 units long and 10 units wide. What is the probability that the point is within 3 units of at least one side of the rectangle?

choices.slip: Found the probability of being in the inner rectangle, 32/140, and did not subtract it from 1.
Removed a strip of width 3 from only one side of each dimension, leaving an 11 by 7 rectangle: 1 - 77/140 is 9/20.
Found the 11 by 7 rectangle left after removing one 3-unit strip per dimension and used its area ratio, 77/140.

steps: The points farther than 3 units from every side form an inner rectangle that is \(14 - 6 = 8\) by \(10 - 6 = 4\), with area 32.
The whole rectangle has area \(14 \times 10 = 140\), so the probability of being in the inner rectangle is \(\frac{32}{140} = \frac{8}{35}\).
The required probability is \(1 - \frac{8}{35} = \frac{27}{35}\).
explanation.why: The strip along each side is 3 units wide, so the inner rectangle loses 3 units from both ends of each dimension, not 3 units in total.
explanation.pattern: Geometric probability is an area ratio; find the complementary region and subtract it from 1.

items.stem: Bag A holds 5 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. Bag B holds 2 red marbles and 6 blue marbles. One marble is chosen at random from bag A and placed in bag B, and then one marble is chosen at random from bag B. Given that the marble chosen from bag B is red, what is the probability that the marble moved from bag A was red?

steps: Moved red (5/8), then red drawn from 9 marbles with 3 red: \(\frac58 \times \frac{3}{9} = \frac{15}{72}\).
Moved blue (3/8), then red drawn with 2 red among 9: \(\frac38 \times \frac29 = \frac{6}{72}\).
explanation.why: Bag B has 9 marbles after the transfer, and its red count depends on the color moved, so the two cases must be weighted by their own probabilities.
explanation.pattern: For a reverse conditional, divide the probability of the path you want by the total probability of all paths to the observed event.

items.stem:
The counts below show how many employees at a firm chose each plan and each work arrangement.

Plan X: x remote and 20 on-site
Plan Y: 45 remote and 75 on-site

The events "chooses Plan X" and "works remotely" are independent. What is the probability that a randomly selected employee chose Plan X?

steps: Independence means the Plan X share is the same in both columns: \(\frac{x}{x + 45} = \frac{20}{20 + 75}\), so \(\frac{x}{45} = \frac{20}{75}\) and \(x = 12\).
The table totals \(12 + 20 + 45 + 75 = 152\) employees.
explanation.why: Independence is a statement about ratios between rows and columns, so x must be found first and then included in both the Plan X count and the total.
explanation.pattern: Independent events have equal conditional and marginal probabilities, which fixes an unknown cell.

items.stem: A device works only if component A works and at least one of components B and C works. The components fail independently. Component A works with probability 0.9, component B with probability 0.8, and component C with probability 0.7. Given that the device works, what is the probability that component B failed?

steps: The device works with probability \(0.9 \times (1 - 0.2 \times 0.3) = 0.9 \times 0.94 = 0.846\).
The device works with B failed only if A works, B fails, and C works: \(0.9 \times 0.2 \times 0.7 = 0.126\).
The conditional probability is \(\tfrac{0.126}{0.846} = \tfrac{7}{47}\).
explanation.why: Given that the device works, B failing is possible only when C works, so the unconditional chance of B failing (0.2) is not the answer.
explanation.pattern: Find the probability of the condition, then the probability of the condition together with the event, and divide.

items.stem: A committee of 4 people is chosen at random from 5 seniors, 4 juniors, and 3 sophomores. What is the probability that the committee includes at least one person from each of the three classes?

choices.slip: Subtracted the committees missing one class (35 + 70 + 126) from the total but did not add back the committees counted twice for missing two classes (6).
Counted only 3 ways to pick which class supplies two members and ignored the choices within that class (10, 6, and 3).
Counted only the 60 ways to pick one person from each class, ignoring the fourth member.

steps: There are \(\binom{12}{4} = 495\) equally likely committees.

With four members and three classes, one class supplies two: seniors \(\binom{5}{2}\cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 120\), juniors \(5\cdot\binom{4}{2}\cdot 3 = 90\), sophomores \(5\cdot 4\cdot\binom{3}{2} = 60\), for 270 committees.
The probability is \(\tfrac{270}{495} = \tfrac{6}{11}\).
explanation.why: A committee of four with all three classes must have exactly one class represented twice, and each of the three cases needs its own count of pairs.
explanation.pattern: Split 'at least one of each' into the patterns that satisfy it, count each with combinations, and divide by the total.

items.stem: A condition affects 2% of a population. A screening test is positive for 90% of people who have the condition and for 5% of people who do not. A randomly chosen person takes the test twice, with the two results independent given the person's condition, and is positive both times. What is the probability that the person has the condition?

steps: Two positives for someone with the condition: \(0.02 \times 0.9 \times 0.9 = 0.0162\).
Two positives for someone without it: \(0.98 \times 0.05 \times 0.05 = 0.00245\).
explanation.why: Both results must be positive, so each branch of the tree contains the test probability twice, and the prevalence is applied once.
explanation.pattern: Multiply along each branch of the tree, then divide the branch you want by the sum of the branches that fit the evidence.

items.stem: A car travels \(168\) miles using \(6\) gallons of gas. At this rate, how many miles can the car travel using \(10\) gallons of gas?

steps: Rate: \(\frac{168}{6} = 28\) miles per gallon.
\(28 \times 10 = 280\) miles.
explanation.why: 28 miles for every gallon, times 10 gallons, is 280 miles.
explanation.pattern: Find the unit rate first, then multiply by the new amount.

items.stem: A leaking faucet drips \(3\) milliliters of water every \(20\) seconds. At this rate, how many liters of water does the faucet drip in one day? (1 liter = 1,000 milliliters)

steps: Per minute: \(3 \times \frac{60}{20} = 9\) milliliters.
Per day: \(9 \times 60 \times 24 = 12{,}960\) milliliters.
explanation.why: There are 4,320 twenty-second periods in a day (86,400 ÷ 20), and 4,320 × 3 mL = 12,960 mL = 12.96 L.
explanation.pattern: Chain the conversions one unit at a time (seconds → minutes → hours → days, mL → L), so the units cancel.

items.stem: A printer prints \(p\) pages every \(s\) seconds. At this rate, which expression gives the number of pages the printer prints in \(m\) minutes?

choices.text: \(\dfrac{60pm}{s}\)

choices.slip: Divided by 60 instead of multiplying: minutes are bigger than seconds, so more pages print.
choices.text: \(\dfrac{pm}{60s}\)

choices.slip: Inverted the time parts of the rate.
choices.text: \(\dfrac{60ps}{m}\)

choices.slip: Used seconds per page instead of pages per second.
choices.text: \(\dfrac{60sm}{p}\)

steps: Rate: \(\frac{p}{s}\) pages per second.
\(m\) minutes is \(60m\) seconds.
Pages \(= \frac{p}{s} \cdot 60m = \frac{60pm}{s}\).
explanation.why: Check with numbers: 10 pages every 5 seconds is 2 pages per second, so 1 minute gives 120 pages, and 60(10)(1)/5 = 120.
explanation.pattern: Write the rate as a fraction with units, convert the time to the same unit, then multiply.

items.stem: A solid aluminum cylinder has a mass of \(1,080\) grams and a height of \(10\) centimeters. The density of aluminum is \(2.7\) grams per cubic centimeter. To the nearest tenth of a centimeter, what is the radius of the cylinder?

choices.slip: Left π out: solved 10r² = 400.
Stopped at r² and didn't take the square root.
Found the base area without π and stopped there.

steps: Volume \(= \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{density}} = \frac{1{,}080}{2.7} = 400\) cubic centimeters.
\(r = \sqrt{12.73} \approx 3.6\) centimeters.
explanation.why: A radius of 3.6 cm gives a volume of π(3.6)²(10) ≈ 407 cm³ and a mass of about 1,099 g, the closest of the choices to 1,080 g.
explanation.pattern: Density links mass and volume (V = m/ρ). Then use the shape's volume formula and solve for the length asked.

items.stem: Alloy X is made of copper and tin in a mass ratio of 3 to 2. Alloy Y is made of copper and tin in a mass ratio of 1 to 4. A metalworker melts 8 kilograms of alloy Y together with some amount of alloy X, and the mixture contains equal masses of copper and tin. How many kilograms of alloy X did the metalworker use?

steps: Alloy X is \(\frac{3}{5}\) copper and \(\frac{2}{5}\) tin by mass; alloy Y is \(\frac{1}{5}\) copper and \(\frac{4}{5}\) tin.
Let \(x\) be the kilograms of X. Copper: \(\frac{3}{5}x + \frac{1}{5}(8)\). Tin: \(\frac{2}{5}x + \frac{4}{5}(8)\).
Set them equal: \(3x + 8 = 2x + 32\), so \(x = 24\).
explanation.why: With 24 kg of X the mixture has 14.4 + 1.6 = 16 kg of copper and 9.6 + 6.4 = 16 kg of tin.
explanation.pattern: Turn each part-to-part ratio into fractions of the whole, then set the two component totals equal.

items.stem: A museum builds a scale model of a storage tank. Every length on the model is \(\frac{1}{50}\) of the corresponding length on the actual tank, and the model holds 2.4 liters of water. How many cubic meters of water does the actual tank hold? (1 cubic meter = 1,000 liters)

choices.slip: This multiplies the volume by 50 only; volume scales with the cube of the length factor.
This uses 50 squared, which is the factor for area, not volume.
This is the volume in liters; the question asks for cubic meters.

steps: Lengths are scaled by 50, so volume is scaled by \(50^3 = 125{,}000\).
The tank holds \(2.4 \times 125{,}000 = 300{,}000\) liters.
Convert to cubic meters: \(300{,}000 \div 1{,}000 = 300\).
explanation.why: Volume scales with the cube of the length factor, and the final answer must be in cubic meters, not liters.
explanation.pattern: Length factor k means area factor k squared and volume factor k cubed; then convert units last.

items.stem: A delivery cyclist rides from a warehouse to a market at an average speed of 12 kilometers per hour, then returns by the same route at an average speed of 24 kilometers per hour. The total riding time for the round trip is 4.5 hours. How many kilometers long is the route from the warehouse to the market?

steps: Let \(d\) be the one-way distance. The trip out takes \(\frac{d}{12}\) hours and the return takes \(\frac{d}{24}\) hours.
Then \(d = 4.5 \times 8 = 36\).
explanation.why: Out: 36/12 = 3 hours. Back: 36/24 = 1.5 hours. Total 4.5 hours.
explanation.pattern: Different speeds over the same distance: write each leg's time as distance over speed and add.

items.stem: Solution X is a mixture of acid and water in the ratio 1 to 4 by volume. Solution Y is a mixture of acid and water in the ratio 3 to 2 by volume. How many liters of Solution Y must be added to 20 liters of Solution X so that the resulting mixture contains equal volumes of acid and water?

choices.slip: This repeats the 20 L of Solution X, as if equal volumes of X and Y were needed.
This divides the 12 L shortfall by 0.4, Y's water fraction, instead of the net gain of 0.2 L of acid per liter.
This treats the 1 to 4 ratio as 1/4 acid (5 L of 20) instead of 1/5 (4 L of 20).

steps: Solution X is 1 part acid in 5 parts, so 20 L of X holds 4 L acid and 16 L water.
Solution Y is 3 parts acid in 5 parts, so each liter holds 0.6 L acid and 0.4 L water.
Set acid equal to water: \(4 + 0.6v = 16 + 0.4v\), so \(0.2v = 12\) and \(v = 60\).
explanation.why: Each liter of Y adds 0.2 L more acid than water, and X is short by 12 L of acid, so 12 / 0.2 = 60 liters.
explanation.pattern: Convert ratios to fractions of the whole (parts out of the sum of parts), then balance the two quantities.

items.stem: A conveyor belt carries boxes at a constant speed of 150 feet per minute. The front edges of consecutive boxes are 45 inches apart. How many boxes pass a fixed point on the belt in one hour? (1 foot = 12 inches)

choices.slip: This is the number of boxes per minute; the question asks about one hour.
This divides 150 by 45 without converting feet to inches, then multiplies by 60.
This multiplies by 12 a second time after already converting feet to inches.

steps: Convert the speed: \(150 \times 12 = 1{,}800\) inches per minute.
Boxes per minute: \(1{,}800 \div 45 = 40\).
Boxes per hour: \(40 \times 60 = 2{,}400\).
explanation.why: The belt moves 1,800 inches each minute and one box passes every 45 inches, so 40 boxes pass each minute and 2,400 each hour.
explanation.pattern: Put distance and spacing in the same unit before dividing, then convert minutes to hours last.

items.stem: At a camp, the ratio of boys to girls was 5 to 7. Then 15 boys left and 9 girls arrived, and the ratio of boys to girls became 1 to 2. How many campers were at the camp originally?

choices.slip: This forgets the 9 girls who arrived, solving 2(5k - 15) = 7k, so k = 10.
The total after the change is 150; the net change was -6, so the original total is 150 + 6, not 150 - 6.
This is the number of campers after the change, not before it.

steps: Let the original numbers be \(5k\) boys and \(7k\) girls.
Original total: \(12k = 156\).
explanation.why: With k = 13 there were 65 boys and 91 girls; after the change there are 50 boys and 100 girls, a 1 to 2 ratio.
explanation.pattern: Write ratio parts as multiples of k, apply the changes to the actual counts, and set up the new ratio as an equation.

items.stem: On a map, 1 centimeter represents 2.5 kilometers. A nature preserve covers 18 square centimeters on the map. How many hectares does the preserve actually cover? (1 square kilometer = 100 hectares)

choices.slip: This is the area in square kilometers; the question asks for hectares.
This converts 112.5 square kilometers using a factor of 10 instead of 100.
This multiplies by the scale 2.5 only once (45 km2), not squared, then converts to hectares.

steps: One square centimeter on the map is \((2.5)^2 = 6.25\) square kilometers.
Actual area: \(18 \times 6.25 = 112.5\) square kilometers.
Convert: \(112.5 \times 100 = 11{,}250\) hectares.
explanation.why: Areas scale by the square of the length scale, and the final conversion multiplies square kilometers by 100.
explanation.pattern: Square the length scale for area, then apply the unit conversion once.

items.stem: A reservoir can be filled by inlet pipe A alone in 6 hours or by inlet pipe B alone in 9 hours. A drain, when open, empties a full reservoir in 18 hours. The reservoir starts empty, and pipe A and the drain are both opened. After 2 hours, pipe B is also opened, and all three stay open until the reservoir is full. How many hours after the start is the reservoir full?

steps: Pipe A and the drain together fill \(\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{18} = \frac{1}{9}\) of the reservoir per hour, so after 2 hours \(\frac{2}{9}\) is full.
With pipe B open too, the net rate is \(\frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{9} = \frac{2}{9}\) per hour.
The remaining \(\frac{7}{9}\) takes \(\frac{7}{9} \div \frac{2}{9} = 3.5\) hours, so the total is \(2 + 3.5 = 5.5\) hours.
explanation.why: Rates add as fractions of the job per hour, and the drain subtracts. The rate changes at 2 hours, so the problem splits into two stages.
explanation.pattern: Work-rate problems: convert each time to a rate (job per hour), add or subtract rates, and handle each stage separately.

items.stem: The scale of a trail map is 1 : 50000, so 1 centimeter on the map represents 50000 centimeters on the ground. The hiking route measures 80 centimeters on the map. A hiker covers the first 60% of the route's actual length at 4 kilometers per hour and the rest at 2 kilometers per hour, without stopping. How many hours does the hike take?

steps: First part: \(0.60 \times 40 = 24\) km at 4 km/h takes 6 hours. Second part: 16 km at 2 km/h takes 8 hours.
Total time: \(6 + 8 = 14\) hours.
explanation.why: The speeds apply to equal-percent shares of the distance, not of the time, so averaging 4 and 2 to get 3 km/h would give 13.3 hours, which is wrong.
explanation.pattern: Convert units first, then compute time = distance / speed for each leg and add the times.

items.stem: A trail mix is made of nuts, raisins, and chocolate chips in the ratio 6 : 3 : 1 by mass. Nuts cost $12 per kilogram, raisins cost $8 per kilogram, and chocolate chips cost $20 per kilogram. The maker then changes the ratio to 4 : 3 : 3, and the price of chocolate chips rises by 25%. By how many dollars does the ingredient cost of 1 kilogram of mix increase?

steps: New chip price: \(1.25 \times 20 = 25\).
Increase: \(14.70 - 11.60 = 3.10\) dollars.
explanation.why: Both the recipe and one price changed. Changing only the ratio gives an increase of 1.60 and changing only the price gives 0.50, and neither alone is the answer.
explanation.pattern: A ratio of parts makes a weighted average: cost per kilogram is the sum of (share times price). Recompute with every change applied.

items.stem: A project was scheduled to take 12 workers 15 days working 8 hours per day, and all workers work at the same rate. After 5 days, 4 of the workers leave. The remaining workers increase their workday to 10 hours. How many more days do the remaining workers need to finish the project?

choices.slip: Used all 12 workers for the longer day, forgetting that 4 workers left: 960 / 120.
Kept the 8-hour day for the remaining workers: 960 / 64.
Divided the total work (1440), not the remaining work, by the new daily output of 80.

steps: Total work: \(12 \times 15 \times 8 = 1440\) worker-hours. Completed in 5 days: \(12 \times 5 \times 8 = 480\). Remaining: 960.
Remaining crew output per day: \(8 \text{ workers} \times 10 \text{ hours} = 80\) worker-hours.
Days needed: \(960 \div 80 = 12\).
explanation.why: The remaining work must be found first, and then divided by the new daily output, which uses both the smaller crew and the longer day.
explanation.pattern: Measure work in worker-hours; subtract what is done, then divide by the new worker-hours per day.

items.stem: A straight trail is 81 miles long. Ifeoma starts at the west end and walks east at 12 miles per hour. Wenceslao starts at the east end 30 minutes after Ifeoma starts and walks west at 18 miles per hour. They both walk without stopping. How many miles from the west end of the trail are they when they meet?

steps: Ifeoma has walked \(12 \times 0.5 = 6\) miles when Wenceslao starts, so \(81 - 6 = 75\) miles remain between them.
They close the gap at \(12 + 18 = 30\) miles per hour, so they meet \(75 \div 30 = 2.5\) hours after Wenceslao starts.
Ifeoma has walked \(6 + 12 \times 2.5 = 36\) miles from the west end.
explanation.why: The head start must be removed from the gap before the speeds are combined, and the answer is measured from Ifeoma's end, not from where they would have met without the delay.
explanation.pattern: Subtract the head start first, close the remaining gap at the combined speed, then convert the meeting time back to a distance from the requested end.

items.stem: A laser printer cartridge holds 21 grams of toner. The toner has a density of 0.75 gram per milliliter, and each printed page uses 0.35 milliliter of toner. A print shop needs to print 1300 pages. How many cartridges must the shop buy, if cartridges can only be bought whole?

choices.slip: Found 16.25 cartridges but dropped the partial cartridge instead of rounding up.
Skipped the density: 21 mL per cartridge gives 60 pages each, and \(1300 \div 60 \approx 21.7\) rounds up to 22.
Multiplied by the density instead of dividing: 15.75 mL per cartridge gives 45 pages each, and \(1300 \div 45 \approx 28.9\) rounds up to 29.

steps: Volume per cartridge: \(21 \div 0.75 = 28\) mL, since density is grams per milliliter.
Pages per cartridge: \(28 \div 0.35 = 80\).
Cartridges needed: \(1300 \div 80 = 16.25\), and a partial cartridge cannot be bought, so 17.
explanation.why: Two traps work against each other: the density must divide the mass (not multiply it), and the final count must be rounded up.
explanation.pattern: Convert units in the right direction, find the capacity of one container, divide, and round up when only whole units can be bought.

items.stem: A cleaning solution is made by mixing concentrate and water in the ratio 1 to 24 by volume. A janitor has 750 milliliters of concentrate and plenty of water. She fills spray bottles that each hold exactly 500 milliliters of finished solution, always using the correct ratio. What is the greatest number of bottles she can fill completely?

choices.slip: Treated 24 parts as the whole bottle, so each bottle needs about 20.8 mL of concentrate and 750 mL fills 36.
Rounded 37.5 up, but the last bottle would be only half filled.
Treated the ratio as 26 parts (adding an extra part for the concentrate), giving 39.

steps: The ratio 1 to 24 means 25 equal parts in all, so one bottle needs \(500 \div 25 = 20\) mL of concentrate.
The concentrate supports \(750 \div 20 = 37.5\) bottles.
Only complete bottles count, so the greatest number is 37.
explanation.why: The ratio compares concentrate to water, so the whole solution is 25 parts, not 24. The half bottle must then be discarded rather than rounded up.
explanation.pattern: A part-to-part ratio needs its parts added to get the whole; then check whether the question wants whole units.

items.stem: Zorica exchanges $800 for euros. The exchange service first takes a 2.5% fee out of the dollar amount and then converts what is left at 0.9 euro per dollar. She spends 480 euros and converts the rest back to dollars at 1.15 dollars per euro, with no fee on the second exchange. How many dollars does she have after the second exchange?

steps: After the fee she converts \(800 \times 0.975 = 780\) dollars, which gives \(780 \times 0.9 = 702\) euros.
After spending 480 euros, \(702 - 480 = 222\) euros remain.
Converted back: \(222 \times 1.15 = 255.30\) dollars.
explanation.why: The fee comes off the dollars before the first conversion, and the two exchange rates are not reciprocals, so the second rate must be used as given.
explanation.pattern: Apply each stated step in order, keeping track of the currency after every step.

items.stem: A cyclist pedals at a steady 70 revolutions per minute. A chain links a chainring with 48 teeth to a rear cog with 16 teeth, so the rear wheel makes \(\frac{48}{16}\) turns for each pedal revolution. Each turn of the wheel moves the bicycle 2.1 meters. At this pace, how many minutes will the cyclist need to ride 39.69 kilometers?

steps: Wheel turns per minute: \(70 \times \frac{48}{16} = 210\).
Speed: \(210 \times 2.1 = 441\) meters per minute, which is \(441 \times 60 \div 1000 = 26.46\) kilometers per hour.
Time: \(39.69 \div 26.46 = 1.5\) hours, which is 90 minutes.
explanation.why: The pedal rate has to be multiplied by the gear ratio before the wheel circumference is used, and the final time is requested in minutes, not hours.
explanation.pattern: Chain the rates in order (pedal turns, wheel turns, meters, kilometers) and convert units only once at the end.

items.stem: On a trip, a car traveled 252 miles on highways at 42 miles per gallon and 63 miles in city traffic at 21 miles per gallon. What was the car's average fuel economy, in miles per gallon, for the whole trip?

choices.slip: Took the simple mean of 42 and 21, ignoring how far the car traveled at each rate.
Multiplied the highway rate by the highway share of the distance, 0.8(42), and stopped.
Weighted the two mpg values by distance, 0.8(42) + 0.2(21), which averages the rates instead of totaling gallons.

steps: Highway fuel: \(252 \div 42 = 6\) gallons. City fuel: \(63 \div 21 = 3\) gallons.
Total distance is \(252 + 63 = 315\) miles on \(6 + 3 = 9\) gallons.
Average economy: \(315 \div 9 = 35\) miles per gallon.
explanation.why: Fuel economy is total miles divided by total gallons. Averaging the two mpg figures, even with weights for distance, ignores that the car uses more gallons per mile in the city.
explanation.pattern: To average a rate, divide the total of the numerator quantity by the total of the denominator quantity.

items.stem: A technician is paid a base hourly rate for the first 40 hours worked in a week and 1.5 times that rate for every hour beyond 40 in that week. Over four weeks she worked 38, 46, 52, and 44 hours and earned a total of $4584. What is her base hourly rate, in dollars?

steps: Hours paid at the base rate: \(38 + 40 + 40 + 40 = 158\), because overtime is counted week by week and the 38-hour week has none.
Overtime hours: \(0 + 6 + 12 + 4 = 22\), each paid at 1.5 times the base rate, which equals \(33\) base-rate hours.
Total pay equals \(158 + 33 = 191\) base-rate hours, so the rate is \(4584 \div 191 = 24\) dollars per hour.
explanation.why: Because the overtime threshold applies to each week separately, the 180 total hours cannot simply be split into 160 regular and 20 overtime hours.
explanation.pattern: Convert premium hours into equivalent base-rate hours, then divide the total pay by that equivalent total.

items.stem: A drone flies in a straight line for 20 seconds at 54 kilometers per hour and then for 40 seconds at 36 kilometers per hour. On a map with scale 1 : 50000, how many centimeters long is the drone's path?

choices.slip: Converted 700 m to 7,000 cm instead of 70,000 cm.
Averaged the speeds to 45 km/h and applied it for the full 60 seconds, ignoring the unequal times.
Treated the seconds as minutes, giving a path of 42 km before applying the scale.

steps: First leg: \(54 \text{ km/h} = 15\) m/s, so \(15 \times 20 = 300\) m. Second leg: \(36 \text{ km/h} = 10\) m/s, so \(10 \times 40 = 400\) m.
Total path: 700 m \(= 70{,}000\) cm.
explanation.why: The two speeds apply for different lengths of time, so they cannot be averaged as 45 km/h, and the distance must be in centimeters before dividing by the scale.
explanation.pattern: Convert speed and time to a distance in one unit, then apply the map scale to that distance.

items.stem: A cyclist leaves a trailhead at 18 kilometers per hour. 20 minutes later, a scooter rider leaves the same trailhead on the same straight path at a steady 7.5 meters per second. How many kilometers from the trailhead is the scooter rider when she catches the cyclist?

steps: Convert the scooter's speed: \(7.5 \text{ m/s} \times 3.6 = 27\) km/h.
The cyclist's head start is \(18 \times \tfrac{20}{60} = 6\) km, and the scooter closes the gap at \(27 - 18 = 9\) km/h, which takes \(6 \div 9 = \tfrac{2}{3}\) hour.
The scooter rider has traveled \(27 \times \tfrac{2}{3} = 18\) km.
explanation.why: The speeds are in different units and the cyclist leaves first, so the head start must be converted to distance and the closing speed used for the catch-up time.
explanation.pattern: Convert to one unit, turn the head start into a gap, divide by the closing speed, then use the chaser's own speed for the distance.

items.stem: Partners A, B and C split the cost of a shared workshop. The ratio of A's payment to B's payment is 3:4, and the ratio of B's payment to C's payment is 6:5. Together, A and C paid $1260 more than B paid. How many dollars did C pay?

choices.slip: Chained the ratios as 3:4:5 without matching B's two different values (4 and 6); that makes A and C pay only 4 units more than B.
Found the unit correctly (180) but gave B's payment of 12 units instead of C's 10 units.
Matched B incorrectly, writing the ratio as 3:6:5; that makes A and C pay only 2 units more than B.

steps: Make B the same in both ratios: A:B = 9:12 and B:C = 12:10, so A:B:C = 9:12:10.
A and C together pay \(9 + 10 = 19\) units and B pays 12 units, so the difference is 7 units, and \(7\text{ units} = 1260\) gives 1 unit = 180 dollars.
C paid \(10 \times 180 = 1800\) dollars.
explanation.why: Two ratios sharing B can be combined only after B is scaled to its least common multiple (12); copying 4 and 6 side by side gives the wrong shares.
explanation.pattern: Link ratios through the shared quantity, convert the stated difference into units, then solve for one unit.

items.stem: An IV bag holds 800 milliliters of fluid, and the tubing delivers 15 drops per milliliter. A nurse sets the flow to 20 drops per minute. After 150 minutes, the nurse increases the flow rate by 50 percent. How many more hours will it take for the remaining fluid to finish dripping at the new rate?

steps: Total drops: \(800 \times 15 = 12{,}000\). Drops delivered in the first 150 minutes: \(20 \times 150 = 3000\), so 9000 drops remain.
The new rate is \(20 \times 1.5 = 30\) drops per minute, so the rest takes \(9000 \div 30 = 300\) minutes.
Convert to hours: \(300 \div 60 = 5\).
explanation.why: The flow rate increases only after part of the fluid is gone, so the remaining drops (not the total) are divided by the new rate, and the answer must be converted from minutes to hours.
explanation.pattern: Convert volume to the rate's unit, subtract what has already run, divide by the new rate, then convert the time unit.

items.stem: A rectangular room is 5 m by 4 m with walls 2.5 m high. The four walls, minus one door of 2 m² and one window of 1.5 m², will be painted with 2 coats. One liter of paint covers 9 m² of wall in one coat, and paint is sold only in 5-liter cans at \(\$28\) per can. What is the total cost, in dollars, of the paint that must be bought?

steps: Wall area: 2(5 + 4)(2.5) = 45 m², minus 2 + 1.5 = 3.5 m² of openings, leaves 41.5 m².
Two coats cover 83 m², which needs 83/9, about 9.22 liters.
Cans hold 5 liters each, so 9.22 liters requires 2 cans (10 liters), and 2 × 28 = 56.
explanation.why: Paint cannot be bought in fractions of a can, so the cost uses the next whole number of cans (2), not 9.22/5 = 1.84 cans (which would give about 51.64).
explanation.pattern: Chain area, coats, liters, then round up to whole packages before pricing.

items.stem: A tank holds 9 cubic meters of water (1 cubic meter = 1,000 liters). Pump A adds 18 liters per minute and Pump B adds 1.2 cubic meters per hour, while a leak removes 8 liters per minute. If the tank starts empty and all three run continuously, how many hours will it take to fill the tank?

steps: Pump B: 1.2 m³ per hour = 1,200 L per 60 min = 20 L per minute.
Net rate: 18 + 20 − 8 = 30 liters per minute.
Tank: 9 m³ = 9,000 L, so it takes 9,000/30 = 300 minutes = 5 hours.
explanation.why: The leak must be subtracted, and Pump B's rate must be converted to liters per minute before the rates can be combined.
explanation.pattern: Convert every rate to one unit, net them, then convert the final time back to the unit asked.

items.stem: Alloy A is 30% copper by mass and costs \(\$6\) per kilogram. Alloy B is 55% copper and costs \(\$9\) per kilogram. A foundry melts the two together to make 200 kilograms of an alloy that is 45% copper. What is the total cost, in dollars, of the alloys used?

steps: Let a be kilograms of A. Copper: 0.30a + 0.55(200 − a) = 0.45(200) = 90, so 110 − 0.25a = 90 and a = 80.
So 80 kg of A and 120 kg of B are used.
explanation.why: The mixture sets the amounts (80 and 120), and only then can the prices be applied; pricing 200 kg at an average of the two prices gives a wrong total.
explanation.pattern: Solve the concentration equation for the amounts first, then price each amount.

items.stem: Car A uses 8 liters of fuel per 100 kilometers and Car B uses 6 liters per 100 kilometers. Fuel costs \(\$1.75\) per liter. For a trip of 450 miles, with 1 mile = 1.6 kilometers, how many dollars more would the fuel cost in Car A than in Car B?

steps: Distance: 450 × 1.6 = 720 kilometers.
Fuel: Car A uses 720 × 8/100 = 57.6 L; Car B uses 720 × 6/100 = 43.2 L, a difference of 14.4 L.
Cost difference: 14.4 × 1.75 = 25.2 dollars.
explanation.why: Using 450 as kilometers instead of converting miles would give 15.75, and forgetting the price gives 14.4.
explanation.pattern: Convert the distance once, then compute the difference in fuel before pricing it.

items.stem: At a fair, the ratio of adults to children was 5 to 3. After 24 adults left, the ratio of adults to children was 4 to 3. Then 18 more children arrived, and no one else came or left. How many children were at the fair then?

steps: Let there be 5k adults and 3k children. After 24 adults leave: (5k − 24)/(3k) = 4/3.
Cross-multiply: 15k − 72 = 12k, so k = 24, giving 120 adults and 72 children at the start.
After 18 more children arrive there are 72 + 18 = 90 children.
explanation.why: The question asks for the count after the arrivals, so the children from the first ratio (72) are not the final answer.
explanation.pattern: Use a ratio multiplier k, set up the changed ratio as an equation, then apply the later change.

items.stem: Two bottles are geometrically similar. The small bottle is 20 cm tall, holds 0.5 liter, and uses 120 cm² of plastic. The large bottle is 30 cm tall. Plastic costs \(\$0.004\) per square centimeter. What is the plastic cost, in dollars, per liter of capacity of the large bottle?

steps: Scale factor 30/20 = 1.5. Area scales by 1.5² = 2.25 and volume by 1.5³ = 3.375.
Large bottle: plastic 120 × 2.25 = 270 cm², costing 270 × 0.004 = 1.08 dollars; capacity 0.5 × 3.375 = 1.6875 L.
Cost per liter: 1.08 / 1.6875 = 0.64 dollars.
explanation.why: Scaling both quantities by the factor 1.5 (instead of its square and its cube) would give 0.96 per liter.
explanation.pattern: Area scales with the square of the scale factor and volume with the cube; use each for the matching quantity.

items.stem: A right triangle has legs of length \(9\) and \(12\). What is the length of its hypotenuse?

steps: Pythagorean theorem: \(c^2 = 9^2 + 12^2 = 81 + 144 = 225\).
explanation.why: 9-12-15 is the 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 3.
explanation.pattern: Hypotenuse² = leg² + leg². Take the square root at the end.

items.stem: In right triangle \(ABC\), angle \(C\) is a right angle and \(\sin A = \frac{8}{17}\). What is the value of \(\cos A\)?

choices.slip: This is tan A (opposite over adjacent).
This is adjacent over opposite, the reciprocal of tan A.
This is the reciprocal of sin A.

steps: \(\sin A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), so take the side opposite \(A\) as 8 and the hypotenuse as 17.
The other leg is \(\sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15\).
\(\cos A = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{15}{17}\).
explanation.why: 8-15-17 is a right triangle, and cos A uses the leg next to A (15) over the hypotenuse (17).
explanation.pattern: Given one trig ratio, sketch the triangle, find the missing side with Pythagoras, then read off the ratio asked for.

items.stem: An isosceles right triangle has a hypotenuse of length \(14\). What is the area of the triangle?

steps: In a \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangle, hypotenuse \(= \text{leg} \cdot \sqrt{2}\), so each leg is \(\frac{14}{\sqrt{2}} = 7\sqrt{2}\).
explanation.why: Each leg squared is 98, and half of that is 49. (The two legs are equal, so the area is leg²/2.)
explanation.pattern: In an isosceles right triangle, leg = hypotenuse/√2, and area = leg²/2 = hypotenuse²/4.

items.stem: In right triangle \(JKL\), angle \(K\) is a right angle, \(JK = 7\), and \(KL = 24\). Triangle \(JKL\) is similar to triangle \(PQR\), where \(J\), \(K\), and \(L\) correspond to \(P\), \(Q\), and \(R\), respectively. What is the value of \(\sin R\)?

choices.slip: This is tan L (opposite over adjacent), not sin L.
This is cos L: it uses the side adjacent to L.
This is the reciprocal of sin L.

steps: Corresponding angles of similar triangles are equal, so \(\sin R = \sin L\).
Hypotenuse \(JL = \sqrt{7^2 + 24^2} = 25\).
The side opposite angle \(L\) is \(JK = 7\), so \(\sin L = \frac{7}{25}\), and \(\sin R = \frac{7}{25}\).
explanation.why: Similarity keeps every angle, so R has the same sine as L: the opposite leg 7 over the hypotenuse 25.
explanation.pattern: For similar triangles, move the question to the triangle whose sides you know, then use SOH-CAH-TOA there.

items.stem: In right triangle \(ABC\), angle \(C\) is a right angle and \(\cos A = 0.6\). The area of triangle \(ABC\) is \(96\) square units. What is the perimeter, in units, of triangle \(ABC\)?

steps: \(\cos A = 0.6 = \frac{3}{5}\), so \(AC : AB = 3 : 5\), and the third side makes a 3-4-5 triangle: \(AC = 3k\), \(BC = 4k\), \(AB = 5k\).
The legs are \(AC\) and \(BC\): area \(= \frac{1}{2}(3k)(4k) = 6k^2 = 96\), so \(k^2 = 16\) and \(k = 4\).
Perimeter \(= 3k + 4k + 5k = 12k = 48\).
explanation.why: The sides are 12, 16 and 20: the area is ½ · 12 · 16 = 96 and cos A = 12/20 = 0.6.
explanation.pattern: A trig ratio fixes the shape (side ratios) but not the size. Use a second fact, here the area, to find the scale factor.

figure.alt: Right triangle with the right angle at A. The legs are 9 and 12, and the hypotenuse is x.

items.stem: In the right triangle shown, what is the value of \(x\)?

steps: Use the Pythagorean theorem: \(x^2 = 9^2 + 12^2 = 81 + 144 = 225\).
explanation.pattern: 9-12-15 is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 3. Spotting the multiple saves the arithmetic.

figure.alt: Right triangle ABC with the right angle at C. Side AC is 8 and the hypotenuse AB is 17.

items.stem: In the right triangle shown, what is the value of \(\tan A\)?

choices.slip: This is cos A (adjacent over hypotenuse).
Flipped the ratio: adjacent over opposite.
This is sin A (opposite over hypotenuse).

steps: Find the missing leg: \(BC = \sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{289 - 64} = \sqrt{225} = 15\).
\(\tan A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{15}{8}\).
explanation.why: The side opposite A is 15 and the side next to A is 8, so tan A = 15/8.
explanation.pattern: Tangent needs the two legs. If one leg is missing, find it with the Pythagorean theorem first.

figure.alt: Right triangle ABC with the right angle at C. AC is 15 and BC is 20. Point D is on the hypotenuse AB, and segment CD, marked x, meets AB at a right angle.

items.stem: In right triangle \(ABC\) shown, \(\overline{CD}\) is perpendicular to \(\overline{AB}\). What is the value of \(x\)?

steps: Hypotenuse: \(AB = \sqrt{15^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25\).
Area of the triangle using the legs: \(\frac{1}{2}(15)(20) = 150\).
Area using \(AB\) as the base and \(CD\) as the height: \(\frac{1}{2}(25)(x) = 150\).
explanation.why: The same area, 150, written two ways gives 25x = 300, so x = 12.
explanation.pattern: The altitude to the hypotenuse equals (leg × leg) ÷ hypotenuse. Writing the area two ways gets it without trigonometry.

items.stem: For a value of \(x\) between 0 and 18, \(\cos(3x + 5)^\circ = \sin(2x + 10)^\circ\). What is the value of \(3x + 5\)?

steps: Sine and cosine of complementary angles are equal: \(\cos\theta = \sin(90^\circ - \theta)\).
\(3x + 5 = 3(15) + 5 = 50\). (The other family of solutions gives \(x\) far outside 0 to 18.)
explanation.why: The angles must sum to 90, so x = 15 and 3x + 5 = 50.
explanation.pattern: Equal sine and cosine values mean the two angles are complementary (sum 90), so set up one linear equation.

items.stem: A \(25\)-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall, with its base on level ground \(7\) feet from the wall. The top of the ladder slides \(4\) feet down the wall, and the ladder keeps touching both the wall and the ground. How many feet does the base of the ladder move away from the wall?

choices.slip: This is the new distance of the base from the wall, not how far it moved.
This is the new height of the top on the wall.
This is the original height of the top on the wall.

steps: At first the top is at height \(\sqrt{25^2 - 7^2} = 24\) feet.
After sliding down 4 feet the top is at height 20, so the base is \(\sqrt{25^2 - 20^2} = 15\) feet from the wall.
The base moved \(15 - 7 = 8\) feet.
explanation.why: The height drops from 24 to 20, so the base goes from 7 to 15 feet out, a move of 8 feet.
explanation.pattern: A sliding ladder keeps its length as the hypotenuse. Use Pythagoras twice, once per position, and subtract.

items.stem: In triangle \(ABC\), angle \(C\) is a right angle, \(AC = 21\), and \(BC = 28\). The bisector of angle \(C\) meets \(\overline{AB}\) at point \(D\). What is the length of \(\overline{AD}\)?

steps: Hypotenuse: \(AB = \sqrt{21^2 + 28^2} = 35\).
The angle bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides: \(\frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AC}{BC} = \frac{21}{28} = \frac{3}{4}\).
explanation.why: AB is 35 and the bisector splits it 3 : 4, so AD is 3/7 of 35, which is 15.
explanation.pattern: The angle bisector theorem: a bisector splits the opposite side in the ratio of the two sides next to the angle.

items.stem: In triangle \(ABC\), \(AB = AC = 10\) and \(BC = 12\). What is the sine of angle \(A\)?

choices.slip: Used area = (1/2)(leg)(leg)(sin A) = 48 but divided by 100 instead of 50.
This is the sine of half of angle A (6 over 10), not of angle A.
This is the cosine of half of angle A, which is also the sine of a base angle.

steps: The altitude from \(A\) to \(\overline{BC}\) has length \(\sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = 8\), so the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(12)(8) = 48\).
The area is also \(\frac{1}{2}(AB)(AC)\sin A = \frac{1}{2}(10)(10)\sin A = 50\sin A\).
explanation.why: Computing the area two ways gives 50 sin A = 48, so sin A = 24/25.
explanation.pattern: When no right angle contains the angle you want, find the area from the altitude, then use area = 1/2 ab sin C.

items.stem: A rectangle is inscribed in an equilateral triangle with side length \(12\). One side of the rectangle lies on a side of the triangle, and the other two vertices of the rectangle lie on the other two sides of the triangle. The rectangle's height (its dimension perpendicular to the side of the triangle it lies on) is \(3\sqrt{3}\). What is the length of the rectangle's side that lies on the triangle's side?

steps: The equilateral triangle's height is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(12) = 6\sqrt{3}\).
The small triangle above the rectangle is also equilateral (similar to the big one), with height \(6\sqrt{3} - 3\sqrt{3} = 3\sqrt{3}\).
Similar triangles: the small triangle's side is \(12 \cdot \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{6\sqrt{3}} = 6\), and the rectangle's top side equals this, so the bottom side (equal to the top) is 6.
explanation.why: The triangle above the rectangle is equilateral with half the full height, so its side is 6, which is also the rectangle's width.
explanation.pattern: A line parallel to a base cuts off a smaller similar triangle. Its height is the full height minus the rectangle's height, and the ratio gives its side.

items.stem: For an acute angle \(\theta\), \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \frac{7}{5}\). What is the value of \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\)?

choices.slip: Subtracted 1 from the sum 7/5 instead of squaring.
Stopped at 2 sinθ cosθ and forgot to halve.
Halved the square of the sum without first subtracting 1.

steps: Square both sides: \(\sin^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta = \frac{49}{25}\).
Since \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\), \(1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{49}{25}\).
\(2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{24}{25}\), so \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{12}{25}\).
explanation.why: Squaring the sum brings in sin² + cos² = 1; what is left is twice the product, 24/25, so the product is 12/25.
explanation.pattern: When a sum of sin and cos is given, square it and use the Pythagorean identity to isolate the product.

items.stem: From a point on level ground, the angle of elevation to the top of a vertical tower has tangent \(\frac{3}{4}\). After walking \(28\) meters straight toward the base of the tower, the angle of elevation to the top has tangent \(\frac{3}{2}\). How tall, in meters, is the tower?

steps: Let the tower have height \(h\) and the first distance to its base be \(d\). Then \(\frac{h}{d} = \frac{3}{4}\) and \(\frac{h}{d - 28} = \frac{3}{2}\).
explanation.why: The distances are 56 m and 28 m from the base; the height is 3/4 of 56, or 3/2 of 28, which is 42.
explanation.pattern: With two elevation angles, write tan = height ÷ distance for each position and eliminate the unknown starting distance.

items.stem: A right triangle has an acute angle \(A\) with \(\tan A = \frac{5}{12}\), and the triangle's perimeter is \(60\). What is the length of the altitude drawn to the hypotenuse?

choices.slip: Divided the area by the hypotenuse without doubling.
Gave the shorter leg, not the altitude to the hypotenuse.
Doubled the area but divided by the unscaled hypotenuse, 13, instead of 26.

steps: A triangle with \(\tan A = \frac{5}{12}\) is similar to a 5-12-13 triangle, whose perimeter is 30. The scale factor is \(\frac{60}{30} = 2\), so the sides are 10, 24, and 26.
The altitude to the hypotenuse \(h\) satisfies \(\frac{1}{2}(26)h = 120\), so \(h = \frac{240}{26} = \frac{120}{13}\).
explanation.why: The sides are 10, 24, 26, so the area is 120 and the altitude to the 26-long hypotenuse is 240/26 = 120/13.
explanation.pattern: Use the tangent to fix the shape, the perimeter to fix the size, then area = ½ × base × height with the hypotenuse as the base.

items.stem: In triangle \(ABC\), point \(D\) lies on \(\overline{AC}\) such that \(\overline{BD}\) is perpendicular to \(\overline{AC}\), \(\angle A = 45^\circ\), and \(\angle C = 30^\circ\). If \(AC = 7 + 7\sqrt{3}\), what is the length of \(\overline{BC}\)?

steps: Let \(BD = h\). In the 45-45-90 triangle \(ABD\), \(AD = h\). In the 30-60-90 triangle \(BDC\), \(DC = h\sqrt{3}\) and \(BC = 2h\).
So \(AC = h + h\sqrt{3} = 7 + 7\sqrt{3}\), which gives \(h = 7\).
explanation.why: The altitude BD splits AC into h and h√3, so the given length 7 + 7√3 means h = 7, and BC (the hypotenuse of the 30-60-90 triangle) is 2h = 14.
explanation.pattern: Drop the altitude to make two special right triangles that share a leg; express every side in terms of that shared leg.

items.stem: A ladder that is \(25\) feet long stands in an alley between two vertical walls on level ground. With its foot at a fixed point on the ground, the ladder's top rests against one wall at a height of \(20\) feet. Without moving the foot, the ladder is tipped across the alley so that its top rests against the opposite wall at a height of \(24\) feet. How wide, in feet, is the alley?

steps: Distance from the foot to the first wall: \(\sqrt{25^2 - 20^2} = 15\).
Distance from the foot to the second wall: \(\sqrt{25^2 - 24^2} = 7\).
The alley's width is the sum, \(15 + 7 = 22\) feet.
explanation.why: The foot is 15 ft from one wall and 7 ft from the other, so the walls are 22 ft apart.
explanation.pattern: Each ladder position is its own right triangle with the same hypotenuse. Find each horizontal leg, then add them because the foot is between the walls.

items.stem: In a right triangle, the two acute angles are \(x\) and \(y\). If \(\sin x = \frac{2}{3}\), what is the value of \(\tan y\)?

choices.slip: This is cos x (equal to sin y), not tan y.
This is tan x, not tan y.
Took the reciprocal of sin x instead of finding tan y.

steps: Because \(x + y = 90^\circ\), \(\tan y = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\).
\(\cos x = \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\).
explanation.why: The tangent of the complement is the cotangent: adjacent over opposite for x, which is √5 over 2.
explanation.pattern: Complementary angles swap sine and cosine, so tan y = cos x ÷ sin x. Use the Pythagorean identity to get cos x.

items.stem: Rectangle \(PQRS\) has \(PQ = 9\) and \(QR = 12\). Its diagonals intersect at point \(O\). What is the value of \(\sin\angle POQ\)?

choices.slip: Found the cosine of ∠POQ instead of the sine.
Used 9/15, the sine of the angle between a diagonal and the 12-long side, not the angle between the diagonals.
Used 12/15, the sine of the angle between a diagonal and the 9-long side.

steps: The diagonal is \(\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = 15\), so \(PO = OQ = 7.5\).
The rectangle's area is 108, and triangle \(POQ\) is one quarter of it: \(27 = \frac{1}{2}(7.5)(7.5)\sin\angle POQ\).
explanation.why: Triangle POQ has two sides of 7.5 and an area of 27, so its sine is 54 divided by 56.25, which is 24/25.
explanation.pattern: Use area = ½ ab sin C on a triangle where two sides and the area are known. Diagonals of a rectangle split it into four equal-area triangles.

items.stem: In right triangle \(ABC\), the right angle is at \(C\), \(AC = 10\), and \(BC = 24\). Point \(G\) is the centroid of the triangle. What is the length of \(CG\)?

steps: The hypotenuse is \(AB = \sqrt{10^2 + 24^2} = 26\).
The median from \(C\) goes to the midpoint of the hypotenuse, which is the circumcenter of a right triangle, so its length is half the hypotenuse: 13.
The centroid is \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the way along the median from the vertex: \(CG = \frac{2}{3}(13) = \frac{26}{3}\).
explanation.why: The median to the hypotenuse is 13, and the centroid sits two-thirds of the way from C, giving 26/3.
explanation.pattern: In a right triangle the median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse; the centroid divides any median 2 : 1 from the vertex.

items.stem: A square is drawn inside a right triangle with legs of length \(15\) and \(20\). One vertex of the square is at the triangle's right angle, two sides of the square lie along the legs, and the opposite vertex of the square lies on the hypotenuse. What is the side length of the square?

steps: Let the square have side \(s\). The part of the 15-leg beyond the square is \(15 - s\), and the small triangle cut off at the top is similar to the whole triangle.
explanation.why: Similar triangles give (15 − s)/15 = s/20, so s = 300/35 = 60/7.
explanation.pattern: The side of a square at a right angle is ab/(a + b); derive it with similar triangles.

items.stem: A rectangular box has a base measuring \(3\) by \(4\) and a height of \(12\). A space diagonal of the box makes an angle \(\theta\) with the plane of the base. What is \(\sin\theta\)?

choices.slip: Used the base edge 4 instead of the height 12 as the opposite side.
Gave the cosine of the angle.
Gave the tangent of the angle instead of the sine.

steps: The diagonal of the base is \(\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\).
The space diagonal is \(\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = 13\). It, the base diagonal, and the vertical edge form a right triangle, and \(\theta\) is the angle between the space diagonal and the base diagonal.
\(\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{12}{13}\).
explanation.why: The height 12 is opposite the angle, and the space diagonal 13 is the hypotenuse.
explanation.pattern: For a box, the angle with the base lives in the right triangle formed by the base diagonal, the vertical edge, and the space diagonal.

items.stem: For an acute angle \(\theta\), \(\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}\). What is the value of \(\frac{\cos\theta}{1 + \sin\theta} + \frac{1 + \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\)?

choices.slip: Evaluated only the first term, cosθ/(1 + sinθ).
Subtracted the two terms (3/2 − 2/3) instead of adding.
Evaluated only the second term, (1 + sinθ)/cosθ.

steps: With hypotenuse 13 and opposite side 5, the adjacent side is 12, so \(\cos\theta = \frac{12}{13}\).
\(1 + \sin\theta = \frac{18}{13}\), so the first term is \(\frac{12/13}{18/13} = \frac{2}{3}\) and the second is \(\frac{3}{2}\).
explanation.why: cosθ = 12/13 makes the terms 2/3 and 3/2, which add to 13/6.
explanation.pattern: Draw the right triangle from the given sine to get the cosine, then evaluate each term separately.

items.stem: A right isosceles triangle has legs of length \(8\). A second right isosceles triangle is built so that each of its legs is equal to the hypotenuse of the first triangle, and a third is built so that each of its legs is equal to the hypotenuse of the second. What is the sum of the hypotenuse lengths of the three triangles?

choices.slip: Added only the first two hypotenuses.
Added the legs 8, 8√2, 16 instead of the hypotenuses.
Multiplied each hypotenuse by 2 instead of √2 to get the next one.

steps: A right isosceles triangle with leg \(L\) has hypotenuse \(L\sqrt{2}\).
First hypotenuse: \(8\sqrt{2}\). Second triangle has legs \(8\sqrt{2}\), so its hypotenuse is \(8\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2} = 16\). Third triangle has legs 16, so its hypotenuse is \(16\sqrt{2}\).
explanation.why: The hypotenuses are 8√2, 16, and 16√2; each step multiplies by √2.
explanation.pattern: Each right isosceles step multiplies lengths by √2, so two steps double the length.

items.stem: A right triangle has side lengths \(x\), \(x + 7\), and \(x + 7 + 1\), where \(x > 0\) and \(x + 7 + 1\) is the hypotenuse. What is the tangent of the smallest angle of the triangle?

choices.slip: Gave the sine of the smallest angle.
Gave the sine of the larger angle, 12/13, instead of the tangent of the smaller angle.
Gave the tangent of the larger acute angle.

steps: The smallest angle is opposite the shortest side (5): \(\tan = \frac{5}{12}\).
explanation.why: The quadratic gives x = 5, so the sides are 5, 12, 13 and the smallest angle's tangent is 5/12.
explanation.pattern: Set up Pythagoras with the algebraic sides, solve for x, then read the trig ratio of the angle opposite the shortest side.

items.stem: In quadrilateral \(ABCD\), angles \(B\) and \(D\) are right angles, \(AB = 15\), \(BC = 20\), and \(AD = 7\). What is the area of the quadrilateral?

steps: Diagonal \(AC\) is the hypotenuse of right triangle \(ABC\): \(AC = \sqrt{15^2 + 20^2} = 25\).
It is also the hypotenuse of right triangle \(ADC\), so \(CD = \sqrt{25^2 - 7^2} = 24\).
explanation.why: The diagonal AC = 25 is shared, which gives CD = 24; the two right triangles have areas 150 and 84.
explanation.pattern: Split the quadrilateral along the diagonal; a diagonal opposite two right angles is a hypotenuse of both triangles.

items.stem: In right triangle \(ABC\), the right angle is at \(C\), \(AC = 75\) and \(BC = 100\). Point \(D\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(C\) to hypotenuse \(AB\), and point \(E\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(D\) to side \(AC\). What is the length of \(DE\)?

choices.slip: Found AE, the other leg of triangle ADE.
Found AD, the hypotenuse of triangle ADE.
Found CD, the altitude to the hypotenuse.

steps: Triangle \(ADE\) is similar to triangle \(ABC\) (both have angle \(A\) and a right angle), so \(\frac{DE}{BC} = \frac{AD}{AB}\).
explanation.why: DE is parallel to BC and 45/125 of its length.
explanation.pattern: Altitude to the hypotenuse creates similar right triangles; a second perpendicular makes another similar triangle, so scale by the same ratio.

items.stem: In trapezoid \(ABCD\), \(AB \parallel CD\), and \(AD\) is perpendicular to both bases. The longer base \(AB = 20\), the slanted side \(BC = 15\), and \(\sin \angle ABC = \frac{4}{5}\). What is the area of the trapezoid?

choices.slip: Treated the figure as a 20 by 12 rectangle, ignoring the taper of the shorter base.
Used the slanted side 15 as the height.
Swapped sine and cosine, giving height 9 and shorter base 8.

steps: Height \(AD = 15 \cdot \frac{4}{5} = 12\). The horizontal run of side \(BC\) is \(15 \cdot \frac{3}{5} = 9\).
The shorter base is \(CD = 20 - 9 = 11\).
explanation.why: Sine gives the height 12, cosine gives the overhang 9, so the short base is 11.
explanation.pattern: Right trapezoid: split off a right triangle from the slanted side; its legs give the height and the difference of the bases.

items.stem: In the \(xy\)-plane, line \(\ell\) has slope \(\frac{5}{12}\). Points \(Q\) and \(P\) lie on \(\ell\), with \(P\) to the right of \(Q\). Point \(R\) lies directly below \(P\) and at the same height as \(Q\), so \(QR\) is horizontal and \(PR\) is vertical. The area of triangle \(QPR\) is \(120\). What is the length of \(QP\)?

steps: The legs satisfy \(PR : QR = 5 : 12\). Let \(PR = 5k\) and \(QR = 12k\).
explanation.why: The legs are 10 and 24, so the hypotenuse is 26 (a 5-12-13 triangle scaled by 2).
explanation.pattern: The slope fixes the leg ratio; the area fixes the scale factor, which then scales the hypotenuse.

items.stem: A lamp post is \(5.4\) meters tall. A person who is \(1.8\) meters tall stands \(6\) meters from the base of the post, and then walks directly away from the post until standing \(15\) meters from its base. Assume the lamp is a point of light at the top of the post and the ground is level. By how many meters does the length of the person's shadow increase?

choices.slip: Gave the distance the person walked.
Found only the final shadow length.
Found only the starting shadow length.

steps: By similar triangles, shadow \(s\) and distance \(d\) satisfy \(\frac{s}{s + d} = \frac{1.8}{5.4} = \frac{1}{3}\), so \(3s = s + d\) and \(s = \frac{d}{2}\).
At 6 meters the shadow is 3 meters; at 15 meters it is 7.5 meters.
Increase \(= 7.5 - 3 = 4.5\) meters.
explanation.why: The shadow is always half the distance from the post, so it grows by half of the 9 meters walked.
explanation.pattern: Lamp-and-shadow: the person's triangle is similar to the lamp's whole triangle (which includes the shadow plus the distance).

items.stem: Square \(ABCD\) has side length \(12\), and \(M\) is the midpoint of side \(CD\). Diagonal \(AC\) is drawn along with segment \(AM\). What is the value of \(\sin \angle CAM\)?

choices.slip: Found tan of angle CAM instead of sin.
Found the sine of angle MAD instead of angle CAM.
Found the tangent of angle MAD instead of the sine of angle CAM.

steps: Triangle \(ACM\) has base \(CM = 6\) on line \(CD\) and height \(12\) (the distance from \(A\) to line \(CD\)), so its area is \(\frac{1}{2}(6)(12) = 36\).

Area \(= \frac{1}{2}(AC)(AM)\sin \angle CAM\), so \(36 = \frac{1}{2}(12\sqrt{2})(6\sqrt{5})\sin\angle CAM = 36\sqrt{10}\sin\angle CAM\), and \(\sin\angle CAM = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} = \frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\).
explanation.why: Computing the area of triangle ACM two ways isolates the sine.
explanation.pattern: When an angle is not part of a right triangle, equate area = 1/2 ab sin C with area = 1/2 base x height.

items.stem: In triangle \(ABC\), \(\angle B = 60^\circ\), \(\angle C = 45^\circ\) and \(AB = 12\). What is the length of \(AC\)?

choices.slip: Used the shorter leg 6 as the altitude (cosine instead of sine), then multiplied by the square root of 2.
Gave the altitude from A, not the side AC.
Assumed AC = AB.

steps: Drop the altitude \(AD\) from \(A\) to \(BC\). In the 30-60-90 triangle \(ABD\), \(AD = 12 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 6\sqrt{3}\).
Triangle \(ADC\) has a \(45^\circ\) angle at \(C\) and a right angle at \(D\), so it is an isosceles right triangle with hypotenuse \(AC = AD\sqrt{2}\).
\(AC = 6\sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 6\sqrt{6}\).
explanation.why: AC is the hypotenuse of a 45-45-90 triangle whose leg is the 60-degree altitude 6 sqrt(3).
explanation.pattern: Split a non-right triangle with an altitude into two special right triangles and chain the side ratios.

items.stem: For an acute angle \(\theta\), \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta = \frac{1}{5}\). What is the value of \(\tan\theta\)?

choices.slip: Stopped after squaring: found sin theta times cos theta.
Inverted the ratio (cos over sin).
Found sin theta + cos theta instead of the tangent.

steps: Square both sides: \(1 - 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{1}{25}\), so \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{12}{25}\).
Then \((\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = 1 + \frac{24}{25} = \frac{49}{25}\), so \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \frac{7}{5}\) (positive for an acute angle).
Adding and subtracting: \(\sin\theta = \frac{4}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta = \frac{3}{5}\), so \(\tan\theta = \frac{4}{3}\).
explanation.why: Squaring and using sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 gives sin + cos, and the pair of equations gives each value.
explanation.pattern: Given a sum or difference of sin and cos, square it and use the Pythagorean identity.

items.stem: Two observers stand on level ground on opposite sides of a vertical tower, in line with its base. The tower is \(30\) meters tall. The angles of elevation from the observers to the top of the tower are \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\). How far apart, in meters, are the observers?

choices.slip: Subtracted the two horizontal distances, as if the observers were on the same side of the tower.
Found only the horizontal distance for the \(30^\circ\) observer.
Used the \(30^\circ\) distance, \(30\sqrt{3}\), for both observers.

steps: The \(30^\circ\) observer is \(30/\tan 30^\circ = 30\sqrt{3}\) meters from the base.
The \(60^\circ\) observer is \(30/\tan 60^\circ = 10\sqrt{3}\) meters from the base.
They are on opposite sides, so the distances add: \(30\sqrt{3} + 10\sqrt{3} = 40\sqrt{3}\).
explanation.why: Opposite sides means the two horizontal distances add; same side would make them subtract.
explanation.pattern: Elevation angles from two points: each horizontal distance is height / tan(angle); add or subtract by position.

items.stem: Triangle \(ABC\) has a right angle at \(C\), hypotenuse \(AB = 26\), and \(\tan A = \frac{5}{12}\). What is the radius of the circle inscribed in the triangle?
