choices.text: , which

steps: The first part is a complete sentence ending with 'two weeks'.
'Gave ... time to resubmit' needs a subject and comments on the whole extension.
A nonrestrictive 'which' clause is introduced with a comma.
explanation.why: ', which' adds a comment on the extension to the complete clause.
explanation.pattern: Complete clause, which + verb: a nonrestrictive comment on the whole clause.

items.passage: Library closures during the pandemic varied widely. The northern archive, as well as the three branch libraries it supervises ______ was closed to the public for most of 2021, according to a county report that also lists the repairs completed since then.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A dash cannot close an interruption opened by a comma.
A semicolon would separate the subject from its verb.
A colon would separate the subject from its verb.

steps: A comma after 'archive' opens the 'as well as' insertion.
The insertion ends after 'supervises', and the verb 'was closed' follows.
The insertion must be closed with a matching comma.
explanation.why: The closing comma matches the opening comma before 'was closed'.
explanation.pattern: An insertion opened with a comma closes with a comma; 'as well as' phrases do not change the subject.

items.passage: The earlier survey tallied only breeding pairs of the two larger gull species, which are easy to count from a boat ______ the 2022 survey counted every adult bird on the island, including four species that nest in burrows.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: ; by contrast,
, by contrast,
choices.slip: A comma cannot join two independent clauses, and 'by contrast' is not a conjunction.

choices.text: : by contrast,
choices.slip: A colon does not introduce a contrast; the second clause neither explains nor lists.

choices.text: ; by contrast
choices.slip: The phrase 'by contrast' opening a clause needs a comma after it.

steps: The first clause ends with 'a boat'; the second begins 'the 2022 survey counted'.
Both are independent clauses joined only by 'by contrast', a transitional phrase.
A transitional phrase between independent clauses takes a semicolon before and a comma after.
explanation.why: '; by contrast,' joins the two clauses correctly.
explanation.pattern: Independent clause; transition, independent clause.

items.passage: At the hearing on the dredging schedule, the harbor engineer was blunt. “The channel was never designed for vessels this deep ______ he told the board, adding that the 1932 survey had assumed a far smaller fleet.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A period would end the sentence and leave 'he told the board' as a fragment without a capital.
In American usage the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
A semicolon after the quotation would separate the quotation from its attribution.

steps: The quotation is interrupted by the attribution 'he told the board'.
The quoted words end before the attribution and the sentence continues.
A comma ends the quoted part, placed inside the closing quotation mark.
explanation.why: ',”' closes the quotation and links it to the attribution.
explanation.pattern: Quoted words, followed by an attribution: comma inside the quotation mark.

items.passage: Only the pumps ______ were installed before 1960 and have not since been rebuilt need replacement this year, the county engineer says, though several newer pumps from the same maker have also begun to fail.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: that
, that
choices.slip: A comma before 'that' would make a restrictive clause nonrestrictive and split subject from its modifier.

choices.text: , which
choices.slip: A comma plus 'which' would suggest that all the pumps were installed before 1960.

choices.text: ; which
choices.slip: A semicolon cannot precede a relative clause.

steps: 'Only the pumps' needs the clause to identify which pumps need replacement.
The 'that' clause restricts the meaning, so it is not set off.
No comma comes before a restrictive clause.
explanation.why: 'that' introduces the restrictive clause with no comma.
explanation.pattern: Restrictive clause: no commas.

items.passage: The cooperative's loan fund is meant for newcomers, not for established growers ______ it will not lend to any farm that has marketed more than a single harvest through the cooperative's stall.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: , that is,
choices.slip: A comma cannot join two independent clauses on its own.

choices.text: ; that is,
: that is,
choices.slip: A colon does not combine with 'that is' to join the clauses.

choices.text: ; that is
choices.slip: 'That is' opening a clause needs a comma after it.

steps: The first clause is complete; so is 'it will not lend ...'.
'That is' glosses the first clause and acts as a conjunctive phrase.
It takes a semicolon before and a comma after.
explanation.why: '; that is,' joins the two clauses.
explanation.pattern: Independent clause; that is, independent clause.

items.passage: The salvage crew expected little from the wreck, which lies in forty meters of cold water and had been picked over twice since 1950. Among the objects raised during the first week of diving ______ a brass sextant, two pewter plates, and a sealed ink bottle whose contents had survived the sinking.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: was
choices.slip: The singular verb agrees only with the first item, 'a brass sextant'; the subject of this inverted sentence is the whole three-part series, which is plural.

choices.text: , were
choices.slip: A comma would separate the introductory phrase from the inverted verb, which follows such a phrase directly.

choices.text: were
; were
choices.slip: A semicolon needs a complete clause before it, and 'Among the objects raised ... diving' is only a phrase.

steps: The sentence opens with a long prepositional phrase and inverts the order, so the verb comes before its subject.
The subject is the series after the blank: a sextant, plates, and a bottle, which is plural.
No punctuation separates the introductory phrase from the inverted verb.
explanation.why: 'were' agrees with the plural series and follows the phrase directly.
explanation.pattern: In inverted order, the verb follows the introductory phrase with no punctuation and agrees with the subject that comes after it.

items.passage: The footbridge was approved in 2004 and, after two redesigns that doubled its cost and a flood that delayed construction for a full year ______ was finally opened in 2011, three years after the contractor who had won the first bid went bankrupt.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A dash cannot close an interruption that a comma opened.
A semicolon would break the compound predicate 'was approved ... was finally opened' and leave the interruption unclosed.

choices.text: , and
choices.slip: A second 'and' would stack on the one before the interruption, producing 'and, ... , and was'.

steps: 'and,' opens an interruption that begins with 'after two redesigns'.
The interruption ends after 'a full year', and the second verb 'was finally opened' follows.
The comma that opened it must be matched by a comma.
explanation.why: One closing comma ends the interruption and leaves the two-verb predicate intact.
explanation.pattern: An interrupter that opens with a comma after a conjunction closes with a comma before the resumed verb.

items.passage: Perrin Haldane, who has surveyed the estuary’s mudflats for nineteen years, says the old tide counts cannot be trusted. “The gauge was moved twice before 1950,” she told the visiting auditors last spring ______ “and nobody recorded where it had stood each time.”
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A period would end the sentence, but the quotation resumes with lowercase 'and', so the quoted sentence has not ended.
A semicolon would treat the attribution as a full clause joined to the rest of the quotation.
A colon would present the resumed words as an explanation of the attribution, when they simply continue the quoted sentence.

steps: The quotation is split by the attribution 'she told the visiting auditors last spring'.
The second part begins with lowercase 'and', so it continues the same sentence.
A comma returns to the quotation after the attribution.
explanation.why: The comma links the attribution to the continuing quoted sentence.
explanation.pattern: When a quoted sentence resumes after an attribution, the attribution is followed by a comma.

items.passage: “The harbor’s depth records were kept in three separate ledgers,” the clerk explained to the visiting auditors ______ “Only one of them survived the fire of 1911, and it covers just the north basin.”
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A comma would join the finished quoted sentence, through the attribution, to a new capitalised sentence, making a comma splice.
A semicolon would join the attribution to a new quoted sentence that begins with a capital letter.

choices.text: , and
choices.slip: 'and' would join the attribution to a quotation that is a separate sentence, which the words do not support.

steps: The first quoted sentence ends before the attribution.
The second quotation begins with a capital, 'Only', so it is a new sentence.
The attribution must end with a period.
explanation.why: The period ends the sentence that the attribution closes, and the new quotation starts a fresh one.
explanation.pattern: When a quotation resumes with a new sentence after an attribution, the attribution ends with a period.

items.passage: Residents of Pell Quay still argue about the breakwater. After the 1998 storm, the weekly paper ran an editorial whose opening line became a local saying. “Who will pay for the dredging ______ the editorial asked, and the answer remains disputed.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A comma after the question mark would double the punctuation; the question mark already ends the quoted part.
A comma would replace the question mark and turn the quoted question into a statement.
A period would turn the quoted question into a statement and leave the lowercase attribution after a full stop.

steps: The quoted words are a question, and the attribution 'the editorial asked' follows.
A quoted question keeps its question mark even when an attribution follows.
The question mark stays inside the closing quotation mark, with no comma added.
explanation.why: '?”' keeps the question and lets the attribution follow in lowercase.
explanation.pattern: A quoted question keeps its question mark before an attribution; no comma is added.

items.passage: The scholarship covers not only the tuition of students admitted to the nursing program ______ the cost of the uniforms, textbooks, and clinical placements that most first-year applicants cannot afford without help.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: , but also
choices.slip: A comma would separate the two parallel noun phrases linked by 'not only ... but also'.

choices.text: ; but also
choices.slip: A semicolon needs a complete clause on each side, and these are noun phrases.

choices.text: and also
choices.slip: 'Not only' pairs with 'but also'; 'and also' breaks the correlative pair.

choices.text: but also

steps: 'not only' opens a pair whose second part is 'but also'.
Both parts are noun phrases: 'the tuition ...' and 'the cost ...'.
Parallel phrases in a correlative pair are not separated by a comma.
explanation.why: 'but also' completes the pair without a comma.
explanation.pattern: A correlative pair joining phrases takes no punctuation between its parts.

items.passage: Of the three clinics the county funds, only the ______ clinic on Calder Street stays open past six in the evening, which matters to the hundreds of women who visit it each week after finishing their shifts.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: women’s
womens’
choices.slip: 'Women' is already plural without an -s, so the possessive adds apostrophe-s rather than an apostrophe alone.

choices.text: woman’s
choices.slip: 'Woman's' is singular, but the clinic serves hundreds of women.

choices.text: womens
choices.slip: This has no apostrophe and is not a standard form.

steps: The clinic belongs to, or serves, women: a possessive modifier is needed.
'Women' is an irregular plural that does not end in -s.
The possessive of such a plural adds apostrophe-s.
explanation.why: 'women's' is the plural possessive of an irregular plural.
explanation.pattern: An irregular plural that does not end in -s takes apostrophe-s.

items.passage: The inspector’s report on the east wall was short and blunt ______ “The mortar has failed in forty places, and the wall will not survive another winter.”
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A comma would join a complete clause to a quotation with no verb of saying to connect them.

choices.text: , that
choices.slip: 'that' would introduce an indirect statement, which does not take quotation marks.

choices.text: , and
choices.slip: 'and' would link the quotation to the clause as if it were an additional fact rather than the content of the report.

steps: 'The inspector's report ... was short and blunt' is a complete clause.
The quotation that follows illustrates what the report said and has no introducing verb.
A colon after a complete clause introduces it.
explanation.why: The colon introduces the quotation that shows the report's bluntness.
explanation.pattern: A colon after a complete clause may introduce a quotation that illustrates it.

items.passage: The vote on the stadium bond having been postponed twice since January because of disputes over the cost estimates ______ the council finally scheduled a special session for the second week of June.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A semicolon needs a complete clause before it, and the opening group has no finite verb.
A colon also needs a complete clause before it.

choices.text: , and
choices.slip: 'and' would join a modifying phrase to a clause, which is not parallel.

steps: 'The vote ... having been postponed' has no finite verb, so it is an absolute phrase.
The main clause begins with 'the council finally scheduled'.
A comma separates a long opening phrase from the main clause.
explanation.why: The comma ends the opening absolute phrase.
explanation.pattern: A long opening phrase without a finite verb is followed by a comma before the main clause.

items.passage: Six farms line the Ruan, but the oldest orchard has belonged since 1884 to the Delgado family, and the ______ carved gate sign has been repainted by each of four generations.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: Delgado’s
choices.slip: The singular possessive names one person, but the owners are the whole family.

choices.text: Delgados’
Delgados’s
choices.slip: This adds an extra s after an apostrophe on a plural that already ends in -s.

choices.text: Delgados
choices.slip: This has no apostrophe, so it does not show possession.

steps: The sign belongs to the Delgado family as a group, so the name is plural.
Plural family names add -s.
A plural noun ending in -s shows possession with an apostrophe alone.
explanation.why: 'Delgados’' is the plural possessive of the family name.
explanation.pattern: A plural family name forms its possessive by adding -s and then an apostrophe.

items.passage: Having spent six summers retracing the 1887 boundary survey with only the original field notes, which the county’s records office lost in a fire and later recovered from a private collection ______ Osric Delamere, a retired surveyor from the lower valley, finally published a corrected map of the old county line this spring, a decade after the dispute began.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A semicolon needs a complete clause before it; the opening phrase has no subject or verb.
A colon also needs a complete clause before it.
A single dash would open an interruption that is never closed, and it cannot close the comma-opened which-clause.

steps: 'Having spent … private collection' is an introductory participial phrase; the subject, 'Osric Delamere', follows it.
Inside it, 'which the county's records office lost…' was opened by a comma, so that clause needs a closing comma.
One comma therefore ends the which-clause and the whole introductory phrase.
explanation.why: The comma closes the which-clause and also sets off the introductory phrase.
explanation.pattern: A comma after a long introductory phrase also closes any comma-opened clause inside it.

items.passage: The council did not postpone the vote ______ two members were absent; it postponed it because the legal opinion on the bond had not yet arrived from the state office.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: because
, because
choices.slip: A comma would present the absence as the reason the council did not postpone, reversing the contrast the second clause sets up.

choices.text: ; because
choices.slip: A semicolon needs a complete clause on each side.

choices.text: , since
choices.slip: The comma would make the absence the reason for not postponing, and 'since' repeats that reading.

steps: The second clause says the real reason for postponing was the missing legal opinion.
So the first clause denies that the absences were the reason: 'did not postpone the vote because ...'.
The reason clause is restrictive and takes no comma.
explanation.why: No comma lets 'because two members were absent' fall inside the negation.
explanation.pattern: A reason clause that the negation applies to takes no comma.

items.passage: At the hearing, the auditors asked the warehouse manager ______ the 1887 ledger had been altered after the fire, who had held the storeroom keys that winter, and whether any earlier copy had survived.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: : how
choices.slip: A colon would separate the verb 'asked' from the embedded questions that are its objects.

choices.text: , how
choices.slip: A comma would also separate 'asked' from the questions that complete it.

choices.text: ; how
choices.slip: A semicolon would separate the verb from its objects and needs a complete clause before it.

choices.text: how

steps: 'asked the warehouse manager' takes three embedded questions as objects: how..., who..., whether...
These are objects of 'asked', not separate sentences.
No punctuation separates a verb from its objects.
explanation.why: 'how' begins the first embedded question directly.
explanation.pattern: A verb is not separated from its objects, including embedded questions.

items.passage: Early surveys of the delta relied on aerial photographs taken at low tide (Teversham 1962 ______ Later teams, working from satellite data, found that many of the channels shown on those photographs had since silted up or shifted by hundreds of meters.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A period inside the parentheses would end a parenthetical sentence, but this citation sits inside the sentence.
A comma would join the sentence to a new sentence with a capital 'Later', making a comma splice.
With no end punctuation, the next sentence would run on.

steps: The parenthesis opens a citation inside the first sentence.
The sentence ends after the citation, so the parenthesis closes and the period follows it.
The next sentence begins with a capital, 'Later'.
explanation.why: ').' closes the citation and then ends the sentence.
explanation.pattern: A citation within a sentence closes with the parenthesis; the sentence's period follows it.

items.passage: Few civic essays outlive their moment, but the 1931 essay “Who Owns the River?” ______ a decade of lawsuits among the three mills upstream, and the question it posed is still cited in water-rights cases.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: , prompted
choices.slip: A comma would separate the title, which is the subject, from its verb.

choices.text: ; prompted
choices.slip: A semicolon would separate the subject from its verb.

choices.text: prompted
: prompted
choices.slip: A colon would separate the subject from its verb.

steps: The subject is the title 'Who Owns the River?' with its essay label.
The question mark ends the title, not a clause.
The verb follows with no punctuation.
explanation.why: 'prompted' follows the title directly.
explanation.pattern: A title that is the subject is not separated from its verb, even if it ends in a question mark.

items.passage: The inspector’s summary called the repairs “adequate ______ the foreman, who had expected praise, took the word as an insult and refused to sign.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: In American usage, semicolons go outside closing quotation marks; only commas and periods go inside.
A comma would join two independent clauses with no conjunction, a comma splice.
A period would end the sentence, but the next words begin in lowercase.

steps: The quoted word 'adequate' ends the first clause.
Two independent clauses are joined without a conjunction, so a semicolon is needed.
The semicolon goes after the closing quotation mark.
explanation.why: '”;' closes the quotation and joins the clauses.
explanation.pattern: A semicolon is placed outside closing quotation marks.

items.passage: Marine biologists surveying the tidal flats at Tessel Sound recorded three conditions that separated the thriving eelgrass beds from the failing ones ______ water clarity above two meters, sediment containing less than five percent silt, and summer temperatures that rarely passed eighteen degrees Celsius. No failing bed met more than one of these conditions, which suggested that all three act together.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; the list that follows is not one.
A comma would leave the list attached to “failing ones” as if it described them, and the passage says the opposite.
A period would leave the list as a fragment, and the next word is lowercase.

steps: The words before the blank form a complete clause that promises three conditions.
What follows is a list of those three conditions with internal commas.
A colon introduces a list after a complete clause.
explanation.why: A colon links the complete clause to the list it announces.
explanation.pattern: Complete clause + list: colon.

items.passage: In its first report on the 2023 culvert failures, filed in March after a seven-month review, the county board received the three ______ joint analysis, which blamed corrosion rather than excessive load, a finding that surprised members who had budgeted for reinforced channels instead of replacement pipe along the entire northern road. Local historians say the board has not revisited the question since.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: engineers
choices.slip: Without an apostrophe the noun cannot own the analysis.

choices.text: engineers’
engineer’s
choices.slip: “Three” requires a plural owner; this form is singular possessive.

choices.text: engineers’s
choices.slip: A plural already ending in s takes only an apostrophe.

steps: “Three” shows more than one engineer.
They jointly own the analysis, so the noun must be a plural possessive.
A regular plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.why: “engineers’” is the plural possessive.
explanation.pattern: Plural possessive: add only an apostrophe.

items.passage: When the first cost estimate for the lighthouse restoration arrived, the mayor dismissed it as “a rounding error ______ which turned out to understate the final bill by nearly forty percent. By the time the contractors submitted a second figure, the council had already voted twice to defer any decision, and the keeper’s cottage had lost its roof. Residents still quote the remark whenever a new project is proposed.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: In American usage a comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
A semicolon cannot set off a which-clause from the noun it describes.
A period would leave “which turned out…” as a fragment.

steps: “Which turned out to understate…” is a nonrestrictive clause modifying the quoted phrase, so a comma must precede it.
The comma comes before the closing quotation mark in American usage.
explanation.why: “,”” places the comma inside the quotation.
explanation.pattern: Commas go inside closing quotation marks.

items.passage: Although the grant committee reviewed each proposal on its merits, Dr. Brandel’s stood apart: it was the only one that put ______ interests ahead of its own, offering to share its sequencing equipment with the three rural hospitals that have no laboratory, and the reviewers, who rarely agreed on anything that spring, scored it identically. Colleagues later said the decision had surprised no one who read the full file.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: everyone’s else
choices.slip: The apostrophe-s goes on the last word of the phrase, not on “everyone.”

choices.text: everyones else’
choices.slip: “Everyone” is singular; this form is garbled.

choices.text: everyone elses’
choices.slip: “Else” does not take a plural s.

choices.text: everyone else’s

steps: “Everyone else” is a single unit naming the owners.
In compound indefinite pronouns, the possessive ending attaches to the final word.
explanation.why: “everyone else’s”.
explanation.pattern: Add ’s to the last word of “everyone else.”

items.passage: The viaduct’s original cables, which the firm that designed them had expected to last a full century ______ began to fray within forty years, and the replacement program now consumes nearly a third of the regional maintenance budget, leaving little for the secondary roads that feed the bridge. Engineers now inspect the remaining spans twice a year. Nobody involved expected the matter to be settled quickly, least of all those who had followed it from the beginning.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A closing dash cannot match an opening comma.
A semicolon would cut the subject “cables” off from its verb “began.”
A colon cannot close an interrupter.

steps: The comma after “cables” opens a nonrestrictive which-clause.
The clause ends after “century,” and the verb “began” follows.
The interrupter needs a matching comma.
explanation.why: A closing comma matches the opening one.
explanation.pattern: Interrupters need matching marks.

items.passage: Vaccine shipments that wait overnight at the regional depot depend on a single refrigeration loop. The cold-storage valves must be inspected every month ______ corrosion goes unnoticed until a seal fails, and by then the loss of refrigerant can spoil an entire shipment before anyone on the loading dock has seen a single warning light on the control panel.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: , otherwise,
choices.slip: A comma would splice two independent clauses.

choices.text: ; otherwise,
: otherwise,
choices.slip: The second clause states a consequence, not an explanation or a list, so a colon is not supported.

choices.text: . otherwise,
choices.slip: A period would require “Otherwise” to be capitalized.

steps: 'The cold-storage valves must be inspected every month' is a complete clause.
'Otherwise, corrosion goes unnoticed…' is also a complete clause introduced by a conjunctive adverb.
Two independent clauses joined by a conjunctive adverb take a semicolon before it and a comma after it.
explanation.why: A semicolon before 'otherwise' and a comma after it join the clauses correctly.
explanation.pattern: Semicolon + conjunctive adverb + comma between independent clauses.

items.passage: The ferry route to Fennick Isle was cut in 1974 ______ leaving the school with eleven pupils by 1980, and the island’s last teacher, who had commuted by rowboat for two winters, retired the following spring without a replacement. Only a handful of families remain there today, and the building is now used mainly as a summer art studio that the district rents out.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A semicolon would leave 'leaving the school…' as a fragment.
A colon needs a complete clause explaining the first; this is a participial phrase.
A period would leave a fragment beginning with a lowercase participle.

steps: 'The ferry route to Fennick Isle was cut in 1974' is a complete clause.
'Leaving the school with eleven pupils by 1980' is a participial phrase that modifies the whole clause, not 1974.
A trailing participial phrase is set off by a comma.
explanation.why: A comma attaches the participial phrase to the clause.
explanation.pattern: Comma before a trailing participial phrase that modifies the whole clause.

items.passage: The restoration of the Pell Street promenade ran two seasons late (it was funded in part by a federal grant and in part by a bequest from a retired schoolteacher ______ the final cost was $4.1 million, nearly double the original estimate, and the reopening ceremony drew only a small crowd because the east wing stayed closed.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A comma after the parenthesis would splice two independent clauses.
The parenthesis must close before the semicolon; the semicolon belongs outside it.
With no mark after the parenthesis, the two clauses run together.

steps: The parenthetical, 'it was funded … schoolteacher', is a complete clause that must be closed.
'The restoration … ran two seasons late' and 'the final cost was $4.1 million' are independent clauses.
Close the parenthesis, then join the clauses with a semicolon placed outside it.
explanation.why: '); ' closes the aside and joins the clauses.
explanation.pattern: Close the parenthesis, then use the clause-joining mark.

items.passage: The old cannery—a sprawling brick complex that employed nearly four hundred people, most of them seasonal workers, at its height in 1950 ______ now houses a museum, a brewery, and a climbing gym, and the city has proposed adding a footbridge to the waterfront so that visitors can reach it from the ferry landing without crossing the highway.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A comma cannot close an interrupter opened by a dash, and it would blur the commas inside the aside.
A semicolon would separate the subject from its verb.
A colon would separate the subject from its verb.

steps: The dash after 'cannery' opens an aside.
The aside already contains commas, and it ends after '1950'; the verb 'houses' follows.
The closing mark must be a dash to match the opening dash.
explanation.why: A closing dash matches the opening dash.
explanation.pattern: Dashes come in matched pairs.

items.passage: The recipe that finally won the county fair’s pie contest turned out to be my ______ ginger crust, a family secret she had refused to write down for thirty years and only shared after the judges, who had tasted it twice that afternoon, begged for the method. Her pie has taken first prize every year since, and the recipe now hangs framed in the fair office.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: sister’s-in-law
choices.slip: The possessive ending goes at the end of the compound, not in the middle.

choices.text: sister-in-laws’
choices.slip: “Sister-in-law” is singular here, as “she” shows; the plural possessive is wrong.

choices.text: sisters-in-law
choices.slip: This lacks any possessive marker.

choices.text: sister-in-law’s

steps: “She” shows one owner.
In a hyphenated compound, the ’s is added to the last word.
explanation.why: “sister-in-law’s”.
explanation.pattern: Possessive of a hyphenated compound goes on the end.

items.passage: After six years of planning, the museum’s curators agreed that the new wing could not open without three objects ______ the 1912 survey globe, whose painted oceans had been retouched by three different hands; a brass transit instrument, still calibrated to the 1887 baseline; and the surveyor’s original field journal, which a collector donated in 2018.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A semicolon requires two independent clauses; the words after the blank form a list.
A comma after a complete clause would not introduce a list whose items are separated by semicolons.
A period would leave a fragment beginning with a lowercase article.

steps: 'The museum's curators agreed that the new wing could not open without three objects' is a complete clause.
What follows names the three objects as a list, and the items are separated by semicolons because they contain commas.

items.passage: The treasurer, who had kept the society’s accounts by hand since the 1980s and who distrusted every spreadsheet that the new board proposed ______ refused to hand over the ledgers, and the board, unwilling to force the matter, hired an outside auditor instead. items.passage: Every October the two neighboring ______ shared orchard, a strip of apple and pear trees that runs along both properties, is picked by relatives who arrive from three states, and the harvest is divided by a schedule that neither household has ever written down. items.passage: In the winter of 1987, when the reservoir dropped to its lowest recorded level since the dam opened ______ crews working along the exposed shoreline found the foundations of a mill that had been flooded for sixty years, and archivists later matched its dimensions to a drawing in the county survey. items.passage: The sealant on the hull cured for two full days under the heat lamps ______ then the crew repainted the lower planks, working from the stern forward so that the seams would not be disturbed before the afternoon tide came in. items.passage: Unlike most coastal surveys of the period, which relied on private funds and volunteer crews ______ the 1840 survey was paid for entirely by the Crown, and its charts of the northern shoals, drawn by naval officers, remained in use for more than a century. The clause ends before “the 1840 survey.”
A comma closes it and ends the introduction.

explanation.pattern: Closing comma in introductory phrase.

items.passage: At a public hearing on drought planning, the council heard from several experts about the region's water supply. “The reservoir will not recover by autumn,” the hydrologist Ilse Brandvold-Ketter told the council on Tuesday, ______ “unless the upstream towns agree to cut their withdrawals by a fifth, and even then only if the snowpack in the northern range reaches ninety percent of its average depth by the end of March.”

steps: The quotation is one sentence split by an attribution: the resumed words begin in lowercase.
The attribution ends and the quotation resumes, which is marked by a comma.
A period or semicolon would break the sentence.
explanation.why: A comma returns to the quotation after the attribution.
explanation.pattern: Split quotation: comma after the attribution, resumed words lowercase.

items.passage: After a three-year dispute over its leaking roof, the city council did not close the Harrowgate Street library, as the budget committee had predicted ______ it moved the branch into the vacant post office, cut its weekend hours, and asked volunteers to staff the children’s room, a compromise that neither the librarians nor the budget hawks had wanted at the start.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: , instead,

choices.text: : instead,

choices.text: instead,
choices.slip: A run-on; nothing separates the clauses, and 'instead' appears to attach to 'predicted'.

choices.text: ; instead,

steps: 'The city council did not close the library' and 'it moved the branch' are independent clauses.
'Instead' is a conjunctive adverb, so a semicolon precedes it and a comma follows.
The 'as … had predicted' clause ends before the semicolon.
explanation.why: A semicolon before 'instead' and a comma after it join the clauses.
explanation.pattern: Independent clause ; conjunctive adverb , independent clause.

items.passage: A structural engineer spent two days examining a water-stained wall in the old bakery and then wrote a short report for the owners. The inspector's finding was simple ______ the wall had never been waterproofed, so every repair since 1990 had treated the symptom and left the cause untouched, a pattern the owners now describe as the most expensive mistake they made.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A comma splice; two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone.

choices.text: that
choices.slip: Ungrammatical; 'that' would make a fragment with no linking logic.

choices.text: , that
choices.slip: The comma and 'that' together leave the clause unattached and unclear.

steps: 'The inspector's finding was simple' is a complete clause; what follows explains the finding.
A colon links the complete clause to its explanation.
The later ', so every repair' is a separate comma-plus-conjunction join and does not affect the blank.
explanation.why: A colon after a complete clause introduces the explanation.
explanation.pattern: Complete clause + colon + explanation.

items.passage: When the legislature created the harbor authority in 1911, it gave the new body very little money and a long list of duties. The harbor authority's first chair, the retired pilot Anselm Qureshi-Boyd ______ inherited a staff of nine, a leaking office, and a charter that gave the authority power to seize any vessel that carried unlisted cargo.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

A closing dash cannot match an opening comma.
A colon would separate the subject from its verb.

steps: The comma after 'chair' opens a nonessential appositive: 'the retired pilot Anselm Qureshi-Boyd'.
Inside it, 'pilot' and the name form a restrictive pair with no comma, which can hide the need to close the appositive.
A comma closes the appositive before the verb 'inherited'.
explanation.why: A closing comma ends the appositive before the main verb.
explanation.pattern: An appositive opened by a comma must be closed by a comma.

items.passage: Industrial museums often build exhibits around a single large machine that explains a whole region's past. The foundry's last working furnace ______ a coal-fired giant that ran without a break from 1887 to 1973, feeding rail yards across three counties—now serves as the centerpiece of a museum that charges no admission and draws more than forty thousand visitors a year.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: A comma cannot open an interrupter that a dash closes.
A semicolon would leave a fragment and break the subject from its verb.
A colon would separate the subject from its verb and cannot open an interrupter.

steps: The sentence contains a closing dash after 'counties', so an opening dash is needed.
The interrupter has its own comma, which can make a comma seem right.
Marks around an interrupter must match.
explanation.why: An opening dash pairs with the closing dash after 'counties'.
explanation.pattern: Dash-set interrupters need a dash at each end.

items.passage: The flood that hit the river towns last March tested every public institution in the county. At a ceremony on Friday, the mayor praised the volunteers who had worked through the flood ______ the county had offered them no equipment or training in the days after the water rose. Several of them had used their own garage tools and borrowed trucks.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: yet
choices.slip: A run-on; 'yet' here joins two independent clauses and needs a comma before it.

choices.text: , yet
; yet
choices.slip: A semicolon is not used before 'yet' when it joins two short clauses as a conjunction.

choices.text: : yet
choices.slip: A colon needs a clause that explains or lists; this clause contrasts.

steps: 'The mayor praised the volunteers…' is a complete clause.
'The county had offered them no equipment…' is a second complete clause with its own subject, so 'yet' here is a coordinating conjunction, not an adverb.
A coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses takes a comma before it.
explanation.why: A comma before 'yet' joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.pattern: Comma + coordinating conjunction (yet) between independent clauses.

items.passage: Ferry schedules on the northern lake change with the weather, and this year the change came early. The ferry stopped running in the second week of November ______ the channel, which is shallow and exposed, froze earlier than it had in any year since the harbor commission began keeping records in 1921. ; for

choices.text: : for
choices.slip: A colon introduces a list or explanation, not a 'for' clause.

choices.text: for
choices.slip: A run-on; 'for' as a conjunction needs a comma.

steps: 'For the channel … froze' is an independent clause, so 'for' is a coordinating conjunction meaning 'because'.
A comma goes before a coordinating conjunction joining independent clauses.
The commas around 'which is shallow and exposed' belong to a nonessential clause.
explanation.why: A comma before 'for' joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.pattern: Comma + for (conjunction) joins independent clauses.

items.passage: The night shift at the testing laboratory spent an hour arguing about a faulty instrument whose readings had wandered for weeks. “Why did the gauge drift so far before anyone ______ the technician asked the room, though no one had an answer and the supervisor, who had been reading the logs since morning, only shook his head.

noticed.”

choices.slip: A question mark already ends the quotation; the comma is unnecessary.

steps: The quoted words are a question, so a question mark closes them inside the quotation marks.
The attribution that follows begins in lowercase and does not change the question mark.
Pairing a question mark with a comma is wrong.
explanation.why: A question mark inside the quotation marks ends the quoted question.
explanation.pattern: A quoted question keeps its question mark even before an attribution.

items.passage: Dredging of the outer channel had been debated for nearly a decade. The harbor commission approved the new dredging schedule in March after two public hearings. The vote was ______ Residents who attended the second hearing, however, said that the commissioners had read none of the written objections, which the county clerk had received in bundles of several hundred pages each.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: No period ends the first sentence, so two sentences run together.

choices.text: unanimous. (The full minutes appear in Appendix C.)
unanimous, (the full minutes appear in Appendix C.)
choices.slip: A comma before the parenthesis leaves a comma splice with a complete sentence inside.

steps: The parenthetical is a complete sentence standing between two other sentences.
The sentence before it needs a period.
Its own period goes inside the closing parenthesis; nothing follows outside.
explanation.why: A freestanding parenthetical sentence is capitalized and ends inside the parentheses.
explanation.pattern: Sentence-length parenthetical between sentences: period before, period inside.

items.passage: The state's regional development fund supported pilot programs in two small fishing towns. Garth Landing and Veyne Quay received foundation grants of $4.2 million and ______ which together covered less than half of each program's projected costs, a gap that both towns hoped the state would help to close before the pilot ended, though the legislature had not yet taken up the request.

$3.6 million respectively,

choices.slip: The comma after 'respectively' is missing before the nonrestrictive which clause.

choices.slip: A semicolon cannot join a modifier to the clause it follows.

steps: 'Respectively' is an interrupter and is set off by commas.
The which clause is nonrestrictive and needs a comma before it, which 'respectively,' supplies.
Only ', respectively,' has both commas.
explanation.why: '... $3.6 million, respectively, which ...' uses a matched pair.
explanation.pattern: 'Respectively' mid-sentence takes a comma on each side.

items.passage: Laboratory space at the university has been scarce since the physics building closed for repairs. In the memo that circulated before the vote, the director described the transfer ______ “a short-term measure” and added that the budget committee, which had met only twice all year, would need to approve the move of the east laboratory’s equipment to the north campus, where space is limited.

as;
choices.slip: A semicolon after 'as' separates the preposition from its object.

A quotation that completes the sentence grammatically takes no punctuation before it.
The compound predicate 'described … and added' takes no comma either.
explanation.why: 'As' flows directly into the quotation.
explanation.pattern: No punctuation between a preposition and its quoted object.

items.passage: Water managers in the valley recorded an unusually sharp split between the two main sources during the long drought. The lower reservoir, which supplies the eastern wards and the university hospital, held only forty days of water in ______ the northern reservoir, fed by two mountain streams, stayed above ninety percent through the whole dry season, according to the annual report.

'Meanwhile' is a conjunctive adverb, so a semicolon goes before it.
A comma follows it.
explanation.why: 'August; meanwhile, the northern reservoir ...' joins correctly.
explanation.pattern: Semicolon before and comma after a conjunctive adverb between clauses.

items.passage: Fire investigators in the harbor district spent nearly three months on the case before releasing a report. After reviewing the fire marshal's findings, the insurer's investigators blamed the building's aging ______ for the blaze that destroyed the Odeon Annex last winter, a conclusion that the owners, who had paid for the pump's replacement in 2020, disputed, citing invoices from that year and the maintenance logs.

choices.slip: A dash opened and a comma closed; the marks must match.

steps: 'Not the pump' is a contrasting phrase that interrupts the clause.
It is nonessential, so it takes commas on both sides.
The marks must match: comma and comma.
explanation.why: 'wiring, not the pump, for the blaze' uses a matched pair.
explanation.pattern: A 'not ...' contrast phrase in mid-sentence takes paired commas.

items.passage: Harbor staff had run the evacuation drill for years without a written rule on when to hold position. In a memo that the staff circulated before the drill, the harbor master wrote, “The only phrase anyone needs to remember is ‘hold ______ The crews, who had ignored three earlier memos, finally read this one aloud at every shift change, and attendance at the briefings rose.

choices.slip: Both quotations would close before the period; American style puts it inside.

choices.text: position.’”

steps: A quotation inside a quotation takes single marks.
Both quotations end together at the end of the sentence.
In American style the period precedes both closing marks, inner first, then outer.
explanation.why: 'hold position.’”' closes inner then outer with the period inside.
explanation.pattern: Nested quotations ending together: period, then single, then double mark.

items.passage: Preservationists in the old transit district won a long campaign last month. The Pennant Street depot, where the city's first electric buses were tested in 1951 and where a retired mechanic still keeps the original ______ will be converted into a museum, a plan that the preservation society has endorsed on the condition that the loading docks remain intact, since they are the only part of the structure that survived the fire of 1974.

choices.slip: A semicolon cannot close an interrupter that opened with a comma.

choices.slip: A dash cannot close an interrupter that opened with a comma.

steps: The comma after 'depot' opens a nonessential 'where' clause.
The clause, with its compound 'where ... and where', must be closed before the main verb 'will be converted'.
The matching mark is a comma.
explanation.why: 'depot, where ... logbooks, will be converted' closes the pair.
explanation.pattern: Closing comma after a long interrupter, before the main verb.

items.passage: Water pressure on Tolliver Row had been poor for years. Residents kept asking the same thing at every meeting: why had the water authority waited until 2020 to replace the main (a repair its own engineers had urgently recommended in ______ Nobody at the authority offered an answer that satisfied them, and the meeting ended without a vote, as it had the month before.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.slip: The parenthetical is a statement; the question mark belongs to the whole sentence, outside.
The sentence is a question, so a period cannot end it.
A period inside the parenthesis and a question mark outside would double up the endings.

steps: The whole sentence after the colon is a question.
The parenthetical inside is a statement, so it takes no mark of its own.
The question mark goes after the closing parenthesis.
explanation.why: '(a repair ... in 2016)?' ends the question outside the parenthesis.
explanation.pattern: Question outside a statement-parenthetical: close the parenthesis, then the question mark.

items.passage: Ana had practiced the speech until she could recite it in her sleep. Yet standing at the podium, she set her notes aside and told the story of her grandmother's bakery instead, the one she had been told was too personal for the occasion. The room, restless a moment earlier, went quiet.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Ana is so nervous that she forgets a speech she has practiced.
choices.slip: She knows the speech perfectly and chooses to set her notes aside.

choices.text: Ana's audience makes clear that it dislikes personal stories.
choices.slip: The restless room goes quiet when she tells the story, a sign of attention.

choices.text: Ana's grandmother taught her how to speak in public.
choices.slip: The grandmother appears only as the subject of the story.

choices.text: Ana swaps her prepared speech for a story that holds the room.

steps: She has the speech memorized.
'Yet' she sets her notes aside and tells a personal story 'instead'. That is a choice.
The restless room 'went quiet': the story holds the listeners.
explanation.why: Ana chooses a personal story over her prepared speech, and the audience responds with attention.
explanation.pattern: A main idea must cover the whole text. Check each part of a choice against the text: 'forgets' fails because she 'set her notes aside'.

items.passage: It was long assumed that the marsh wren sings its hundred-odd songs in no particular order. Recordings analyzed by ornithologist Pia Lund suggest otherwise: neighbors answer one another with the song that follows the rival's in a sequence both birds share. A wren's repertoire, on this view, is less a collection than a common script, and singing is a matter of keeping one's place in it.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Lund's analysis suggests that marsh wrens sing in a shared order, which neighbors follow in reply.
Lund's analysis suggests that each wren arranges its songs in a private order rivals cannot predict.
choices.slip: The sequence is one 'both birds share', not a private one.

choices.text: Lund's recordings confirm that marsh wrens choose among their songs more or less at random.
choices.slip: Her recordings 'suggest otherwise' than the old assumption of no order.

choices.text: Lund's recordings show that marsh wrens with more songs tend to defeat their neighbors.
choices.slip: The text says nothing about which birds win.

steps: Old assumption: the songs come in no particular order.
Lund's finding: neighbors reply with the next song in 'a sequence both birds share'.
The last sentence restates it: the repertoire is 'a common script'.
So the main idea is a shared order that the birds follow.
explanation.why: The text presents Lund's evidence that wrens' songs follow a sequence shared by neighbors.
explanation.pattern: When choices differ by one word ('shared' or 'private'), go back to the sentence that settles it.

items.passage: Economist Noor Hadley studied what happened in forty towns after a rail line closed. Shops near the old stations lost customers, as expected. But shops on the towns' edges, where new bus stops were placed, gained almost exactly as many, leaving each town's total sales nearly flat. Hadley concludes that the closures moved commerce more than they reduced it.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The rail closures sharply reduced the total amount of shopping in the towns.
choices.slip: Total sales stayed 'nearly flat'.

choices.text: Shoppers in the forty towns came to prefer traveling by bus over rail.
choices.slip: The text reports where sales went, not which transport people liked.

choices.text: Shops near the old stations soon won back the customers they lost.
choices.slip: The text says those shops lost customers and doesn't say they returned.

choices.text: The rail closures changed where people shopped more than how much.

steps: Shops near stations lost customers.
Shops near the new bus stops gained 'almost exactly as many'.
Totals were 'nearly flat', so commerce 'moved' rather than shrank.
explanation.why: Hadley's conclusion is that the closures relocated commerce without much reducing it.
explanation.pattern: The last sentence often states the main idea. Here 'moved … more than they reduced' is the point to match.

items.passage: The letter had sat unopened on the mantel for three days. Tobias dusted around it, straightened the candlesticks on either side of it, and once moved it an inch to the left so that it sat square. He told his sister he had simply been too busy to read it.
items.question: Based on the text, what is true about Tobias?

choices.text: He has read the letter and wants to keep its contents from his sister.
choices.slip: The letter is 'unopened'.

choices.text: His reason for not reading the letter doesn't match how he behaves.
He hasn't noticed that a letter is waiting for him on the mantel.
choices.slip: He dusts around it and moves it, so he has noticed it.

choices.text: He has been told by his sister that he must not open the letter.
choices.slip: His sister only hears his excuse; she gives no instruction.

steps: He says he was 'too busy' to read the letter.
But he has time to dust around it, tidy beside it and adjust it.
So being busy isn't the real reason: his actions contradict his words.
explanation.why: Tobias gives the letter careful attention for three days while claiming to have no time for it.
explanation.pattern: In fiction, compare what a character says with what the character does. A gap between them is usually the point.

items.passage: Historians of the Calder Bay fishery have tended to date its decline to the 1920s, when catches fell by half. Archivist Ilya Brandt argues that this confuses the symptom with the onset. Harbor ledgers show that crews had been sailing steadily farther for the same catch since the 1890s; by the time totals fell, the nearer grounds had been empty for a generation. The catch figures, Brandt notes, had stayed level precisely because the fleet was working harder to keep them so.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Brandt argues that the decline was caused by crews sailing farther out for their catch, a practice that began in the 1890s.
choices.slip: Crews sailed farther because the near grounds were giving out; the text presents longer trips as a response to decline, not its cause.

choices.text: Brandt argues that historians have misdated the fall in catches, which the harbor ledgers place in the 1890s, not the 1920s.
choices.slip: Brandt accepts that catches fell in the 1920s; until then the figures 'had stayed level'.

choices.text: Brandt argues that the decline began well before the catch totals showed it, since growing effort had kept those totals level.
Brandt argues that the fall in catches in the 1920s was milder than historians hold, since the fleet's effort offset part of it.
choices.slip: Extra effort held catches level before the 1920s; nothing says the 1920s fall was smaller than reported.

steps: Historians: decline began in the 1920s, when catches fell.
Brandt: that is the 'symptom', not the 'onset'.
Evidence: since the 1890s crews sailed farther 'for the same catch'; near grounds were already empty.
Catches stayed level only 'because the fleet was working harder', so the decline started earlier and was masked.
explanation.why: Brandt holds that the fishery was declining from the 1890s and that greater effort kept the catch totals from showing it.
explanation.pattern: Sort out the order of events and what caused what. Wrong choices here reuse the text's facts but swap cause and effect or shift the dates.

items.passage: For decades, ecologists assumed that the small mollusks of rocky shores were bit players: grazers whose effect on the seaweed around them was minor next to that of predators such as sea stars. Marine ecologist Teodora Valcourt tested this at a site in southern Chile by fencing off thirty tide-pool plots and, in half of them, excluding a small grazing snail for two years. Where the snails were removed, brown algae covered nearly 70% of the rock, compared with roughly 25% in plots where snails remained. Valcourt cautions, however, that her plots lay on a sheltered shore; on exposed shores, where waves tear algae loose whether or not it is grazed, the snails' influence may be far smaller. She argues that the older assumption was therefore not so much wrong as untested outside the settings in which it had been formed.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Valcourt's experiment suggests that small snails may control seaweed growth more strongly than sea stars do on rocky shores generally, a result she says should now replace the older assumption.
choices.slip: The experiment never compared snails with sea stars, and Valcourt limits the result to sheltered shores.

choices.text: Removing a small grazer from tide pools let algae spread widely, challenging a long-held view of such grazers, though the result may not hold on exposed shores.
Valcourt's results suggest that the older assumption about small grazers is likely to prove mistaken on exposed shores as well as on the sheltered shore she studied.
choices.slip: Reverses her caveat: she says the snails' influence may be far smaller on exposed shores.

choices.text: Ecologists have long disagreed about whether waves or grazing animals do more to limit the spread of algae on rocky shores around the world.
choices.slip: Not in the text: no disagreement between ecologists is described, only a shared assumption.

steps: The text reports an old assumption (small grazers matter little), Valcourt's experiment (algae roughly 70% vs 25%), and a caveat (sheltered shore).
The main idea has to carry the finding and its limit.
One choice reaches the whole world, one throws the result away, and one adds a dispute the text never mentions.
explanation.why: It states the result, what it challenges, and the limit Valcourt herself gives.
explanation.pattern: Main-idea answers keep both the finding and the author's caveat; wrong choices drop the caveat (overreach) or inflate it (overcorrection).

items.passage: Historians have long credited the spread of cheap almanacs in eighteenth-century Varnholt to the town's new paper mill, which opened in 1741 and lowered the cost of printing. Archivist Ignatius Brelle's survey of 1,900 surviving print-shop invoices complicates that account. Almanac output did rise sharply after 1741, but Brelle found that it had already doubled in the five years before the mill opened, when printers were still importing paper at higher prices. What changed in that period, he argues, was a 1736 municipal ruling that let printers sell directly to peddlers instead of through the booksellers' guild. The mill, in his view, let a trade that was already growing grow faster; it did not start it.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Brelle's survey of invoices shows that the paper mill had no effect on almanac output, which was determined entirely by the 1736 ruling on direct sales to peddlers.
choices.slip: 'Entirely' and 'no effect' overreach: Brelle says the mill let growth continue faster.

choices.text: Brelle argues that printers began selling almanacs directly to peddlers only after the new mill had lowered the cost of paper, which then weakened the booksellers' guild.
choices.slip: Reverses the sequence: the selling ruling came in 1736, before the mill, and the text does not say the mill weakened the guild.

choices.text: Brelle argues that the mill lowered printing costs in Varnholt but that almanac output had already begun to climb before 1741, because cheaper imported paper had reached the town's printers.
choices.slip: Reverses the facts: imported paper was still expensive before the mill, and the earlier rise followed the 1736 ruling on direct sales.

choices.text: Invoices show almanac output rising before the mill opened, which Brelle attributes chiefly to a change in who could sell almanacs; the mill sped up growth already under way.

steps: Older account: mill lowered costs, so almanacs spread.
Brelle: output doubled in the five years before the mill, after the 1736 selling rule.
So the mill sped up growth rather than starting it.
explanation.why: It gives Brelle's finding (growth before the mill), his explanation (the selling rule), and the mill's reduced role.
explanation.pattern: When a text revises an earlier explanation, the main idea is the revision, not the old account and not an extreme version of the new one.

items.passage: Many spring wildflowers produce seeds bearing a fatty appendage that ants carry to their nests; there the ants eat the appendage and discard the seed. Botanist Keiko Wardlaw placed 600 marked seeds of one such wildflower on a forest floor and followed them for a year. Ants moved 41% of the seeds, a median of 1.8 meters, far enough to escape the dense shade of the parent plant. But few seedlings appeared near the nests themselves: more than half of the carried seeds ended up in nest refuse piles, where the soil was so rich in dissolved salts that little could germinate. The best-surviving seedlings grew from seeds that ants dropped along the way, before reaching a nest. Wardlaw concludes that the ants disperse the wildflower effectively, but that the benefit comes mostly from the carrying and not from the nest.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Ants move this wildflower's seeds far enough to be useful to it, but the seeds that fare best are those dropped on the way to a nest rather than those deposited in it.
Ants harm the wildflower's chances of reproducing by carrying its seeds to nests, where salty soil keeps most of them from germinating.
choices.slip: Contradicts Wardlaw's conclusion that the ants disperse the plant effectively; the harm applies to seeds left in refuse piles, not to dispersal overall.

choices.text: The fatty appendage on the wildflower's seeds benefits the plant less than it benefits the ants, which eat it and then discard the seed, so the plant gains little from being moved.
choices.slip: Not argued: the text never weighs the appendage's benefit to plant against ant.

choices.text: Wardlaw's year-long tracking showed that ants carry 41% of the seeds to nests, where roughly 41% of them go on to germinate successfully.
choices.slip: The 41% is the share of seeds moved, not a germination rate; most seeds left in nests did not germinate.

steps: Ants moved 41% of seeds a median of 1.8 m, escaping parent shade.
Seeds left in nest refuse piles mostly failed (salty soil).
Seeds dropped en route did best. So dispersal helps; the nest does not.
explanation.why: It combines the dispersal benefit with the finding that the best seedlings came from seeds dropped before the nest.
explanation.pattern: Check each choice for a number or comparison the text doesn't make (41% reused as a germination rate; 'harm' where the text says 'effective').

items.passage: Lichenometry dates exposed rock surfaces by measuring the largest lichen growing on them, on the assumption that lichens expand at a steady rate. Geomorphologist Orsolya Pemberton checked the method on thirty gravestones whose carving dates were known, from 1790 to 1950. For stones under about a century old, her lichen-based dates fell within a decade of the true date. For older stones, the errors grew to several decades, because growth slows as a lichen ages and the steady-rate assumption fails. Pemberton does not recommend abandoning the method, but she urges that dates older than a century be reported as wide ranges.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Pemberton's test of thirty gravestones showed that lichenometry is too unreliable to date any rock surface and should be replaced by other methods.
choices.slip: Contradicts the text: she does not recommend abandoning it, and it worked well for younger stones.

choices.text: Lichens grow at a steady rate throughout their lives, which is why lichenometry can date gravestones carved after 1790 to within a decade.
choices.slip: Reverses the finding: growth slows with age, which is why older dates fail.

choices.text: Lichenometry gave accurate dates for young surfaces but grew unreliable for older ones, so Pemberton recommends keeping it while widening the stated uncertainty for older dates.
Gravestones carved before 1850 are less suitable for lichen dating than those carved later because their carving dates are less certain.
choices.slip: Invents a reason: the carving dates were known; the problem is slowing lichen growth.

steps: Method assumes steady lichen growth.
Test: accurate for stones under about a century, errors of decades for older ones.
Pemberton keeps the method but asks for wide ranges on old dates.
explanation.why: It states both the accuracy for young surfaces and the recommended handling of older dates.
explanation.pattern: Main idea = finding plus the author's response to it; wrong choices keep only one half or reverse the cause.

items.passage: When the Delmarch Quartet premiered Hanne Vossler's String Quartet No. 2 in 1962, critics called its slow movement unfocused. Vossler agreed. Over the next nine years she cut the movement from 212 measures to 140, removing a long middle section and moving its most striking theme to the opening. Musicologist Renzo Abila, comparing the five surviving manuscripts, notes that every revision shortened the movement and none added new material. He reads this as evidence that Vossler saw her task not as improving the movement by adding to it, but as uncovering a shorter piece that the first version had buried.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Abila reads the manuscripts as showing that Vossler revised by cutting, not adding, to reveal a shorter work buried in the first version.
Vossler rewrote the slow movement of her quartet several times because critics disliked it and she wished to win back their favor.
choices.slip: Not supported: she agreed with the critics; nothing says she was seeking favor.

choices.text: Abila claims that the quartet's slow movement was best in its original 212-measure form and that later cuts weakened the piece.
choices.slip: Reverses Abila's reading: he sees the cuts as uncovering the better piece.

choices.text: Musicologists have found that five manuscripts of the quartet survive, which is more than exist for any other work by Vossler.
choices.slip: Not in the text: no comparison with her other works is made.

steps: First version called unfocused; Vossler agreed.
Revisions: 212 to 140 measures, nothing added.
Abila: she was uncovering a shorter piece, not adding.
explanation.why: It gives Abila's inference from the manuscripts about how Vossler revised.
explanation.pattern: Check whose claim the main idea reports: here Abila's reading of the evidence, not the facts alone.

items.passage: At the Ketsel site, excavators in the 1970s found forty clay vessels buried in a row beneath the floor of a house and concluded that the row was a ritual offering. Archaeologist Nasrin Halloran-Quist recently reexamined the vessels and found residues of fermented barley in all forty, along with wear marks on their rims that match those on vessels used daily for drinking. She argues that the row was most likely a storage cache buried for safekeeping during a crisis, not an offering. She concedes, however, that she cannot explain why the vessels were set in so even a line, a pattern that fits ritual practice better than hurried hiding.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Halloran-Quist has shown that the Ketsel vessels were never used for drinking and were made only to be buried beneath the floor of the house in a single season.
choices.slip: Contradicts the wear marks she found.

choices.text: Evidence from residues and wear leads Halloran-Quist to reinterpret the Ketsel vessels as stored goods rather than an offering, though the orderly arrangement remains unexplained.
The even line of vessels beneath the Ketsel house proves that the 1970s excavators were right to treat the row as a ritual offering.
choices.slip: She argues against the offering reading; the line is the leftover puzzle.

choices.text: Residues of fermented barley in the Ketsel vessels show that the household was brewing in secret, which explains why the vessels were buried.
choices.slip: Invents secret brewing; she proposes a crisis cache.

steps: 1970s reading: ritual offering.
New evidence: barley residue and drinking wear point to stored goods.
She admits the even line is unexplained.
explanation.why: The correct choice carries both the revised reading and the admitted gap.
explanation.pattern: Main idea with a concession must include the caveat, not only the headline claim.

items.passage: Glassmaker Ilona Brandhorst-Yee spent six years trying to reproduce the deep red of medieval cathedral windows, which medieval glassmakers achieved by adding gold. Following the recipes in a surviving twelfth-century manual, she produced a glass of the right color, but microscope analysis showed that her gold particles were nearly twice as large as those in the original panes and more evenly spaced. She suspects that the medieval makers, whose wood-fired furnaces swung widely in temperature, got their particles from uneven heating, something her electric kiln, held steady within five degrees, cannot supply. She plans to add deliberate temperature swings to her next trials.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Medieval glassmakers achieved red glass more reliably than modern makers because their wood-fired furnaces held temperatures steadier than any electric kiln can.
choices.slip: Reverses the contrast: the kiln is steady, the medieval furnaces were not.

choices.text: Brandhorst-Yee has shown that the medieval manual's recipes are incomplete, since following them produced glass of the wrong color.
choices.slip: The color was right.

choices.text: Brandhorst-Yee's reproduction of medieval red glass matches the original in color but not in particle structure, a difference she attributes to furnace conditions she intends to imitate.
Gold particles in medieval red glass were larger than those in her reproduction because medieval makers added more gold to each batch.
choices.slip: Reverses particle size and invents the gold amount.

steps: Followed the manual: color right.
Particles were larger and more even than in originals.
She blames steady kiln heat and will add swings.
explanation.why: The color matched, the microstructure did not, and she links that to furnace temperature.
explanation.pattern: Main idea: summarize the result, the gap, and the explanation offered.

items.passage: Two research teams measured the age of the same layer of volcanic ash on the Tessaly plateau. One team, using the radioactive decay of potassium in ash crystals, reported 41,000 years; the other, counting annual bands of mud in a lake sediment core that contained the ash, reported 38,500 years. Geochemist Imelda Vasquez-Thorne argues that the gap does not show an error by either team: the potassium method dates when the crystals formed in the magma, which may precede the eruption by centuries or longer, while the sediment count dates the ash's arrival in the lake. On this reading, the results are compatible, and the gap roughly measures how long the crystals sat in the magma chamber.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The sediment-core count of 38,500 years is more reliable than the potassium result, since layers of lake mud record the passage of time directly.
choices.slip: She does not rank the methods.

choices.text: Potassium dating is generally less precise than layer counting, so Vasquez-Thorne recommends that the plateau's ash be dated only by sediment cores.
choices.slip: Not stated; she keeps both results.

choices.text: The two teams' results differ by 2,500 years, which shows that at least one team made an error that Vasquez-Thorne has now identified.
choices.slip: She denies that either team erred.

choices.text: Vasquez-Thorne argues that two different ages for the same ash layer can both be correct, because the two methods date different events rather than the same one.

steps: Two methods, two ages, same ash.
She says the gap is not an error.
Each method dates a different event, so both can be right.
explanation.why: Her point is that the methods date different events, so the discrepancy is not a contradiction.
explanation.pattern: Main idea: capture the author's reinterpretation of an apparent conflict.

items.passage: Ragna had promised herself she would clear her late uncle's boat shed in a single weekend. By Saturday noon she had filled four bags with rotted rope and rusted tins and felt pleased with herself. Then she found his logbooks, twenty-one of them, each entry a line or two about wind and catch, written in a hand so neat it seemed a stranger's. She sat on an upturned crate and read until the light failed, then carried the logbooks to the car one at a time, as though they might wake. The four bags stayed where they were, by the door.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Ragna, who expected to clear her uncle's shed briskly and without sentiment, is slowed and moved by finding his logbooks.
Ragna regrets promising to clear her uncle's shed so quickly and decides to keep everything that he left behind in it.
choices.slip: Overreach: she carries off logbooks, not everything.

choices.text: Ragna is frustrated that her uncle's logbooks are so brief and impersonal that they reveal nothing about him.
choices.slip: She reads until dark and treats them tenderly.

choices.text: Ragna finds the work of clearing the shed unexpectedly satisfying until the loss of daylight forces her to stop.
choices.slip: She stops because of the logbooks, and the pleasure was early, not the point.

steps: She planned a brisk clearing and began well.
The logbooks stop her; she reads and carries them gently.
The bags are left, so the plan has been abandoned.
explanation.why: Her actions, not stated feelings, show the shift from brisk clearing to quiet attachment.
explanation.pattern: Fiction main idea: read the actions for the change in the character.

items.passage: Urban planner Gwendolen Farquhar-Roth studied what happened after the city of Halstow built an express ferry that cut the crossing time from 40 minutes to 25. Rather than shortening commutes, the ferry's main effect in the long run was to lengthen them: within three years, residents of the far shore, drawn by the faster crossing, had moved to homes about 8 miles farther out, so that average door-to-door commutes returned to roughly their earlier length of 62 minutes. Farquhar-Roth reads this as evidence that commuters tend to spend a roughly constant amount of time traveling, using any gain in speed to live farther from their jobs.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The express ferry failed because too few residents of the far shore chose to ride it after its crossing time was cut to 25 minutes.
choices.slip: Contradicts the account: residents responded to it.
