choices.text: Farquhar-Roth found that a faster ferry did not shorten commutes in the long run, because residents used the saved time to settle farther from their jobs.
Farquhar-Roth concludes that commuters in Halstow prefer living farther out and would have moved even if the ferry had never been built.
choices.slip: Overreach: the move was tied to the faster crossing.

choices.text: Faster crossings reduced average commutes only temporarily, which Farquhar-Roth blames on overcrowding aboard the new ferry.
choices.slip: Invents overcrowding as the cause.

steps: Ferry cut crossing from 40 to 25 minutes.
Residents moved 8 miles farther out; commutes returned to about 62 minutes.
She reads this as constant travel time.
explanation.why: The time saved was spent on distance, so commutes were no shorter.
explanation.pattern: Main idea: the surprising result and the author's explanation.

items.passage: For years, ornithologist Benedikt Lindroth-Ames believed that the red patch on male Larkspur finches signaled good health to females, since males with brighter patches carried fewer blood parasites. His team then painted the patches of 60 males, making dull birds look bright, and dulled the patches of 60 bright ones. Females chose the males at the same rates as before, regardless of the paint. Lindroth-Ames now thinks that females attend mainly to the males' songs, and that patch brightness tracks parasite load only because both depend on the same diet. He published the revised view in a journal of field ornithology.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Lindroth-Ames's experiment confirmed that females prefer males with brighter patches and that bright patches signal low parasite loads.
choices.slip: The experiment found no preference for the paint.

choices.text: Parasite load, not diet, determines the brightness of the patches, and females have learned to read it by listening to the males' songs.
choices.slip: Reverses diet and parasite load and invents the reading by song.

choices.text: An experiment altering patch color led Lindroth-Ames to doubt that females choose by the patch, and to propose that song matters more and the patch merely reflects condition.
Painting the patches harmed the males' health, which is why females showed no preference for the painted birds.
choices.slip: Invents harm; females simply ignored the paint.

steps: Old view: bright patch signals health to females.
Painted males were chosen as before.
New view: song matters; patch tracks diet and so parasites.
explanation.why: The experiment undercut the patch as a signal and shifted his view to song and a shared diet.
explanation.pattern: Main idea: a researcher's revision after a test.

items.passage: In the 1930s, growers in the Orrin valley began sowing tall rye grass between rows of apple trees to hold soil on steep slopes, and the practice spread because it worked. Agronomist Perpetua Salgado-Whitlock, reviewing three decades of growers' records, found that orchards with rye also had about 30 percent fewer codling moth larvae, a major apple pest, because the grass sheltered ground beetles that feed on them. Most growers had credited the rye only with preventing erosion, and many mowed it short each summer, which reduced beetle numbers. Salgado-Whitlock says the practice persisted because erosion control alone justified it, but that growers who recognize the pest benefit may manage the grass differently.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Growers who mow rye grass short each summer are making a mistake, because the practice increases erosion on the steep slopes of the Orrin valley.
choices.slip: Erosion from mowing is never claimed; the cost of mowing is to beetles.

choices.text: Ground beetles, not rye grass, are the main reason apple orchards in the Orrin valley have fewer codling moth larvae than they once did.
choices.slip: Overreach: the beetles depend on the grass, and no 'main reason' contrast is drawn.

choices.text: Rye grass was adopted in the Orrin valley mainly to control pests, although growers later found that it also holds soil on steep slopes.
choices.slip: Reverses the order of purposes.

choices.text: A grass sown to prevent erosion in orchards also appears to reduce a pest, a benefit growers overlooked and one that could change how they manage it.

steps: Rye was sown for erosion control.
Records show it also cuts a pest by sheltering beetles.
Growers missed this, and some mowing hurts it.
explanation.why: It states the original purpose, the overlooked benefit, and the possible change in management.
explanation.pattern: The main idea covers the whole arc; wrong choices reverse the order or invent a cost or a dispute.

items.passage: Astronomer Leopold Achterberg-Mensah studied a faint star whose light dimmed unpredictably nine times over four years, by between 2 and 14 percent each time. Two explanations were proposed: that a cloud of dust was passing in front of the star, and that planets in orbit were crossing it. Achterberg-Mensah notes that the dips differed widely in depth and length, which fits a shifting dust cloud far better than a planet, since a planet crossing the star dims it by the same amount on each pass. Two of the nine dips, however, were nearly identical in depth and were separated by exactly 41 days, a pattern a dust cloud would have little reason to produce. He suggests that the two explanations may not exclude each other.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Planets crossing a star can be ruled out as a cause of its dimming, because the nine dips varied so widely in depth and in length.
choices.slip: Overreach; two dips do suggest a planet.

choices.text: Most of a star's dimming events fit a passing dust cloud better than a planet, but two matching dips leave open that both explanations apply.
A pair of dips that repeated at an interval of 41 days shows that a planet, not a dust cloud, caused all nine of the dimming events.
choices.slip: Overreach in the other direction; seven dips do not fit a planet.

choices.text: Astronomers disagree about whether dust or planets explain dimming stars, and Achterberg-Mensah has not tried to decide between the two.
choices.slip: Not in the text; he does weigh the evidence.

steps: Seven irregular dips favor dust.
Two matching dips 41 days apart point to a planet.
He proposes that both may be at work.
explanation.why: It gives the main finding, the exception, and his tentative conclusion.
explanation.pattern: Main-idea answers keep the finding and its qualification; overreach in either direction is wrong.

items.passage: When I was a child, I took my grandmother Odile's cooking as proof that she did not care for us. She boiled vegetables until they collapsed, reused the same strip of foil for weeks, and served the previous night's soup at breakfast without comment. I remember asking my mother why Grandmother never made anything nice, and my mother changing the subject. It was only after Odile's death, when I found her ration books from the war years in a biscuit tin, each page annotated in tiny, careful handwriting, that I began to see that her habits were not indifference. They were the discipline of someone who had once watched her own children go hungry, and who could not stop counting.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The narrator's mother avoided discussing Odile's cooking because she was embarrassed by her mother's habits and by the household's lack of money.
choices.slip: Her mother's motive is never stated.

choices.text: The narrator's resentment of her grandmother's cooking faded after she discovered ration books proving that Odile had been a skilled cook during the war.
choices.slip: Skill as a cook is not claimed; the ration books show careful counting.

choices.text: Looking back, the narrator comes to see that habits she once read as carelessness were shaped by her grandmother's memory of hardship.
Odile's refusal to waste food was a habit the narrator inherited and now practices in her own kitchen, despite the objections of her family.
choices.slip: Nothing about the narrator's own habits or her family's objections.

steps: The narrator once read Odile's habits as not caring.
The ration books changed that reading.
The habits come from wartime hunger.
explanation.why: The passage turns on a changed understanding: indifference becomes the discipline of hardship.
explanation.pattern: In narrative main-idea items, find the shift in understanding and reject choices that add motives or events.

items.passage: When the city of Veldrin introduced a daily fee for private cars entering its old quarter, officials reported that traffic there fell by 14 percent in the first year. A closer analysis by transport economist Fiona Rasmussen-Adeyinka found that the decline was not spread evenly: trips made by commuters who drove to work every day fell by only 3 percent, while trips by drivers whose purpose was shopping or sightseeing fell by 31 percent. She attributes the difference to the fact that regular commuters have few alternatives and typically absorb the fee, whereas occasional visitors can easily shift to trams, to other districts, or to staying home. She cautions that the overall 14 percent figure therefore conceals what the fee actually changed.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A fee that cut traffic overall did so mainly by discouraging occasional trips, and the overall figure hides how little it changed commuters' driving.
Veldrin's fee failed to change driver behavior, since commuters who drive to work every day cut their trips by only 3 percent after it began.
choices.slip: Overgeneralizes from one group; visitors cut trips by 31 percent.

choices.text: Officials in Veldrin overstated the fee's effect on traffic by counting trams and other alternatives in the first year's totals for the old quarter.
choices.slip: Not in the text; no miscounting is claimed.

choices.text: Occasional visitors to Veldrin's old quarter respond more to price than commuters do because they have higher incomes and make shorter trips overall.
choices.slip: Invents causes; the text says alternatives, not income or trip length.

steps: Overall traffic fell 14 percent.
The fall was 3 percent for commuters and 31 percent for occasional visitors.
The average hides the uneven effect.
explanation.why: It reports the overall result and the author's caution about the uneven breakdown.
explanation.pattern: Averages can hide opposite or uneven group effects; the main idea includes the breakdown.

items.passage: Critics have long described the late poems of Ottoline Fairbrother-Nkemelu as plainer than her early work, with short words, regular lines, and almost no figurative language. Literary scholar Cormac Ellsworth-Diallo argues that this reading mistakes the surface for the whole. The late poems, he notes, rely on syntax that suspends a sentence across several lines, so that a reader cannot tell what a clause modifies until a final line that arrives only after several readings. The simplicity of the vocabulary, he claims, is a deliberate technique: by removing difficult words, the poet moves the difficulty into the structure of the sentences, where it is harder to notice and harder to resolve.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Ellsworth-Diallo shows that critics were right to call the late poems plainer than the early ones, but wrong about which words made them plainer.
choices.slip: He disputes that they are plainer overall.

choices.text: Ellsworth-Diallo argues that the plain wording of the poet's late work is deliberate and shifts the poems' difficulty from vocabulary to sentence structure.
The late poems of Fairbrother-Nkemelu are harder to read than her early poems because they use more figurative language and more uncommon words.
choices.slip: Contradicts the text, which says the late poems use almost no figurative language.

choices.text: Readers who return to the late poems several times eventually find that their syntax is as regular and straightforward as their vocabulary.
choices.slip: Reverses his claim: the syntax stays hard to resolve.

steps: Critics call the late poems plain.
Ellsworth-Diallo says plain words are deliberate.
The difficulty moves into sentence structure.
explanation.why: It captures his thesis about where the difficulty lies.
explanation.pattern: When a scholar rejects the usual reading, the main idea states the new reading and what it replaces.

items.passage: Conservators at the Halloran Gallery noticed that the blue robes in a set of oil panels painted in 1880 had faded to gray in some areas but not others. The gallery's owners assumed that sunlight was responsible, since the faded areas faced the windows. Chemist Zoltan Pemberton-Achieng tested this by comparing the panels with two identical test boards painted with the same blue pigment: one stored for ten years in a dark, damp cellar and one hung in a dry, sunlit room. The board from the cellar had faded much more. Pemberton-Achieng concluded that moisture, which had slowly altered the pigment, was the main cause, and that the faded patches in the gallery matched places where damp had gathered behind the panels rather than places that received the most light.
items.question: According to the text, what did the comparison of the two test boards show?

choices.text: Sunlight alters the blue pigment more quickly than moisture does, but only in oil paintings that are kept in sunlit rooms.
choices.slip: Reverses the finding.

choices.text: The faded patches on the gallery panels were the areas that had received the most direct light from the gallery's windows.
choices.slip: The text says they matched damp, not light.

choices.text: Panels stored in damp conditions fade at about the same rate as panels hung in sunlit rooms when the same pigment is used.
choices.slip: The cellar board faded much more, not equally.

choices.text: The board kept in the dark, damp cellar faded more than the board hung in the dry, sunlit room, pointing to moisture rather than light.

steps: Two identical boards: one dark and damp, one dry and sunlit.
The damp board faded much more.
So moisture, not light, is the main cause.
explanation.why: The cellar board faded more, which points to moisture.
explanation.pattern: Read comparison results exactly; a tempting assumption (sunlight) is what the test overturns.

items.passage: Rooftop beekeeping is often promoted as a way to help struggling pollinators, but ecologist Valeria Pruitt-Nnamdi doubted that honeybees help wild bees. She surveyed wild bee species in 24 neighborhoods of a large city and compared the counts with the number of managed hives per square kilometer. In neighborhoods with one to four hives per square kilometer, wild bee diversity was about 15 percent higher than in neighborhoods with no hives, which she attributes to the flowering plants hive owners add to roofs and gardens. In neighborhoods with more than eight hives per square kilometer, however, diversity fell below that of neighborhoods with none, and she suspects that honeybees were taking most of the available nectar. She cautions that the survey was observational.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Rooftop beekeeping reduces wild bee diversity in cities, because honeybees at high densities consume the nectar that wild bees need in order to survive and reproduce in the city's neighborhoods.
choices.slip: Ignores the benefit at low density and states the cause as proven.

choices.text: Wild bee diversity was highest in the neighborhoods with the most hives, which suggests that managed honeybees help wild pollinators wherever they are kept in the city's neighborhoods.
choices.slip: Reverses the high-density result.

choices.text: Ecologists remain divided over whether rooftop beekeeping helps pollinators, because the neighborhoods in the survey differed too much in their plantings to be fairly compared with one another.
choices.slip: Invents a dispute and a reason not in the text.

choices.text: A survey links rooftop hives to greater wild bee diversity only at low densities, with diversity falling at high densities, though its design cannot prove cause.

steps: Low density: diversity higher. High density: diversity lower.
The author adds that the survey is observational, so causes are suspected, not shown.
The main idea must hold the benefit, the threshold, and the caution.
explanation.why: The text reports a pattern that reverses with density and flags it as unproven.
explanation.pattern: A main idea that includes a reversal or a caveat must state both sides of it.

items.passage: When the Calloway Footbridge opened in 2006, it swayed so sharply on its first day that engineers closed it within hours. The first explanation was wind, since the bridge spans an open estuary, but wind-tunnel tests on a scale model produced only small movements. Engineer Bettina Okonkwo-Hartl then recorded the bridge with accelerometers while 200 volunteers crossed it, and found that as the deck began to move, walkers unconsciously widened their stance and fell into step with the motion, pushing the deck further. She notes, however, that on windless days the same crowd produced far milder swaying, which suggests that a gust may have been needed to start the motion that the walkers then amplified.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Wind-tunnel tests showed that wind alone caused the footbridge's sway, which engineers then confirmed by recording crowds as they crossed the bridge during windy days that year.
choices.slip: Reverses the finding of the tests.

choices.text: Walkers falling into step amplified the bridge's sway more than wind alone could have, though a gust may have been needed to start the motion.
Walkers falling into step were the sole cause of the footbridge's sway, since the bridge moved little in wind-tunnel tests and on windless days.
choices.slip: Overstates: windless swaying was milder, not absent.

choices.text: Engineers were unable to determine what caused the footbridge to sway, since wind and pedestrians each produced only small movements when tested separately in the trials.
choices.slip: Contradicts the finding that walkers pushed the deck further.

steps: Wind alone fails the model test.
Crowd behavior amplifies the sway, and the windless days show milder motion.
So the crowd is the main cause, with wind a likely starter.
explanation.why: The text revises the cause to pedestrians while keeping a role for wind.
explanation.pattern: When a text revises an explanation but keeps a qualification, the main idea must include the qualification.

items.passage: In a 10-week trial, nutrition scientist Haldis Ferreira-Okoye assigned 36 healthy adults to one of two diets: one rich in fermented foods such as yogurt, kimchi, and kefir, or one rich in fiber from beans, whole grains, and vegetables. Adults in the fermented-food group showed a clear increase in the diversity of their gut microbes and lower levels of several inflammation markers in their blood. Those in the fiber group showed smaller changes in both measures. Ferreira-Okoye cautions, however, that the trial was short and small, that its participants were all healthy, and that it did not follow them after it ended, so whether the benefits last or would appear in people with existing conditions remains unknown.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A small trial found that fermented foods improved gut microbes and lowered inflammation more than fiber, but lasting effects and effects in unwell people are unknown.
Fiber-rich diets are inferior to fermented-food diets for health, since adults eating fiber saw smaller changes in both gut microbes and inflammation markers over the ten weeks of the trial.
choices.slip: Overstates a modest comparison as a verdict.

choices.text: Fermented foods permanently lower inflammation in healthy adults, as shown by a trial that measured gut microbes and blood markers in 36 volunteers over ten weeks.
choices.slip: Contradicts the caution about duration.

choices.text: Gut microbial diversity and inflammation are unrelated in healthy adults, since the two diets changed each measure by different amounts in the trial's participants over the ten weeks.
choices.slip: Draws a conclusion the text never states.

steps: Result: the fermented group improved more on both measures.
Qualification: small, short, healthy participants, no follow-up.
The main idea combines the result with that limit.
explanation.why: The text reports a favorable finding and then limits how far it can be trusted.
explanation.pattern: Do not stop at the finding; the author's caution is part of the main idea.

items.passage: Archaeologists studying the Teshuan cave long assumed that its red animal paintings were no more than 15,000 years old, since that was the age of similar art elsewhere in the region. Geochemist Aurelia Dunsmuir-Achebe dated thin mineral crusts that had formed over the pigment, using uranium-thorium decay, and obtained ages of 27,000 and 26,400 years for two crusts. Because the crusts grew after the paint was applied, she says, the paintings must be at least that old. She adds that the method cannot say how much older the paintings are, since there is no way to know how long the paint lay exposed before a crust began to form.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The Teshuan paintings are 27,000 years old, a date that overturns earlier estimates by showing that the paint was applied only shortly before the crusts began to form there.
choices.slip: Treats a minimum age as an exact age.

choices.text: Uranium-thorium dating of mineral crusts is too unreliable to give a firm age for cave paintings, so the age of the Teshuan paintings remains as it was first assumed to be.
choices.slip: Misreads the caveat as a rejection of the method.

choices.text: Mineral crusts over the Teshuan paintings date to about 27,000 years so the paintings are at least that old, though the method cannot show their real age.
The Teshuan paintings are older than any other cave art in the region, since the crusts that formed over the pigment are at least 27,000 years old, a record for the region.
choices.slip: Adds a comparison the text does not make.

steps: Crusts date to about 27,000 years and formed after the paint.
So the paint is at least that old; it could be older.
The main idea states the age as a minimum.
explanation.why: The crusts give a floor for the paintings' age, not a precise date.
explanation.pattern: Distinguish a minimum from an exact value when a method only bounds the answer.

items.passage: Students often study by cramming a topic into one long session, but cognitive psychologist Hesper Brannigan-Sule found that this habit trades long-term learning for short-term performance. In her experiment, 80 students learned 60 vocabulary words in a language new to them, either in a single 90-minute session or in three 30-minute sessions spread over a week. On a test an hour after the final session, the crammers scored slightly higher, averaging 51 words correct against 48. When tested a month later, however, the spaced group averaged 39 words and the crammers only 22. Brannigan-Sule suggests that students judge study methods by how fluent they feel right away, which makes cramming seem more effective than it is.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Cramming is the more effective way to learn new vocabulary, since the crammers scored higher than the spaced group on the test given an hour after the final session.
choices.slip: Takes only the short-term result.

choices.text: Spacing study sessions over time produces much better long-term retention than cramming does, even though cramming can give slightly better scores on a test taken right afterward.
Students should divide their study time into three short sessions each week, because the spaced group outperformed the crammers on tests of vocabulary learned in a new language.
choices.slip: Turns a finding into advice and ignores the short-term advantage.

choices.text: Students judge study methods accurately because they feel most fluent after the method that works best, as shown by the results of Brannigan-Sule's experiment.
choices.slip: Reverses the claim about fluency being misleading.

steps: One hour later: crammers 51, spaced 48.
One month later: spaced 39, crammers 22.
The main idea holds both results with the long-term one favored.
explanation.why: The text pairs a small early edge for cramming with a large later edge for spacing.
explanation.pattern: A main idea can require keeping an initial result alongside the reversal that matters more.

items.passage: In the 1880s the Garrick Railway began running refrigerated cars that carried slaughtered beef from the grasslands of the interior to cities in the east. Economic historian Joaquina Oyelowo-Brandt found that retail beef prices in eastern cities fell by roughly a quarter within a decade, and that households in the lowest income group, which had rarely bought fresh beef before, doubled their purchases. Yet the same period saw the number of independent butchers who slaughtered local cattle in those cities fall by nearly half, as large interior packers undersold them. Oyelowo-Brandt concludes that although the railway brought real gains to eastern consumers, much of the lower price was achieved by the loss of an established local trade.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Refrigerated rail cars mainly benefited interior packers, who undersold local butchers and then raised beef prices for eastern households once local competition had closed down for good.
choices.slip: The text reports prices falling, not rising afterward.

choices.text: Eastern consumers gained from refrigerated rail cars, which cut beef prices by about a quarter and doubled beef purchases among every income group in the eastern cities.
choices.slip: Omits the cost and extends the doubling beyond the lowest group.

choices.text: Refrigerated rail cars lowered beef prices and widened access for eastern consumers, but cheaper shipped meat also destroyed much of the local butchers' trade.
Local butchers in eastern cities closed in large numbers in the 1880s because lower-income households switched from fresh beef to cheaper preserved meats instead.
choices.slip: Gives a cause the text never names.

steps: Gain: prices fell about a quarter and poor households bought more.
Cost: nearly half of local butchers disappeared.
The historian ties the two together; the main idea must too.
explanation.why: The text presents a real consumer benefit and the local trade that paid for it.
explanation.pattern: When the author pairs a benefit with a cost, the main idea needs both.

items.passage: For decades, historians of navigation have debated whether medieval Norse sailors crossed the North Atlantic with a sun compass, a bearing dial that reads the sun's shadow, or relied on landmarks and bird flight alone. In 1948, a fragment of a carved wooden disc was recovered from a Greenland monastery site. Researcher Ingeborg Halvorsen-Tse, reconstructing the disc, found that its notches line up with the sun's noon shadow at the site's latitude only for the months May through August, which was the sailing season. She concludes that the disc supports the sun-compass view, while admitting that one fragment cannot show how widely sailors used such an instrument.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Norse sailors crossed the North Atlantic using sun compasses, as proved by a carved disc recovered from a Greenland monastery site in 1948.
choices.slip: Overstates: the text calls the disc support, not proof.

choices.text: A reconstructed disc whose notches match the sailing-season noon shadow lends some support to the sun-compass theory of Norse navigation, though it cannot show how common the instrument was.
Historians have debated Norse navigation for decades because the only surviving evidence, a single wooden disc, is too damaged to interpret.
choices.slip: The disc could be reconstructed and interpreted.

choices.text: A carved disc found in Greenland shows that Norse sailors who relied on landmarks and bird flight also owned instruments that worked only from May through August of each year.
choices.slip: Mixes the two rival theories into one claim the text does not make.

steps: Two theories: sun compass or landmarks and birds.
The disc fits the sun-compass theory for the sailing months.
One fragment cannot show how common it was.
explanation.why: It reports the disc as support for one theory and keeps the caveat about one fragment.
explanation.pattern: A main idea includes the conclusion and its stated limit.

items.passage: Translators of the 1923 epic The Salt Orchard have long disagreed about its closing line, whose last word in the original language can mean either harvest or rest. The first English translator, Ardith Cresswell-Moy, chose rest, which gives the poem a quiet ending. Gustav Eckersley later chose harvest, after finding in the poet's notebooks that she had crossed out an earlier ending about sleep. Translator Lidia Rosvall now argues that neither choice is right, because the poet may have intended the ambiguity itself, and she renders the word as a phrase that carries both senses, even though the English line becomes twice as long as the original.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Eckersley's choice of harvest is better supported than Cresswell-Moy's choice of rest, because it rests on evidence from the poet's own notebooks.
choices.slip: Overreaches: the text reports the notebook evidence but does not call his choice better.

choices.text: The poet crossed out an early ending about sleep because she wished the poem to end quietly instead of on a note of harvest, a wish that Eckersley's later translation set aside.
choices.slip: Reverses the order and invents a motive.

choices.text: Rosvall's phrase is the first English rendering to remain faithful to the original, because earlier translators ignored the ambiguity of the final word.
choices.slip: The text never says earlier translators ignored the ambiguity.

choices.text: Because the poem's last word can mean either harvest or rest, translators have chosen differently, and one now proposes keeping both meanings at the cost of a longer line.

steps: The last word is ambiguous.
Two translators picked one sense each.
A third keeps both, with a longer line.
explanation.why: It covers the ambiguity, the differing choices, and the newest proposal with its cost.
explanation.pattern: A main idea covers the whole progression, not a single detail.

items.passage: Volcanologist Torun Eklund-Maddox tested the potassium-argon dating method on 14 lava samples of known age, erupted on a Pacific island between 1790 and 1950. The method, which assumes that no argon was present in the rock when it cooled, gave ages within the expected error for 9 of the samples. For the other 5, all from flows that cooled rapidly, it gave ages as great as 300,000 years because bubbles of argon from deep magma had been trapped in the rock. Eklund-Maddox concludes that the method is dependable for rock that lost its gas while cooling slowly, but that for rapidly cooled flows it can badly overstate age and should be checked by a second method.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A test on lava of known age showed that potassium-argon dating can badly overstate the age of rapidly cooled flows that trapped argon, so those flows need a second check.
Potassium-argon dating is unreliable and should be abandoned, because it gave ages of up to 300,000 years for lava that erupted within the past two centuries on a single island.
choices.slip: Overstates: the method worked for 9 of 14 samples.

choices.text: Most lava samples from Pacific islands contain trapped argon, which explains why the method gave correct dates for 9 samples and incorrect dates for 5.
choices.slip: The trapped-argon problem was tied to rapid cooling, not to most samples.

choices.text: Volcanologists tested the method on 14 samples because they believed its assumption that no argon is present at cooling was true for every kind of flow.
choices.slip: Invents a belief the text does not report.

steps: Known-age lavas let her test the method.
9 right; 5 wrong, all rapidly cooled with trapped argon.
Conclusion: fine for slow-cooled rock, check rapid-cooled flows.
explanation.why: It gives the test, the failure condition, and the recommended second check.
explanation.pattern: Keep the condition under which a method fails, not only that it fails.

items.passage: Economist Ragnhild Delacour-Fell compared two fish markets on the same coast. At Wennick Bay, sellers pay a flat fee for each crate they bring to the morning auction, whatever the crate holds. At Hollen Reach, sellers pay a fixed percentage of each crate's sale price. Over one season, the average crate sold at Wennick Bay was worth 22 percent more than the average crate at Hollen Reach, although both markets drew fish from the same boats and buyers paid similar prices per kilogram for fish of the same species. Delacour-Fell attributes the difference to the effect of the fee structure on what sellers chose to bring.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Because the percentage fee at Hollen Reach rose with price, sellers there brought mostly low-priced fish in order to avoid paying it.
choices.slip: Misreads the percentage fee: it rises with price but does not target cheap fish.

choices.text: The flat fee at Wennick Bay was lower than the percentage fee at Hollen Reach, so sellers could afford to bring larger crates of fish.
choices.slip: The text never compares the size of the two fees.

choices.text: Because the fee at Wennick Bay was the same for every crate, it took a larger share from low-value crates, so sellers had less reason to bring them.
Buyers at Wennick Bay paid higher prices per kilogram than buyers at Hollen Reach, which raised the worth of each crate sold at the morning auction throughout the whole season.
choices.slip: The text says prices per kilogram were similar.

steps: Crates were worth 22 percent more at Wennick Bay.
Boats, buyers, and prices were similar.
The fee structure, flat versus percentage, is credited.
explanation.why: A flat fee falls hardest on cheap crates, so fewer were brought, raising the average value.
explanation.pattern: Use the cause the text names, not a plausible outside one.

items.passage: When a pedestrian footbridge swayed noticeably under crowds on its opening day, engineers found that the structure was sound. The swaying had grown because walkers, without noticing, began to step in time with the sway, which then grew larger. Stiffening the bridge would have cost 9 million dollars. Instead, the engineers installed dampers costing 1.5 million, aiming not to remove all motion but to hold it below the level at which walkers begin to fall into step. In a later count of 4,000 crossings, no synchronized sway appeared, although the bridge still moves visibly in strong wind.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Footbridges that sway are structurally weak and must be stiffened, a conclusion engineers reached after the events of the opening day.
choices.slip: Contradicted: the structure was sound.

choices.text: The dampers removed the swaying entirely, at a lower cost than stiffening, since no synchronized sway appeared in the 4,000 crossings counted afterward.
choices.slip: The bridge still moves in strong wind, so not all motion was removed.

choices.text: Engineers rejected stiffening because walkers' synchronized steps showed that rigid bridges are more likely to sway, a pattern confirmed in 4,000 later crossings.
choices.slip: Invents a link between rigidity and swaying.

choices.text: After a footbridge swayed because walkers fell into step, engineers chose a cheaper fix that kept motion below the level that triggers synchronization instead of making the bridge rigid.

steps: Sway grew because walkers synchronized.
Stiffening: 9 million; dampers: 1.5 million.
Goal changed from no motion to motion below the trigger.
explanation.why: It states the cause, the cheaper approach, and the redefined goal.
explanation.pattern: Notice when a fix changes the goal rather than meeting the original one.

items.passage: Planting street trees lowers summer air temperature by shading pavement, but trees also release water vapor, which raises humidity and can make hot weather feel worse. Climatologist Ruairi Kessinger-Bell measured both effects in 12 neighborhoods. Shading cooled afternoon air by 1.8 degrees Celsius on average, but the added humidity canceled about 1.2 degrees of that cooling in the perceived heat index, leaving a net reduction of about 0.6 degrees. She notes that in dry regions, where added humidity is easily absorbed, the humidity penalty is much smaller, so the net benefit there is larger.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Street trees cool the air by shading pavement, but the added humidity cancels much of the benefit in perceived heat, leaving a smaller net improvement.
Street trees raise humidity so much that neighborhoods with trees feel hotter than neighborhoods without them, despite the cooling effect of shade on the pavement beneath them.
choices.slip: The net effect is still a reduction of 0.6 degrees.

choices.text: Trees cooled the measured neighborhoods by 1.8 degrees Celsius, which shows that planting them is the most effective way to reduce urban heat.
choices.slip: Ignores the humidity penalty and compares with no other method.

choices.text: Climatologists measured 12 neighborhoods because the effect of added humidity on perceived heat is greatest in dry regions where trees are scarce.
choices.slip: Twists the dry-region point: the penalty is smaller there.

steps: Shade cools by 1.8; humidity cancels 1.2.
Net is 0.6.
Dry regions fare better.
explanation.why: It states both opposing effects and the smaller net result.
explanation.pattern: When two effects oppose, the main idea is the net.

items.passage: A letter describing the 1871 collapse of Hollin Bridge was long credited to the surveyor Edith Marwood because its handwriting resembles hers. Archivist Sibyl Ravenscroft-Ito noted that the same handwriting also resembles that of Marwood's assistant, Cyril Pendleton, whom Marwood had trained to write in her style. The letter also describes an inspection of the bridge's piers, and the firm's records show that only Pendleton attended that inspection. Ravenscroft-Ito concludes that Pendleton more likely wrote the letter, but she cautions that only one page of his writing survives for comparison.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Pendleton's handwriting is identical to Marwood's because she trained him, which proves that the author of the Hollin Bridge letter can never be known.
choices.slip: Overstates: the text says resemblance, and the author may be inferred.

choices.text: The letter's description of the inspection is unreliable, because its author is now believed not to have attended the inspection of the piers.
choices.slip: Reverses it: the author is believed to have attended.

choices.text: Evidence about who attended an inspection suggests a letter long credited to a surveyor was more probably written by her assistant, though a single surviving writing sample leaves some doubt.
The firm's records show that Marwood was absent from the 1871 collapse, which explains why the letter in question is signed only with an initial and why no copy was kept.
choices.slip: Invents details about her absence and the signature.

steps: Handwriting fits both, since she trained him.
Only he attended the inspection described.
One page of his writing leaves doubt.
explanation.why: It combines the new evidence, the revised attribution, and the stated limit.
explanation.pattern: When attribution changes, keep both the reason and the caveat.

items.passage: In 2012, conservation managers at Cobhurst Marsh began removing an invasive reed they believed was crowding out native sedges. By 2018 the reed had been cleared from 70 percent of the marsh, and sedge cover had risen modestly. During the same years, however, counts of a rare marsh wren fell by nearly half. Ecologist Dalia Rutherglen-Nair found that the wrens nested almost entirely in the reed stands, whose tall stems sheltered nests from wind, and that few wrens nested in the shorter sedges. She does not call the removal a mistake, noting that restoring sedge was the managers' goal and had begun to succeed, but she proposes that the remaining 30 percent of the reed be left in place until wrens begin nesting in the sedge.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Removing an invasive reed to restore sedges seems to have harmed a rare bird that nested in it, so an ecologist suggests keeping part.
Removing the invasive reed from Cobhurst Marsh was a mistake, because it caused the marsh wren's decline and did very little for native sedges.
choices.slip: Overstates: she does not call it a mistake and sedge cover rose.

choices.text: Marsh wrens declined at Cobhurst Marsh because sedges grew too densely after the reed was removed, leaving no room for nests in the marsh.
choices.slip: Invents a cause; the text ties the decline to the loss of reed cover.

choices.text: Ecologist Rutherglen-Nair found that the managers' belief that the invasive reed crowded out native sedges was wrong, since sedge cover rose only modestly after removal.
choices.slip: Misreads the modest rise as evidence against the managers' belief.

steps: Reed removal modestly helped sedge; wrens fell by nearly half.
Wrens nested in the reed, so removal removed their nesting cover.
She suggests leaving 30 percent, without calling the removal a mistake.
explanation.why: It captures the unintended harm and the measured proposal, without overstating.
explanation.pattern: Main idea: keep the author's qualifications and do not upgrade a suggestion to a verdict.

items.passage: In 1958, chemist Ottoline Sjoberg-Achebe was trying to develop a stronger glue for aircraft panels. One batch failed to harden, remaining a soft, tacky film that peeled cleanly from every surface she tested, including steel. She nearly discarded it, but a colleague used a scrap to hold a paper note to a laboratory wall, where it stayed for weeks and came off without damage. Sjoberg-Achebe then spent two years refining the formula, and by 1961 the adhesive was being tested for reusable labels. She said later that she never did produce the aircraft glue she had set out to make, though the project that she had been assigned to ended without any complaint from her employer.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Sjoberg-Achebe eventually succeeded in making a stronger aircraft glue after testing a failed batch on several surfaces, including steel.
choices.slip: She never made the aircraft glue.

choices.text: Credit for the adhesive belongs to Sjoberg-Achebe's colleague, who recognized its use, and whose two years of work completed it.
choices.slip: The colleague suggested a use; she spent the two years refining it.

choices.text: Many useful products begin as failures, since batches that fail at their intended purpose are often discarded before other properties are tested.
choices.slip: A general claim about discarded failures that the text does not make.

choices.text: A batch that failed as a strong glue became a different product once its weak, removable hold was seen as useful.

steps: She aimed at a stronger glue and got a weak, tacky film.
A colleague's use of it showed a removable hold; she refined it for labels.
She never made the aircraft glue.
explanation.why: The failure became useful for a different purpose.
explanation.pattern: Distinguish what the text reports from general lessons or credit assigned beyond it.

items.passage: Historian Ludmila Hollenbeck-Ashdown examined the 1,140 surviving apprenticeship contracts from the port of Kellmoor between 1700 and 1790 and found that 92 percent were for boys. She cautions against concluding that few girls learned trades. The contracts survive because they were filed with the town court, and filing was required only when the apprentice's family paid a fee to the master. Wills and account books show that such fees were seldom paid for girls, whose training was usually arranged informally with relatives and neighbors. She estimates that for every filed contract for a girl there were at least several unfiled arrangements, and she urges that the filed contracts not be treated as a sample of all training in the port.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Girls in Kellmoor between 1700 and 1790 were apprenticed in greater numbers than boys, though almost always through informal arrangements with relatives.
choices.slip: Overreaches: she says girls were undercounted, not that they outnumbered boys.

choices.text: A historian argues that Kellmoor's surviving contracts undercount girls' training, because filing was required only for fee-paying arrangements, which were seldom made for girls.
Historians who study apprenticeship contracts reach unreliable conclusions because the surviving contracts are too few to represent any single trade.
choices.slip: 1,140 contracts is not described as too few; the problem is who is missing.

choices.text: The Kellmoor town court required every apprenticeship to be filed, though families often neglected to file the arrangements that were made for girls.
choices.slip: Filing was required only when a fee was paid.

steps: 92 percent of 1,140 contracts were for boys.
Filing applied only to fee-paying arrangements, seldom made for girls.
So the record undercounts girls' training.
explanation.why: It reports her caution and its reason.
explanation.pattern: Check why the record has the shape it has before reading its numbers literally.

items.passage: Two research teams dated the same cave painting. Team Kowal measured radiocarbon in the charcoal pigment and obtained an age of 14,200 years, plus or minus 300. Team Ibarra dated the thin calcite crust that had formed over the painting using uranium-thorium decay and obtained 14,900 years, plus or minus 150. The ranges do not quite overlap. However, a crust can form only after a painting exists, so its age is a minimum for the painting, whereas charcoal samples are easily contaminated by younger carbon, which makes radiocarbon ages appear too young. The teams now agree that the two results can be reconciled, and that further sampling of both the pigment and the crust would be worthwhile.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The radiocarbon date should be rejected, because charcoal pigment from a cave painting cannot be dated reliably at all by any method.
choices.slip: Overstates: contamination makes dates too young, not unusable.

choices.text: The uranium-thorium date shows the painting is exactly 14,900 years old, since the crust formed immediately after the painting was made and sealed it.
choices.slip: The crust gives a minimum age, not an exact one.

choices.text: The two dates seem to conflict, but the limits of each method let both hold, with the painting at least as old as the crust.
The two teams' results agree within their margins of error, so the painting's age is settled at about 14,500 years.
choices.slip: The ranges do not overlap, and the text does not settle on 14,500.

steps: The two ranges do not overlap.
Crust age is a minimum; charcoal can read too young.
So both can be right if the painting is at least as old as the crust.
explanation.why: It explains the apparent conflict by the direction of each method's bias.
explanation.pattern: A main idea can be a reconciliation, not a choice between two claims.

items.passage: When Ilsabet's brother returned from the northern camps after three years, she set a second plate at the table, as she had every evening of his absence, and he looked at it without comment. They ate. He asked about the harvest, and she said the barley had come in thin; she asked about the roads, and he said they were bad above the river. Afterward he washed both plates himself, drying each slowly, and stood a moment with the second one in his hands before he set it on the shelf, where it lay on top of the others rather than beneath them. She noticed that, said nothing, and turned down the lamp.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: The brother is disappointed by the poor harvest and bad roads, though he declines to say so.
choices.slip: The remarks about harvest and roads are routine talk, not complaint.

choices.text: Ilsabet resents her brother's long absence and shows it by setting a second plate each evening.
choices.slip: She set the plate for him; the text shows no resentment.

choices.text: The siblings quarrel over how the household was run while he was away, and he shows displeasure by washing the plates himself.
choices.slip: No quarrel appears; washing is quiet care.

choices.text: Though neither speaks of it, the siblings' small actions at their reunion convey how much they feel for each other.

steps: She kept a place for him for three years; he notices it silently.
Their talk is about the harvest and roads, while the plate holds the emotion.
Small gestures carry the feeling that neither names.
explanation.why: The restrained talk and the plate gestures together convey unspoken feeling.
explanation.pattern: In fiction, the main idea may be in what actions suggest, not in what is said.

items.passage: A team led by hydrologist Cormac Ilunga-Preston compared stream temperatures in two forested valleys over four summers. Streams in the Larkmoor valley, where about 40 percent of the trees along the banks had been cut for timber, averaged 3.1 degrees Celsius warmer than comparable streams in the uncut Berrow valley. The team had expected the difference to come mainly from lost shade. Yet readings taken at night, when shade is irrelevant, showed a gap of 2.6 degrees, not far below the daytime gap of 3.4. The team concluded that cutting had mainly reduced the flow of cold groundwater into the streams, since the cut slopes now shed rain as surface runoff.
items.question: According to the text, what did the nighttime readings show?

choices.text: The gap between the valleys was nearly as large at night as by day, so lost shade could not be its main cause.
The streams in the cut valley cooled more quickly after dark than the streams in the uncut valley did, because of the lost trees.
choices.slip: No such comparison of cooling speed is reported.

choices.text: The temperature gap between the valleys disappeared at night, which confirmed that lost shade was the main cause of warming.
choices.slip: The gap persisted at 2.6 degrees.

choices.text: The temperature gap between the valleys was larger at night than during the day, which pointed to reduced groundwater inflow.
choices.slip: Night gap, 2.6, was smaller than the day gap, 3.4.

steps: Day gap 3.4 degrees; night gap 2.6 degrees.
Shade does not matter at night, yet the gap remained.
So lost shade could not be the main cause.
explanation.why: The night gap stayed nearly as large, which counts against the shade explanation.
explanation.pattern: Detail questions: match the exact figures and what the authors say they imply.

items.passage: Food scientists studying how a bakery's bread loses crispness separated the process into two stages: moisture first moves from the crumb into the crust, and moisture then leaves the crust into the surrounding air. A sealed bag blocks the second stage, whereas an open basket permits it, and humid air slows it. In dry conditions, crusts on 20 sealed loaves softened within 2 hours, but crusts on 20 loaves in open baskets stayed crisp for 5 hours. The scientists predicted that in a room at 85 percent humidity the advantage of open storage would largely vanish. In that room, sealed loaves softened at 2 hours and open loaves at 2.5 hours.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Sealed storage is better than open storage for keeping crust crisp, since sealed loaves softened more slowly in the humid room.
choices.slip: Sealed loaves softened in 2 hours, faster than open loaves.

choices.text: Moisture moving from the crumb into the crust is the main cause of softening, and the way a loaf is stored has no effect on it.
choices.slip: Storage method changed how quickly crusts softened.

choices.text: Open storage delays softening by letting moisture leave the crust, but humid air removes most of that benefit, as the scientists' tests bore out.
Humidity has no effect on how quickly crusts soften, since sealed loaves softened at 2 hours in both dry and humid rooms.
choices.slip: Open loaves softened much sooner in humid air; sealed loaves are shielded from humidity.

steps: Open baskets let moisture leave the crust; sealed bags do not.
Humidity slows that escape, so open loaves lose their advantage.
Tests: open loaves, 5 hours dry and 2.5 hours humid.
explanation.why: It reports the benefit of open storage and its loss in humid air.
explanation.pattern: Main idea needs both the effect and the condition that limits it.

items.passage: Marine biologist Cleo Haverkamp-Ndiaye tested whether tide-pool snails change their shells in response to the scent of crabs, their main predator. She raised 60 juvenile snails and 60 adult snails in tanks, half of each group in water carrying crab scent and half in plain seawater. After eight weeks, juveniles in scented water had shells about 22 percent thicker than juveniles in plain water, but they had grown about 30 percent less in length. Adults in scented and plain water did not differ in shell thickness or in length. Haverkamp-Ndiaye notes that adult shells are already thick enough to resist most crab attacks.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Crab scent caused snails of all ages to grow thicker shells, though the extra thickness slowed their growth in length over the eight weeks.
choices.slip: Adults showed no change in shell thickness.

choices.text: Juvenile snails exposed to crab scent grew more slowly than juveniles in plain water, which shows that the scent disrupts the growth of young snails.
choices.slip: This omits the thicker shells and treats the slower growth as damage rather than a trade-off.

choices.text: Young snails exposed to crab scent grew thicker shells at the cost of slower growth, a response adults, with already thick shells, did not show.
Adult snails are better protected from crabs than juveniles are, because adult shells are thick enough that crab scent does not change them.
choices.slip: The text doesn't compare how well adults and juveniles are protected.

steps: Juveniles: shells 22 percent thicker, growth 30 percent less.
Adults: no difference, and their shells are already thick.
The main idea: a juvenile-only response with a growth cost.
explanation.why: The trade-off between thickness and growth appeared in juveniles only.
explanation.pattern: A main idea must keep both the effect and its limit (who it applied to).

items.passage: Economic historian Perpetua Halvorsen-Oduya compared prices at the weekly market of the town of Ebbingholt before and after a railway station opened there in 1862. Using merchants' account books, she found that the price of wheat flour fell by about 11 percent within two years of the station's opening, while the price of locally woven cloth did not change. She attributes the difference to the fact that flour could now be shipped cheaply by rail from distant mills, whereas the cloth was made in the town itself and faced no new rail competition. Prices in the neighboring town of Yarrowby, which had no station, rose slightly over the same period.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: A railway station lowered prices in Ebbingholt only for goods that could be shipped in, not for locally made goods, unlike a town without a station.
Railways lower prices mostly by increasing competition among local producers, as the fall in flour prices in Ebbingholt and the unchanged price of cloth both show.
choices.slip: The competition came from distant mills, not local producers.

choices.text: Prices in Yarrowby rose because the town lacked a railway station, while prices in Ebbingholt fell because it had one, so stations determine price trends.
choices.slip: This credits the station for every price movement; the passage ties the effect to goods that could be shipped in.

choices.text: Locally woven cloth kept its price in Ebbingholt because the town's weavers resisted competition from cloth shipped in by rail, as the unchanged price shows.
choices.slip: Nothing in the text says weavers resisted anything; the cloth faced no new rail competition.

steps: Flour (shippable) fell 11 percent; cloth (local) did not change.
Yarrowby, with no station, saw no such fall.
The main idea combines the contrast between goods with the comparison town.
explanation.why: The price fall appeared only for goods that rail could bring in.
explanation.pattern: Main idea captures the pattern across cases, not one case alone.

items.passage: Engineers at Strandell Materials tested a concrete mix in which 30 percent of the cement is replaced by fly ash, a powdery by-product of coal burning. Cylinders of the new mix cured at 25 degrees Celsius reached 35 percent less compressive strength than standard cylinders after 7 days but 8 percent more after 90 days. In cylinders cured at 5 degrees Celsius, the fly-ash mix still trailed the standard mix by 25 percent after 90 days. The engineers conclude that fly ash raises long-term strength only if the concrete cures in warm conditions, and that builders working in cold seasons should not assume the benefit.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Fly ash makes concrete weaker than standard cement, since the new mix trailed the standard mix after 7 days and in cold curing.
choices.slip: This ignores the 8 percent gain at 90 days in warm curing.

choices.text: Concrete cured at 25 degrees Celsius is stronger after 90 days than concrete cured at 5 degrees, regardless of what it is made from.
choices.slip: The text compares mixes at each temperature, not temperatures for each mix.

choices.text: Builders should use fly ash only in warm seasons, since early strength matters less than the strength measured at 90 days.
choices.slip: The engineers advise against assuming the benefit; the claim that early strength matters less is not in the text.

choices.text: Fly ash slows early strength gain and raises strength at 90 days, but the later benefit appeared only under warm curing conditions.

steps: Warm curing: weaker at 7 days, stronger at 90 days.
Cold curing: still weaker at 90 days.
So fly ash's benefit is delayed and depends on warmth.
explanation.why: The benefit is late and conditional on warm curing.
explanation.pattern: Main idea keeps both the timing and the condition of a result.

items.passage: Developmental psychologist Ines Dumont-Mbeki compared the vocabularies of 90 four-year-olds: 30 who spoke only English, 30 who spoke English and Spanish, and 30 who spoke English and Vietnamese. On a test of English words alone, the bilingual children scored on average 15 percent below the English-only children. When the researchers counted every concept a child could name in either language, counting a concept once even if the child knew the word in both languages, the three groups' scores were nearly identical. Dumont-Mbeki concludes that the bilingual children's lower English scores reflect a vocabulary divided between two languages, not a smaller total store of concepts.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Learning two languages slows vocabulary growth in each language, as the bilingual children's lower scores on the English-only word test show.
choices.slip: Total concepts were nearly equal; only English-word scores were lower.

choices.text: Bilingual four-year-olds scored lower on English words alone yet knew about as many concepts overall, so their vocabularies are divided, not smaller.
English-only children know more words than bilingual children do, so a vocabulary test given in English alone fairly measures every child's knowledge.
choices.slip: A test in English alone understates bilingual children's knowledge, the opposite of this claim.

choices.text: Spanish-English and Vietnamese-English bilingual children had equal conceptual vocabularies, which shows that the languages a child speaks have no effect on word learning.
choices.slip: The text compares total concepts across groups; it does not show that language has no effect on word learning.

steps: English-only test: bilinguals 15 percent lower.
Concept count across both languages: nearly identical.
So knowledge is divided, not smaller.
explanation.why: Lower English scores combined with equal total concepts show a divided vocabulary.
explanation.pattern: Main idea reconciles two findings rather than reporting one.

items.passage: Botanist Rune Aldersey-Oyelowo recorded visitors to the flowers of the dusk lily, which blooms for a single night in the desert of Tarsk. Over 40 nights, hawk moths made 71 percent of the recorded visits and bats made 29 percent. But when the team measured the pollen deposited on the flowers' stigmas after each visit, a bat visit left about 9 times more pollen than a moth visit did. Flowers covered with mesh that excluded bats but let moths through set seed in 12 percent of cases, while flowers open to both set seed in 58 percent.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Although moths made most visits to dusk lilies, bats appear to provide most of the pollination, since each bat visit deposits far more pollen.
Moths are the main pollinators of dusk lilies, because they made 71 percent of the recorded visits to the flowers.
choices.slip: Visit counts alone mislead; bats leave about 9 times more pollen per visit.

choices.text: Bats and moths contribute about equally to the pollination of dusk lilies, since flowers open to both set seed in 58 percent of cases.
choices.slip: The 58 percent figure applies to flowers open to both visitors and says nothing about an equal split.

choices.text: Dusk lilies depend on bats because moths deposit no pollen when they visit the flowers, as the mesh experiment shows.
choices.slip: Moths do deposit some pollen, and seed set was 12 percent with moths alone.

steps: Visits: moths 71 percent, bats 29 percent.
Pollen per visit: bats about 9 times more, so bats deliver roughly three-quarters of the pollen.
Seed set drops from 58 to 12 percent without bats.
explanation.why: Pollen per visit and the exclusion test both show bats matter more than visit counts suggest.
explanation.pattern: Count of events can mislead; weight by the effect each event has.

items.passage: Ecologist Mireille Okonkwo-Brandt estimates penguin colony sizes from satellite images by measuring the area of guano stains on the ice and converting it to a number of breeding pairs. To test the method, her team compared satellite estimates with ground counts at 12 colonies. At the 8 colonies with more than 5,000 pairs, the estimates fell within 10 percent of the ground counts. At the 4 colonies with fewer than 1,000 pairs, the estimates were on average 45 percent too low, because the stained areas were smaller than the images could reliably detect. Okonkwo-Brandt concludes that the method is suited to surveying large colonies.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Satellite images of guano stains are too inaccurate to estimate penguin colony sizes, since estimates at 4 of 12 colonies were far too low.
choices.slip: The method worked well at 8 of 12 colonies.

choices.text: Ground counts of penguin colonies should be replaced by satellite estimates, because the estimates fell within 10 percent at the large colonies.
choices.slip: The test supports the method only for large colonies, not as a general replacement.

choices.text: Small penguin colonies produce smaller guano stains than large colonies do, which is why small colonies are harder to count from the ground.
choices.slip: The difficulty described is satellite detection, not counting on the ground.

choices.text: Satellite estimates from guano stains track ground counts closely for large penguin colonies but underestimate small ones, so the method suits large colonies.

steps: Large colonies: within 10 percent.
Small colonies: 45 percent too low.
The method is reliable for large colonies only.
explanation.why: The method is accurate for large colonies and unreliable for small ones.
explanation.pattern: Main idea states the finding together with its limit.

items.passage: Urban planner Hugo Marsh claims that adding benches to a shopping street increases the time people spend there, not merely the number of people who pass through.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Marsh's claim?

choices.text: After benches were added to one street, the number of daily visitors rose by 30 percent.
choices.slip: This is about how many people came, which Marsh sets apart from how long they stay.

choices.text: Most shop owners on streets with benches said that they were glad to have them.
choices.slip: Owners' opinions don't measure how long people stay.

choices.text: Streets that have benches are more often found in a city's wealthier neighborhoods.
choices.slip: This is about where benches are, not their effect on time spent.

choices.text: After benches were added to one street, the average visit grew from 20 to 35 minutes.

steps: Marsh's claim is about time spent, 'not merely the number of people'.
So the evidence must measure the length of visits.
Visits growing from 20 to 35 minutes does that.
explanation.why: Longer average visits after benches were added is direct evidence about time spent.
explanation.pattern: Watch for 'not merely X'. Evidence about X alone is the tempting wrong answer.

items.passage: Agronomist Dana Okoye hypothesizes that barley in the Pell valley yields more in fields bordered by hedges because the hedges shelter the crop from wind.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Okoye's hypothesis?

choices.text: Wind speeds measured inside the hedged fields were lower than those measured in open fields.
choices.slip: This fits the hypothesis: hedges do reduce wind.

choices.text: In side valleys with almost no wind, hedged fields outyielded open ones just as much.
Barley yields in the Pell valley differed a good deal from one year to the next.
choices.slip: Yearly variation doesn't bear on why hedged fields yield more.

choices.text: Most farmers in the valley first planted their hedges to mark where fields ended.
choices.slip: Why hedges were planted doesn't affect what they do for the crop.

steps: The hypothesis: hedges raise yields by blocking wind.
If so, hedges should help little where there is no wind to block.
Finding the same advantage in windless valleys means something other than wind shelter explains it.
explanation.why: If hedges help just as much where there is no wind, shelter from wind can't be the reason.
explanation.pattern: To weaken a 'because' claim, look for the same effect appearing without the proposed cause.

items.passage: Psychologist Ines Valdez hypothesizes that people remember a list of words better when they expect to teach it to someone than when they expect to be tested on it. She further proposes that this is because expecting to teach leads people to organize the material, not simply to study it for longer.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Valdez's account?

choices.text: People who expected to teach recalled more words, and they also studied the list for nearly twice as long.
choices.slip: Longer study would explain the better recall, which is the explanation Valdez rules out.

choices.text: People who expected to teach studied no longer but grouped the words by type more often and recalled more.
People who went on to teach the list recalled more than people who only expected to teach it.
choices.slip: This compares teaching with expecting to teach, not expecting to teach with expecting a test.

choices.text: People who expected a test and people who expected to teach grouped the words equally often.
choices.slip: If both groups organized equally, organizing can't explain any difference.

steps: The account has two parts: expecting to teach improves recall, and the reason is organizing, not extra study time.
Support needs better recall, more organizing, and no extra study time.
Only one choice has all three.
explanation.why: Equal study time rules out the rival explanation, and more grouping with better recall fits Valdez's proposed reason.
explanation.pattern: When a hypothesis includes a 'because … not …', the evidence must support the cause and rule out the alternative.

items.passage: In an essay, critic Runa Ostby writes that the narrator of the novel Low Water describes her hometown with affection even as she lists its faults.
items.question: Which quotation from Low Water most effectively illustrates Ostby's claim?

choices.text: "I loved the town best in spring, when the river ran high and every orchard on the hill was white with bloom."
choices.slip: This shows affection but lists no faults.

choices.text: "The roofs leaked and the buses never came; I counted the days until I was old enough to leave."
choices.slip: This lists faults but shows a wish to leave, not affection.

choices.text: "People who visit say the town is charming, though I notice that they never stay for the winter."
choices.slip: This reports visitors' views, not the narrator's own affection.

choices.text: "The roofs leaked, the buses never came, and still I would know that crooked skyline anywhere and be glad."

steps: The claim needs both at once: faults listed, and affection.
Faults: 'The roofs leaked, the buses never came'.
Affection: 'and still I would know that crooked skyline anywhere and be glad'.
explanation.why: This quotation names the town's faults and, in the same breath, the narrator's gladness at the sight of it.
explanation.pattern: For 'X even as Y' claims, a quotation showing only X or only Y is the trap. The right one shows both.

items.passage:
Harvest at four community gardens in one season
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Garden} & \text{Volunteers} & \text{Vegetables harvested (kg)} \\ \hline \text{Elm Street} & 18 & 310 \\ \hline \text{Mill Road} & 12 & 450 \\ \hline \text{Park Avenue} & 25 & 280 \\ \hline \text{Quay Lane} & 9 & 300 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
A community group tracked the harvest at four gardens for one season. A student reviewing the results notes that the garden with the most volunteers was not the one with the largest harvest: ______
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?

choices.text: Park Avenue had 25 volunteers but harvested 280 kg, while Mill Road harvested 450 kg.
Mill Road had 12 volunteers and harvested 450 kg, the most of the four gardens.
choices.slip: True, but it doesn't mention the garden with the most volunteers.

choices.text: Quay Lane had 9 volunteers, the fewest, and harvested 300 kg of vegetables.
choices.slip: True, but the claim is about the garden with the most volunteers.

choices.text: Park Avenue had 25 volunteers and also harvested 450 kg, the most of any of the four gardens.
choices.slip: Park Avenue harvested 280 kg, not 450 kg.

steps: Most volunteers: Park Avenue (25).
Largest harvest: Mill Road (450 kg).
The right choice shows both facts: Park Avenue's harvest (280 kg) was smaller than Mill Road's.
explanation.why: It names the garden with the most volunteers and shows another garden harvested more.
explanation.pattern: First find the rows the claim is about. Then reject choices that are true but about other rows, and choices that misread the table.

items.passage:
Average daily riders on three bus routes
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Route} & \text{Before fare cut} & \text{After fare cut} \\ \hline \text{Route 4} & \text{2,000} & \text{2,400} \\ \hline \text{Route 9} & 500 & 800 \\ \hline \text{Route 12} & \text{1,200} & \text{1,500} \\ \hline \end{array}\)
After a city cut bus fares, a transit analyst reported that ridership grew most, in proportion to its earlier level, on the route that had been used least: ______
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?

choices.text: Route 4 gained 400 daily riders, more than either of the other two routes gained.
choices.slip: True, but this is the largest gain in number, not in proportion, and Route 4 was the most used route.

choices.text: Route 9 rose from 500 to 800 daily riders, a larger proportional gain than any other.
Route 12 rose from 1,200 to 1,500 daily riders, the same increase in number as Route 9.
choices.slip: True, but it doesn't show which route grew most in proportion.

choices.text: Route 9 carried 800 daily riders after the fare cut, the fewest of the three routes.
choices.slip: True, but it gives no comparison of growth.

steps: The least-used route before the cut: Route 9 (500).
Proportional gains: Route 4, 400 of 2,000 = 20%; Route 9, 300 of 500 = 60%; Route 12, 300 of 1,200 = 25%.
Route 9 grew most in proportion.
explanation.why: Route 9's rise from 500 to 800 is a 60% gain, well above 20% and 25% on the other routes.
explanation.pattern: 'In proportion' means percent change, not the raw difference. The largest raw gain is the trap.

items.passage:
Average height gain of ferns after eight weeks (cm)
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Soil} & \text{Full sun} & \text{Shade} \\ \hline \text{Moist} & 12 & 11 \\ \hline \text{Dry} & 5 & 9 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
Botanist Sela Arden hypothesized that shade helps this fern grow only when the soil is dry. The results of her eight-week trial support the hypothesis: ______
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?

choices.text: ferns in moist soil gained more height than ferns in dry soil, in sun and in shade alike.
choices.slip: True, but it compares soils, not the effect of shade.

choices.text: ferns in shade gained more height than ferns in full sun in both kinds of soil.
choices.slip: In moist soil, shaded ferns gained slightly less (11 cm against 12 cm).

choices.text: in dry soil, ferns in shade gained 9 cm over the eight weeks, well above the 5 cm gained by the ferns left in full sun.
choices.slip: True, but it shows only that shade helps in dry soil, not that it helps only there.

choices.text: shade made little difference in moist soil (11 cm against 12 cm) but raised growth in dry soil from 5 cm to 9 cm.

steps: 'Only when the soil is dry' makes two claims: shade helps in dry soil, and it doesn't help in moist soil.
Dry soil: 5 cm in sun, 9 cm in shade. Shade helps.
Moist soil: 12 cm in sun, 11 cm in shade. Shade doesn't help.
The right choice reports both comparisons.
explanation.why: Both rows are needed: a clear gain from shade in dry soil and none in moist soil.
explanation.pattern: 'Only when' needs evidence for both sides: the effect appears in one condition and is absent in the other.

items.passage:
Survey of residents in three towns
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Town} & \text{Residents surveyed} & \text{Own a bicycle} & \text{Cycle to work} \\ \hline \text{Aldham} & 400 & 300 & 40 \\ \hline \text{Brock} & 200 & 100 & 50 \\ \hline \text{Carrow} & 500 & 300 & 100 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
A researcher argues that owning a bicycle does not by itself lead people to cycle to work. She points out that the town where the largest share of residents own a bicycle is also the town where the smallest share cycle to work: ______
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?

choices.text: in Aldham, 300 of 400 residents own a bicycle, but only 40 of 400 cycle to work.
in Carrow, 300 residents own a bicycle and 100 cycle to work, the most of any town.
choices.slip: These are counts, not shares; Carrow's ownership share (300 of 500) is lower than Aldham's.

choices.text: in Brock, only 100 residents own a bicycle, but half that number cycle to work.
choices.slip: True, but Brock has the smallest ownership share, so it isn't the town the claim describes.

choices.text: in Aldham, 300 residents own a bicycle and more cycle to work than in Brock.
choices.slip: Fewer Aldham residents cycle to work (40) than Brock residents (50).

steps: The claim is about shares, so divide by residents surveyed.
Ownership: Aldham 300/400 = 75%; Brock 100/200 = 50%; Carrow 300/500 = 60%.
Cycling to work: Aldham 40/400 = 10%; Brock 50/200 = 25%; Carrow 100/500 = 20%.
Aldham is highest in ownership and lowest in cycling to work.
explanation.why: Aldham has the largest share of owners (75%) and the smallest share of cycle commuters (10%).
explanation.pattern: When towns differ in size, 'share' means a fraction of each town's total. Equal counts (300 and 300) can hide unequal shares.

items.passage:
Spring rainfall and change in Lake Orrin's summer level
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Year} & \text{Spring rainfall (mm)} & \text{Change from previous summer (m)} \\ \hline \text{2015} & 340 & \text{+0.4} \\ \hline \text{2016} & 300 & \text{-0.3} \\ \hline \text{2017} & 310 & \text{-0.2} \\ \hline \text{2018} & 250 & \text{+0.1} \\ \hline \text{2019} & 365 & \text{+0.6} \\ \hline \end{array}\)
Hydrologist Tamar Reiss states that in every year in which spring rainfall exceeded 300 mm, Lake Orrin stood higher that summer than the summer before, with a single exception that she attributes to a release of water from the dam. The exception is shown in the table: ______
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?

choices.text: in 2016, when spring rainfall was 300 mm and the lake's level fell by 0.3 m.
choices.slip: 300 mm does not exceed 300 mm, so Reiss's statement doesn't cover 2016.

choices.text: in 2018, when spring rainfall was 250 mm and the lake's level rose by 0.1 m.
choices.slip: Reiss's statement is only about years with rainfall above 300 mm; 2018 isn't one of them.

choices.text: in 2017, when spring rainfall was 310 mm and the lake's level fell by 0.2 m.
in 2019, when spring rainfall was 365 mm and the lake's level rose by 0.6 m.
choices.slip: This year fits the rule; it isn't an exception.
