steps: The rule covers only years in which spring rainfall exceeded 300 mm: 2015 (340), 2017 (310) and 2019 (365).
2016 had exactly 300 mm, which does not exceed 300, so the rule doesn't apply to it.
In 2015 and 2019 the lake rose, as the rule says.
In 2017 the lake fell by 0.2 m. That is the exception.
2018 looks odd (low rain, lake rose), but the rule says nothing about years at or below 300 mm.
explanation.why: 2017 is the one year with rainfall above 300 mm in which the lake fell.
explanation.pattern: A rule of the form 'whenever A, then B' is broken only by a case with A and without B. Check the boundary too: 'exceeded 300' leaves out exactly 300.

items.passage: Many deep-sea sponges host dense communities of bacteria, and biologist Ximena Ferreira's team has proposed that these bacteria allow sponges to survive where food is extremely scarce. In a 2023 study, the team compared two sponge species collected from the same seafloor plateau, 1,900 meters below the surface: Hexactinella orla, whose tissue is roughly 40% bacteria by volume, and Aphrocallistes vena, whose tissue is under 2% bacteria by volume. The two species are similar in size and age. Over eighteen months in tanks supplied with almost no particulate food, H. orla specimens lost little mass, whereas A. vena specimens lost about a third of theirs. The team concluded that H. orla's bacteria sustain the sponge by supplying nutrients that it cannot gather on its own.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the team's conclusion?

choices.text: When fed regularly, A. vena specimens gained mass at about the same rate as H. orla specimens kept under identical feeding conditions in the tanks.
choices.slip: This is about feeding conditions; it doesn't bear on whether H. orla's bacteria were what sustained it without food.

choices.text: H. orla specimens whose bacteria were reduced by more than 90 percent with antibiotics lost no more mass in the tanks than untreated specimens did.
The bacteria in H. orla tissue belong to several groups that have not been found in A. vena or in other sponge species collected from the plateau.
choices.slip: That the bacteria are unusual would fit the team's idea that they do something special; it doesn't weaken it.

choices.text: H. orla specimens in the tanks lost mass more slowly during the first six months of the study than they did during the last twelve months.
choices.slip: A change in rate over time doesn't separate the bacteria from other explanations; both species could have slowed at the start.

steps: The conclusion: H. orla's bacteria are what let it do without food.
To weaken it, find evidence that H. orla survives just as well when the bacteria are mostly gone.
A: removing over 90% of the bacteria made no difference to the mass lost, so the bacteria weren't doing the sustaining.
B, C and D are consistent with the team's conclusion or irrelevant to it.
explanation.why: If H. orla loses no more mass with most of its bacteria removed, the bacteria can't be what sustains it.
explanation.pattern: To weaken a causal claim, look for the cause removed with the effect staying. Findings that are true but don't touch the proposed cause are the wrong choices.

items.passage: In 2018, the city of Marlowe Ridge installed 300 bat houses along its river corridor. Ecologist Pilar Soto argues that the bat houses, and not a regional change in weather or mosquito numbers, reduced the number of mosquito complaints that residents filed with the city. To compare, Soto's team gathered yearly complaint rates from Marlowe Ridge and from a neighboring city of similar size and climate that installed no bat houses.
items.question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Soto's argument?

choices.text: From 2014 through 2018, the rates in both cities stayed within a range of about 3 complaints per 10,000 residents, with neither city's rate moving far from the other's.
choices.slip: True of the years before the bat houses; it shows the cities were alike beforehand but not what happened afterward.

choices.text: In 2018 the rates in the two cities were equal, and after 2018 Marlowe Ridge's rate fell below the neighboring city's and stayed below it in every later year.
choices.slip: The rates were not equal in 2018 (41 in Marlowe Ridge against 43 in the neighboring city).

choices.text: After 2018, the complaint rate in Marlowe Ridge fell steadily, while the rate in the neighboring city stayed within a narrow band of about 41 to 43.
In 2018, the complaint rate in Marlowe Ridge was lower than the rate in the neighboring city, and it was lower than the neighboring city's rate in every other year shown.
choices.slip: In 2014, 2016 and 2017 Marlowe Ridge's rate was equal to or higher than the neighboring city's rate (for example, 43 against 41 in 2015).

steps: Soto's claim: the bat houses caused the drop, not region-wide weather or mosquito numbers.
Support needs two things: Marlowe Ridge's rate fell after 2018, and the comparison city (no bat houses, same region) did not change.
A states both. B is true but covers only the years before 2018. C is false. D is true but weaker, since it compares only the end points.
explanation.why: Marlowe Ridge's rate fell after 2018 while the comparison city's stayed level, which rules out a regional cause.
explanation.pattern: For data that supports a cause, use the comparison group: the treated group changes after the intervention and the comparison group doesn't. Check each choice against the actual points on the graph.

items.passage:
Peak water temperature and coral bleaching (percent of colonies bleached)
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Peak temperature} & \text{Colonies that had survived an earlier heat wave} & \text{Colonies with no earlier heat wave} \\ \hline 30^{\circ}\text{C} & 12 & 31 \\ \hline 31^{\circ}\text{C} & 18 & 40 \\ \hline 32^{\circ}\text{C} & 55 & 58 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
Marine biologist Inés Valderrama hypothesizes that coral colonies that survived an earlier heat wave bleach less in later heat waves than colonies with no such history, but that this advantage disappears when the later heat wave is much hotter.
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Valderrama's hypothesis?

choices.text: At 30°C and 31°C, smaller shares of earlier-survivor colonies bleached than of colonies with no earlier heat wave (12% and 18%, against 31% and 40%), and the gap between the two kinds of colony was wider at 32°C than at 31°C.
choices.slip: The gap narrowed to 3 points at 32°C (55% against 58%); it did not widen.

choices.text: At 30°C and 31°C, fewer earlier-survivor colonies bleached than colonies with no earlier heat wave (12% and 18% against 31% and 40%), but at 32°C the shares were nearly equal (55% and 58%).
Bleaching was more common at 32°C than at 30°C or 31°C among colonies of both kinds, and 55% of earlier-survivor colonies bleached at 32°C.
choices.slip: Accurate but shows only that hotter water bleaches more, not how the earlier-survivor advantage changes.

choices.text: At 32°C, 55% of colonies that had survived an earlier heat wave bleached, compared with 58% of colonies with no earlier heat wave.
choices.slip: Supports only the second half (advantage disappears at 32°C), not the claim that an advantage existed at cooler temperatures.

steps: Claim has two parts: earlier survivors bleach less; the advantage vanishes at much hotter temperatures.
Only one choice covers both the gap at cooler temperatures and the near-equality at 32°C.
explanation.why: It cites the gap at 30°C and 31°C and the near-equal shares at 32°C, covering both parts.
explanation.pattern: If a claim has two parts, the best evidence covers both; a choice that is accurate for one part is only half an answer.

items.passage: Researchers studying a species of crow that makes hooked tools from twigs have proposed that the skill is learned from other crows rather than being inherited as a fixed behavior. Adults of the species use the hooks to pull grubs from rotting logs, a task that juveniles attempt with little success during their first months. Earlier fieldwork could not tell whether juveniles improve by watching adults or simply because they grow stronger and more coordinated. Crows in different regions are known to make hooks of somewhat different shapes, and young crows are known to spend long periods near adults that are using tools. Behavioral scientist Joaquim Neves-Bright set out to test the proposal directly.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the researchers' proposal?

choices.text: Wild crows in two separate regions that differ in the kinds of twigs available make hooks of different shapes, although the researchers did not record which twig types were available in each region.
choices.slip: Differences between regions could come from different twigs, so this does not separate learning from inheritance.

choices.text: Young crows raised near adults begin making simple hooks at about the same age at which they begin flying long distances, and both milestones come sooner in regions where suitable twigs are plentiful.
choices.slip: Matching ages does not show the skill is learned from adults; it could be a maturation timetable.

choices.text: Adult crows that make hooked tools spend more time foraging for insects in tree bark than adults that do not make such tools, and they forage in larger groups.
choices.slip: Concerns foraging habits of adults, not how the skill is acquired by young crows.

choices.text: Young crows raised without adult contact made hooked tools much less skillfully than crows raised near adults, and improved only after watching an adult demonstrate the technique.

steps: Proposal: tool skill is learned from other crows, not inherited.
Best test: remove the chance to learn, then give it back.
Isolated crows are worse; they improve after watching: the sign of learning from others.
explanation.why: Isolation lowers skill and demonstration raises it, which isolates social learning from inheritance.
explanation.pattern: Supporting evidence for 'learned, not innate' must manipulate learning opportunities; regional differences and timing coincidences leave inheritance open.

items.passage: Starting in 2019, cafés in the town of Pellam Cross offered a discount to customers who brought their own reusable cups; cafés in the nearby town of Ossen Dale offered no such discount. Public-policy researcher Lars Okonkwo-Reyes argues that the discount, and not a general rise in environmental awareness across the region, accounts for most of the growth in reusable-cup use in Pellam Cross. Okonkwo-Reyes notes that the two towns share a regional newspaper and a waste-reduction program begun in 2017, and that both have run the same public campaigns about cutting waste.
items.question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Okonkwo-Reyes's argument?

choices.text: In every year from 2018 to 2022, a larger share of customers used reusable cups in Pellam Cross than in Ossen Dale, and the difference between the two towns grew from 1 point in 2018 to 16 points in 2022.
choices.slip: False: the shares were equal in 2018 (10% and 10%) and in 2019 (11% and 11%).

choices.text: The share of customers using reusable cups rose every year from 2017 to 2022 in both Pellam Cross and Ossen Dale, and in every year the share in Pellam Cross was equal to or greater than the share in Ossen Dale.
choices.slip: True of both towns, so it fits a regional rise in awareness as well as the discount.

choices.text: The share of customers using reusable cups was nearly the same in both towns through 2019, but from 2019 to 2022 it rose by 20 percentage points in Pellam Cross and by only 4 in Ossen Dale.
From 2017 to 2019, the share of customers using reusable cups rose by 2 points in Pellam Cross and by 3 points in Ossen Dale.
choices.slip: Shows the towns were alike before the discount, but says nothing about what happened after it.

figure.alt: Line graph of the percent of café customers using reusable cups by year, 2017 to 2022, for two towns. Pellam Cross: 2017, 9; 2018, 10; 2019, 11; 2020, 19; 2021, 26; 2022, 31. Ossen Dale: 2017, 8; 2018, 10; 2019, 11; 2020, 12; 2021, 14; 2022, 15.

steps: Argument: the discount, not regional awareness, drove Pellam Cross's growth.
Best evidence: similar before 2019 (11% and 11%), then divergence.
Pellam Cross 11 to 31 (+20); Ossen Dale 11 to 15 (+4).
explanation.why: Equal levels through 2019 and a 20-point versus 4-point rise after the discount supports the argument.
explanation.pattern: For a comparison-town argument, look for evidence of similarity before the change and divergence after it; either half alone is weaker.

items.passage: In her published 1893 report on the birds of the Thornwick marshes, the naturalist Ottilie Wrenfield states that every identification in the report was 'made with certainty.' Ornithologist Pavel Ndlovu-Hart, who has studied Wrenfield's surviving field notebooks, argues that her private notes show more doubt about some identifications than the published report admits. Wrenfield, a self-taught naturalist who worked alone, kept pencil notebooks during her visits and wrote the published report over the following winter; its preface says that doubtful sightings were 'left out.'
items.question: Which quotation from Wrenfield's field notebooks, if accurate, would most directly support Ndlovu-Hart's argument?

choices.text: 'Wren, I think; though the tail is wrong and the song is not one I know. Will enter it as wren until shown otherwise.'
'Wren. Singing from the hedge at ten past six; third pair on this side of the marsh since the weekend.'
choices.slip: Records an identification and a sighting without doubt.

choices.text: 'Small brown bird again in the sedge, probably the wren seen on the second; flew before I could check for the eye-stripe.'
choices.slip: Shows mild doubt, but about a repeat sighting of a bird already identified, a weaker match than the key.

choices.text: 'Fog until noon. Heard the marsh harrier distinctly at eight though I could not see it, and have noted it as heard only.'
choices.slip: Shows care in separating hearing from seeing, which supports her reliability, not doubt about identification.

steps: Claim: notes show more doubt about identifications than the report ('with certainty') admits.
Need a note that expresses doubt about an identification yet records it as one.
'Wren, I think; though the tail is wrong...' does that.
explanation.why: The note questions an identification yet enters it in the record, which contrasts with the published claim of certainty.
explanation.pattern: Quotation questions: find the one that matches the claim's exact point (doubt about an identification), not just any hedged or careful language.

items.passage: Marine biologist Yusra Thorne hypothesizes that the loud clicking of a certain shrimp is used mainly to defend territory rather than to attract mates.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Thorne's hypothesis?

choices.text: Shrimp click far more often when an unfamiliar shrimp enters their burrow area than when a potential mate does.
Shrimp click at about the same rate whether or not another shrimp is nearby.
choices.slip: Clicking unrelated to other shrimp supports neither purpose.

choices.text: Male shrimp that click more often are chosen as mates more often than quieter males.
choices.slip: This supports the mate-attraction idea Thorne doubts.

choices.text: Shrimp can hear each other's clicks from several meters away.
choices.slip: Distance of hearing says nothing about what the clicks are for.

steps: Hypothesis: territory defense, not mating.
Support = clicking rises in response to intruders and not in response to mates.
explanation.why: More clicking toward intruders than toward mates points to defense.
explanation.pattern: Evidence that supports a 'rather than' claim must favor one side and not the other.

items.passage: A study of 120 office workers at an insurance firm tracked afternoon attention over eight weeks, using a computer task that counted lapses (responses slower than 800 milliseconds). Workers who took a daily outdoor walk of at least fifteen minutes before lunch had fewer lapses than workers who stayed at their desks, but only among workers who averaged seven or more hours of sleep a night; among workers who averaged less, walkers and non-walkers did not differ. Researcher Maren Lundgaard concludes that a daily walk improves afternoon attention only when workers are otherwise well rested.
items.question: Which choice best describes data from the study that support Lundgaard's conclusion?

choices.text: Among workers who averaged less than seven hours of sleep, walkers had fewer lapses than non-walkers, while among workers who averaged seven or more hours the two groups did not differ.
choices.slip: Reverses the pattern the text reports.

choices.text: Among workers who averaged seven or more hours of sleep, walkers had fewer lapses than non-walkers, and among workers who averaged less, walkers had slightly fewer lapses as well.
choices.slip: A walking benefit in both sleep groups contradicts 'only when rested'.

choices.text: Walking was linked to fewer lapses only in the group averaging seven or more hours of sleep; in the group averaging less, walkers' and non-walkers' lapse counts were similar.
Non-walkers who averaged seven or more hours of sleep had fewer lapses than walkers who slept as much, while walkers and non-walkers who averaged less sleep did not differ.
choices.slip: Reverses the direction of the walking effect among rested workers.

steps: Claim: walks help only when rested.
Needed: walk effect present with enough sleep, absent without.
Only the key compares walkers with non-walkers inside each sleep group.
explanation.why: It shows the walk effect appearing in the rested group and vanishing in the other.
explanation.pattern: To test an 'only when' claim, compare the groups within each condition.

items.passage: Plant biologist Zofia Kratochvil hypothesizes that the ultraviolet patterns visible on the petals of a certain wildflower serve mainly to guide bees toward the flower's nectar, not to attract bees from a distance. To test this, her team painted over the ultraviolet patterns on some blossoms in a meadow, left other blossoms untouched, and recorded how bees behaved around each group.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kratochvil's hypothesis?

choices.text: Bees approached painted and untouched blossoms at similar rates, but bees landing on painted blossoms spent noticeably longer searching before reaching the nectar.
Bees approached untouched blossoms far more often than painted ones, though those that landed reached the nectar equally quickly in both groups.
choices.slip: This supports the idea that the patterns attract bees from a distance, the view Kratochvil doubts.

choices.text: Bees approached painted and untouched blossoms at similar rates and reached the nectar equally quickly on both, whatever the state of the patterns.
choices.slip: No effect of the patterns would leave the hypothesis unsupported.

choices.text: Bees that landed on untouched blossoms stayed longer overall than bees that landed on painted ones, though both kinds of blossom were approached at similar rates.
choices.slip: Staying longer does not show the patterns help bees find nectar.

steps: Hypothesis: patterns guide bees to nectar once there, not draw them in.
Support needs similar approach rates (no attraction effect) and slower nectar-finding when patterns are removed.
explanation.why: Equal approach rates show the patterns do not attract; longer searching on painted blossoms shows they guide.
explanation.pattern: For a 'mainly X, not Y' hypothesis, evidence must show an effect on X and none on Y.

items.passage: Historian Ludmila Fairchild argues that the fourteenth-century decline of the port of Karsholm was driven mainly by the silting of its harbor rather than by the plague that struck the region in 1349. Her evidence is that customs receipts at the port began falling in 1331, eighteen years before the plague, and that dredging expenses in the town's accounts rose steadily over the same period.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Fairchild's argument?

choices.text: Plague deaths in Karsholm in 1349 were among the highest recorded in the region, with roughly half the town's population lost.
choices.slip: The decline started before 1349, so high plague deaths do not touch her argument about the earlier fall.

choices.text: Customs receipts at neighboring ports with clear harbors also began falling in the early 1330s, when a regional trade slump reduced shipping everywhere.
Dredging expenses at Karsholm kept rising after 1349, and customs receipts continued to fall at about the same pace as before the plague.
choices.slip: Fits the silting story and offers no rival cause for the earlier fall.

choices.text: Several other ports with silting harbors also saw customs receipts fall before 1349, even though the plague spared those ports.
choices.slip: This supports her view that silting, not plague, drives such declines.

steps: Her claim: silting, not plague, caused the decline.
Weakening = a rival cause that explains the pre-1349 fall: a regional slump that hit ports with clear harbors too.
explanation.why: If ports without silting also declined, silting is not needed to explain Karsholm's fall.
explanation.pattern: A weakener offers another cause that fits the same evidence; a choice that supports the claim, or says nothing about the evidence, does not.

items.passage: A student claims that, in Marguerite Oyelaran's novel The Salt Gate, the narrator looks back on her youthful ambitions with a mixture of embarrassment and tenderness.
items.question: Which quotation from The Salt Gate most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: “I burned the plans the year I turned thirty, and I have never regretted it, nor wished to see a single line of them again, nor to explain why.”
choices.slip: Shows only rejection, with no tenderness.

choices.text: “Those plans remain the best thing I ever made, and I keep them by my bed as one keeps the face of someone loved, reading a page each night.”
choices.slip: Shows only tenderness, with no embarrassment.

choices.text: “The plans ran to four hundred pages and sat in a cedar chest in the attic until the house was finally sold.”
choices.slip: Reports facts without any feeling about them.

choices.text: “I cannot read those old plans without wincing, yet I would not tear a single page from them; they were so sure of everything I never was.”

steps: Claim needs both feelings in one quotation.
Only one choice combines wincing (embarrassment) with refusing to destroy the pages (tenderness).
explanation.why: The quotation joins wincing with keeping every page, showing both embarrassment and tenderness.
explanation.pattern: For a mixed-feeling claim, reject quotations that show one feeling or none.

items.passage: After a town installed speed cameras at six intersections, collisions at those intersections fell from 62 in the year before to 41 in the year after. A resident wrote that the figures prove the cameras prevent collisions.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the resident's claim?

choices.text: Collisions at the six monitored intersections had averaged about 60 per year in each of the previous five years.
choices.slip: This shows the drop broke a steady pattern, which supports the claim.

choices.text: Collisions at comparable intersections in the town that had no cameras also fell by about a third over the same two years, from 58 to 39.
Drivers surveyed at the monitored intersections said they slowed down when they saw a camera, though most disliked the fines.
choices.slip: This supports the claim that cameras change driver behavior.

choices.text: The cameras issued 1,100 tickets in their first year, most of them to drivers who lived outside the town.
choices.slip: Ticket numbers say nothing about whether collisions would have fallen anyway.

steps: Claim: the drop proves the cameras worked.
A weakener shows the drop also happened without cameras, so something else may explain it.
explanation.why: A similar fall at camera-free intersections suggests the drop is not due to the cameras.
explanation.pattern: When a before-and-after change is claimed as a cause, look for a comparison group that changed too.

items.passage: Archaeologist Imani Odhiambo-Rees proposes that the settlement at Ketterby was abandoned gradually, over a generation or more, rather than suddenly in a single season. Her team excavated forty houses across the site, recording the objects on each floor and in the layers of fill above it.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Odhiambo-Rees's proposal?

choices.text: Most of the houses held few tools or valuable goods on their floors, and household objects grew steadily scarcer in the layers closer to the top of the occupation.
Pottery on the floors of many houses was broken and scattered, and some houses had been rebuilt after earlier damage.
choices.slip: Neither detail says how fast the site emptied.

choices.text: Coins found in the houses were all minted within a single twenty-year span, which closely matches the dates of the settlement's earliest construction.
choices.slip: Coin dates address when the town was built, not how it was abandoned.

choices.text: Many houses showed signs of repeated repair and reuse of building stone over the settlement's long history.
choices.slip: Repair and reuse say nothing about the pace of abandonment.

steps: Proposal: slow abandonment.
Support = signs that people removed goods over time and the site thinned out.
explanation.why: Emptied floors and thinning objects layer by layer fit a slow departure.
explanation.pattern: For a gradual-versus-sudden claim, match the evidence to the pace, not just the event.

items.passage: Wildlife biologist Fabrizio Sandoval-Reyes measured bat activity near a wind farm and found that it was about 40% lower on nights when the turbines were running than on nights when they were idle. He concluded that the sound of the turbines deters bats from the area.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Sandoval-Reyes's conclusion?

choices.text: Noise levels near the running turbines were measured at about 55 decibels, a level that other studies have linked to reduced feeding in bats.
choices.slip: This supports the noise explanation.

choices.text: Bat activity fell by a similar amount near running turbines that had been fitted with dampers cutting their noise roughly in half.
Bat activity near the idle turbines was about the same as at control sites located several kilometers from the wind farm.
choices.slip: This shows idle turbines do nothing, which fits the conclusion.

choices.text: Bats were observed foraging near the wind farm on most of the nights on which the turbines were running, although in smaller numbers.
choices.slip: Lower activity is already part of the finding; it does not challenge the cause.

steps: Conclusion: turbine noise deters bats.
A weakener shows the drop continues when noise is reduced.
explanation.why: If halving the noise leaves the drop unchanged, noise is probably not the cause.
explanation.pattern: To weaken a cause, remove or change the cause and see whether the effect stays.

items.passage: A student claims that, in Ottoline Brae's short story 'Low Water,' the narrator portrays the river as indifferent to human concerns.
items.question: Which quotation from 'Low Water' most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: “The river rose against us all night as though it had sworn to drive us from the house and every one of our quarrels with it.”
choices.slip: This shows the river as hostile, not indifferent.

choices.text: “The river kept us company through the long evening, murmuring beneath the window as if it meant to comfort us.”
choices.slip: This shows the river as kindly, not indifferent.

choices.text: “We spoke of the river so often that winter that it seemed, on certain nights, to be listening to our plans.”
choices.slip: This treats the river as attentive, the opposite of indifferent.

choices.text: “The river went on carrying its leaves and silt past the open door, taking no notice of the argument that filled the house.”

steps: Claim: the river does not care about human affairs.
Only one quotation has the river carrying on while the people argue.
explanation.why: The river keeps moving and ignores the quarrel, which shows indifference.
explanation.pattern: Pair the claim's key word (indifferent) with the quotation showing neither hostility nor care.

items.passage: Ornithologist Henrike Valdivia hypothesizes that birds living in noisy cities adjust to the noise mainly by singing at a higher pitch, rather than by singing more loudly. She recorded songs of one species in several districts of a large city, measuring both pitch and loudness.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Valdivia's hypothesis?

choices.text: Birds in noisy districts sang at a slightly higher pitch and also noticeably louder than birds in quiet districts.
choices.slip: If loudness rose as well, the adjustment is not 'mainly' pitch.

choices.text: Birds in noisy and quiet districts sang at nearly the same pitch and at nearly the same loudness, whatever the level of traffic around them.
choices.slip: No adjustment at all would not support her hypothesis.

choices.text: Birds in noisy districts sang at a noticeably higher pitch than birds in quiet districts, while the loudness of their songs differed little between the two kinds of district.
Birds in quiet districts sang at a higher pitch than birds in noisy districts, and their songs were also somewhat louder.
choices.slip: Reverses the expected direction of the pitch difference.

steps: Hypothesis: pitch, not loudness.
Support: pitch rises with noise and loudness does not.
explanation.why: A pitch difference without a loudness difference matches 'mainly pitch, not loudness'.
explanation.pattern: For a 'mainly X rather than Y' hypothesis, evidence needs a difference in X and none in Y.

items.passage: Ecologist Anahita Nandakumar hypothesizes that a native wasp's attack on the eggs of an invasive moth is limited by the availability of nectar-producing plants near crop fields, since adult wasps feed on nectar. She counted moth egg masses, and the number of those that had been parasitized, at twelve fields: six bordered by flowering hedgerows and six bordered by bare grass.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nandakumar's hypothesis?

choices.text: More egg masses were parasitized at fields bordered by flowering hedgerows than at fields bordered by bare grass, though egg masses were about equally numerous at both.
Egg masses were more numerous at the fields bordered by bare grass, but the share of them that was parasitized was similar at both kinds of field.
choices.slip: No difference in parasitism between field types does not support a nectar effect.

choices.text: Wasps were more numerous at the fields bordered by flowering hedgerows, but the share of egg masses parasitized there was no higher than at the other fields.
choices.slip: Having more wasps without more parasitism does not show that nectar raises parasitism.

choices.text: A larger share of egg masses was parasitized at the fields bordered by bare grass than at the fields bordered by flowering hedgerows, where the moths were more numerous.
choices.slip: Reverses the expected direction of the effect.

steps: Hypothesis: nectar availability limits parasitism.
Support: more parasitism where nectar plants border the field, with moth numbers similar.
explanation.why: A higher parasitism share with hedgerows, and moths comparable, points to nectar as the limiting factor.
explanation.pattern: Match evidence to the variable in the hypothesis and check for rival differences.

items.passage: Education economist Tomasz Verhoeven studied eighteen school districts that switched to a four-day week and found that their average student attendance rose from 91% to 94% in the following year. He concluded that the shorter week caused the improvement in attendance.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Verhoeven's conclusion?

choices.text: Attendance in the four-day districts had held steady at about 91% in each of the five years before the schedule changed.
choices.slip: This shows the rise was a break from trend, which supports the conclusion.

choices.text: A survey found that many families moved into the four-day districts after the change, and those families reported high attendance for their children in their previous districts as well.
After the schedule change, the four-day districts reported fewer student discipline problems, although patterns of absence by day of the week stayed the same.
choices.slip: Discipline records do not explain why average attendance rose.

choices.text: Within the four-day districts, attendance rose more among older students than among younger ones after the change.
choices.slip: A difference among age groups does not show that the schedule was not the cause.

steps: Conclusion: the shorter week caused higher attendance.
Weakener: the districts' student population changed in a way that explains higher attendance.
explanation.why: If high-attendance families moved in, the rise may reflect who attends, not the schedule.
explanation.pattern: Look for a change in who is being measured, not only in what is being done.

items.passage: A student claims that, in Cordelia Verhoef's novel The Lamplighter's Debt, the narrator describes his sister's generosity as a form of calculation.
items.question: Which quotation from The Lamplighter's Debt most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: “She gave freely, and when I asked what she expected in return, she looked at me as if I had spoken in another language.”
choices.slip: Shows pure generosity with no calculation.

choices.text: “She kept a small blue notebook on her shelf in which she entered every loan and every debt, though she never once asked for repayment.”
choices.slip: Shows careful tracking but says she never sought repayment, so no calculation behind her giving.

choices.text: “She gave freely, though I sometimes suspected that she enjoyed being thanked more than she enjoyed giving.”
choices.slip: Suggests vanity, not a calculated expectation of return.

choices.text: “She gave freely, and I knew by the small blue notebook on her shelf that every favor was entered there against some future day.”

steps: Claim needs generosity and calculation together.
Only one quotation shows her tracking favors as loans.
explanation.why: The quotation joins giving freely with counting favors as a loan to be called in.
explanation.pattern: For a two-part claim, reject quotations that show only one part.

items.passage: Researchers studying whether background music improves accuracy on repetitive tasks asked 60 workers to enter the same kind of records in two sessions, one with a playlist of instrumental music and one in silence. The order of the two sessions was randomized for each worker. Workers made an average of 3.1 errors per hundred records with music and 4.4 without, and the researchers concluded that instrumental music improves accuracy on repetitive tasks.
items.question: Which question would be most useful to answer in evaluating the researchers' conclusion as it is presented in the text?

choices.text: Did the instrumental playlist used in the music sessions include pieces that most of the workers had heard before the study?
choices.slip: Familiarity with the pieces does not bear on whether music or something else changed accuracy.

choices.text: Did most workers report that they preferred working with instrumental music to working in silence?
choices.slip: Preference does not bear on whether accuracy improved because of the music.

choices.text: Did the records entered in the music sessions contain about the same number of difficult or ambiguous entries as the records entered in the silent sessions?
Were the 60 workers in the study more experienced at data entry than the typical data-entry worker?
choices.slip: This concerns generalization to other workers, not whether music caused the improvement in this study.

steps: Conclusion: music improved accuracy.
A valid test needs sessions that differ only in music.
The difficulty of the records could differ and explain the error rates.
explanation.why: If the music sessions had easier records, the lower errors might not be due to music.
explanation.pattern: Ask what else could differ between conditions besides the variable being tested.

items.passage: Cognitive psychologists claim that the benefit of spaced practice over massed practice depends on how long students wait before being tested. In an experiment, students learned vocabulary lists using either massed practice (one long session) or spaced practice (the same total time split across several days), and each student was tested either one day or one week after the final session.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the psychologists' claim?

choices.text: Spaced practice produced higher scores than massed practice when the test came one week later, but scores did not differ between the two when the test came one day later.
Spaced practice produced higher scores than massed practice at both test delays, and scores were lower overall at the one-week delay than at the one-day delay.
choices.slip: A benefit at both delays does not show that the benefit depends on the delay.

choices.text: Scores were higher at the one-day delay than at the one-week delay for both practice schedules, with spaced practice scoring above massed practice at each delay.
choices.slip: A forgetting effect for both schedules and a benefit at every delay do not show dependence on the delay.

choices.text: Massed practice produced scores equal to those of spaced practice at both test delays, though scores at one week were lower than at one day for both schedules.
choices.slip: Shows no benefit of spaced practice at either delay.

steps: Claim: the spaced-practice benefit depends on delay.
Support: a benefit at one delay and none at the other.
explanation.why: A benefit that appears at one delay and vanishes at the other shows dependence on the delay.
explanation.pattern: 'Depends on' claims need a difference that changes across conditions.

items.passage: Hydrologist Pilar Ansgar-Weiss proposes that the rise in winter-spawning trout in Sedgemoor Creek between 2018 and 2021 resulted from the 2019 removal of a small weir, which opened an upstream stretch of spawning gravel. Survey crews walked the same 12 reaches of the creek each February, using electrofishing gear of the same model and the same sampling time in both years, and counted 310 adult trout in 2018 and 434 in 2021, an increase of 40 percent. Two of the 12 reaches lie upstream of the former weir; the other ten lie downstream. The creek is about 14 kilometers long and is fed mainly by snowmelt.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Ansgar-Weiss's proposal?

choices.text: Fifteen of the 434 trout counted in 2021 carried marks showing that they had been released from a hatchery rather than born in the creek.
choices.slip: Removes only 15 fish; the count still rose by about 35 percent and no other cause is shown.

choices.text: Adult trout in a nearby stream whose weir was left in place also increased by about 40 percent between February 2018 and February 2021.
Spawning nests were more numerous in 2021 in the upstream stretch opened by the weir's removal than in any downstream stretch of the creek.
choices.slip: Supports the proposal: more nests where the weir came out.

choices.text: Water temperature in the creek stayed within half a degree of its 2018 level throughout the 2021 spawning season, so temperature cannot explain the difference.
choices.slip: Rules out one rival cause, so it supports the proposal.

steps: Claim: the weir removal caused the 40 percent rise.
A rival cause that raised counts where there was no weir change would weaken it.
A stream with its weir intact rose by the same amount, so something other than the weir fits the rise.
explanation.why: A matching untreated stream showing the same rise suggests a cause common to both streams, not the weir.
explanation.pattern: Weaken-a-cause: look for the comparison group that changes the same way without the proposed cause.

items.passage: Literary critic Dalia Mwangi-Roth argues that in poet Evander Leask's first collection, the sea is not a literal setting but a figure for the way memory returns unbidden. Leask grew up in an inland town, and the 1952 collection contains twenty poems that mention water in some form. Mwangi-Roth contends that the sea imagery in these poems consistently describes arrival and withdrawal, as of waves, rather than harbors, ships, or shorelines a reader could place on a map, and she adds that the speaker never claims to be near the water. Her essay quotes eleven of the twenty poems in full and discusses the rest briefly.
items.question: Which quotation from the collection would most directly support Mwangi-Roth's argument?

choices.text: 'The gray boats lean at the quay in Ardmore, and the gulls / argue over what the fishermen throw back.'
choices.slip: Literal harbor, boats and a named place: the opposite of her claim.

choices.text: 'I stood a long time on the shingle, wanting nothing, / and the water kept its distance from my shoes.'
choices.slip: Puts the speaker on a real shore, which contradicts the claim.

choices.text: 'What I had put away comes in again at its own hour, / and goes out, leaving the sand darker.'
'Remember the lamp-lit kitchen, the kettle, your voice rising / over the stairs, and how it all returns without being called.'
choices.slip: Shows memory returning unbidden but uses no sea imagery, so it misses the figure.

steps: Claim: sea imagery stands for memory coming and going, not for a real place.
Need a quotation with both memory-like content and wave-like arrival and withdrawal.
Only the first links returning and leaving to something put away.
explanation.why: It joins the sea image to memory's unbidden return without a place a reader could map.
explanation.pattern: Quotation evidence must match both halves of the claim, not just one.

items.passage: Behavioral ecologist Thandiwe Ormerod-Vance hypothesizes that honeybee foragers judge a food source by comparison with other sources nearby, not against a fixed minimum reward. In a field experiment, she trained marked bees to visit a feeder offering 25 percent sugar solution, then placed a second feeder two meters away and recorded whether the trained bees kept visiting the first. Only bees that had visited the first feeder at least five times before each hour-long test were followed, and the second feeder's concentration varied from test to test. The study ran over two summers at the same meadow site, with the second feeder's side alternated between trials.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ormerod-Vance's hypothesis?

choices.text: Most trained bees stopped visiting the first feeder whether the second offered 45 percent or 15 percent solution, as though 25 percent had fallen below an absolute minimum.
choices.slip: Abandonment regardless of the alternative points to a fixed standard.

choices.text: Most trained bees kept visiting the first feeder whether the second offered 45 percent or 15 percent solution, though they visited the richer feeder more often than the poorer.
choices.slip: Staying in both cases shows no dependence on the alternative.

choices.text: Fewer trained bees kept visiting the first feeder when the second offered 15 percent solution than when it offered 45 percent solution.
choices.slip: Reverses the predicted pattern.

choices.text: Most trained bees stopped visiting the first feeder when the second offered 45 percent solution, but most kept visiting it when the second offered 15 percent solution.

steps: Hypothesis: a source is judged relative to nearby alternatives.
Prediction: the same 25 percent feeder is dropped or kept depending on the alternative.
Only the first choice shows the same feeder judged differently by alternative.
explanation.why: The same feeder is abandoned next to a richer alternative and kept next to a poorer one, which shows comparison.
explanation.pattern: Relative-standard claims need the same item treated differently as the comparison changes.

items.passage: Education researcher Gunnar Aberdeen-Pryce credits a tutoring program for a rise in reading scores at eight Marlowe County schools. The schools were chosen for the program in 2021 because their students had the lowest reading scores in the county that year, and their average score rose from 61 to 70 on a 100-point scale by 2023. Aberdeen-Pryce notes that the tests were identical in both years and were scored by the same state office, and that no school changed its principal or its reading curriculum. The county's other 41 schools were not offered the program.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the credit Aberdeen-Pryce gives the program?

choices.text: Nine other county schools whose 2021 scores were only slightly higher, and which did not receive the program, also gained about nine points by 2023.
Students at the eight schools who attended at least twenty tutoring sessions gained more points than students who attended fewer sessions.
choices.slip: A dose pattern supports the program rather than weakening it.

choices.text: Three of the eight schools raised their average scores by more than 12 points, while two raised them by fewer than 5 points.
choices.slip: Variation among the eight schools says nothing about a rival cause.

choices.text: Reading scores across the county as a whole rose by only one point between 2021 and 2023, while those at the eight schools rose by nine.
choices.slip: Compares the eight with the county and favors the program.

steps: Claim: tutoring raised scores at the lowest-scoring schools.
Weakening: a comparable group without tutoring improved just as much.
Nearby schools with near-identical scores gained the same nine points without the program.
explanation.why: Untutored schools starting from similar scores gained as much, so the program is not needed to explain the rise.
explanation.pattern: Weaken-with-comparison: look for similar untreated cases showing the same change.

items.passage: Pollination biologist Esperanza Vondrak-Lund proposes that bumblebees choose between blue and yellow flowers according to color only when nectar is scarce. In her experiment, bees visited artificial flowers that were either blue or yellow and were filled with either a rich 30 percent sugar solution or a poor 5 percent solution. The colors differed only in dye, flower positions were swapped every hour, and visits were counted per flower per hour over three days. Nectar volumes were matched by adding a tasteless thickener, so that the flowers looked equally full, and twelve bumblebee colonies took part.
items.question: Which result, if true, would best support Vondrak-Lund's proposal?

choices.text: Blue flowers received about twice as many visits as yellow with both rich and poor solution, though rich flowers of either color drew more visits than poor ones.
choices.slip: Color matters under both conditions, not only when nectar is scarce.

choices.text: With rich solution, blue and yellow flowers received similar visit counts; with poor solution, blue flowers received about twice as many visits as yellow.
With poor solution, blue and yellow flowers received similar visit counts; with rich solution, blue flowers received about twice as many visits as yellow.
choices.slip: Reverses the proposal: color matters only when nectar is rich.

choices.text: Both colors received about twice as many visits with rich solution as with poor, and blue and yellow flowers received similar visits within each solution.
choices.slip: Shows nectar matters but color never does.

steps: Claim: color guides choice only when nectar is scarce.
Needs no color preference with rich nectar and a preference with poor nectar.
Only the first choice has that split.
explanation.why: Similar visits to both colors at rich nectar and a clear preference at poor nectar is exactly 'only when scarce'.
explanation.pattern: 'Only when' claims need a difference in one condition and none in the other.

items.passage: Critic Rosalind Wetherby-Nunes argues that Teodor Maclaine's second novel keeps the setting of his first, a fishing village in decline, but abandons its detached narrator for one who is openly part of the village. She rests her case on the novels' opening paragraphs. The first novel, she notes, begins with an unnamed observer describing the village from the hills above it, and she says the second begins by placing its narrator among the villagers on the quay. Both novels run to about 300 pages, and both were published by the same small press in the 1980s.
items.question: Which quotation from the opening of Maclaine's second novel would most directly support Wetherby-Nunes's argument?

choices.text: 'From the ridge the village looked smaller than anyone there believed, its cannery roof gone dark and its quay empty of boats and its nets drying on the stones.'
choices.slip: Keeps the setting but also the detached outside viewpoint.

choices.text: 'I came to the city in March, a stranger to its streets, and kept an account of what people there said about the sea.'
choices.slip: First-person narrator, but the setting is no longer the declining village.

choices.text: 'We kept the quay swept and the nets mended, and no one in our village ever spoke of leaving.'
choices.slip: Villager narrator in the village, but no decline, so continuity of setting is missing.

choices.text: 'We had lost the cannery by Easter, and by midsummer none of us at the quay still pretended that the boats would be mended.'

steps: Claim: same declining village, but now a narrator who belongs to it.
Need both a 'we' or insider voice and decline in the village.
Only the first choice has both.
explanation.why: The quotation has an insider 'we' at the quay and a village losing its cannery and boats.
explanation.pattern: Two-part claims need evidence matching both the change and the continuity.

items.passage: Soil scientist Cormac Ilyushin-Bate proposes that a fungus living on the roots of young pine seedlings boosts their growth by supplying phosphorus. In a greenhouse experiment, he grew seedlings in sterilized soil with or without the fungus, in soil that either was or was not supplemented with phosphorus. After 20 weeks he measured each seedling's dry mass. All pots received the same light and water, and each of the four combinations included 30 seedlings. The seedlings were grown from seed collected in a single stand, and the fungus was cultured from roots taken from that same stand.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Ilyushin-Bate's proposal?

choices.text: Seedlings grown with the fungus still reached a greater dry mass than seedlings grown without it in the soil that had been supplemented with phosphorus.
Seedlings in unsupplemented soil reached greater dry mass with the fungus than without it, and fungus-free seedlings reached greater mass when phosphorus was added to the soil.
choices.slip: Both results fit a fungus that supplies phosphorus.

choices.text: Seedlings grown with the fungus in unsupplemented soil had higher phosphorus concentrations in their tissues than seedlings grown without it.
choices.slip: The fungus delivering phosphorus supports the proposal.

choices.text: Seedlings with the fungus in supplemented soil reached about the same dry mass as seedlings with the fungus in unsupplemented soil.
choices.slip: Fits the proposal: fungus seedlings already had enough phosphorus.

steps: Claim: the fungus helps because it supplies phosphorus.
If so, adding phosphorus should erase the fungus advantage.
The advantage persists with phosphorus added, so another mechanism is needed.
explanation.why: If extra phosphorus does not remove the fungus's benefit, phosphorus supply is not the whole mechanism.
explanation.pattern: Mechanism claims are weakened when removing the mechanism's job leaves the effect intact.

items.passage: Historian Lucian Faulkner-Adeyemi claims that the sharp drop in apprentices registered with the weavers' guild of Brenwick after 1846 was caused by a new national law ending guild monopolies, not by workers moving to factory towns. Registered apprentices in Brenwick fell from 140 in 1845 to 52 in 1850. Faulkner-Adeyemi has compared the Brenwick guild register with that of Stoneleigh, a similar town whose guild, under an earlier royal charter, was exempt from the law, and he has census data on both towns' populations for these years. Both towns lie on the same river, and woven wool cloth was the main product of each.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Faulkner-Adeyemi's claim?

choices.text: Brenwick's census population fell by 15 percent between 1845 and 1850, while the number of factory jobs in nearby towns rose sharply over the same years.
choices.slip: Supports the rival explanation of migration.

choices.text: Stoneleigh's registered apprentices fell from 130 to 50 between 1845 and 1850, though its guild was exempt from the law.
choices.slip: An exempt guild also collapsing weakens the law explanation.

choices.text: Stoneleigh's registered apprentices stayed near 130 through 1850, even though its census population fell by about as much as Brenwick's did over the same years.
Brenwick's census population changed little between 1845 and 1850, and the number of apprentices registered there fell in every year of that period.
choices.slip: Rules out migration but gives no link to the law, since no comparison town is used.

steps: Claim: the law, not migration, caused the drop.
Need an exempt town with similar population loss but no apprentice drop.
Only the first choice shows both.
explanation.why: An exempt town that lost population yet kept its apprentices separates the law from migration.
explanation.pattern: Compare a town that lacks one cause but shares the other.

items.passage: Soil scientist Odalys Fenwright-Amadi hypothesizes that the lupine plants growing thickly on the volcanic slopes of Mount Ellery raise the nitrogen content of the soil enough to let other plant species establish themselves there. She surveyed 60 plots, each 10 meters square, and counted the plant species other than lupine in each one. Plots with no lupine held an average of 2 other species; plots where lupine covered about a quarter of the ground held 5; and plots where it covered more than three quarters held 9. All the plots lie at similar elevation, receive similar rainfall, and are within reach of seeds from the same surrounding vegetation.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Fenwright-Amadi's hypothesis?

choices.text: Soil in the densest lupine plots held about three times as much nitrogen as soil in lupine-free plots, but it also held more water and organic matter.
choices.slip: Nitrogen is confounded with water and organic matter, so it does not isolate nitrogen as the cause.

choices.text: Lupine-free plots given nitrogen fertilizer for two growing seasons came to hold about as many other species as the plots densely covered by lupine.
On a neighboring volcano, plots with more lupine also held more species of other plants, although the nitrogen content of the soil there was not measured.
choices.slip: Repeats the correlation but says nothing about nitrogen as the mechanism.

choices.text: Most of the species found alongside dense lupine grow poorly in nitrogen-poor soil, but several of them also grow well in plots that have no lupine at all.
choices.slip: Partly fits, but species that thrive without lupine weaken the link to its nitrogen.

steps: The hypothesis is that nitrogen from lupine is what lets other species establish.
The best support removes lupine but supplies nitrogen, and shows the species count rising.
Only the fertilizer result does that; the others leave other causes open.
explanation.why: Adding nitrogen to lupine-free plots reproduces the effect without lupine, which points to nitrogen as the mechanism.
explanation.pattern: To test a mechanism, supply the proposed cause alone and see whether the effect follows.

items.passage: Economist Dalila Montenegro-Vail argues that opening a bank branch in a village raises its households' incomes. In a survey of 48 villages in the Ardel highlands, she found that villages with a branch had median household incomes 30 percent higher than villages without one, and the gap persisted after she adjusted for population and for distance to the nearest market town. She reports that the branches, which belong to a single lender, were all opened between 2012 and 2015, and she concludes that access to formal credit helps households earn more.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Montenegro-Vail's argument?

choices.text: Households in villages without a branch were more likely to borrow from informal lenders, who typically charge higher rates of interest than banks do.
choices.slip: This fits the idea that credit access matters; it does not weaken it.

choices.text: Loans made by the lender to households in the surveyed villages averaged about 8 percent of a household's annual income in the years after 2012.
choices.slip: The size of loans says nothing about whether branches or prior wealth explain the income gap.

choices.text: Villages with a branch had a larger share of households that held a bank account than villages without a branch did at the time of the survey.
choices.slip: Consistent with the claim; account-holding does not show which came first.

choices.text: Before opening any branch, the lender ranked highland villages by household income and chose its first sites from the highest-income villages.

steps: The claim is that the branch causes higher income.
Weaken it by showing the direction of cause could run the other way.
If the lender picked already-richer villages, the income gap predates the branches.
explanation.why: Choosing branch sites by income would produce the same gap even if branches did nothing for households.
explanation.pattern: Reverse causation weakens a causal claim: show that the supposed effect came first and drove the supposed cause.

items.passage: Archaeologist Nandini Peverell-Oyelaran proposes that the people of Skerrow Head, a coastal settlement occupied about 1,100 years ago, relied heavily on seafood. She measured a chemical ratio in bone collagen from 31 skeletons buried there; higher values indicate more marine foods in the diet. The average was 15.2. For comparison, she cites an average of 9.8 for 40 skeletons from an inland cemetery 30 kilometers away, and notes that values near 9 are typical of people who ate mainly crops and livestock raised on land. Peverell-Oyelaran takes the gap as evidence of heavy seafood consumption at Skerrow Head.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously undermine Peverell-Oyelaran's interpretation?

choices.text: Sheep and cattle grazing the salt marshes around Skerrow Head have collagen values near 15, so people eating their meat would show similar values.
Bone collagen from six Skerrow Head skeletons was too degraded to measure, so those individuals were left out of the average she reports.
choices.slip: Small exclusion of unmeasurable bones does not suggest a bias toward high values.

choices.text: Fish bones and shells were found in large quantities in the settlement's refuse deposits, along with the remains of cattle and sheep.
choices.slip: This supports seafood eating, with livestock a side detail.

choices.text: The inland cemetery's skeletons were of people who died on average about ten years younger than the people buried at Skerrow Head.
choices.slip: An age difference has no link to the marine ratio in the passage.

steps: The ratio is used as a sign of seafood in the diet.
To undermine it, find another food source at Skerrow Head that gives the same high ratio.
Salt-marsh livestock would give high values with no seafood.
explanation.why: If land animals at the site also give high values, the ratio no longer separates a seafood diet from a livestock diet.
explanation.pattern: A proxy measure supports a claim only if no other source produces the same reading.

items.passage: In her study of nineteenth-century lighthouse keepers' letters, historian Wilhelmina Odukoya-Stahl argues that keepers rarely described their isolation outright. Instead, she contends, they revealed it through an intense attention to the supply boat that brought mail and company, so that the boat's arrival became the emotional center of their letters. Her examples come from the correspondence of Edmund Rathbone-Ikeda, who kept a light on a rocky islet for eleven years and wrote to his sister at the end of each month. Odukoya-Stahl treats his letters as typical of the keepers she studied, noting that he almost never wrote the word 'lonely' and that he reported daily routines in a steady, practical tone.
items.question: Which quotation from Rathbone-Ikeda's letters would best illustrate Odukoya-Stahl's claim?

choices.text: 'The tender was a week late again, and I have counted the biscuit twice to be certain that it will last.'
choices.slip: Shows attention to the boat, but about supplies, not an emotional focus.

choices.text: 'I am well, and the lamp has not failed once this winter, though the nights are very long.'
choices.slip: A steady practical report with no link to the boat.

choices.text: 'The tender is due Thursday if the sea allows, and I find I have swept the landing twice already in readiness.'
'No one has spoken to me in a month, and I confess that the silence has begun to weigh upon me.'
choices.slip: States isolation outright, the opposite of her claim.

steps: Her claim: isolation is shown through eager attention to the boat, not stated.
The quotation must be about the boat and carry feeling indirectly.
Sweeping the landing in readiness does that.
explanation.why: The keeper's preparation for the boat expresses longing without naming it.
explanation.pattern: Match the quotation to the exact claim: indirect expression, not direct statement and not mere logistics.

items.passage: Educational psychologist Gunnhild Abernathy-Soto claims that short quizzes at the start of class improve retention because retrieving information strengthens memory, not simply because quizzes lead students to spend more time on the material. In a 2024 study across six sections of a statistics course, sections that began each class with a five-minute quiz averaged 78 on the final exam, compared with 71 in sections that began with a five-minute review of notes. However, study logs showed that students in the quiz sections spent about 20 more minutes per week studying outside class than students in the review sections.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Abernathy-Soto's claim?

choices.text: Within the quiz sections, the students who spent the most time studying outside class earned the highest scores on the final exam of the term.
choices.slip: Ties scores to study time, which supports the rival explanation.

choices.text: Quiz sections also outscored review sections on a midterm exam given halfway through the term, by a margin similar to the final-exam gap.
choices.slip: Repeats the gap but leaves the extra study time unaddressed.

choices.text: Students in the review sections said that they found the notes review less helpful for preparing for exams than the quizzes seemed to be.
choices.slip: Opinion about usefulness does not separate retrieval from extra time.

choices.text: In a second course where out-of-class study time was equal across sections, quiz sections still outscored review sections on the final by about 7 points.

steps: The rival explanation is that quiz students simply studied more.
Support requires a comparison where study time is the same and the quiz advantage remains.
Only the second course does this.
explanation.why: With study time equalized, the remaining 7-point gap cannot come from extra study time.
explanation.pattern: Strong support removes the confound by holding it constant.

items.passage: Ornithologist Casimir Delacroix-Nwosu claims that the low number of chicks raised by seabirds on the Haskeling Islands is caused mainly by black rats, which were accidentally introduced to the islands in the nineteenth century, rather than by a shortage of the small fish the birds feed on. Across the 14 islands he surveyed, colonies on the eight islands with rats raised an average of 12 chicks per 100 nests in a season, whereas colonies on the six rat-free islands raised an average of 58. Delacroix-Nwosu notes that the rat-free islands lie in the same stretch of ocean as the rat-infested ones and that the birds on all 14 islands forage over the same waters.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Delacroix-Nwosu's claim?

choices.text: Camera traps on three of the rat-infested islands recorded rats entering nests and eating eggs on dozens of nights during the breeding season.
choices.slip: Shows rats do harm; strengthens the claim.

choices.text: Colonies on the rat-free islands raised between 40 and 75 chicks per 100 nests, a wider spread than colonies on the rat-infested islands showed.
choices.slip: Spread in rat-free colonies is not about what causes the gap.

choices.text: On two islands where rats were eradicated in 2015, colonies were still raising fewer than 15 chicks per 100 nests four years afterward.
Rats were introduced to the different islands at different times between 1830 and 1920, and the oldest rat populations are now the densest.
choices.slip: Differences in timing and density do not bear on whether rats cause the low numbers.

steps: The claim is that rats cause the low chick numbers.
Weaken it with a case where rats are removed and the low numbers continue.
The eradication islands show exactly that.
explanation.why: If chick numbers stay low after the rats are gone, the rats were not the main cause.
explanation.pattern: Remove the proposed cause; if the effect persists, the causal claim is weakened.

items.passage: Urban planner Ravindra Kessler-Ogunbanjo argues that planting street trees lowers summer afternoon temperatures on residential blocks, a conclusion that critics dispute because wealthier neighborhoods tend to have more trees and also more air-conditioned buildings, parks, and light-colored roofs. Using satellite measurements in the city of Lantry, he found that blocks with dense tree canopy averaged 3.1 degrees Celsius cooler on summer afternoons than blocks with little canopy. He adds that the 40 blocks he compared are drawn from six neighborhoods across the city with a wide range of median household incomes.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Kessler-Ogunbanjo's argument against the critics' objection?

choices.text: Among the 40 blocks, those in higher-income neighborhoods were cooler on average than those in lower-income neighborhoods, whether or not they had dense canopy.
choices.slip: Income affects temperature independent of trees, which supports the critics.

choices.text: Within each of the six neighborhoods, blocks that gained new street trees in 2020 were cooler in 2023 than comparable blocks in that neighborhood that gained none.
Residents of the cooler blocks reported spending less on air conditioning during the summer than residents of the warmer blocks did.
choices.slip: Fits either explanation, since cooler blocks could be cooler for any reason.

choices.text: Surveys showed that most residents of the 40 blocks, whatever their income, said they preferred streets lined with trees to streets without trees.
choices.slip: Preference is irrelevant to temperature.

steps: The objection: income, not trees, explains the cooling.
A fair test compares blocks in the same neighborhood, so income is held fixed.
New trees producing cooling within each neighborhood does that.
explanation.why: Comparing like with like inside each neighborhood removes wealth as an explanation.
explanation.pattern: Answer a confound by comparing groups that match on it.

items.passage: Marine ecologist Taini Valdrecht-Oyelaran proposes that kelp forests along Cape Hollin shrank after 2012 mainly because sea urchins multiplied once a disease killed the sea stars that preyed on them, and not because the water grew warmer. Surveys of 30 reefs found that average kelp cover fell from 62 percent to 21 percent while urchin density rose from 4 to 31 per square meter. Over the same years the water on every reef warmed, by amounts that ranged from 0.4 to 1.6 degrees Celsius depending on the reef. Surveyors visited each reef once a year in late summer and counted urchins and measured kelp cover along the same 50-meter transect each time.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Valdrecht-Oyelaran's proposal?

choices.text: Reefs where the water warmed the most lost the most kelp, and those same reefs were also the ones on which urchin density increased most steeply.
choices.slip: Warming and urchins rose together, so it fits the rival cause equally.

choices.text: Reefs on which urchin density rose the most lost the most kelp, and this was true whether a reef had warmed by about 0.4 degrees or by about 1.6 degrees.
In laboratory tanks, urchins ate kelp faster at water temperatures like those now found on the reefs than at the cooler temperatures typical before 2012.
choices.slip: Makes warming the driver of grazing, favoring the rival.

choices.text: On every one of the 30 reefs, kelp cover was lower in the final survey than in the first, and urchin density was higher in the final survey than in the first.
choices.slip: Restates the shared trend that both causes explain.

steps: Warming varied from reef to reef, so it can be separated from urchin numbers.
Support needs reefs that differ in warming but show the same urchin-kelp link.
Urchin-linked kelp loss at both low and high warming does that.
explanation.why: If kelp loss tracks urchin increase at every level of warming, warming is not what drives the loss.
explanation.pattern: To separate two causes that rose together, find cases where one varies while the other is held steady.

items.passage: Literary scholar Solveig Palavecino argues that in her 1931 essay on the fishing town of Wenlow Harbor, the writer Winifred Rennick presents herself as a loyal booster of the town while quietly conveying that she regards its prosperity as fragile. Rennick calls the cannery the town's livelihood, praises her neighbors' thrift and cheer, and ends with a toast to the harbor's future. Palavecino notes that the essay never states a doubt outright, and that any doubt appears only in what Rennick chooses not to say or to look at. Her essay, written for a regional magazine, runs to eleven pages and quotes several of the town's longtime residents.
items.question: Which quotation from Rennick's essay, if used by Palavecino, would best illustrate her claim?

choices.text: "I tell every newcomer that the cannery will outlast us all, and the newcomers, hearing it from me and seeing my pride, have never once thought to doubt it for a moment."
choices.slip: Loyal boosterism only; no hint of doubt.

choices.text: "The pilings beneath the cannery have been rotting since my father's day, and the town council, which I have never trusted, has declined to pay for new ones."
choices.slip: States the doubt outright and is not boosterish.

choices.text: "Some in Wenlow will tell you the cannery is a fragile thing, but I have noticed that the ones who say so are never the ones who fish."
choices.slip: Names the fragility outright, only to dismiss it.

choices.text: "I tell every newcomer that the cannery will outlast us all, and I say it with a smile, though I have never gone down to look at the pilings."

steps: The claim has two parts: public loyalty and an unstated doubt.
Eliminate quotations that voice the doubt outright or show only loyalty.
Only one praises the cannery while avoiding the pilings.
explanation.why: The speaker boosts the cannery but her refusal to look at the pilings quietly signals fear.
explanation.pattern: For a two-part claim, the quotation must show both parts, and doubt that is only implied must stay implied.

items.passage: Archaeologist Pelagia Strandmark-Oduya argues that the 11 painted vessels found in the Dunmoor burial were made by potters living in the valley, not brought in from elsewhere. Chemical analysis shows that the clay in all 11 vessels matches the riverbank clay found throughout the valley, and the vessels' painted spirals appear on no pottery found outside the valley. She adds that the burial dates to about 1400 BCE, a period for which no kiln has yet been excavated anywhere in the valley. She also notes that the spirals were painted on before firing, in a mineral pigment that would not survive being applied to fired clay.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly undermine Strandmark-Oduya's argument?

choices.text: The valley's riverbank clay was sold in bulk to potters in a coastal town 60 kilometers away, where the spiral style was also painted then.
The riverbank clay of the valley has a mineral signature that has not been found in any other clay deposit within 200 kilometers of the burial site.
choices.slip: Strengthens a local origin.

choices.text: Two of the 11 vessels differ slightly in mineral content from the other nine, though both still match clay deposits found at several points in the valley.
choices.slip: Both still match local clay, so the claim stands.

choices.text: Potters in the valley in later periods worked in the spiral style and fired their vessels in kilns built beside the riverbank clay pits, a custom that continued for several centuries.
choices.slip: Suggests a local tradition, so it supports the argument.

steps: The evidence is that clay and style are local.
To undermine, show that local clay and style could also belong to vessels made somewhere else.
Bulk-sold clay and the same style on the coast does that.
explanation.why: Local clay does not prove local making if the clay was traded and the style was shared.
explanation.pattern: Evidence for where a material comes from does not show where it was worked; find the rival site.

items.passage: A school district tested a reading program in 12 schools and used 12 matched schools as a comparison. At the end of the year, research director Leopold Achterberg-Nwosu reported that the program "helped struggling readers more than it helped strong readers." Average gains in test points were as follows. Struggling readers gained 8 points in program schools and 2 points in comparison schools. Strong readers gained 10 points in program schools and 7 points in comparison schools. The district gave the same end-of-year test in all 24 schools and classified readers as struggling or strong using the previous year's scores.
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses the data to support the director's claim?

choices.text: Struggling readers in program schools gained 8 points, four times the 2-point gain of struggling readers in comparison schools, so the program clearly raised their scores.
choices.slip: Never compares with strong readers' benefit.

choices.text: Struggling readers in program schools gained 8 points, more than the 7 points gained by strong readers in comparison schools, so the program narrowed the gap between groups.
choices.slip: Mixes a program group with a comparison group.

choices.text: The program added 6 points to struggling readers' gains (8 versus 2) but only 3 points to strong readers' gains (10 versus 7).
Struggling readers in comparison schools gained only 2 points while strong readers there gained 7, showing that struggling readers need the program more than strong readers do.
choices.slip: Uses comparison schools only, so it shows need, not effect.

steps: The claim is about the program's effect, which means program gain minus comparison gain.
Struggling readers: 8 - 2 = 6. Strong readers: 10 - 7 = 3.
The choice stating both differences supports the claim.
explanation.why: Only a within-group program-versus-comparison difference measures the program's effect for each group.
explanation.pattern: To judge which group benefits more, compute each group's gain over its own comparison.

items.passage: Geologist Barnaby Wrightsborough-Teko argues that the thick layer of sand in the bed of Lake Pelham was laid down in a single catastrophic storm surge rather than accumulating slowly over several centuries. The layer is 14 centimeters thick and holds pollen, charcoal fragments, and scraps of leaves. Cores taken at five sites show the layer at the same depth below the surface, buried under about 60 centimeters of finer mud that settled afterward. Wrightsborough-Teko adds that no comparable sand layer appears anywhere else in the cores, and that her team measured the layer's thickness at each core site and found that it varied by less than 2 centimeters.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Wrightsborough-Teko's argument?

choices.text: Cores from the lake bed show 22 similar sand layers over the past 3,000 years, each separated from the next by a thin band of organic mud.
choices.slip: Points to repeated events, not to the one layer.

choices.text: Within the layer, sand grains grade smoothly from coarse at the bottom to fine at the top with no breaks, and the leaf scraps inside all come from one season.
The sand in the layer matches the mineral makeup of the riverbed where the river that feeds the lake enters along its northern shore.
choices.slip: Gives the source, not the timing.

choices.text: Radiocarbon dates for charcoal at the bottom of the layer and charcoal at the top of the layer differ by about 40 years, with the top charcoal the younger of the two.
choices.slip: Implies slow accumulation over decades.

steps: The claim is about timing: one event, not slow buildup.
Evidence must show the layer formed in one continuous episode.
Smooth grading with no breaks and leaves from one season does that.
explanation.why: Unbroken grading and single-season leaves indicate that the sand settled in one episode.
explanation.pattern: For event-versus-gradual claims, choose evidence about continuity and timing, not about source.

items.passage: Psychologist Philomena Obuya-Strand hypothesizes that sleep strengthens newly learned memories through processes that occur only during sleep, and not merely by sparing them from interference by new experiences. In a study, 60 volunteers memorized 40 word pairs in the evening. Half then slept for eight hours; the other half spent the same eight hours at ordinary daytime activities.
