All volunteers were healthy adults aged 18 to 30, and none took sleep medication or caffeine in the 12 hours before the test. The next day the sleepers recalled an average of 31 pairs and the other volunteers an average of 24.
items.question: Which additional finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?

choices.text: Volunteers who slept only four hours recalled an average of 27 pairs, more than the awake group but fewer than the volunteers who slept eight hours.
choices.slip: More awake hours also meant more interference.

choices.text: Volunteers who learned the pairs in the morning and stayed awake all day recalled fewer pairs eight hours later than volunteers who learned them at night and slept.
choices.slip: Still confounds sleep with ordinary daytime activity.

choices.text: Within the awake group, volunteers who reported more distracting events during the day recalled fewer pairs than volunteers who reported fewer such events.
choices.slip: Supports the interference explanation, the rival.

choices.text: Volunteers who stayed awake eight hours in a dim, quiet room, without reading or conversation, recalled fewer pairs than the sleepers, 26 on average against 31.

steps: The rival explanation is interference from new experiences.
Support needs awake volunteers with little interference who still recall less.
The dim, quiet room awake group removes interference.
explanation.why: If quiet wakefulness still leaves recall below sleep, interference alone cannot explain the sleep advantage.
explanation.pattern: To support a mechanism, remove the rival (here, interference) and check that the effect remains.

items.passage: Developmental psychologist Rosamund Achebe-Thorvaldsen claims that being bilingual itself improves children's ability to switch between tasks, a conclusion critics dispute because the bilingual children in her sample were more likely to have parents with advanced degrees, a factor linked to stronger task-switching in many studies. In a sample of 200 eight-year-olds, bilingual children completed a switching task about 14 percent faster than monolingual children. The task asked children to sort cards by color and then by shape, with the sorting rule changing without warning, and every child was tested individually. Achebe-Thorvaldsen notes that the sample included families across a wide range of parental education.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Achebe-Thorvaldsen's claim against the critics' objection?

choices.text: The bilingual advantage appeared in each of the three cities where the sample children lived, even though the cities differ greatly in size and in the languages spoken.
choices.slip: Replication across cities does not hold parental education fixed.

choices.text: Among the bilingual children, those who used both languages every day completed the task faster than those who used their second language only rarely or not at all.
choices.slip: Parental education could still explain who uses both languages daily.

choices.text: Among children whose parents had the same level of education, bilingual children completed the task faster than monolingual children, at every level in the sample.
Children of parents with advanced degrees completed the task faster than children of parents with less education, whether the children in the sample were bilingual or monolingual.
choices.slip: Shows parental education matters, which supports the critics.

steps: The objection: parental education, not bilingualism, explains the speed.
A fair test compares bilingual and monolingual children with the same parental education.
Only one choice does that at every level.
explanation.why: Comparing within levels of parental education removes that factor as an explanation.
explanation.pattern: Answer a confound by comparing groups that match on it.

items.passage: Historian Evander Offenbach-Wray argues that in 1887 the Valmere harbor commission postponed dredging the channel not because of a shortage of funds, as the standard account holds, but because its members feared that a deeper channel would draw trade away to the rival port of Brindle Quay. He points out that the commission's published statements never mentioned the rival port, though its private minutes survive. The commission deferred the dredging contract at four consecutive meetings that year. The surviving minute book records the commission's discussions in the secretary's own words, and a report that year put the cost of the work at fourteen hundred pounds.
items.question: Which quotation from the commission's minutes would best support Offenbach-Wray's argument?

choices.text: "The treasurer reports a surplus of sixteen hundred pounds in the dredging account; nevertheless it was resolved that no contract be let until Brindle Quay's trustees declare their intentions."

"The treasurer reports the dredging account stands at three hundred pounds, short of the contractor's estimate of fourteen hundred; it was resolved to postpone the work until the spring tolls are collected."
choices.slip: Fits the standard funding account.

choices.text: "Mr. Garrow observed that a deeper channel would admit larger vessels and bring a good deal of new trade to the port, a view the commission received with general approval and some enthusiasm."
choices.slip: Shows approval of dredging, not fear of the rival.

choices.text: "The commission resolved to invite the Brindle Quay trustees to share in the cost of dredging, since both harbors would gain a share of the larger ships' trade in future years."
choices.slip: Shows cooperation with the rival, not fear.

steps: The claim has two parts: funds were not the obstacle, and the rival port was.
A surplus rules out money; waiting on Brindle Quay points to the rival.
Only one quotation does both.
explanation.why: The surplus removes the funding explanation while the wait for Brindle Quay shows the real concern.
explanation.pattern: Quotation evidence must fit every part of the claim, including the part it denies.

items.passage: Ornithologist Dagny Foulkes-Amari proposes that first-year garden warblers choose their autumn departure direction chiefly from the rotation of the night sky rather than from Earth's magnetic field. She raised 60 warblers indoors with no view of the real sky, then tested each bird alone in a round cage during the migration season and recorded the direction of its hops. Half the birds were tested under a projected planetarium sky matching the real sky for their latitude, and half under a uniformly dark ceiling. In both rooms, the magnetic field was left at its natural strength and orientation.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Foulkes-Amari's proposal?

choices.text: Birds under the planetarium sky hopped mostly toward the southwest, the direction in which wild warblers of that region depart, while birds under the dark ceiling showed no preferred direction.
Birds in both rooms hopped mostly toward the southwest, although birds under the planetarium sky did so somewhat more consistently than birds under the dark ceiling.
choices.slip: Direction without the sky shows the magnetic field is enough.

choices.text: Birds under the planetarium sky hopped toward the southwest, as did 40 wild adult warblers tested in the same kind of cage under the real night sky at that latitude, a result she took to show that her planetarium sky was realistic.
choices.slip: No dark-ceiling comparison, so the sky is not isolated as the cue.

choices.text: Birds under the planetarium sky hopped toward the southwest, and a third group tested under the same sky with the magnetic field reversed hopped toward the northeast.
choices.slip: Following the reversed field points to magnetism, not the sky.

steps: Her claim is that the sky, not the magnetic field, sets direction.
The magnetic field is the same in both rooms, so only the sky differs.
Direction only under the sky, and none without it, isolates the sky.
explanation.why: Only the sky varies between rooms, so a direction found under it and absent without it supports her proposal.
explanation.pattern: For 'support' items, pick the result in which only the proposed cause varies.

items.passage: Transportation analyst Emeka Lindfors-Barr argues that the protected bike lanes built along Merrion Row in 2019 made cycling there safer, not merely less common. Critics reply that injuries on the corridor fell only because fewer people rode it after construction disrupted the street. City records show 72 reported cycling injuries on the corridor in 2018 and 54 in 2021. Automated counters recorded about 410,000 bike trips on the corridor in 2018 and about 360,000 in 2021; the counters were the same type and in the same locations in both years.
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the text to support Lindfors-Barr's argument against the critics?

choices.text: Injuries fell from 72 to 54, a drop of 25 percent, which shows the lanes made cycling safer no matter how many people rode the corridor.
choices.slip: Ignores that ridership also fell, so it does not answer the critics.

choices.text: Injuries fell by 18 while trips fell by about 50,000, so roughly one injury was avoided for every 2,800 trips that were lost.
choices.slip: Treats the injury drop as a result of lost trips, which supports the critics.

choices.text: Injuries fell by 25 percent while trips fell by only about 50,000, a small share of the 410,000 total, so fewer trips cannot account for any of the decline.
choices.slip: Overstates: some of the drop could still come from fewer trips.

choices.text: Injuries fell by 25 percent, from 72 to 54, while trips fell by only about 12 percent, from 410,000 to 360,000, so injuries per trip declined.

steps: Critics say fewer riders explains fewer injuries.
Compare the change in injuries with the change in trips: 25 percent versus about 12 percent.
Injuries fell faster than riding, so the rate per trip fell.
explanation.why: Only the key compares injuries with trips as percentages, which shows the rate fell.
explanation.pattern: When critics cite a changed denominator, choose the rate comparison.

items.passage: Fisheries biologist Soren Vandekamp argues that the perch population of Lake Orrow has collapsed, citing the annual gill-net survey: the survey caught 1,840 perch in 2015 and 610 in 2023. The survey uses nets of the same mesh size set at the same 15 sites each year, and every net is left out overnight. Vandekamp notes that anglers' reports from the lake describe slower fishing in recent years, and he concludes that the lake now holds only about a third as many perch as it did eight years ago.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously undermine Vandekamp's conclusion?

choices.text: Two other lakes in the region, surveyed with identical nets and procedures, also showed a drop of more than half in perch catch between 2015 and 2023.
choices.slip: Matching declines elsewhere support a real decline.

choices.text: Perch caught in the 2023 survey were, on average, four centimeters longer than perch caught in the 2015 survey, although both surveys caught perch of many sizes.
choices.slip: Fish length does not show whether the number of perch fell.

choices.text: The survey set 120 nets overnight in 2015 but only 40 in 2023, so the catch per net was about the same in the two years.
Perch in Lake Orrow feed mainly on insect larvae, and the larvae were as abundant in 2023 as they were in 2015.
choices.slip: Plentiful food gives a reason to doubt a collapse but is not evidence about the number of perch.

steps: Catch per year depends on how many nets were set.
1,840 over 120 nets and 610 over 40 nets are both about 15 fish per net.
So the catch fell because effort fell, not necessarily the population.
explanation.why: If catch per net is unchanged, the drop in total catch reflects less netting rather than fewer perch.
explanation.pattern: Check whether a drop in a total count comes from a drop in effort.

items.passage: Critic Hjalmar Teague-Osei argues that in Imogen Rathmell's novel The Tidewater Ledger, the narrator Pru, a bookkeeper, presents her loyalty to her employer as a matter of principle while the story shows that fear of losing her lodging is what actually keeps her there. Pru rents an attic room above the firm's offices for far less than the going rate in town. She describes herself as bound by duty to the owner, Mr. Arkwright, who rarely speaks to her. Teague-Osei contends that readers should watch what Pru does, not what she says, when the owner announces that the building will be sold.
items.question: Which quotation from the novel would most directly illustrate Teague-Osei's claim?

choices.text: "I owe Mr. Arkwright more than any wage," Pru said, but when he mentioned the sale of the building she asked at once, before he had finished, what notice the tenants would be given.

"I owe Mr. Arkwright more than any wage," Pru said, and when he mentioned the sale of the building she thanked him for telling her himself and returned quietly to her ledgers for the rest of that afternoon.
choices.slip: Her action matches her stated principle.

choices.text: Pru told herself each morning that the firm's work mattered, though in the evenings she admitted in her diary that she envied the clerks who had left to start their own businesses.
choices.slip: Private restlessness is not fear of losing lodging.

choices.text: When the sale was announced, Pru wrote to Mr. Arkwright offering to stay on at lower pay, saying she could not imagine the offices without a clerk who understood their accounts.
choices.slip: Reads as professional pride, with no link to the attic room.

steps: The claim: her stated principle hides fear of losing her room.
Look for words and action pulling apart at the news of the sale.
Only the key has her ask about tenants' notice, her room, right after professing duty.
explanation.why: Her first reaction to the sale concerns her housing, which contradicts her stated principle.
explanation.pattern: For quotation items, match the exact tension the claim describes.

items.passage: Archaeologist Basil Quenneville proposes that the incised-rim and smooth-rim pottery found on the Verlow terrace were made by two communities living there at the same time, not by one community whose style changed over the centuries. Excavators recovered 140 incised-rim and 95 smooth-rim sherds. The terrace was built up by repeated river floods, each leaving a separate band of silt; the bands are numbered 1 (oldest) to 6 (newest). Charcoal from bands 2 through 5 gave radiocarbon dates spanning about 300 years.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Quenneville's proposal?

choices.text: Incised-rim sherds made up most of the pottery in the older bands and smooth-rim sherds most of the pottery in the newer bands, though bands 3 and 4 each held a few sherds of both styles.
choices.slip: Gradual replacement with only a brief overlap suggests succession.

choices.text: The two styles overlapped only in band 4, with incised-rim sherds found in bands 1 through 4 and smooth-rim sherds in bands 4 through 6.
choices.slip: A single overlapping band fits a hand-over from one style to the other.

choices.text: Both styles occurred in every one of bands 2 through 5, and in several bands sherds of the two styles lay together in the same hearths.
Both styles occurred in bands 2 through 5, and the clay used for both styles came from the same stretch of riverbank.
choices.slip: Shared clay points to one community, which opposes the proposal.

steps: Coexistence means both styles share the same time slices.
Succession would show one style replacing another.
Both styles in each band, even at shared hearths, shows they were used at once.
explanation.why: Finding both styles throughout the bands and at shared hearths indicates simultaneous use.
explanation.pattern: For contemporaneity, look for overlap across many layers, not a gradient or a single overlap.

items.passage: Exercise physiologist Teodoro Wennerstrom claims that a compound in tart cherry juice speeds muscle recovery after hard running. In his trial, 48 runners completed a punishing 20-kilometer run and then drank either tart cherry juice or an equal volume of water over the next two days. Runners given the juice reported that their leg soreness returned to normal about 11 hours sooner, on average, than did runners given water. Assignment to the two drinks was random. Runners knew which drink they had received, and soreness was measured only by a questionnaire the runners completed themselves.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously undermine the claim that a compound in the juice speeds recovery?

choices.text: Blood samples taken from the juice group showed higher levels of the compound than blood samples taken from the water group.
choices.slip: Shows the compound was absorbed, which supports the claim.

choices.text: A second group of 12 runners given a juice with the compound removed reported times to normal soreness similar to those of the water group.
choices.slip: Supports the claim by removing the compound removes the benefit.

choices.text: Runners in the juice group reported sleeping about 20 minutes longer on average on each of the two recovery nights than did runners in the water group.
choices.slip: Extra sleep could be a result of the compound, so it need not undermine the claim.

choices.text: In an earlier study, runners who were told that a drink would speed recovery reported faster return to normal soreness even when the drink was only colored water.

steps: The trial was unblinded and relied on self-report.
A belief that a drink helps can by itself change reports of soreness.
Expectation alone producing the same result gives a rival explanation for the 11 hours.
explanation.why: The expectation effect offers a rival cause for the self-reported difference.
explanation.pattern: Look for a rival explanation that fits the same data when design flaws are described.

items.passage: Plant pathologist Ludovica Haverstraw-Osei suspects that a root fungus has spread through the Orrel highlands mainly on the boots of hikers rather than by windborne spores. Surveying 90 forest plots, she recorded the share of trees infected in each plot and the plot's distance from the nearest hiking trail. The highlands' prevailing wind blows from west to east, and the plots lie on both sides of a long north-south ridge crossed by two trails. Spores of similar fungi are known to travel several kilometers before settling.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Haverstraw-Osei's suspicion?

choices.text: Infection rates were higher in plots east of the ridge than in plots west of it, regardless of each plot's distance from the nearest trail.
choices.slip: Higher infection downwind points to wind dispersal.

choices.text: Infection rates were highest in plots beside trails and fell steadily with distance from the trails, whether a plot lay east or west of the ridge.
Infection rates were higher in plots near trails than in plots far from them, and the plots nearest the trails were also the ones with the oldest trees.
choices.slip: Tree age is a rival explanation for the pattern near trails.

choices.text: Plots beside the two busiest trails had higher infection than plots beside the two quietest trails, but infection did not vary with distance from the trails within either pair.
choices.slip: The lack of any distance pattern is what wind spread would also produce.

steps: Boot spread should center on trails; wind spread should follow the wind.
Infection that depends on trail distance on both sides of the ridge fits boots.
Other choices have a different cause that fits equally well or better.
explanation.why: Infection highest near trails and declining with distance, on both sides of the ridge, fits spread by hikers and not by wind.
explanation.pattern: Support a transmission route with a spatial pattern the rival route cannot produce.

items.passage: Trade economist Philippa Orlowska-Beck argues that the 2020 tariff on steel pipe from Dorvenia did not reduce the country's total steel pipe imports but redirected them to other suppliers. Customs records show that Dorvenia supplied 420,000 tonnes of steel pipe in 2019 and 150,000 tonnes in 2021, and that total steel pipe imports from all countries were 1.10 million tonnes in 2019. The tariff applied to Dorvenian pipe only. Pipe is used mainly in construction, and Orlowska-Beck acknowledges that construction activity was somewhat lower in 2021 than in 2019.
items.question: Which choice most effectively uses data to support Orlowska-Beck's argument?

choices.text: Imports from other suppliers rose from 680,000 tonnes in 2019 to 950,000 tonnes in 2021, a rise equal to the fall in imports from Dorvenia, so total imports were unchanged at 1.10 million tonnes.
Imports from Dorvenia fell by 270,000 tonnes between 2019 and 2021, a drop of about 64 percent, which shows the tariff sharply cut purchases from the supplier it targeted.
choices.slip: True, but it says nothing about where the lost pipe came from.

choices.text: Imports from other suppliers rose from 680,000 tonnes in 2019 to 800,000 tonnes in 2021, a rise of about 18 percent that partly offset the fall in imports from Dorvenia over the same two-year period.
choices.slip: A partial offset means total imports fell, against her claim.

choices.text: Domestic steel pipe production rose by about 270,000 tonnes between 2019 and 2021, roughly the amount by which imports from Dorvenia fell over those years.
choices.slip: Suggests domestic output replaced it, not other importers.

steps: Her claim: total imports stayed the same.
Dorvenian pipe fell by 270,000, so others must rise by 270,000.
680,000 to 950,000 does that exactly.
explanation.why: Only the key shows the other suppliers' gain exactly matching the Dorvenian loss, leaving the total unchanged.
explanation.pattern: Check that a 'redirected, not reduced' claim needs the offset to be complete.

items.passage: Agronomist Bertil Hallgrimsen-Sule reports that applying biochar, a charcoal-like soil additive, raised maize yields. Across 24 field plots, the 12 plots that received biochar averaged 7.9 tonnes of maize per hectare, compared with 6.8 tonnes for the 12 plots that received none. Plots were assigned at random, and all plots received the same fertilizer and irrigation. Hallgrimsen-Sule concludes that biochar reliably raises maize yield by about one tonne per hectare.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Hallgrimsen-Sule's conclusion?

choices.text: The highest-yielding plot in the whole trial, at 12.3 tonnes per hectare, was one of the plots that received biochar.
choices.slip: One high plot alone does not show the average depends on it.

choices.text: Plots with biochar drained water more slowly after heavy rain than plots without it, which is a known effect of the additive in clay soils.
choices.slip: A mechanism detail that does not bear on the yield figures.

choices.text: Two of the biochar plots yielded over 12 tonnes per hectare, while the other ten yielded between 6.4 and 7.6 tonnes, a range overlapping that of the plots without biochar.
In a trial in a different region with 40 plots, biochar raised maize yields by only about 0.4 tonnes per hectare.
choices.slip: A smaller but still positive effect elsewhere does not undermine this trial.

steps: The average of 7.9 could come from two extreme plots.
Ten of twelve biochar plots resemble the controls.
So the gain is not reliable across plots.
explanation.why: The advantage comes from two plots, so biochar does not reliably raise yield.
explanation.pattern: An average gain can hide that only a few plots drive it.

items.passage: Historian Casper Lindqvist-Oyelaran claims that the Quillhaven wool mill closed in 1887 because of rising coal costs, not because of the five-week strike that took place that spring. The mill's owner, in letters from 1887, blamed the strike. Lindqvist-Oyelaran notes that the mill's account books survive, that the strike lasted from mid-April to late May, and that coal prices in the region roughly doubled between 1885 and 1887. He argues that the account books, not the owner's letters, should guide historians.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Lindqvist-Oyelaran's claim?

choices.text: The owner's letters blame the strike for the closure and mention coal prices only once, in passing.
choices.slip: Reflects the owner's view, which the claim rejects.

choices.text: The account books show that, the winter before the strike began, production was cut to two days a week and coal purchases were halved.
Several other mills in the district closed between 1885 and 1887, a period when coal prices there doubled.
choices.slip: Fits coal costs but says nothing about this mill's timing relative to the strike.

choices.text: After the strike ended, the workers offered to return at lower wages, but the owner refused and sold the machinery within a month of the settlement.
choices.slip: Suggests the owner wanted to close, which fits either cause.

steps: The claim: coal costs, not the strike, caused the closing.
Evidence must show trouble at this mill before the strike.
Cuts in output and coal purchases before the strike do that.
explanation.why: Production and coal cuts before the strike point to fuel costs as the earlier cause.
explanation.pattern: Support a cause by showing it came first at the same site.

items.passage: Agronomist Marisol Ekwueme-Hart claims that sowing hairy vetch between corn seasons raises the next corn crop's yield by adding nitrogen to the soil. She surveyed 24 fields in the Tarnley basin. The 12 fields that had been sown with vetch averaged 11.2 tonnes of corn per hectare; the 12 that had not averaged 9.8. All 24 fields were planted with the same corn variety, received the same fertilizer rate, and were harvested in the same week during a single growing season. Each grower in the basin had decided for himself or herself whether to sow vetch, and Ekwueme-Hart concludes that the 1.4-tonne gap reflects the effect of the vetch.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Ekwueme-Hart's conclusion?

choices.text: Growers who sowed vetch were mostly those farming the basin's deeper, better-drained soils, where corn has long outyielded corn on thinner soils whatever the previous cover.

Four of the 12 unsown fields had grown soybeans the previous season, a crop that also leaves added nitrogen in the soil after it is harvested, though the soybeans were not sown deliberately for that purpose.
choices.slip: Raises unsown yields yet they still lagged, so it favors the vetch claim.

choices.text: Among the 12 vetch fields, the six that received above-average rainfall during the summer averaged higher corn yields than the six that received below-average rainfall.
choices.slip: Varies within the vetch group and says nothing about the gap between groups.

choices.text: Eight of the 12 vetch fields were larger than any of the unsown fields, though field size in the basin ranges widely, from about 4 hectares to about 40 hectares.
choices.slip: Size is not tied to yield here, so no rival cause is offered.

steps: Claim: vetch caused the 1.4-tonne gap; growers chose their own treatment.
A weakener offers a rival reason the vetch fields would yield more anyway.
Better soils among vetch growers explain the gap without vetch.
explanation.why: Vetch-sowing growers farming better soils would out-yield others whatever the cover crop.
explanation.pattern: Self-selection: when subjects choose the treatment, look for a trait that goes with the choice and the outcome.

items.passage: Limnologist Ravi Dellacourt-Ng hypothesizes that fish die-offs in Dunmere Lake are triggered by sudden drops in dissolved oxygen, not by high water temperature. Over one summer his team recorded dissolved oxygen and water temperature at dawn on 30 mornings and noted whether dead fish were found along the shore. Oxygen fell below 2 milligrams per liter on 8 of the mornings, and temperature exceeded 26 degrees Celsius on other mornings, and the two conditions sometimes occurred together. The team did not alter any conditions in the lake, and no other water-quality measurement, including pH and turbidity, showed a change on the mornings when dead fish were found along the shore.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Dellacourt-Ng's hypothesis?

choices.text: Dead fish were found on 7 of the 8 mornings with oxygen below 2 milligrams per liter, and on 8 of the 10 mornings with temperature above 26 degrees.
choices.slip: Both conditions predict die-offs here, so it cannot separate oxygen from heat.

choices.text: Dead fish were found on 7 of the 8 mornings with oxygen below 2 milligrams per liter, including 3 of the 4 such mornings with cool water, and on 1 of the other 22 mornings.
Dead fish were found on all 6 mornings when oxygen was below 2 milligrams per liter and temperature was above 26 degrees, and on none of the other 24 mornings.
choices.slip: Only the joint condition is tested; no morning isolates oxygen.

choices.text: Dead fish were found on 5 of the 9 mornings when temperature exceeded 26 degrees but oxygen stayed above 2 milligrams per liter, and on 2 of the 5 mornings when oxygen was low but temperature was cooler.
choices.slip: Die-offs are more frequent with heat alone than with low oxygen alone, which favors temperature.

steps: The hypothesis: oxygen, not heat, triggers die-offs.
Support must compare low oxygen with cool water against the other conditions.
Die-offs on 3 of 4 cool, low-oxygen mornings and almost none otherwise isolate oxygen.
explanation.why: It shows die-offs with low oxygen even when the water was cool, and almost none elsewhere.
explanation.pattern: Separate two overlapping causes by finding cases where one occurs without the other.

items.passage: Critic Henrik Salvatore-Obi argues that in the poem "Winter Allotment," the speaker's grief for her father is expressed not through statements of sorrow but through her insistence on finishing his unfinished garden work. The poem does not mention the death in its first three stanzas, and the speaker describes only his tools and the rows he left half-dug. In the final stanza she completes the work without once naming the man she is doing it for, a restraint that Salvatore-Obi finds typical of the poem as a whole. He contends that the speaker uses labor to avoid saying what she feels, yet that the exactness of her attention to each task gives the feeling away anyway.
items.question: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: "Each time I lift his spade I say aloud that I miss him, and the empty shed answers me only with a cold draft beneath the door."
choices.slip: States the grief outright instead of conveying it through labor.

choices.text: "I leave the half-dug rows exactly as they lie and walk the road the long way round, so as not to pass his gate at dusk."
choices.slip: Shows avoidance but not the finishing of his work.

choices.text: "I turned the last four rows he'd left, each furrow as straight as the string he'd pulled, and did not look up until the light was gone."
"I set the beans at six-inch intervals and the peas along the south wall, as the seed packets advise, and the work went well enough this year."
choices.slip: Shows labor but no avoidance and no trace of him or of feeling.

steps: Claim has two halves: labor stands in for stated grief, and precision betrays the feeling.
The quotation must show finishing his work, avoidance of looking up, and care in his manner.
Only the third choice finishes his rows to his standard and avoids looking up.
explanation.why: The speaker finishes his rows exactly as he would have, working until dark without pausing.
explanation.pattern: For a two-part claim, reject quotations that satisfy only one part.

items.passage: Astronomer Ilse Bramwell-Ojo hypothesizes that a small, close-orbiting planet has no substantial atmosphere. Given the planet's distance from its star, a bare rock that does not move heat around should reach about 1,190 kelvin on its sunlit side and be extremely cold on its night side, while a thick atmosphere circulating heat would hold the sunlit side near 900 kelvin and warm the night side considerably. Her team measured infrared light from the planet at several points in its orbit, which allows the two sides to be measured separately. The team also confirmed that the planet's orbit is nearly circular, so its distance from the star changes little, and that the star's brightness was steady during the observations.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Bramwell-Ojo's hypothesis?

choices.text: The sunlit side measured about 1,170 kelvin, and the night side measured about 700 kelvin, consistent with heat reaching the dark side.
choices.slip: A warm night side points to heat circulation by an atmosphere.

choices.text: The sunlit side measured about 900 kelvin, and the night side was too cold to detect, which shows a bare surface can be cooler than predicted.
choices.slip: Day-side temperature matches the atmosphere prediction, not the bare-rock one.

choices.text: The planet's measured mass and radius together indicate a rocky composition similar to Earth's, with a surface of silicate rock.
choices.slip: Rocky composition does not decide whether an atmosphere is present.

choices.text: The sunlit side measured about 1,170 kelvin, and the night side was too cold to detect, consistent with almost no heat moving between the sides.

steps: Bare rock predicts a hot day side near 1,190 K and a frigid night side.
An atmosphere predicts a cooler day side near 900 K and a warm night side.
Only a hot day side with an undetectable night side matches both halves of the bare-rock prediction.
explanation.why: Both sides match the bare-rock prediction and neither matches the atmosphere prediction.
explanation.pattern: Check both predictions of a model; a mixed result does not support it.

items.passage: Education researcher Marguerite Adeyemi-Lund claims that a 12-week tutoring program raised students' math scores. Sixty students were assigned by lottery to tutoring, which took place after school three times a week, and sixty to no tutoring; both groups followed the same curriculum with the same teachers, and the two groups had nearly identical mean scores on a math test at the start. A second test at 12 weeks was completed by 48 tutored students and 58 untutored students; the tutored group's mean was 74 and the untutored group's was 68. Adeyemi-Lund's analysis included only students who completed the second test, and she reports that the tutored group's gain was statistically significant.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously undermine Adeyemi-Lund's claim?

choices.text: Of the 2 untutored students who did not complete the second test, both had been in the bottom quarter of the group on the first test.
choices.slip: Their absence raises the untutored mean, so the true gap is, if anything, larger.

choices.text: Of the 12 tutored students who did not complete the second test, 9 had been in the bottom quarter of the group on the first test.
Tutored students who completed the second test had attended an average of 31 of the 36 scheduled sessions, and most said they found the sessions helpful.
choices.slip: Attendance among completers says nothing about who dropped out.

choices.text: Several tutored students scored lower on the second test than on the first test, though the tutored group's mean still rose over the period.
choices.slip: Individual declines are compatible with a higher group mean.

steps: Only completers were analyzed; 12 tutored students left versus 2 untutored.
If the tutored dropouts were mostly weak scorers, the tutored mean is inflated by their absence.
Nine of 12 from the bottom quarter does exactly that.
explanation.why: Losing mostly low scorers from the tutored group would raise its mean without any tutoring effect.
explanation.pattern: Attrition bias: check who left each group, not just how many.

items.passage: Botanist Anselm Kowalczyk-Reyes hypothesizes that seeds of the desert shrub Brandle's sage germinate after wildfires because of chemicals in smoke, not because of the intense heat of the fire. In a greenhouse, his team treated seeds from the same parent plants in different ways and then watered all seeds identically for 30 days. Seeds were kept on moist filter paper in identical dishes at 20 degrees Celsius, and a seed counted as germinated once a root emerged. Earlier work indicates that heating seeds to 80 degrees Celsius for five minutes reproduces the heat that seeds near the soil surface experience in a fire, and that smoke water is a standard stand-in for the chemicals in smoke.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Kowalczyk-Reyes's hypothesis?

choices.text: Seeds that were both heated at 80 degrees and soaked in smoke water germinated at 64 percent, while untreated seeds germinated at only 6 percent.
choices.slip: Applies both treatments at once, so it cannot show which one matters.

choices.text: Seeds heated at 80 degrees germinated at 58 percent regardless of whether they were afterward soaked in smoke water or in plain water.
choices.slip: Heat alone raises germination, which favors the heat explanation.

choices.text: Smoke water alone raised germination to 61 percent, whereas heating to 80 degrees alone gave 7 percent, close to the 6 percent of untreated seeds.
Seeds soaked in smoke water germinated at 61 percent, while seeds soaked in water drawn from burned soil with the ash filtered out germinated at only 12 percent.
choices.slip: Compares smoke with ash water and never tests heat.

steps: The hypothesis: smoke chemicals, not heat, trigger germination.
Support requires smoke without heat to work and heat without smoke to fail.
61 percent for smoke alone and 7 percent for heat alone, near the 6 percent baseline, show both.
explanation.why: Smoke alone raises germination far above baseline while heat alone does not.
explanation.pattern: Test each factor separately against an untreated baseline.

items.passage: Critic Beatriz Lanfranchi-Quist argues that the narrator of the novel The Long Meadow recalls her childhood summers with real fondness while repeatedly signaling that she knows her memory has improved them. The narration is built from the narrator's own recollections, and she often pauses to compare them with letters, photographs, and other people's accounts. The narrator, now in her sixties, never says her recollections are false, and she does not abandon them even when the evidence she cites cuts against them. Lanfranchi-Quist contends that the novel's emotional force comes from this double stance: the narrator keeps the summers she loves even as she concedes that the record may not support them.
items.question: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.text: "Every morning the meadow was gold, and every evening my mother called us in from the hay as the swifts came down low over the hedge."
choices.slip: Fond recollection with no sign that she doubts it.

choices.text: "The meadow is a car park now, and the swifts, I'm told, went elsewhere years ago, and nobody my age remembers the place as I do."
choices.slip: Reports change and loss, not an improved memory she keeps.

choices.text: "I cannot be sure the house had a green door; the photographs show it grey, and after all these years I have stopped arguing with them."
choices.slip: Doubts her memory but shows no fondness and gives it up.

choices.text: "The summers I keep were all warm; my sister says it rained a week in 1974, and I suppose she is right, but I cannot make that week come back."

steps: The claim needs fondness, awareness of improvement, and keeping the memory anyway.
A quotation can fail by lacking awareness, lacking fondness, or abandoning the memory.
The last choice keeps the warm summers, concedes the rainy week, and will not restore it.
explanation.why: She keeps her warm summers while conceding the record contradicts them.
explanation.pattern: A two-sided claim needs a quotation that shows both sides at once.

items.passage: Behavioral ecologist Joaquim Retzlaff-Imai hypothesizes that a cuttlefish chooses its disruptive body pattern according to the size of the light and dark patches on the surface beneath it relative to its own body, and not according to the colors of those patches. In tank trials, animals were placed over checkerboards whose squares were either small (about one-tenth of the animal's body width) or large (about one-half), printed either in gray tones or in red and green tones matched for brightness. Each trial lasted ten minutes, with every animal tested over each checkerboard in random order. The team recorded the percentage of trials in which each animal adopted the disruptive pattern.
items.question: Which result, if true, would most strongly support Retzlaff-Imai's hypothesis?

choices.text: Animals adopted the disruptive pattern on large squares in about 80 percent of trials in both the gray and red-green versions, and on small squares in under 10 percent of trials in both versions.
Animals adopted the disruptive pattern on large gray squares in about 80 percent of trials but on large red-green squares in about 20 percent, and on small squares of either type in under 10 percent.
choices.slip: Color changes the response, which the hypothesis rules out.

choices.text: Animals adopted the disruptive pattern on large and small gray squares in about 80 percent of trials each, but on neither large nor small red-green squares.
choices.slip: Color matters and size does not, the reverse of the hypothesis.

choices.text: Animals adopted the disruptive pattern in about 80 percent of trials on large squares and about 75 percent on small squares, in both the gray and red-green versions.
choices.slip: Color does not matter, but neither does size.

steps: Hypothesis: size matters, color does not.
So the response must differ between large and small squares and match across colors.
Only the first choice has a big size effect and no color effect.
explanation.why: It shows a large size effect that is the same for both color sets.
explanation.pattern: A claim that one factor matters and another does not needs evidence of both.

items.passage: Coastal engineer Noor Haldorsen-Mbeki claims that the seawall completed at Garnet Sands in 2019 reduced beach erosion. The 640-meter wall was built after a severe storm in 2018 removed much of the beach, and the beach has been surveyed each autumn since. In a five-year survey before the wall, the beach lost an average of 2.4 meters of width per year. In the two years after the wall, it lost 0.9 and 1.1 meters. Haldorsen-Mbeki notes that the survey method, the survey dates, and the stretch of beach measured were the same before and after, and she attributes the lower losses to the wall rather than to any change in how the beach was measured.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Haldorsen-Mbeki's claim?

choices.text: An unwalled beach 3 kilometers away lost an average of 2.2 meters per year over the five years before the wall and 2.1 meters per year in the two years after.
choices.slip: A comparison beach with no decline suggests the wall mattered.

choices.text: Annual losses in the five years before the wall ranged from 1.8 to 3.1 meters, so each of the two later years falls below that earlier range.
choices.slip: Shows the later losses are unusually low, which favors the wall.

choices.text: In the five years before the wall the coast averaged 14 storm days per year, but only 5 and 6 in the two years after, and erosion there tracks storms closely.
The two pre-wall years with the highest erosion, both above 3 meters, were also the two pre-wall years with the most storm days recorded on this coast.
choices.slip: Links storms to erosion but does not show the later years were unusually calm.

steps: Pre-wall losses averaged 2.4 m; post-wall losses 0.9 and 1.1 m.
A rival cause must change between the periods and affect erosion.
Far fewer storm days after the wall, with erosion tied to storms, explains the drop.
explanation.why: Fewer storms after the wall would reduce erosion with or without the wall.
explanation.pattern: Before/after comparisons need the rival cause to differ between the periods.

items.passage: Textual scholar Eadlin Prosser-Okonjo hypothesizes that the manuscript known as B was copied directly from manuscript A, rather than A and B each being copied independently from a lost earlier manuscript. Only three copies of the text survive: A, B, and C, all of which appear to date from the same century. Prosser-Okonjo compared them line by line, noting where scribes made mistakes such as skipped words or misread letters. A scribe who copies a manuscript reproduces most of its mistakes, though a careful scribe may silently fix a few obvious ones, and every scribe also adds new mistakes of his or her own as the pages go by.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Prosser-Okonjo's hypothesis?

choices.text: Manuscripts A and B agree on about 600 readings that differ from those of C, and none of those shared readings is a clear mistake.
choices.slip: Shared sound readings could have come from the lost source.

choices.text: Manuscript A contains nine mistakes that manuscript C does not, and manuscript B reproduces eight of those nine mistakes.
Manuscript B contains 22 mistakes that appear in neither A nor C, which suggests that its scribe worked quickly.
choices.slip: B's own new mistakes say nothing about which manuscript it was copied from.

choices.text: Manuscript C contains seven mistakes that manuscript A does not, and manuscript B reproduces none of those seven mistakes.
choices.slip: B would lack C's mistakes under either hypothesis.

steps: If B copied A, B should carry A's own mistakes.
If both came from a lost source, A's mistakes would be A's alone and B would not share them.
A's nine distinctive mistakes, eight of them in B, point to A as B's source.
explanation.why: Reproducing nearly all of A's distinctive mistakes is what direct copying predicts.
explanation.pattern: Shared errors, not shared correct readings, reveal copying.

items.passage: Ecologist Ravindra Okafor-Lindt proposes that caffeine in the nectar of citrus flowers benefits the trees by improving honeybees' memory of the flowers' scent, so that bees keep returning to the same trees. In a 2024 orchard experiment, his team trained honeybees to associate a floral scent with a sugar reward. One group of 120 bees received sugar water containing caffeine at the concentration found in citrus nectar, and another group of 120 received sugar water of the same sweetness without caffeine. A day later, when the scent was presented alone, 68 percent of the caffeine group extended their tongues in anticipation of food, compared with 41 percent of the other group. The team concluded that caffeine strengthens bees' memory of the scent that accompanied it.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the conclusion?

choices.text: Among bees given caffeinated sugar water, those trained in the morning extended their tongues to the scent more often the next day than those trained in the afternoon did.
choices.slip: Time of training differs within the caffeine group only; it says nothing about whether caffeine changed memory.

choices.text: Bees given caffeinated sugar water extended their tongues almost as often, about 65 percent, when presented with a scent they had never been trained on.
Bees fed caffeine at twice the concentration found in citrus nectar extended their tongues to the trained scent no more often than bees fed the natural concentration.
choices.slip: A plateau at higher doses doesn't show that the natural dose did not help memory.

choices.text: Bees that received caffeinated sugar water drank about the same volume during training as bees that received sugar water without caffeine did.
choices.slip: This rules out a rival (more drinking) and so supports the team.

steps: Conclusion: caffeine strengthened memory of the specific scent.
A rival explanation: caffeine just made bees more excitable, so they stick out their tongues at any odor.
If caffeinated bees respond almost as often to an untrained scent, the 68 percent does not show memory of the trained scent.
The other findings leave the link between caffeine and the trained scent untouched or support it.
explanation.why: A response to an untrained scent shows the higher rate reflects general arousal, not better memory.
explanation.pattern: To weaken a causal claim about a specific effect, find evidence that the same outcome appears without the specific mechanism.

items.passage: Marine biologist Teodoro Brightwater-Nunez argues that fish become more numerous on a reef when coral fragments grown on underwater frames are planted there, and that the increase does not simply come from fish relocating from nearby reefs. His team planted frame-grown coral on Ketterin Reef in 2020 and left Pellarin Reef, about 3 kilometers away, untouched. Divers counted fish along fixed transects each year. At Ketterin, the average count rose from 210 fish per transect in 2020 to 340 in 2023. Before 2020 the two reefs had similar coral cover and similar fish counts, and a channel of open sand lies between them. The same divers surveyed both reefs in the same month each year, using identical methods.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the argument?

choices.text: Over the same three years, the average count at Pellarin Reef fell from 205 fish per transect to 150, while the count at Ketterin Reef rose.
choices.slip: This pattern fits fish moving from Pellarin to Ketterin, which is the rival explanation.

choices.text: Coral cover at Ketterin Reef increased from 12 percent to 31 percent between 2020 and 2023, while coral cover at Pellarin Reef rose only from 13 to 15 percent.
choices.slip: It shows the planting worked on coral but not whether the extra fish were new or relocated.

choices.text: Most of the increase at Ketterin Reef occurred in the first year after planting, with counts rising more slowly in 2022 and 2023 than in 2021.
choices.slip: The timing of the rise doesn't distinguish new fish from relocated fish.

choices.text: Over the same three years, the average count at Pellarin Reef rose slightly, from 205 fish per transect to 215, with no decrease in any year.

steps: The argument has two parts: planting raised fish numbers, and the rise isn't just fish moving over from nearby reefs.
If fish had moved from Pellarin, its count should have dropped as Ketterin's rose.
A steady or slightly rising count at Pellarin shows it did not lose fish, so the added fish at Ketterin were not drawn from it.
The other choices don't test the relocation rival.
explanation.why: Pellarin's count did not fall, so relocation from the nearest reef does not explain Ketterin's gain.
explanation.pattern: Support for a causal claim often comes from showing that the rival explanation's predicted side effect did not occur.

items.passage: Urban planner Imogen Falk-Adeyemi claims that planting rooftop gardens lowers the temperature inside the buildings beneath them. Her team monitored 40 apartment buildings in the city of Marenhall. Twenty of the buildings added rooftop gardens in 2021, and twenty did not. During the summer of 2022, apartments on the top floors of the garden buildings averaged 3.1 degrees Celsius cooler than top-floor apartments in the other buildings, a gap far larger than the gap between the lower floors of the two groups. Falk-Adeyemi concluded that the gardens caused the cooling, since the two groups of buildings stood in the same neighborhoods and faced the same weather. Sensors recorded indoor temperature every hour, and the team averaged the readings across July and August.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the conclusion?

choices.text: Before any gardens were planted, top-floor apartments in the buildings that later added gardens were already about 3 degrees Celsius cooler than those in the other buildings.
Within the garden buildings, top-floor apartments were cooler where the garden covered a larger share of the roof than where it covered a smaller share.
choices.slip: This dose-response pattern supports the claim.

choices.text: Residents of the garden buildings reported running their air conditioners about as often during summer 2022 as residents of the other buildings did.
choices.slip: This doesn't bear on whether the gardens, or something else, produced the temperature difference.

choices.text: Summer 2022 was warmer than summer 2021 in Marenhall, and top-floor temperatures rose in both groups of buildings between those two summers, by about the same amount.
choices.slip: A shared rise affects both groups and leaves the gap unexplained.

steps: Conclusion: the gardens caused the 3.1-degree gap.
A rival: the garden buildings were already cooler (better insulation, shading, design) before the gardens.
If the gap existed before planting, the gardens can't account for it.
Other choices either support the claim or leave the gap unexplained.
explanation.why: A gap that existed before the gardens were planted cannot have been caused by them.
explanation.pattern: Weaken a before/after or group comparison by showing the groups already differed before the treatment.

items.passage: Education researcher Soledad Varga-Imoru claims that a vocabulary app improves students' vocabulary. In one district, 2,400 students chose to use the app for about twenty minutes a day during a semester. Her team compared them with 2,400 students who did not use it and who had matching scores on a vocabulary test taken before the semester began. On a second vocabulary test at the semester's end, app users' scores had risen by an average of 11 points, and the comparison students' scores had risen by an average of 4 points. A skeptic notes that students who volunteer for an app may simply be more motivated learners, whose scores would have risen faster with or without it.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the argument?

choices.text: App users who completed more than 60 sessions gained an average of 14 points, compared with 8 points for users who completed fewer than 20 sessions.
choices.slip: More motivated students would also complete more sessions, so the skeptic's rival explanation predicts this pattern too.

choices.text: App users and comparison students had the same average score on the vocabulary test taken before the semester began, at about 62 out of 100.
choices.slip: The passage already says the scores matched; matching on earlier scores doesn't address motivation.

choices.text: On a math test the app does not cover, users' scores rose by about 3 points on average, the same as the comparison students' scores.
Fewer than 5 percent of the 2,400 students who began using the app stopped using it before the semester ended.
choices.slip: Low dropout doesn't separate the app's effect from the effect of motivation.

steps: Claim: the app raised vocabulary scores. Rival: volunteers are more motivated and would improve more anyway.
If motivation alone made users improve faster, users should also improve faster in a subject the app doesn't teach.
Equal math gains show users were not generally faster improvers, which weakens the rival.
A dose-response pattern fits both the app and motivation.
explanation.why: Equal gains in math show the users' vocabulary edge isn't just general motivation.
explanation.pattern: Handle a stated rival cause with a control outcome the treatment shouldn't affect; a dose-response pattern can fit the rival too.

items.passage: Ornithologist Hamish Duvall-Nkosi observed that male house finches in a noisy city sing at a higher minimum pitch, averaging 3.4 kilohertz, than males of the same species in quiet nature reserves, which average 2.9 kilohertz. Higher-pitched songs carry better through the low-frequency rumble of traffic. Duvall-Nkosi argues that each city finch raises its pitch in response to the noise it hears, rather than that city finches have inherited a tendency to sing higher. The city and reserve males were recorded in the same season of the same year. Each male was recorded singing on his own territory, and the team analyzed 20 songs per bird for 60 males in each setting.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the argument?

choices.text: Within the city, finches at the noisiest sites sang at a higher minimum pitch than finches at quieter sites, by an average of about 0.2 kilohertz.
choices.slip: Birds with higher-pitched songs might settle at noisy sites, so this fits an inherited tendency as well.

choices.text: When 15 city finches were later housed for three weeks in quiet aviaries, their minimum pitch fell to an average of 3.0 kilohertz.
City finches sang about 4 decibels louder than reserve finches, an adjustment that also helps songs carry through noise.
choices.slip: Loudness is a different adjustment and doesn't show whether the pitch difference is learned or inherited.

choices.text: Reserve finches recorded in autumn sang at the same minimum pitch, 2.9 kilohertz, as reserve finches recorded in spring.
choices.slip: It says nothing about city finches or about noise.

steps: Claim: individual finches adjust pitch to noise (flexible), not inherited.
If so, the same birds should sing lower when the noise is removed.
City finches' pitch dropped from 3.4 to 3.0 in quiet aviaries, which only makes sense if pitch responds to noise.
Choice A (noisier sites, higher pitch) is compatible with birds sorting themselves by inherited pitch.
explanation.why: The same city birds lowered their pitch when the noise was removed, so the pitch was a response to noise.
explanation.pattern: Distinguish 'adjusted by the individual' from 'inherited' by changing the condition for the same individuals.

items.passage: In 2021, the Harlan Valley school district moved the start of its high school day from 7:30 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. Superintendent Delia Fontaine-Abara credited the later start for improved attendance, pointing out that the district's average daily attendance among high school students rose from 91 percent in the 2020-2021 school year to 94 percent in 2021-2022. A state report found that attendance in other districts in the region that kept earlier start times stayed at about 91 percent in both years. Fontaine-Abara argues that the later start, and not some other change in how students or the district behaved, accounts for the increase. The district has four high schools, which together enroll about 3,800 students.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the conclusion?

choices.text: Reported flu cases in the Harlan Valley district were about the same in the winter of 2021-2022 as in the winter of 2020-2021.
choices.slip: This eliminates a rival explanation (a milder flu season), so it supports the superintendent.

choices.text: The increase in attendance was about 3 percentage points at each of the district's four high schools, rather than being concentrated at one school.
choices.slip: A uniform increase fits the start-time explanation as well as any other.

choices.text: Attendance among the district's middle school students, whose start time did not change, rose from 92 percent to 93 percent over the same two school years.
choices.slip: A one-point rise elsewhere in the district could explain only a small part of the three-point rise.

choices.text: In the same year, the district began counting students who arrived within thirty minutes of the first bell as present for the day.

steps: Claim: the later start time caused the three-point attendance gain; no other change in how students or the district behaved.
A change in how attendance was counted is exactly such a change by the district.
If late arrivals now count as present, attendance would rise even if no student behaved differently.
The middle-school rise is real but too small to account for the high school gain.
explanation.why: A more lenient definition of 'present' could produce the three-point rise by itself.
explanation.pattern: Beware of changes in how a quantity is measured: they can replace a causal story with an artifact.

items.passage: Archaeologist Nasrin Hargreave-Obi argues that the stone fort at Karst Hollow was abandoned because of a volcanic eruption. Her team found a layer of volcanic ash about 5 centimeters thick covering the floors of all 14 excavated rooms. Chemical analysis shows that the ash came from an eruption that occurred about 1,180 years ago, and charcoal from the rooms' hearths, found beneath the ash, dates to between 1,200 and 1,190 years ago. Hargreave-Obi argues that the people living in the fort left soon after the ash fell, because the charcoal shows that the hearths were in use until the eruption and no later hearth charcoal was found. The fort was built of local stone and, by the team's estimate, housed about 60 people.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the conclusion?

choices.text: In all 14 rooms, the fort's pottery and tools were found lying on top of the ash layer rather than beneath it.
The ash layer was about 8 centimeters thick in rooms on the north side of the fort and about 3 centimeters thick in rooms on the south side.
choices.slip: Variation in thickness doesn't tell us whether the fort was abandoned.

choices.text: Several settlements within 20 kilometers of the fort have ash layers from the same eruption, and most of them show no signs of occupation after it.
choices.slip: This supports the claim that the eruption caused abandonment.

choices.text: The fort's outer wall was repaired about 1,250 years ago after an earthquake, several decades before the date of the hearth charcoal.
choices.slip: An earlier repair doesn't bear on what happened after the ash fell.

steps: Claim: people left soon after the ash fell.
If pottery and tools lie on top of the ash, they were left or used after the ash was down, so the fort was still in use.
The settlements nearby support abandonment; the north/south thickness and the earlier repair are irrelevant.
explanation.why: Objects lying above the ash show the fort was in use after the eruption.
explanation.pattern: An argument from absence of later evidence is weakened by direct evidence of later use.

items.passage: Botanist Linnea Tavares-Quist hypothesizes that a soil fungus helps pepper plants mainly by protecting them from drought rather than by boosting their growth in general. Her team grew pepper plants in four conditions, 30 plants per condition, and measured the fruit mass produced per plant. Plants grown with the fungus produced an average of 410 grams of fruit when well watered and 380 grams under drought. Plants grown without the fungus produced an average of 400 grams when well watered and 240 grams under drought. The plants were identical in variety and age, and the soil was the same in every condition. Drought plants received one-third of the water that well-watered plants received.
items.question: Which choice best describes data from the passage that support the hypothesis?

choices.text: Plants without the fungus produced 160 grams less fruit under drought than when well watered, showing that drought sharply reduces the yield of pepper plants.
choices.slip: True, but it describes the effect of drought, not of the fungus.

choices.text: Plants with the fungus produced 410 grams of fruit when well watered, more than any other group, which shows that the fungus boosts growth in general.
choices.slip: The 10-gram edge in good conditions is small and contradicts 'mainly drought protection'.

choices.text: The fungus raised average fruit mass by only 10 grams with ample water but by 140 grams under drought.
Under drought, plants without the fungus produced 240 grams and plants with it 380 grams, so the fungus raised yield by about 58 percent.
choices.slip: True, but it doesn't show the effect is specific to drought; the same comparison under good watering is needed.

steps: Hypothesis: the fungus mainly helps under drought, not in general.
To support it, compare the fungus effect in each watering condition: +10 g when well watered, +140 g under drought.
Choice C reports only the drought comparison, so it can't show the effect is specific to drought.
A and B describe drought's effect, or misread the small 10 g edge.
explanation.why: The fungus's benefit is small with ample water and large under drought, matching 'mainly drought protection'.
explanation.pattern: For a conditional effect, compare the treatment effect within each condition, not across conditions.

items.passage: Viticulturist Ottoline Kessler-Abara claims that the date of the grape harvest in the Cerrone Valley depends mainly on spring temperatures, not summer temperatures. Using records from 40 years, her team sorted years by whether spring and summer were warmer or cooler than average and calculated the mean harvest date, counted in days from January 1. Years with a warm spring and a warm summer averaged day 240; a warm spring and a cool summer, day 243; a cool spring and a warm summer, day 256; and a cool spring and a cool summer, day 259. A season counted as warm or cool by comparison with the 40-year average for that season, and each of the four kinds of year occurred 10 times.
items.question: Which choice best describes data from the passage that support the hypothesis?

choices.text: Harvest came about 16 days earlier after warm summers than after cool summers whichever kind of spring preceded, but only about 3 days earlier after warm springs.
choices.slip: This reverses the pattern in the data.

choices.text: Harvest came earliest, on day 240, in years with both a warm spring and a warm summer, and latest, on day 259, in years with both a cool spring and a cool summer.
choices.slip: Both factors change together between the extremes, so it can't separate spring from summer.

choices.text: Harvest averaged day 248 in the two kinds of year with a warm summer and day 251 in the two kinds with a cool summer, a gap of only 3 days.
choices.slip: This shows summer matters little but never shows that spring matters.

choices.text: Harvest came about 16 days earlier after warm springs than after cool springs whichever kind of summer followed, but only about 3 days earlier after warm summers than after cool summers.

steps: Claim: spring temperature matters more than summer temperature.
Hold one season fixed: warm vs cool spring gives 16 days either way (240/256 and 243/259); warm vs cool summer gives 3 days either way.
D reports both comparisons. C reports only the summer half; B changes both seasons at once; A swaps the seasons.
explanation.why: Changing spring moves the harvest 16 days in either summer, while changing summer moves it only 3 days.
explanation.pattern: To show one factor matters more than another, vary each while holding the other fixed.

items.passage: Marine ecologist Bertrand Sallow-Pereira claims that noise from tidal turbines installed in the Sedge Narrows channel in early 2020 drove harbor porpoises away from the channel. Acoustic monitors within 5 kilometers of the turbines recorded an average of 18 porpoise detections per day in 2019 and 7 per day in 2021. A monitor in a similar channel 30 kilometers away, which has no turbines, recorded 17 detections per day in 2019 and 16 per day in 2021. Sallow-Pereira concludes that the turbines, rather than a change in the porpoises' food supply or in regional conditions, caused the decline near the turbines. The turbines began operating in March 2020, and the acoustic monitors were in place throughout.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the conclusion?

choices.text: Detections within 5 kilometers of the turbines were lower on days when the turbines were turning than on days when they were stopped for maintenance.
choices.slip: This fits the turbine explanation, so it supports it.

choices.text: Detections within 5 kilometers of the turbines had already fallen from 41 per day in 2016 to 18 per day in 2019, a decline at least as steep as the later one.
Before and after installation, detections within 5 kilometers of the turbines were higher in summer than in winter, by about 4 per day in both years.
choices.slip: A seasonal pattern shared by both years leaves the drop between years unexplained.

choices.text: Detections at the monitor 30 kilometers away stayed between 15 and 18 per day in every month of the two years.
choices.slip: Stable counts at the distant site support the idea of a local cause.

steps: Claim: the turbines caused the local decline.
A drop that was already under way, at the same pace, before installation points to some earlier local cause.
41 to 18 over three years (about 8 per year) is at least as steep as 18 to 7 over two years (about 5.5 per year).
The other choices support the turbines or are neutral.
explanation.why: The decline predates the turbines and is no slower, so installation need not have caused it.
explanation.pattern: A pre-existing trend can account for a before/after change; a comparison site doesn't rule out a local pre-trend.

items.passage: Infection-control researcher Dalbir Sunderland-Echeme argues that hand-sanitizer dispensers installed at ward entrances at Pemberwick General Hospital cut bloodstream infections there. Across the hospital's nine wards, infections fell from 4.2 to 2.9 per 1,000 patient-days between the year before installation and the year after. A hospital administrator replies that the drop reflects a new central-line care protocol that all nine wards adopted in the same month as the dispensers. Sunderland-Echeme had observers record how often people entering each ward used the dispenser. Use ranged from about 35 percent of entries on the least compliant ward to about 85 percent on the most compliant ward.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Sunderland-Echeme's argument over the administrator's?

choices.text: Infections fell on all nine wards, including the three wards where dispensers were used on fewer than half of entries, and no ward's infection rate rose during the year.
choices.slip: Drops on low-use wards point to the protocol, which every ward shared.

choices.text: Before the dispensers and the protocol were introduced, the wards with the highest infection rates were also the wards with the highest staff turnover.
choices.slip: A pre-existing pattern doesn't separate dispensers from the protocol.

choices.text: Dispenser use was highest on the wards where infections fell most and lowest where they fell least, though all nine wards followed the new protocol equally.
A nearby hospital adopted the same protocol without installing dispensers, and its infections fell from 4.1 to 2.8 per 1,000 patient-days over the same period.
choices.slip: The protocol alone matched the drop, which supports the administrator.

steps: Rival cause: the protocol, which all wards adopted equally.
To favor dispensers, find variation in dispenser use that tracks variation in the drop while the protocol is held constant.
A dose-response pattern across wards does that; the other choices fit the protocol or are unrelated.
explanation.why: Infection drops that scale with dispenser use, with the protocol constant, favor the dispensers.
explanation.pattern: Separate two causes by finding variation in one cause while the other is held constant.

items.passage: Transportation analyst Folasade Merriweather-Lund argues that the protected bike lanes added to downtown streets in the city of Wexmoor made cycling safer there. Police records show 310 reported cyclist injuries on those streets in the year before the lanes opened and 240 in the year after, a drop she attributes to physical separation from traffic. She also notes that motor-vehicle volume on the streets was unchanged. Injuries on streets without new lanes held steady at about 150 a year. Her report does not include counts of how many trips people made by bicycle on any street in either year.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the conclusion?

choices.text: Automated counters on the affected streets recorded about 35 percent fewer bicycle trips in the year after the lanes opened than in the year before.
Of the 240 injuries reported after the lanes opened, about 60 percent involved a collision with a turning car, close to the share in the year before.
choices.slip: The share of injury types doesn't show whether injuries per trip changed.

choices.text: Counters on streets without new lanes recorded about 10 percent fewer bicycle trips in the year after, while injuries there held steady at about 150.
choices.slip: Fewer trips elsewhere only hints at a general decline; it doesn't show what happened on the lane streets.

choices.text: Police were called to roughly the same share of cyclist injuries in both years, so the records cover a similar portion of all injuries.
choices.slip: Consistent reporting supports comparing the two years.

steps: Safer cycling means fewer injuries per trip, not just fewer injuries.
If trips on the lane streets fell about 35 percent, 240 injuries is a higher rate than 310 injuries before (240/0.65, about 369 versus 310).
The other choices don't give trip counts for the lane streets.
explanation.why: With 35 percent fewer trips, 240 injuries is a higher injury rate than 310 injuries was.
explanation.pattern: A drop in a count says nothing about risk until the exposure (trips, people) is known.

items.passage: Hospital director Ilse Vandermeulen-Oko claims that a mentoring program raised first-year retention among night-shift nurses but made little difference for day-shift nurses. The program enrolled 400 new nurses, 100 in each of four groups formed by shift and mentoring status, and nurses were assigned to mentors by random draw within each shift. Twelve months after hire, the share still employed was 88 percent of mentored day-shift nurses, 86 percent of unmentored day-shift nurses, 79 percent of mentored night-shift nurses, and 61 percent of unmentored night-shift nurses.
items.question: Which choice best describes data from the passage that support the director's claim?

choices.text: Mentored nurses overall were retained at 83.5 percent, compared with 73.5 percent for unmentored nurses overall, a 10-point difference across both shifts combined.
choices.slip: This overall gap mixes both shifts and doesn't show the effect is confined to nights.

choices.text: Unmentored night-shift nurses, at 61 percent, were retained at a lower rate than any other group, including the unmentored day-shift nurses, whose rate was 86 percent.
choices.slip: This compares unmentored groups with each other and says nothing about mentoring.

choices.text: Mentored day-shift nurses were retained at 88 percent, a higher rate than the 79 percent of mentored night-shift nurses.
choices.slip: This compares mentored groups across shifts and doesn't show the effect of mentoring.

choices.text: Among night-shift nurses, 79 percent of mentored and 61 percent of unmentored nurses were retained, an 18-point gap; among day-shift nurses the gap was 2 points.

steps: The claim has two halves: a large effect at night and little effect by day.
Compare mentored with unmentored within each shift: 18 points at night, 2 points by day.
Each other choice either blends the shifts or compares groups that differ in shift rather than mentoring.
explanation.why: Only the within-shift comparison shows a large gap at night and a negligible gap by day.
explanation.pattern: To support an 'only for group X' claim, compare treated and untreated within each group.

items.passage: Art historian Rosalind Wetherell-Nwosu argues that an unsigned panel painting was made in the workshop of Pieter Vossel. Tree-ring dating shows the panel's oak was felled in the 1620s. Her team analyzed the ground layer of 12 paintings securely attributed to Vossel's workshop, all painted between 1615 and 1635, and found the pigment lead-tin yellow in 11 of them. They found it in none of 9 securely attributed paintings from the rival workshop of Anselm Draeger. The unsigned panel's ground layer contains lead-tin yellow, and Wetherell-Nwosu concludes that the pigment points to Vossel's workshop rather than Draeger's.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the conclusion?

choices.text: Vossel's workshop is documented to have employed several painters who had trained in other cities before they joined the workshop and brought their own methods.
choices.slip: Staff training doesn't bear on which workshop used the pigment.

choices.text: All nine of the sampled Draeger paintings date from 1675 to 1700, decades after painters in the region had largely stopped using lead-tin yellow.
The oak used for the panel came from a forest region where both Vossel's workshop and Draeger's workshop bought wood throughout the 1620s.
choices.slip: A shared wood source doesn't tell us which workshop used the pigment.

choices.text: The one Vossel painting without lead-tin yellow was painted in 1630, which is in the same decade as the unsigned panel's tree-ring date.
choices.slip: One exception in a sample of 12 leaves the pattern largely intact.

steps: The argument rests on Draeger's paintings lacking the pigment.
If those paintings come from decades after the pigment went out of use, their lack says nothing about Draeger's practice in the 1620s.
The rival comparison group then fails to rule Draeger out.
explanation.why: Draeger's sampled works postdate the pigment's use, so their lack of it is uninformative about the 1620s.
explanation.pattern: A comparison group is weak evidence if it comes from a different time or condition than the case.

items.passage: Education researcher Ewan Brightmore-Mbeki argues that moving the first bell from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m. raised attendance at the six high schools of the Marlow Basin district because students slept longer. Average daily attendance rose from 91.2 percent to 93.8 percent in the year after the change, and surveyed students reported sleeping an average of 38 minutes more on school nights. A school board member counters that the rise came from a new bus schedule, introduced the same autumn, that shortened ride times. The new schedule applied only to the four schools whose students mostly ride district buses; students at the other two schools mostly walk or cycle.
items.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Brightmore-Mbeki's argument over the board member's?

choices.text: Attendance rose by about 2.6 points at both schools whose students mostly walk or cycle, just as at the four schools with the new bus schedule.
Across the four bus-dependent schools, attendance gains were largest at the schools where the new bus schedule cut ride times the most and smallest where it changed ride times little.
choices.slip: Gains that scale with the bus change support the board member.
