Text 2: charcoal only gives a maximum age, but seeds from the same hearth give 11,900.
Weakness raised, but conclusion survives.
explanation.why: Text 2 raises a known weakness and then shows an independent sample largely confirms Text 1.
explanation.pattern: A caveat in Text 2 does not always oppose Text 1; check what the second piece of evidence does.

items.passage:
Text 1
Biologist Evander Obuya-Leclair argues that the bright colors of poison frogs evolved as a warning to predators that hunt by sight. By his account, color benefits a frog only where such predators are present, so frogs in places without them should be duller, since bright coloring also costs energy to produce.
items.passage2:
Text 2
On Quillon Island, where the only predators of poison frogs hunt by smell, Henrietta Szabo-Nakagawa found frogs as brightly colored as those on the mainland. Males with the brightest color, she observed, were chosen as mates about twice as often as duller males. She suggests that color on Quillon Island is maintained by mate choice rather than by predators.
items.question: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?

choices.text: It reports an observation that Text 1's account does not predict and offers a separate function of color that could account for it.
It reports an observation that confirms Text 1's prediction that frogs living without sight-hunting predators are duller than mainland frogs.
choices.slip: The island frogs are as bright as the mainland frogs, contrary to the prediction.

choices.text: It shows that the predators on Quillon Island hunt by sight, which supports Text 1's account of the origin of the frogs' coloring.
choices.slip: The island's predators hunt by smell.

choices.text: It rejects Text 1's account by showing that the frogs on Quillon Island are not poisonous to the predators that hunt them there.
choices.slip: Nothing about toxicity on the island is reported.

steps: Text 1 predicts duller frogs without sight-hunting predators.
Text 2: Quillon frogs are as bright.
Text 2 adds mate choice as another function.
explanation.why: The island observation conflicts with the prediction, and Text 2 supplies a rival function.
explanation.pattern: Apply the model in Text 1 to the new case first, then see whether the case fits.

items.passage:
Text 1
Historian Alistair Penhaligon-Dube attributes the decline of the Merrick Canal to railway competition. Traffic on the canal, he notes, fell by about half in the years after the railway line opened in 1851, and shippers' letters complain of the railway's lower rates.
items.passage2:
Text 2
Historian Winifred Calder-Ogunbanjo points out that the canal's toll records show tonnage had already fallen by nearly a third in the five years before 1851, when silt closed the lower channel to loaded barges. After the railway opened, she finds, the fall continued at a similar pace. She agrees that the railway hastened the end but argues that it did not begin the decline.
items.question: Based on the texts, how would Calder-Ogunbanjo most likely respond to Penhaligon-Dube's attribution?

choices.text: By denying that the railway ever affected the canal's tonnage and attributing the whole decline to the silting of the lower channel
choices.slip: She agrees the railway hastened the end.

choices.text: By arguing that the railway was built only because silting had already closed the canal's lower channel to loaded barges
choices.slip: Nothing in Text 2 gives a reason for the railway's construction.

choices.text: By accepting the attribution because tonnage fell by about half in the years after the railway line opened in 1851
choices.slip: She finds an earlier fall and says the railway did not begin the decline.

choices.text: By granting that the railway added to the canal's decline while arguing that a different problem had already started it

steps: Text 1: rail caused the decline, shown by traffic after 1851.
Text 2: traffic fell a third before 1851 due to silt; fall continued after.
She credits both, with silt first.
explanation.why: She grants the railway a role but places the start of the decline earlier, with silting.
explanation.pattern: Timing evidence separates causes: what happened before the supposed cause cannot be explained by it.

items.passage:
Text 1
Critic Rafaela Ostrowski-Kimani reads the repeated image of closed doors in the novella The Lantern Year as a symbol of confinement. She points to the scenes in which the heroine, Odile, is shut in her aunt's house, where doors are mentioned in nearly every paragraph.
items.passage2:
Text 2
Scholar Thaddeus Linnell-Abara counted every mention of a door in the novella and found that doors appear at the same rate in the chapters of travel and escape as in those set in the aunt's house. He accepts that doors are important to the book but concludes that they mark moments of passage, not confinement in particular.
items.question: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?

choices.text: It denies that doors recur in the novella and argues that Text 1 has invented the image on which its reading depends.
choices.slip: He accepts that doors are important and counts them.

choices.text: It accepts that doors recur prominently but offers evidence that they appear as often in scenes of freedom as in scenes of confinement.
It agrees that doors symbolize confinement but argues that they also come to symbolize confinement in the chapters of travel and escape.
choices.slip: He concludes that doors mark passage, not confinement in particular.

choices.text: It shows that the critic miscounted the mentions of doors in the scenes set in the aunt's house and so overstated the image's frequency.
choices.slip: He does not dispute the frequency in the aunt's house; he finds equal frequency elsewhere.

steps: Text 1 reads doors as confinement from the aunt's-house scenes.
Text 2: same rate in travel chapters.
So the frequency does not single out confinement.
explanation.why: Text 2 grants the image's prominence but shows it is not specific to confinement.
explanation.pattern: A symbol claim based on where an image appears is weakened if it appears just as often elsewhere.

items.passage:
Text 1
Educator Florentine Okafor-Haas reports that third graders who used the Lumen Reader app for a semester gained an average of 12 points on a reading test, compared with 4 points for classmates who did not use it. She concludes that the app substantially improves reading ability.
items.passage2:
Text 2
Researcher Idris Vanterpool-Sato notes that the test was written by the app's developer and that about two-thirds of its vocabulary items were words the app drills. On an independent reading test, the app group's advantage over classmates was 1 point. He accepts that the app teaches the words it drills but doubts that the gain reflects broader reading ability.
items.question: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?

choices.text: It rejects the 12-point figure as miscalculated and argues that the app group gained no more than their classmates on any test.
choices.slip: He accepts the gain on the developer's test and reports a 1-point advantage on the other.

choices.text: It confirms Text 1's conclusion by showing that the app group also outperformed classmates on an independent test by a small margin.
choices.slip: A 1-point advantage on an independent test does not support the claim of substantial improvement.

choices.text: It accepts that the app group gained on the developer's test but argues that the test overlaps with the app's content, so the gain overstates general improvement.
It accepts that the app improves general reading ability but argues that the developer's test overstates how large the improvement is, since only some of its vocabulary items were drilled.
choices.slip: He doubts that the gain reflects broader ability at all.

steps: Text 1: 12 vs 4 points, so reading ability improves.
Text 2: test is drilled vocabulary; independent test shows 1 point.
So the gain is real on the test but not broad.
explanation.why: Text 2 accepts the measured gain but questions what it measures.
explanation.pattern: Ask whether the outcome measure overlaps with the thing being tested before accepting the generalization.

items.passage:
Text 1
Columnist Montgomery Tsegaye-Blum argues that the Wexcombe district's reading reform has failed: the share of students passing the state reading exam fell from about 72 percent to about 69 percent in the three years since the reform began.
items.passage2:
Text 2
Statistician Neriah Castellanos-Weir notes that the pass rate rose at both of the district's high schools, at West High from 80 to 82 percent and at East High from 50 to 53 percent. But East's share of the district's students grew from 25 to 45 percent over the same years, and a larger share of students at the lower-scoring school pulls the district average down. She concludes that the district figure alone cannot show whether the reform failed.
items.question: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?

choices.text: It accepts the district-wide decline in Text 1 but argues that the decline reflects a shift in enrollment between schools, not lower pass rates within each school.
It disputes the district-wide figure in Text 1, showing that the pass rate across both schools actually rose from about 72 percent to about 74 percent once the two schools' results are combined.
choices.slip: The district average did fall; she explains why.

choices.text: It accepts the decline in Text 1 and attributes it to East High, whose pass rate fell by three points while West High's rose.
choices.slip: East's pass rate rose from 50 to 53 percent.

choices.text: It argues that the reform should be judged by East High alone, where the pass rate rose by three points over the three years.
choices.slip: She says the district figure alone cannot show whether the reform failed; she does not single out East.

steps: District: 72 to 69.
Both schools rose.
East's enrollment share grew from 25 to 45 percent, pulling the average down.
explanation.why: The overall decline is a weighting effect; each school improved.
explanation.pattern: When an overall figure falls while each part rises, the mix of the parts has changed.

items.passage:
Text 1
Anthropologist Ulrike Dasgupta-Faye argues that the Kellaran islanders' custom of sharing fish catches among households evolved as insurance against uneven fishing luck. If that is right, she says, households should share more widely in seasons when catches vary most from boat to boat.
items.passage2:
Text 2
Fieldworker Joaquim Oduya-Lindholm recorded sharing across eight seasons. The share of each catch given away stayed near 30 percent whether boat-to-boat variation was high or low, but households gave about three times as much to kin as to nonkin in every season. He suggests that obligations of kinship, rather than insurance, best account for the pattern he recorded.
items.question: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?

choices.text: It reports a result that confirms Text 1's prediction and shows that sharing was widest in the seasons when catches varied most.
choices.slip: The share given away stayed near 30 percent regardless of variation.

choices.text: It shows that the Kellaran islanders do not share catches outside their kin, which contradicts the custom described in Text 1.
choices.slip: Households gave to nonkin as well, at about one third the rate.

choices.text: It accepts Text 1's explanation but reports that islanders share more with kin because the catches of kin vary less from boat to boat, which would make the sharing a form of insurance.
choices.slip: Text 2 offers kinship as an alternative to insurance, not as an addition to it.

choices.text: It reports a result that Text 1's account does not predict and proposes a different factor as the better explanation of how sharing is distributed.

steps: Text 1 predicts more sharing when variation is high.
Text 2: no change in sharing with variation; kin get more.
Kinship better explains the pattern.
explanation.why: The prediction from Text 1 fails, and kinship is offered as the better explanation.
explanation.pattern: Turn the theory into a prediction and check whether Text 2's data match it.

items.passage: The north gallery of the Eastmere library, once a reading room, now holds the library's collection of local landscapes. Each of the paintings in the north gallery of the Eastmere library ______ a small brass label giving the artist's name and the year the work was finished.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: have
choices.slip: The subject is 'Each', which is singular; 'paintings' is part of a phrase between the subject and the verb.

choices.text: has
are having
choices.slip: 'Are' is plural, and 'having' is not used this way for something a label simply shows.

choices.text: were having
choices.slip: 'Were' is plural and past tense, and 'having' doesn't fit.

steps: The subject is 'Each' (each one), not 'paintings'.
'Of the paintings in the north gallery of the Eastmere library' is a phrase between the subject and the verb.
'Each' is singular, so the verb is 'has'.
explanation.why: 'Has' agrees with the singular subject 'Each'.
explanation.pattern: Cross out the 'of …' phrase to find the real subject. 'Each', 'every' and 'one of' take singular verbs.

items.passage: The Ostrander town council keeps residents informed through a monthly newsletter delivered to every household. In its February newsletter, the Ostrander town council announced that ______ would hold an extra meeting in March to vote on the new library budget.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: it
they
choices.slip: 'The town council' is a single group, so it is referred to as 'it', not 'they'.

choices.text: he or she
choices.slip: The council is a group, not one person.

choices.text: we
choices.slip: The newsletter is described from outside, so 'we' doesn't match 'the town council'.

steps: The pronoun refers back to 'the town council'.
A council is one group, and the sentence already calls it 'its' ('In its February newsletter').
So the matching pronoun is 'it'.
explanation.why: 'It' matches the singular group 'the town council', as 'its' earlier in the sentence does.
explanation.pattern: A group noun (council, team, committee) is singular: it / its. Earlier pronouns in the sentence are a clue.

items.passage: River monitoring in the county depends heavily on trained volunteers, who work in teams of three. The volunteers, after measuring the depth of the Tanager River at a dozen points along its banks, ______ their results with the county's water office.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: sharing
choices.slip: 'Sharing' can't be the main verb; the sentence would have no main verb.

choices.text: to share
choices.slip: 'To share' can't be the main verb; the sentence would have no main verb.

choices.text: shared
having shared
choices.slip: 'Having shared' can't be the main verb; the sentence would have no main verb.

steps: The subject is 'The volunteers'.
'After measuring … along its banks' is a phrase between the subject and its verb.
The sentence still needs a main verb for 'The volunteers': 'shared'.
explanation.why: 'Shared' gives the subject 'The volunteers' the main verb the sentence needs.
explanation.pattern: Skip the phrase between the commas and ask: does the subject have a real verb? -ing and 'to' forms can't be the main verb.

items.passage: Lost property turns up often on the county's trails, and rangers keep a careful log of what is found. The map and the brass compass that the hikers found near the trail ______ to a ranger who had lost them a week earlier during a snowstorm.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: belongs
choices.slip: There are two things (the map and the compass), so the verb must be plural.

choices.text: belonging
choices.slip: 'Belonging' can't be the main verb of the sentence.

choices.text: has belonged
choices.slip: 'Has' is singular, but the subject is two things.

choices.text: belonged

steps: The subject is 'The map and the brass compass': two things joined by 'and', so it is plural.
The story is told in the past ('found', 'had lost').
'Belonged' is past tense and works with a plural subject.
explanation.why: 'Belonged' fits both the plural subject and the past-tense story.
explanation.pattern: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb, even if the nearest noun ('compass') is singular.

items.passage: Surveys of the island's shoreline have been under way since the early spring. Having mapped every tide pool along the northern shore of Gannet Island, ______
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: a survey of the southern beaches was begun next by ecologist Ines Varga.
choices.slip: This says the survey mapped the tide pools; the person who did the mapping must come right after the comma.

choices.text: ecologist Ines Varga began a survey of the southern beaches.
the southern beaches were the next site of Ines Varga's survey.
choices.slip: This says the beaches mapped the tide pools.

choices.text: Ines Varga's next survey covered the southern beaches.
choices.slip: The subject here is 'survey', not Ines Varga, so it says the survey mapped the tide pools.

steps: The opening phrase 'Having mapped every tide pool …' describes whoever did the mapping.
That person must be the subject that comes right after the comma.
Only 'ecologist Ines Varga' is someone who could have mapped the tide pools.
explanation.why: Placing 'ecologist Ines Varga' right after the opening phrase makes clear who did the mapping.
explanation.pattern: After an opening -ing or -ed phrase, the next noun must be the one doing that action. Watch for possessives ('Varga's survey'): the subject is the survey.

items.passage: Small presses rarely survive for a century, and fewer still keep to a fixed publishing calendar. Founded in 1922 by three sisters who had trained as printers in a small shop on the coast, the Calloway ______ more than four hundred books of poetry and has never once missed its spring catalog.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: Press, having published
choices.slip: This leaves the subject 'the Calloway Press' without a main verb before 'and has never …'.

choices.text: Press publishing
choices.slip: 'Publishing' can't be the main verb, so the subject has no verb of its own.

choices.text: Press has published
Press, which has published
choices.slip: 'Which has published …' only describes the press; the sentence would still lack a main verb for it.

steps: The long opening phrase 'Founded in 1922 … on the coast' describes the subject, the Calloway Press.
The subject needs a main verb that matches the second verb, 'has never … missed'.
'Has published' is a full verb and parallels 'has never … missed'.
explanation.why: 'Has published' gives the subject a main verb that matches 'has never once missed'.
explanation.pattern: After a long opening phrase, find the subject and make sure it gets a real verb. -ing forms and 'which' clauses only describe.

items.passage: Quarries often sit idle for decades before a town decides what to do with them. Along the far edge of the old Brannock quarry, behind a fence the town put up decades ago, ______ a row of birch trees planted by the town's first schoolchildren.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: stand
choices.slip: The subject is 'a row', which is singular; 'trees' is part of a phrase describing it.

choices.text: are standing
choices.slip: 'Are' is plural, but the subject 'a row' is singular.

choices.text: have stood
choices.slip: 'Have' is plural, but the subject 'a row' is singular.

choices.text: stands

steps: This sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb.
Ask what stands along the edge: 'a row' (of birch trees).
'A row' is singular, so the verb is 'stands'.
explanation.why: 'Stands' agrees with the singular subject 'a row', which comes after the verb.
explanation.pattern: When a sentence starts with a place ('Along …', 'Behind …'), the subject may come after the verb. Find it before choosing singular or plural.

items.passage: Counting seals is difficult work, because the animals spend half of their time at sea. The results of the survey team's two-winter count of the harbor seals along the Wrenhaven coast ______ that the colony, along with this year's pups, has nearly doubled in size since the netting ban.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: suggest
suggests
choices.slip: This agrees with the nearby 'count' or 'coast', but the subject is the plural 'results'.

choices.text: suggesting
choices.slip: 'Suggesting' can't be the main verb, so 'The results' would have no verb.

choices.text: having suggested
choices.slip: 'Having suggested' can't be the main verb, so 'The results' would have no verb.

steps: The subject is 'The results'; everything from 'of the survey team's' to 'Wrenhaven coast' describes it.
The sentence needs a real main verb for that subject, which rules out the -ing forms.
'Results' is plural, so the verb is 'suggest', not 'suggests'.
explanation.why: 'Suggest' is a full verb and agrees with the plural subject 'results', not the singular nouns closer to the blank.
explanation.pattern: Two checks: does the subject have a real verb, and does that verb agree with the subject rather than the nearest noun?

items.passage: Tidal energy has been studied for decades, but long-term evidence about its effects on wildlife remains thin. The Dunmarrow Sound report is one of the few studies of tidal turbines that ______ the effect of the machines on fish migration across a full decade.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: has measured
choices.slip: The relative clause modifies 'studies' (plural), not 'one'.

choices.text: measuring
choices.slip: Leaves the clause without a finite verb.

choices.text: is measuring
choices.slip: Singular and wrong tense for a completed study.

choices.text: have measured

steps: 'that' refers to 'studies', not to 'one'.
'studies' is plural, so the verb is plural.
Present perfect fits an effect measured up to now.
explanation.why: The relative pronoun 'that' stands for the plural 'studies', so the verb is plural.
explanation.pattern: In 'one of the few X that ___', the verb agrees with X.

items.passage: Educators have long debated whether schools should emphasize facts or skills. The new history curriculum is designed to build skills as well as knowledge. It asks students to interpret primary sources, compare competing accounts of the same event, and ______
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: to write arguments that are grounded in evidence that they have gathered.
choices.slip: Breaks the parallel with 'interpret' and 'compare' by adding 'to' and an extra clause.

choices.text: write arguments grounded in evidence.
writing grounded arguments.
choices.slip: An -ing form does not match the bare verbs 'interpret' and 'compare'.

choices.text: the writing of arguments grounded in evidence.
choices.slip: A noun phrase does not match the verbs in the series.

steps: The series has bare verbs: 'interpret', 'compare'.
The last item must be a bare verb with its object.
'write arguments grounded in evidence' matches.
explanation.why: 'Write' matches 'interpret' and 'compare' in form.
explanation.pattern: Items in a series need the same grammatical form; check the first two, then the last.

items.passage: Funding agencies often rely on outside readers to catch weaknesses in proposals before they are judged. The grant application asks each applicant to propose a reviewer, and the instructions are specific. Applicants must name the colleague ______ the finished proposal will be sent for informal comment before the deadline.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: who
choices.slip: The colleague is the receiver of the proposal, so an object form is needed after 'to'.

choices.text: whom
choices.slip: Without 'to', 'name the colleague whom the proposal will be sent' leaves the sentence incomplete.

choices.text: to whom
to who
choices.slip: 'Who' is a subject form and cannot follow 'to'.

steps: 'the proposal will be sent to [the colleague]'.
After a preposition, use 'whom'.
'to whom' links 'colleague' to the clause.
explanation.why: The proposal is sent to the colleague, and after a preposition the object form is whom.
explanation.pattern: Rebuild the clause as a statement: 'The proposal will be sent to him/her.' Him/her points to whom.

items.passage: A party of twelve left the coast in January with enough food for eleven weeks. The expedition's records show that the weather turned in February. By the time the party reached the plateau in March, it ______ most of its supplies and had begun rationing what remained.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: had lost
has lost
choices.slip: Present perfect does not fit a sentence set in the past.

choices.text: lost
choices.slip: Simple past does not show that the loss came before reaching the plateau.

choices.text: would lose
choices.slip: A future-in-the-past form does not match 'had begun rationing'.

steps: 'By the time the party reached... in March' sets a past reference point.
The loss happened before that point.
Past perfect: 'had lost', matching 'had begun'.
explanation.why: The loss came before the March arrival, and 'had begun' also uses the past perfect.
explanation.pattern: 'By the time' + past event signals past perfect for the earlier event.

items.passage: Cold storage at the field station is meant to protect eight years of soil and water samples. The failure of the freezer on the night of the outage went unnoticed for hours. Neither the lead researchers nor the graduate assistant ______ aware that the samples had begun to thaw.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: were
choices.slip: With 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'assistant', which is singular.

choices.text: was
have been
choices.slip: Wrong tense and number for a single past event.

choices.text: are
choices.slip: Present tense does not fit a night that has passed.

steps: With 'neither... nor', the verb matches the nearer subject.
The nearer subject is 'the graduate assistant', singular.
So 'was'.
explanation.why: The nearer subject is singular, so the verb is singular and past.
explanation.pattern: For 'neither/nor' and 'either/or', agree with the subject closest to the verb.

items.passage: Ice thickness is one of the clearest signs of how quickly a polar region is warming. Core samples taken at two stations show a clear contrast in the ice. The thickness of the ice at the northern station is greater than ______ at the southern station by nearly a meter.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: the southern station
choices.slip: Compares the thickness with a station, not with a thickness.

choices.text: those
choices.slip: 'Those' is plural but the compared noun, 'thickness', is singular.

choices.text: which
choices.slip: 'Which' cannot stand in for the thickness in a comparison.

choices.text: that

steps: Compare thickness with thickness.
'that of' stands for 'the thickness of'.
'that' is singular to match 'thickness'.
explanation.why: 'That' stands for 'the thickness' so the two quantities are compared like for like.
explanation.pattern: Comparisons must be logical: use that/those to stand for the noun being compared.

items.passage: Organizers of the harbor cleanup had set a goal of two hundred volunteers. Although a number of local businesses have pledged support, the number of volunteers who signed up before the deadline ______ still well below what the organizers had hoped.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: was
were
choices.slip: 'The number' is singular; the plural 'volunteers' is inside the modifier.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: Plural verb, and the tense does not fit the past setting.

choices.text: are
choices.slip: Plural, and wrong tense.

steps: 'The number of volunteers... was'.
'a number of businesses have' is the plural trap.
explanation.why: 'The number' is singular, and the context is past.
explanation.pattern: 'The number of' takes a singular verb; 'a number of' takes a plural one.

items.passage: Ant colonies vary in how they feed themselves. Unlike the northern colony, which relies almost entirely on a single species of aphid for food, ______
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: the southern colony's diet includes many species of insect.
choices.slip: Compares a colony with a diet, not a colony with a colony.

choices.text: many species of insect are what the southern colony feeds on.
choices.slip: Compares a colony with insect species.

choices.text: it is many species of insect that the southern colony eats.
choices.slip: 'It' has no clear referent and the opening comparison is lost.

choices.text: the southern colony feeds on many species of insect.

steps: 'Unlike the northern colony' invites a colony.
Only one choice names the southern colony as the subject.
explanation.why: The opening phrase compares colonies, so the main clause must name a colony.
explanation.pattern: After 'Unlike X', the subject must be something comparable to X.

items.passage: The town council asked two outside firms to review the redesign before the vote. Engineers consulted on the redesign say it has two advantages. The new proposal not only reduces the cost of building the bridge but also ______ the time required to finish it.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: it shortens
choices.slip: Adds a subject that breaks the parallel with 'reduces'.

choices.text: will shorten
choices.slip: Changes the tense so it no longer matches 'reduces'.

choices.text: shortens
to shorten
choices.slip: An infinitive does not match 'reduces'.

steps: 'reduces' is a present-tense verb.
So the second verb must also be present-tense, with no new subject.
explanation.why: 'Shortens' matches 'reduces' after not only... but also.
explanation.pattern: In 'not only X but also Y', X and Y must have the same form.

items.passage: Each year the Society of Hydraulic Engineers honors one member whose work has changed how the field operates. This year's award goes to the engineer ______ the committee, after reviewing forty nominations over six months, believes designed the most efficient turbine of the decade.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: who
whom
choices.slip: 'Who' is the subject of 'designed'; 'the committee, after reviewing forty nominations over six months, believes' is an interruption.

choices.text: whomever
choices.slip: 'Whomever' is a different construction and fails here.

choices.text: which
choices.slip: 'Which' does not refer to people.

steps: Drop 'the committee believes'.
'___ designed the turbine': the pronoun is the subject.
explanation.why: Remove the interrupter: 'the engineer designed...', so the subject form 'who' is needed.
explanation.pattern: Delete the interrupting clause and see whether the pronoun is a subject (who) or object (whom).

items.passage: Floods often change how a town thinks about its own history. The town's flood of 1931 was blamed on poor planning. Historians argue that if the dam ______ built a decade earlier, the town would have been spared the worst of the damage.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: was
choices.slip: A counterfactual about the past requires the past perfect after 'if'.

choices.text: had been
would have been
choices.slip: 'Would have' belongs in the result clause, not the 'if' clause.

choices.text: were
choices.slip: 'Were' belongs to present or future counterfactuals.

steps: Result clause: 'would have been spared'.
So the if-clause is the past perfect: 'had been'.
explanation.why: A past counterfactual uses 'if + had + past participle', and 'would have' in the result.
explanation.pattern: If-clause: had been. Result: would have been.

items.passage: Scholars of the colonial period have relied on one institution for more than a century. The national archive, which holds more than two million documents on the colonial period and ______ researchers from around the world, will close next year for a three-year renovation.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: welcoming
choices.slip: A participle does not match 'holds' in a 'which' clause.

choices.text: to welcome
choices.slip: An infinitive does not match 'holds'.

choices.text: welcome
choices.slip: A plural form does not agree with 'which', whose antecedent is 'archive'.

choices.text: welcomes

steps: 'which holds... and ___': two verbs for 'which'.
Antecedent 'archive': singular.
'welcomes'.
explanation.why: 'Welcomes' matches 'holds' and agrees with the singular 'archive'.
explanation.pattern: In a compound predicate, verbs must match in form and agree with the same subject.

items.passage: Nocturnal pollinators are declining in many regions, and artificial light has long been a suspected cause, though few studies have tested the idea outside a laboratory. In a recent field study, ecologists ______ the effect of streetlamps on moths set out sixty traps along a rural road, pairing each trap with either a lit lamp or a shielded control.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: investigating
investigated
choices.slip: Adds a second finite verb before the main verb 'set out'.

choices.text: were investigating
choices.slip: Adds a second finite verb before the main verb 'set out'.

choices.text: have investigated
choices.slip: Adds a second finite verb before the main verb 'set out'.

steps: Main verb: 'set out'.
The blank describes 'ecologists'.
Participle: 'investigating'.
explanation.why: 'Set out' is the main verb, so the blank needs a participle modifying 'ecologists'.
explanation.pattern: Find the main verb first; a word before it that describes the subject must not be a second main verb.

items.passage: Rare mineral deposits lie beneath the high plateau, and who may mine them has never been settled. The network of deposits that underlie the plateau, along with the narrow canyons that cut through them, ______ the focus of a long-running dispute between the regional government and several mining companies.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: are
choices.slip: The subject is 'network' (singular); 'along with' and the plural nouns nearby do not change that.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: Plural, so it does not agree with 'network'.

choices.text: is
were
choices.slip: Plural and past, so it does not agree with 'network' or fit the present context.

steps: Subject: 'network'.
'along with... canyons' is an add-on.
Singular verb.
explanation.why: The head noun is 'network', so the verb is singular.
explanation.pattern: Find the head of the subject; phrases introduced by 'along with' do not make it plural.

items.passage: Field recordings now make it possible to compare whole regions rather than single sites. Researchers wanted to know whether birds in different regions sing differently. After analyzing four hundred hours of recorded calls from forest birds at twelve sites, ______
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: a regional pattern in the birds' songs was identified by the research team.
choices.slip: The opening phrase would modify 'pattern', but patterns don't analyze recordings.

choices.text: the team's identification of a regional pattern in the songs was announced.
choices.slip: The opening phrase would modify 'identification', which can't analyze recordings.

choices.text: regional patterns in the birds' songs were among the team's findings.
choices.slip: The opening phrase would modify 'patterns', which can't analyze recordings.

choices.text: the research team identified a regional pattern in the birds' songs.

steps: Who analyzed the recordings?
The team.
So 'the research team' must be the subject.
explanation.why: The subject right after the opening phrase must be the one who analyzed: the team.
explanation.pattern: After an opening -ing or 'After -ing' phrase, the next noun must be its doer.

items.passage: The team tested forty soil samples from an orchard abandoned in 1974 to learn whether past pesticide use had left lasting traces. Each of the samples that the team collected from the orchard's lower terraces ______ contaminated with arsenic, though at widely varying levels.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: was
were
choices.slip: 'Each' is singular, whatever plural nouns follow it.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: Plural, and the present perfect does not fit the past tests.

choices.text: are
choices.slip: Plural and present, which does not fit the past tests.

steps: Subject: 'each'.
Singular, past: 'was'.
explanation.why: 'Each' is the subject and is singular.
explanation.pattern: 'Each of the ___' takes a singular verb, even when the phrase after it is long and plural.

items.passage: Reviewers praised the novel's treatment of language. Critics said the author's strength was exposing readers to unfamiliar dialects rather than ______ them with glossaries and footnotes.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: overwhelm
choices.slip: A bare verb does not match 'exposing' after 'rather than'.

choices.text: overwhelming
to overwhelm
choices.slip: An infinitive does not match 'exposing'.

choices.text: having overwhelmed
choices.slip: A perfect participle changes the timing and does not match 'exposing'.

steps: 'exposing readers... rather than ___'.
Match -ing with -ing.
explanation.why: 'Overwhelming' matches 'exposing' on each side of 'rather than'.
explanation.pattern: The two sides of 'rather than' must be in the same form.

items.passage: The audit was requested after a gift of rare maps went unrecorded for two years. An independent audit of the regional library system found gaps in how new acquisitions were recorded. The auditor recommended that the system ______ its acquisition records every quarter and report any discrepancies to the board.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: reviews
choices.slip: After 'recommended that', the base form is used, not the -s form.

choices.text: reviewed
choices.slip: Past tense does not fit a recommendation about future practice.

choices.text: review
will review
choices.slip: 'Will' does not belong after 'recommended that'.

steps: 'recommended that the system ___'.
Base form: 'review'.
explanation.why: After a verb of recommendation, 'that' clause uses the base form.
explanation.pattern: 'Recommend/suggest/insist that + subject + base verb.'

items.passage: Meltwater on the Orrin glacier refreezes at night, and how quickly it does so affects how much ice the glacier loses over a summer. Hoping to measure the refreezing rate across a full melt season, ______ and logged readings every ten minutes from June to September.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: the glacier's margin received forty thermometers from the research team
choices.slip: 'Hoping' would modify the margin, which cannot hope.

choices.text: forty thermometers were buried along the glacier's margin by the research team
choices.slip: 'Hoping' would modify the thermometers, which cannot hope.

choices.text: the research team buried forty thermometers along the glacier's margin
a line of forty thermometers along the glacier's margin was set out
choices.slip: 'Hoping' would modify the line of thermometers.

steps: The opening phrase 'Hoping to measure...' needs a subject that can hope.
The same subject also 'logged readings'.
Only 'the research team' can both hope and log.
explanation.why: The research team is the logical subject of both 'hoping' and 'logged'.
explanation.pattern: An opening modifier must be followed by the noun it logically describes.

items.passage: The restoration team's survey of the archive's basement, now in its second month, has already turned up more than the catalogue promised. In the northernmost room ______ forty crates of unsorted letters and a locked cabinet containing hand-drawn maps of the old harbor.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: is
choices.slip: The subject is the compound 'crates... and a cabinet', which is plural.

choices.text: are
has been
choices.slip: This form needs a singular subject and a participle.

choices.text: was
choices.slip: This is past singular and does not agree with a compound subject.

steps: The verb comes before its subject ('there' inversion).
The subject is 'crates and a cabinet': two things, so plural.
explanation.why: A compound subject takes a plural verb even when it follows the verb.
explanation.pattern: In inverted sentences, find the real subject after the verb before choosing agreement.

items.passage: Among the university library's most requested holdings are the Aldwyn family papers. The collection of letters, photographs, and survey maps that the family donated in three installments between 1998 and 2004 ______ now catalogued in full, and a finding aid describing every folder can be downloaded from the library's website.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: is
are
choices.slip: 'Collection' is the singular subject; the plural nouns inside the modifier are not.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: This is plural and needs a plural subject.

choices.text: were
choices.slip: This is plural and past, and does not agree with 'collection'.

steps: Subject: 'The collection'.
Everything from 'of letters' to '2004' modifies it.
Singular subject: 'is'.
explanation.why: The singular subject 'collection' takes 'is', whatever plural nouns come between it and the verb.
explanation.pattern: Cross out the modifying phrases to find the subject before choosing the verb.

items.passage: Hydrologists who surveyed the island in 2022 found that its water supply is unusually concentrated. Roughly two-thirds of the island's freshwater ______ drawn from a single aquifer beneath the central plateau, and the remainder comes from small seasonal streams that run dry by August.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: are
choices.slip: 'Two-thirds of the freshwater' takes its number from 'freshwater', which is singular.

choices.text: is
were
choices.slip: Past plural; the passage describes the present and 'freshwater' is singular.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: This plural form does not agree with 'freshwater'.

steps: With a fraction, the number depends on the noun after 'of'.
'Freshwater' is a mass noun: singular.
explanation.why: A fraction of a mass noun takes a singular verb.
explanation.pattern: With fractions and 'most of', agree with the noun inside the 'of' phrase.

items.passage: The river's spring flood has changed noticeably in the decades since engineers completed the Brantley Dam. Since the dam opened in 1964, the average peak flow at the lower gauge ______ by nearly a third, and the floodplain meadows that once depended on the annual surge have begun to give way to shrubland.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: fell
choices.slip: A simple past tense does not fit 'since' plus a change that continues to the present.

choices.text: had fallen
choices.slip: The past perfect needs a later past reference point, which the passage lacks.

choices.text: has fallen
falls
choices.slip: Present simple does not express a change over the period since 1964.

steps: 'Since 1964' marks a period that continues to now.
That calls for the present perfect.
explanation.why: 'Since' with a change that continues to the present takes the present perfect.
explanation.pattern: Match the tense to the time frame: 'since X' with an ongoing result takes the present perfect.

items.passage: The planning board prides itself on consistency, and its minutes support the claim. Rarely ______ the board reverse a ruling once it has been entered in the record, and in the past ten years it has done so only twice, both times after the discovery of a clerical error.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: do
choices.slip: The subject 'the board' is singular.

choices.text: did
choices.slip: The tense should be present to match 'prides itself' and 'has done'.

choices.text: has
choices.slip: 'Has' would need a participle ('reversed'), not the base form 'reverse'.

choices.text: does

steps: 'Rarely' begins the clause, so the helping verb comes before the subject.
Subject: 'the board' (singular), present tense.
explanation.why: After a negative adverb, the helping verb precedes the subject and agrees with it.
explanation.pattern: After 'rarely', 'seldom', 'never', check the inverted helping verb for tense and number.

items.passage: At its meeting in March 1912, the geographical society announced that it ______ its annual conference to Geneva the following spring, since the hall in which it had always met would be closed for repairs until at least the autumn of 1913.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: will move
choices.slip: The announcement is in the past, so the future in the past ('would') is needed.

choices.text: would move
moved
choices.slip: A simple past does not express a plan for the following spring.

choices.text: has moved
choices.slip: The present perfect does not fit a past announcement about a future event.

steps: The announcement is past.
The plan was for a later time.
So 'would move'.
explanation.why: A plan reported from the past takes 'would'.
explanation.pattern: In reported speech, shift 'will' to 'would'.

items.passage: Written in 1887 and revised twice before its final publication in 1893, ______ was never seriously challenged by the owners of Hallam's textile mills, who answered its claim that they were underpaying their workers only with attacks on the author's character.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: critics of the pamphlet
choices.slip: 'Written' would wrongly modify critics, who did not write it.

choices.text: the author's central argument
choices.slip: The argument was not itself written and revised; the pamphlet was.

choices.text: the owners' reply to the pamphlet
choices.slip: 'Written... and revised' cannot describe the owners' reply.

choices.text: the pamphlet

steps: The opening phrase is 'Written in 1887 and revised'.
What was written? The pamphlet.
The noun that follows must be the pamphlet.
explanation.why: The opening participial phrase must be followed by the noun it describes.
explanation.pattern: Ask what the opening phrase describes, then pick the choice that starts with that noun.

items.passage: Glaciologists who study the plateau have long searched for a single feature that sets certain ice masses apart from the rest, and the survey was designed to settle that question. What distinguishes the Brask glaciers from their neighbors, according to the 2021 survey of the plateau, ______ not their size but the thin band of volcanic ash that runs through their upper layers and darkens the surface each summer.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: is
are
choices.slip: The subject is the 'what' clause, which is singular; the plural 'glaciers' and 'neighbors' inside it do not control the verb.

choices.text: being
choices.slip: 'Being' is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: The subject is singular and the sentence describes a present contrast, so 'have been' fails twice.

steps: The subject is the noun clause 'What distinguishes ... according to the 2021 survey'.
A 'what' clause acting as subject is singular.
The complement 'band' is singular too; the plural nouns 'glaciers' and 'neighbors' sit inside the clause and do not change the verb.
explanation.why: The singular noun clause takes 'is'.
explanation.pattern: A what-clause subject takes a singular verb, whatever plural nouns appear inside it.

items.passage: Field botanists rarely become famous, and many spend their careers on projects that few outside the discipline ever notice or read about. In 2020 the Brask Institute published a long-awaited monograph on the lichens of its plateau. Having spent two decades cataloguing the lichens and publishing little beyond a handful of field notes, ______
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: the monograph, which she released in 2020, came as a surprise to colleagues who had assumed she had stopped working.
choices.slip: The monograph did not spend two decades cataloguing lichens; the botanist did.

choices.text: Marit Esker surprised colleagues, who had assumed she had stopped working, by releasing a monograph in 2020.
Marit Esker's monograph, released in 2020, came as a surprise to colleagues who had assumed she had stopped working.
choices.slip: The possessive 'Marit Esker's' is not the subject; 'monograph' is, so the opening phrase still dangles.

choices.text: colleagues who had assumed she had stopped working were surprised by Marit Esker's 2020 monograph.
choices.slip: The opening phrase would describe the colleagues, who did not do the cataloguing.

steps: 'Having spent two decades cataloguing...' needs a person as its subject.
Only Marit Esker spent the two decades.
The word right after the comma must name her as the subject, not her possessive.
explanation.why: The opening phrase correctly modifies 'Marit Esker', the subject of the main clause.
explanation.pattern: Ask who did the action in the opening phrase; that person must be the grammatical subject, not a possessive.

items.passage: Government audits are usually written in a flat and cautious tone, but one report on the water system stood out for how plainly it assigned praise and blame. The inspector's report both criticizes the ministry for ignoring warnings that were raised as early as 2014 and ______ it with acting quickly once the first leaks were reported in 2019.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: is crediting
choices.slip: 'Is crediting' is a different verb form from 'criticizes', so the pair is not parallel.

choices.text: then crediting
choices.slip: The first verb is finite, so 'crediting' is not parallel.

choices.text: credits
has credited
choices.slip: 'Has credited' is a different verb form from 'criticizes', so the pair is not parallel.

steps: 'Both ... and' joins two parallel verb phrases.
The first is 'criticizes the ministry for ignoring...'.
The second must also be a simple present verb: 'credits it with...'.
explanation.why: 'Credits' matches 'criticizes' in form.
explanation.pattern: After 'both', match what follows 'and' to the first element exactly.

items.passage: Funding for harbor improvements had been scarce for years, and the council knew that any plan would face tough questions about its cost and benefit. Of the two proposals the council considered in March, the one submitted by the harbor engineers, though neither was likely to be funded in full, was clearly ______ costly to carry out over the first decade.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: lesser
choices.slip: 'Lesser' does not combine with 'costly' this way.

choices.text: least
choices.slip: 'Least' is a superlative, and only two proposals are being compared.

choices.text: the least
choices.slip: 'The least' is a superlative, and only two proposals are being compared.

choices.text: the less

steps: Two proposals are compared.
With two items the comparative is used, not the superlative.
'The less costly of the two' is the correct pattern.
explanation.why: 'The less' is the comparative form for a comparison of two items.
explanation.pattern: With two items, use the comparative (the more, the less); the superlative is for three or more.

items.passage: River towns in the interior had traditionally depended on barges to move grain, and arguments about whether larger boats could ever reach them divided local opinion. By the time the first steamship reached Verdane in 1851, the town's merchants, who had long assumed that the river was too shallow for anything larger than a barge, ______ already begun lobbying the provincial government to fund a deeper channel.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: had
have
choices.slip: 'Have' is present perfect, which cannot be tied to a past arrival in 1851.

choices.text: were
choices.slip: 'Were already begun' is not a correct verb form.

choices.text: would
choices.slip: 'Would already begun' is not a correct verb form.

steps: 'By the time ... reached ... in 1851' sets a past point.
The lobbying came before that point, so past perfect is needed.
The embedded 'who had long assumed' also uses past perfect, matching the main verb.
explanation.why: 'Had begun' places the lobbying before the steamship's arrival.
explanation.pattern: With 'by the time' plus a past event, use past perfect for what came earlier.

items.passage: Literary awards vary widely in how they select winners, and some of the most respected prizes use procedures that outsiders find surprising. The Sable Prize, ______ judges are chosen by lot from among past winners and are forbidden to discuss a nomination until the shortlist is announced, went this year to a collection of essays on migration.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: which
choices.slip: 'Which judges are chosen' would make the prize itself the thing that chooses judges, and it leaves 'judges' without a possessive link.

choices.text: whose
who's
choices.slip: 'Who's' means 'who is' or 'who has', not a possessive.

choices.text: that the
choices.slip: 'That' cannot follow a comma to open a nonrestrictive clause.

steps: The clause tells us about the prize's judges.
A possessive relative pronoun is needed.
'Whose' is the possessive form; 'who's' is a contraction.
explanation.why: 'Whose' links the prize to its judges.
explanation.pattern: Use 'whose' for possession in a relative clause, including for things; 'who's' is a contraction.

items.passage: Remote lighthouses run on routines that are strict in every detail, and the logs show how closely equipment is monitored from one year to the next. Every instrument kept in the lighthouse's lower store, together with the spare parts and the brass fittings that the keepers inherit from the previous crew, ______ inspected twice a year by the district engineer.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: are
choices.slip: 'Every' makes the subject singular, and 'together with' does not add a second subject, so 'are' does not agree.

choices.text: were
choices.slip: The subject is singular and the present-tense passage rules out the past tense.

choices.text: is
have been
choices.slip: 'Have been' is plural, and 'twice a year' signals a repeated present habit.

steps: The subject is 'Every instrument'.
'Together with the spare parts and the brass fittings' is an insert and adds no second subject.
The singular subject and the present-tense context call for 'is'.
explanation.why: The singular present-tense subject takes 'is inspected'.
explanation.pattern: 'Together with' and similar phrases do not make a singular subject plural.

items.passage: A routine survey in 2022 found rust along the lower cables of the Aldwick footbridge, though none of the strands had yet broken. Concerned that the cables might fail under heavier traffic, ______
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: a new inspection schedule was drawn up by the county's engineers, who also limited the bridge to pedestrians.
choices.slip: The schedule is not the one concerned; the engineers are.

choices.text: the bridge was limited to pedestrians by the county's engineers, who also drew up a new inspection schedule.
choices.slip: The bridge is not the one concerned; the engineers are.

choices.text: a limit to pedestrians was set by the county, whose engineers also drew up a new inspection schedule.
choices.slip: The limit is not the one concerned; the engineers are.

choices.text: the county's engineers drew up a new inspection schedule and limited the bridge to pedestrians.

steps: 'Concerned that...' describes people, not objects.
The engineers are the ones concerned.
The noun right after the comma must be the engineers.
explanation.why: The engineers are the subject, so the opening phrase modifies them correctly.
explanation.pattern: An opening adjective phrase describes the first noun that follows the comma; it must be someone who can be concerned.

items.passage: Tidal gauges are cheap to buy and expensive to keep running. Hydrologists comparing the records from the nine gauges along the Ostrel estuary found that the gauge at Pier Four is the only one of the nine that ______ unbroken readings for the full period since 1998. The other eight were moved, repaired, or replaced at least once, and each interruption left a gap that analysts could not fill reliably.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: have recorded
choices.slip: 'That' refers to 'the only one', not to 'the nine', so the verb is singular.

choices.text: has recorded
are recording
choices.slip: The plural verb is wrong for the same reason, and the progressive tense does not fit a completed period.

choices.text: having recorded
choices.slip: 'Having recorded' is not a finite verb, so the clause would have no verb.

steps: 'The only one of the nine that ___' : the relative clause describes 'the only one'.
'One' is singular, so the verb is singular.
The plural 'nine' is the trap.
explanation.why: 'That' refers to the singular 'only one', so the verb is 'has recorded'.
explanation.pattern: With 'the only one of the ...', the relative pronoun takes a singular verb.

items.passage: Eels hatch in the open ocean and cross thousands of miles to reach European rivers, and for most of the twentieth century no one could follow a single fish for more than a few days. In 1974 the Fennick Institute ______ the first tags small enough for young eels, and every major study of their routes since then has relied on that design.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: has developed
choices.slip: A present perfect verb cannot be paired with a fixed past year like 1974.

choices.text: had developed
choices.slip: The past perfect needs a later past event as a reference, and none is given.

choices.text: was developing
choices.slip: The progressive describes work in progress, but the tags were finished and used from then on.

choices.text: developed

steps: 'In 1974' names a finished moment in the past.
A completed past action at a stated time takes the simple past.
'Since then ... has relied' is a separate present-perfect clause and does not change this verb.
explanation.why: A completed event at a fixed year takes the simple past, 'developed'.
explanation.pattern: Use the simple past with a stated past date; the present perfect is for unspecified or ongoing time.

items.passage: Turtles come ashore on the Vellan coast only at night and only for a few weeks, which makes the work hard to organize. Tracking the tagged turtles, their nests, and the hatchlings that emerge each August ______ a team of eleven volunteers working in shifts from dusk until dawn, because the beaches are too long for a smaller crew to cover in a single night.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: takes
take
choices.slip: The subject is the single gerund phrase 'Tracking ...', which is singular, not the plural nouns inside it.

choices.text: are taking
choices.slip: The plural verb fails, and the progressive implies a single current event rather than a general fact.

choices.text: have taken
choices.slip: The plural verb fails, and the perfect tense does not fit a general present fact.

steps: The subject is the gerund phrase 'Tracking the tagged turtles, their nests, and the hatchlings ...'.
A gerund phrase as subject is singular.
The plural nouns inside it are traps.
explanation.why: One singular activity takes the singular verb 'takes'.
explanation.pattern: A gerund phrase used as a subject takes a singular verb, whatever nouns follow the gerund.

items.passage: Conservators examine old paintings with raking light, tiny samples, and long patience, and they usually expect to find damage. Despite three centuries of exposure to candle smoke, the pigments in the chapel's ceiling still looked ______ to the conservators who examined them in 2021, though the plaster beneath had begun to flake along several of the old repair lines, and the diocese was already weighing whether to fund a second round of cleaning.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: remarkable vivid
choices.slip: 'Remarkable' cannot modify the adjective 'vivid'; an adverb is needed.

choices.text: remarkable vividly
choices.slip: Both words are wrong: 'looked' needs an adjective, and 'vividly' is an adverb.

choices.text: remarkably vividly
choices.slip: 'Vividly' is an adverb, but 'looked' here is a linking verb that needs an adjective.

choices.text: remarkably vivid

steps: 'Looked' here means 'appeared', a linking verb, so it takes an adjective: vivid.
To intensify that adjective an adverb is needed: remarkably.
The combination is 'remarkably vivid'.
explanation.why: An adverb modifies the adjective that follows the linking verb.
explanation.pattern: After a linking verb use an adjective, and modify it with an adverb.

items.passage: Planners in the valley describe the dam as a thirty-year project, and its monitoring network is the least visible part. The Karn dam will not store water until 2032, but the project's schedule is already fixed. By the time the reservoir begins to fill, engineers ______ more than four hundred sensors along the valley walls and tested every one of them against the baseline readings taken in 2027.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: will have installed
will be installing
choices.slip: The progressive means the work is still going on, but 'tested every one' shows it will be finished.

choices.text: have installed
choices.slip: The present perfect cannot refer to a completed action before a future time.

choices.text: would have installed
choices.slip: 'Would have' is for unreal or past conditions, not for a plain future plan.

steps: 'By the time the reservoir begins to fill' sets a future deadline.
Work completed before that deadline takes the future perfect.
'Tested every one of them' confirms the work is finished by then.
explanation.why: Completed-before-then action takes 'will have installed'.
explanation.pattern: Use the future perfect for an action that will be finished before a stated future time.

items.passage: Historians of the grasslands rely heavily on local sources, many of which were never published outside the counties where they were written. Ten Thousand Furrows, the 1958 collection of farm diaries that its editors gathered from sixty families across the prairie, ______ still the most cited source on early settlement diets. Its editors worked without pay and, by their own account, rejected nearly a third of the entries submitted.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: are
choices.slip: The title is one book, so a plural verb is wrong despite 'Furrows', 'diaries', and 'families'.

choices.text: is
have been
choices.slip: A plural verb is wrong, and 'still' signals a present state.

choices.text: were
choices.slip: A plural verb is wrong, and the past does not fit 'still the most cited'.

steps: The subject is the title 'Ten Thousand Furrows', one work.
The plural words nearby are traps.
'Still' signals present tense.
explanation.why: One work takes a singular verb, 'is'.
explanation.pattern: A title takes a singular verb even if it looks plural.

items.passage: Critics in the capital dismissed such artists as amateurs, and gallery owners who disagreed risked their reputations. In the 1880s the Wexmere gallery, whose director distrusted the polished canvases favored by the academy, began buying work by self-taught painters rather than academy graduates. A former shipwright who had taught himself to paint by copying engravings in the town library, ______
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: the gallery bought forty canvases from Tobias Renk in 1884, hanging them all in the east wing.
choices.slip: The opening phrase would describe the gallery, which did not teach itself to paint.

choices.text: Renk's forty canvases of harbor scenes were bought by the gallery in 1884.
choices.slip: The possessive 'Renk's' is not the subject; 'canvases' is, so the phrase describes the canvases.

choices.text: forty canvases were sold to the gallery by Tobias Renk in 1884, and all were hung.
choices.slip: The opening phrase would describe the canvases, which cannot paint.

choices.text: Tobias Renk sold forty canvases to the gallery in 1884.

steps: The opening phrase describes a person who taught himself to paint.
The first noun after the comma must name that person.
Only 'Tobias Renk' as a subject fits; the other choices put something else there or use a possessive.
explanation.why: The shipwright is the subject, so the opening phrase is attached correctly.
explanation.pattern: An opening phrase about a person must be followed by that person as the subject.

items.passage: The Sorrel Theatre faces a budget gap of nearly two hundred thousand dollars after a year of falling attendance, and its trustees have rejected the idea of cutting any productions. They plan to raise ticket prices at the three largest venues, sell naming rights to the main foyer, and ______ the free weekday matinees that have drawn few visitors since spring.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: trimming
choices.slip: In a series after 'plan to', every item is a bare verb, so an -ing form breaks the parallel.

choices.text: will trim
choices.slip: 'Plan to raise, sell, and will trim' mixes an infinitive series with a finite verb.

choices.text: trim
trims
choices.slip: 'Trims' is a singular finite verb and does not match 'raise' and 'sell'.

steps: 'plan to raise ..., sell ..., and ___' is a series sharing one 'to'.
Each item must be a bare verb.
So the last item is 'trim'.
explanation.why: 'Raise', 'sell' and 'trim' match.
explanation.pattern: Items in a series must have the same form.

items.passage: Cores are drilled in tubes about a meter long, and each is logged, sliced, and dated before anyone draws a conclusion. Glaciologists who study ice cores often assume that the oldest layers lie only in the deepest boreholes. Forty percent of the cores that the Ravick team has drilled from the glacier since 2016 ______ ice older than eight thousand years, a proportion that surprised the team's glaciologists.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: contains
choices.slip: 'Cores' is plural, so the verb must be plural.

choices.text: has contained
choices.slip: 'Has' is singular, but the percentage refers to the plural 'cores'.

choices.text: have contained
is containing
choices.slip: 'Is' is singular and the progressive does not fit a completed count.

steps: The percentage refers to 'cores'.
'Cores' is plural, so the verb is plural.
'The Ravick team has drilled' is a separate clause.
explanation.why: The percentage takes its number from 'cores', so the verb is 'have contained'.
explanation.pattern: With 'percent of', the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'.

items.passage: The council spent most of the spring weighing two proposals for the old cannery district. Neither of the two plans that the staff presented in April, despite months of lobbying by local developers and a petition signed by nearly four hundred residents, ______ enough support to pass. The council will meet again in June.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: has won
have won
choices.slip: 'Neither' is singular; the plural 'residents' and 'developers' are in the interrupter.

choices.text: win
choices.slip: 'Neither' needs a singular verb, and 'win' is plural.

choices.text: were winning
choices.slip: The verb is plural and 'were winning' does not fit the completed vote.

steps: The subject is 'Neither'.
The interrupter beginning 'despite' does not change it.
The singular present perfect is 'has won'.
explanation.why: 'Neither' takes 'has won'.
explanation.pattern: Neither is singular, whatever intervenes.

items.passage: The park's winter program trains volunteers to map snow-covered trails, repair damaged signs after storms, and ______ hikers who have lost their way. Applicants must be at least eighteen and complete a two-day course before the first snowfall.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: guiding
choices.slip: The series of bare verbs breaks with an -ing form.

choices.text: will guide
choices.slip: 'Will guide' is finite and does not match 'map' and 'repair'.

choices.text: guides
choices.slip: 'Guides' does not match the bare verbs 'map' and 'repair'.

choices.text: guide

steps: 'trains volunteers to map ..., repair ..., and ___' is a series.
Each item is a bare verb.
So the last is 'guide'.
explanation.why: 'guide' matches 'map' and 'repair'.
explanation.pattern: Items in a series must have the same form.

items.passage: Built without a spillway, ______ during the flood of 1911, when the river rose four meters in two days. Later engineers added a concrete channel, and the dam has held since.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: the flood overwhelmed the dam
choices.slip: The flood was not built without a spillway, so the opening phrase misattaches.

choices.text: engineers saw the dam fail
choices.slip: The engineers were not built without a spillway, so the opening phrase misattaches.

choices.text: the dam failed
the river topped it
choices.slip: The river was not built without a spillway, so the opening phrase misattaches.

steps: The opening phrase describes something that was built.
The next noun must be that thing.
Only the dam was built.
explanation.why: 'the dam' is the thing built without a spillway.
explanation.pattern: An opening modifier must describe the subject that follows it.

items.passage: Since the new pump was installed in the village well in 2015, water use in the village ______ by nearly a third, and residents no longer queue before dawn.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: has fallen
fell
choices.slip: A simple past tense does not link the 2015 start to the present as 'since' requires.

choices.text: had fallen
choices.slip: The past perfect needs a later past reference, and none is given.

choices.text: falls
choices.slip: The present tense does not match an event with a starting point in 2015.

steps: 'Since 2015' marks a period running to now.
That calls for the present perfect.
'Has fallen' fits.
explanation.why: 'has fallen' links 2015 to the present.
explanation.pattern: 'Since' with a past starting point takes the present perfect.

items.passage: The variety of crops grown on the narrow terraces above the river, some of them found nowhere else in the region, ______ remarkable for a valley so steep. Visitors often assume that the terraces are newer than they are.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: are
choices.slip: 'Variety' is singular; the plural 'crops' and 'some of them' are in modifiers.

choices.text: were
choices.slip: The passage is in the present tense.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: 'Have been' is plural.

choices.text: is

steps: The subject is 'The variety'.
'of crops ... region' modifies it.
So the verb is singular present: 'is'.
explanation.why: 'is' agrees with 'variety'.
explanation.pattern: The subject is the head noun, not the noun in a modifying phrase.

items.passage: The tern colony produced ______ chicks this year than last, even though the number of nesting pairs rose slightly and the weather stayed mild through June.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: less
choices.slip: 'Less' is for amounts that cannot be counted, but chicks are countable.

choices.text: fewer
lower
choices.slip: 'Lower' does not modify a countable noun in this way.

choices.text: smaller
choices.slip: 'Smaller' describes size, not number.

steps: Chicks are countable.
The comparison needs a word for a smaller number.
'Fewer' is correct.
explanation.why: 'fewer' modifies countable chicks.
explanation.pattern: Use 'fewer' with countable nouns and 'less' with mass nouns.

items.passage: A series of small tremors, each weaker than the one before it and none strong enough to be felt in the valley town, ______ recorded at the station in March before the main shock arrived in April.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: were
choices.slip: 'Series' is singular; the plural 'tremors' sits in a modifier.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: 'Have been' is plural and does not fit the past time.

choices.text: was
are
choices.slip: 'Are' is plural and present.

steps: The subject is 'A series'.
'of small tremors ...' modifies it.
The past singular verb is 'was'.
explanation.why: 'was' agrees with 'series'.
explanation.pattern: A singular collective head noun takes a singular verb.

items.passage: Restoring a degraded wetland is usually far more expensive than ______ one from scratch, according to the engineers who studied sites in four states.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: to create
choices.slip: The comparison begins with an -ing form, so the second term must match.

choices.text: create
choices.slip: A bare verb does not match 'Restoring'.

choices.text: creation of
choices.slip: This makes the sentence unparallel and awkward.

choices.text: creating

steps: 'Restoring' is a gerund.
A comparison needs matching forms.
So 'creating' completes it.
explanation.why: 'creating' matches 'Restoring'.
explanation.pattern: Compared items must have the same grammatical form.

items.passage: After the hearing, the rangers gave the survey results, along with the original field maps that had been stored in the basement for decades, to the county biologist and ______. We spent the following week comparing the two sets of figures line by line.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: me
I
choices.slip: 'I' is a subject pronoun, but the blank is an object of 'to'.

choices.text: myself
choices.slip: 'Myself' is reflexive and has no subject to reflect.

choices.text: my own
choices.slip: 'My own' is incomplete without a noun.

steps: 'to the county biologist and ___' is a compound object of 'to'.
An object pronoun is needed.
'Me' is the object form.
explanation.why: 'me' is the object of 'to'.
explanation.pattern: Use object pronouns after prepositions, even in compound objects.

items.passage: Several engineers had signed off on the revised foundation drawings, so the failure came as a surprise to the owners. Not the architects but the site foreman, whom the owners had hired only in March and who answered to no one on the design team, ______ the first to notice the cracks in the east wall last winter.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: were
choices.slip: The verb agrees with 'architects', but with 'not ... but' it agrees with the nearer subject, 'foreman'.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: A plural verb again follows 'architects'; the subject is the singular foreman.

choices.text: was
were being
choices.slip: A plural verb does not agree with 'foreman', and the progressive does not fit.

steps: In 'not X but Y' the verb agrees with Y.
Y is 'the site foreman', which is singular.
The event was last winter, so the simple past 'was' fits.
