explanation.why: 'Foreman' is singular, so 'was'.
explanation.pattern: With 'not X but Y', the verb agrees with the noun nearer to it.

items.passage: Few documents from the early port survive intact. The archive's oldest ledger, a water-stained volume that records every cargo unloaded at the Marrick quay between 1802 and 1819, ______ to the museum in 1974 by a retired customs officer who had found it in his attic while clearing the house of a distant cousin.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: was donated
having been donated
choices.slip: A participle cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence has no finite verb.

choices.text: donated
choices.slip: 'Donated' would make the ledger the donor, and the 'by' phrase shows it was donated.

choices.text: being donated
choices.slip: A participle cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence has no finite verb.

steps: The subject is 'the archive's oldest ledger'; the appositive and the 'that' clause only describe it.
The sentence still needs a finite main verb.
The 'by a retired customs officer' phrase calls for the passive 'was donated'.
explanation.why: 'Was donated' supplies the passive main verb.
explanation.pattern: A long subject with a modifier still needs a finite main verb.

items.passage: The Larkin Foundation changed its application procedure for 2025. Under the revised rules, a grant applicant must either submit a written statement describing the project's budget and expected community benefits to the foundation's regional office by March 1 ______ with the review panel in person during the first week of April. Staff expect about two hundred applications.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: or to interview
choices.slip: 'Either submit' is followed by a bare verb, so 'to interview' breaks the parallel.

choices.text: or interviewing
choices.slip: A gerund does not match the bare verb 'submit'.

choices.text: or interviewed
choices.slip: A past participle does not match the bare verb 'submit'.

choices.text: or interview

steps: 'Either' opens the first option: 'submit a written statement'.
'Or' must open a parallel second option.
The first option is a bare verb after 'must', so the second must be too.
explanation.why: 'Or interview' matches 'submit'.
explanation.pattern: Items joined by either...or take the same form.

items.passage: The Mereth Prize, awarded every three years by an international society of river scientists, goes to the ecologist ______ the selection panel believes has done the most to restore degraded river habitat during the preceding decade. This year's panel, which met for two days in Geneva, was unusually divided. Several members had proposed candidates from their own institutions.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: whom
choices.slip: 'Whom' is tempting beside 'the panel believes', but the pronoun is the subject of 'has done'.

choices.text: who
whoever
choices.slip: 'Whoever' cannot follow the noun 'ecologist' this way.

choices.text: whomever
choices.slip: 'Whomever' cannot follow the noun 'ecologist' this way and is the wrong case.

steps: Drop 'the selection panel believes': 'the ecologist ___ has done the most'.
The blank is the subject of 'has done'.
A subject takes 'who'.
explanation.why: 'Who' is the subject of 'has done'.
explanation.pattern: A parenthetical like 'she believes' does not change the case of the pronoun.

items.passage: The twelve letters found in the Oswin attic are unsigned, and the sender is unknown. Because they are postmarked in 1911 and refer to private matters that few outsiders would have known, the letters ______ by someone close to the family, though the handwriting does not match any surviving member's. Archivists have so far catalogued the letters by date only.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: must have written
choices.slip: The letters cannot write; they were written.

choices.text: must have been writing
choices.slip: The letters were not the writers, so a progressive active form fails.

choices.text: must have been written
must be written
choices.slip: A present form does not express an inference about the past.

steps: The letters receive the action, so the verb is passive.
The inference concerns 1911, a past time.
'Must have been written' combines the perfect for the past and the passive.
explanation.why: Past inference plus passive voice gives 'must have been written'.
explanation.pattern: Use modal + have + been + participle for a passive inference about the past.

items.passage: Auditors reviewing the city's shipping contracts found that early cost estimates were often unreliable. The more the council relied on those estimates when it signed a contract, ______ the final cost differed from the amount the council had approved, a pattern the auditors traced to bidders who submitted low figures in order to win the work.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: the less
choices.slip: The estimates were unreliable, so more reliance should mean more difference, not less.

choices.text: so much more
choices.slip: The correlative pair needs 'the more' to answer 'the more'.

choices.text: the more that
choices.slip: The extra 'that' breaks the paired comparative.

choices.text: the more

steps: 'The more ... , the ___' is a paired comparative.
The estimates were unreliable, so greater reliance meant a larger gap.
The second half needs 'the more'.
explanation.why: 'The more' pairs with 'The more' and fits the logic.
explanation.pattern: Paired comparatives take 'the' in both halves, and the second half must match the logic.

items.passage: The review board met nine times last year, and its minutes show a pattern. More than one member of the board's three-person finance committee, including two who had voted for the original budget, ______ for a formal audit of the transit fund.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: have since asked
choices.slip: 'More than one' takes a singular verb; 'two' and 'members' pull toward the plural.

choices.text: has since asked
has since been asked
choices.slip: The verb agrees, but the passive reverses the meaning: the members requested the audit, they were not asked for one.

choices.text: have since been asking
choices.slip: The plural verb does not agree with 'More than one member'.

steps: The subject is 'More than one member', which is singular.
The plural 'two who had voted' is inside an interrupter and does not control the verb.
The members did the asking, so the verb must be active: 'has since asked'.
explanation.why: 'More than one member' is singular and active: 'has since asked'.
explanation.pattern: 'More than one' takes a singular verb, whatever plural words follow.

items.passage: Engineers who inspected Harcourt Weir in 1998 recommended replacing its timber gates with steel ones. Had the water board accepted that advice at the time, the weir ______ standing today, and the 2019 flood would not have breached it.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: would still have been
choices.slip: 'Today' marks a present result; the perfect form puts the result in the past.

choices.text: will still be
choices.slip: 'Will' is future and ignores the unreal past condition.

choices.text: would still be
had still been
choices.slip: 'Had been' is a past-perfect condition form and cannot be the result clause.

steps: 'Had the board accepted' is an unreal past condition (1998).
'Today' makes the result present.
An unreal past condition with a present result takes 'would' plus the base verb: 'would still be'.
explanation.why: The present result of an unreal past condition is 'would still be standing'.
explanation.pattern: Mixed conditional: past perfect condition, 'would + base verb' for a present result.

items.passage: The mill's grinding stones are rated for a limited load. Roughly 4,000 kilograms of grain, together with the wooden hoppers that feed the stones and the chutes that carry the flour away, ______ the most the mill can safely process in an hour, according to its 1952 manual.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: are
choices.slip: The plural nouns in the 'together with' phrase do not make the subject plural.

choices.text: were
choices.slip: The plural is wrong and the past tense does not fit 'can safely process'.

choices.text: have been
choices.slip: The plural does not agree with the singular amount, and the tense does not fit.

choices.text: is

steps: The subject is 'Roughly 4,000 kilograms', a single amount.
'Together with' adds nouns without changing the subject's number.
The present tense matches 'can safely process': 'is'.
explanation.why: The single amount takes 'is'.
explanation.pattern: An amount treated as one quantity is singular; 'together with' phrases do not change number.

items.passage: The farms along the ridge keep their hay in barns of every size. Few of the buildings are ______ the Orsini family's barn, which was built in 1912 to hold the harvest from three neighboring estates.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: as large as, if not larger than,
as large, if not larger than,
choices.slip: The first comparison is left incomplete: 'as large' needs its own 'as'.

choices.text: as large if not larger than
choices.slip: The phrase 'as large' has no 'as' to complete it, and the insertion needs its commas.

choices.text: larger than, if not as large as,
choices.slip: The inserted comparison is reversed, so 'larger than' fails to complete either comparison correctly.

steps: Two comparisons share one object: 'as large as' and 'larger than'.
Each comparison needs its own complete idiom.
The interrupting phrase is set off with commas: 'as large as, if not larger than, the barn'.
explanation.why: Both comparisons are complete: 'as large as, if not larger than,'.
explanation.pattern: In 'as X as, if not Y-er than', each comparison keeps its own 'as ... as' or 'than'.

items.passage: The wreck found off Marlowe Flats is generally believed ______ the harbor in about 1740 carrying salt, though no manifest has survived, and the hull's oak planking, dated by its growth rings, supports that estimate.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: to enter
choices.slip: The simple infinitive fails to place the entry earlier than the present belief.

choices.text: to have entered
to be entering
choices.slip: The progressive infinitive suggests an action in progress now.

choices.text: having entered
choices.slip: A participle cannot follow 'is believed' this way.

steps: The belief is held now; the ship's entry happened about 1740.
An action earlier than the main verb takes the perfect infinitive.
'To have entered' fits 'is believed'.
explanation.why: The perfect infinitive 'to have entered' marks the earlier event.
explanation.pattern: Use 'to have + past participle' for an event that happened before the verb it depends on.

items.passage: Three municipal crews were assigned to the flood repairs. The Harcourt Road crew, the Eastgate crew, and the lakeshore crew each ______ responsible for a separate stretch of the channel, and a supervisor from the water board inspected every stretch in May.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: was
choices.slip: 'Each' after a plural subject does not make the verb singular.

choices.text: has been
choices.slip: The singular verb ignores the plural compound subject, and the present perfect conflicts with the past narrative.

choices.text: were
is
choices.slip: The singular present tense ignores the plural subject and the past narrative.

steps: The subject is the three crews, a plural compound.
'Each' follows the subject; it does not replace it.
The narrative is past, so 'were'.
explanation.why: The plural subject takes 'were'.
explanation.pattern: 'Each' placed after a plural subject leaves the verb plural.

items.passage: Few navigational records from the old port survive. The only surviving copies of the 1911 harbor charts, a set of six hand-colored sheets that once hung in the pilots' office, ______ now kept in climate-controlled storage, and the museum admits visitors to see them by appointment only.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: are
is
choices.slip: The appositive 'a set' is singular but does not govern the verb; the plural 'copies' does.

choices.text: has been
choices.slip: The singular verb ignores the plural subject 'copies'.

choices.text: were
choices.slip: The past tense conflicts with 'now kept' and 'admits'.

steps: The subject is 'copies', plural.
'A set of six ... office' only renames it and does not change its number.
'Now kept' and 'admits' are present, so 'are'.
explanation.why: The plural subject 'copies' takes 'are'.
explanation.pattern: An appositive does not change the number of its head noun.

items.passage: The shipyard museum's pride is its replica of an 1890 steam launch. Assembled from donated parts over fourteen years, ______ the shipyard's most visited exhibit, and its brass fittings are polished by volunteers every Saturday.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: volunteer labor from retired welders has made the replica
choices.slip: 'Assembled' would describe 'labor', not the replica.

choices.text: the launch replica, a favorite of school groups, has become
the builders, many of them retired welders, made it
choices.slip: 'Assembled' would describe the builders, not the replica.

choices.text: visitors from school groups now regard the replica as
choices.slip: 'Assembled' would describe the visitors, not the replica.

steps: 'Assembled from donated parts' must modify the noun right after the comma.
Only the replica was assembled from parts.
The long insertion 'a favorite of school groups' does not change the subject.
explanation.why: 'The launch replica ... has become' makes the replica the thing assembled.
explanation.pattern: A modifier at the start of a sentence describes the subject that follows the comma.

items.passage: Output at the Wragby Lane mill has more than doubled, and the payroll, once limited to nine workers, now covers forty, ever since the owners ______ the old turbines for a single modern unit in 1987.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: replace
choices.slip: The present tense does not fit a completed event in 1987.

choices.text: had replaced
choices.slip: The past perfect needs a later past reference, but the main clause is in the present perfect.

choices.text: replaced
have replaced
choices.slip: The present perfect cannot take the fixed past time 'in 1987'.

steps: The main clause uses the present perfect ('has doubled').
The 'since' clause names a completed past event with a date, 'in 1987'.
The simple past is required.
explanation.why: 'Replaced' places the event at a fixed time in 1987.
explanation.pattern: Since + simple past clause; present perfect in the main clause.

items.passage: The 1904 ledgers, which the last clerks tied with twine and stacked on the vault's bottom shelf, ______ undisturbed there ever since the old bank closed in 1931.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: has lain
choices.slip: The singular verb ignores the plural subject 'ledgers'.

choices.text: have lain
have laid
choices.slip: 'Laid' needs an object; the ledgers are simply resting.

choices.text: has laid
choices.slip: The verb is singular and 'laid' needs an object.

steps: The subject is 'ledgers', plural; the relative clause in between is a distraction.
The intransitive verb 'lie' (to rest) has the participle 'lain'.
'Ever since' calls for the present perfect: 'have lain'.
explanation.why: 'Have lain' agrees with 'ledgers' and uses the correct form of 'lie'.
explanation.pattern: Lie, lay, lain (rest); lay, laid, laid (place). Agreement follows the head noun.

items.passage: The inspector's report praised the mill's safety record far more warmly than it ______ the mill's profits, which the report noted had fallen in each of the last three years.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: did
does
choices.slip: The present tense does not match the past 'praised'.

choices.text: has done

Comparative adverb: 'more precisely'.
explanation.why: 'More precisely' is the comparative adverb for a two-way comparison.
explanation.pattern: Action verb takes an adverb; compare two things with the comparative.

items.passage: Most of the island's orchards belong to the Zelenko family, whose apple trees were planted in the 1880s and whose cider is sold across the region. explanation.why: 'The Pennistons' vineyards' is the plural possessive.
explanation.pattern: Plural family name + possession = -s plus apostrophe.

items.passage: The reservoir above Wrenfall was full by April, and hydrologists at the county office confirmed that the snowpack had melted early and that no drought was expected. The clauses are in the past ('was', 'through September of that year'), so the verb is past.
'The town still restricted' meets both.

explanation.pattern: Although/though + clause, main clause with no but/yet; keep tense consistent.

items.passage: When the Tessarine Narrows canal opened in 1901, its engineers promised shipping companies that the new locks they had designed ______ the passage between the two seas to under a day, and for nearly a decade the companies, trusting those promises and the published tide tables for both coasts, rerouted their freight accordingly, signing contracts for the following three seasons at fixed rates.

Future-in-the-past uses 'would' plus the base verb.
'Would shorten' states a promised future without implying it failed.
explanation.why: 'Would shorten' is the backshifted future after 'promised'.
explanation.pattern: After a past reporting verb, 'will' becomes 'would'.

items.passage: Insurers had expected the divers to find a breach in the freighter’s hull, since the leak began after the ship struck a reef. 'To date' needs the present perfect.
'Has shown' is singular present perfect.

items.passage: In the novel's last chapter, the narrator, a mapmaker who left her family's farm in 1960, returns to the valley, finds the orchard cut down, and ______ that nobody in the village remembers her father, whose letters she has carried for decades without once answering them, though everyone recalls the dog that followed him everywhere, a detail the narrator finds almost unbearable.

The blank is the last verb in a series and must match.
'Learns' keeps the simple present.
explanation.why: 'Learns' is parallel with 'returns' and 'finds'.
explanation.pattern: Series of verbs: keep one tense; literary events use the present.

items.passage: The report that the three hydrologists drafted after a decade of fieldwork on the Ketterly River, a project that cost the university nearly two million dollars and employed forty students, ______ that the river be classified as a protected watercourse before any new dams are approved, and the state legislature will debate it in March, when the three authors are due to testify.

'Report' is singular; 'hydrologists' and 'dollars' are distractors.
The subject must not be repeated by 'it'.
explanation.why: 'Report ... recommends' is a singular finite verb with no repeated subject.
explanation.pattern: Long subject + one finite verb; no pronoun repetition.

items.passage: After the main pump failed in March, the inspector from the water board asked the contractor how long ______, since the town's reservoir held only five days of reserve water at the rate residents were then using it and the next delivery of replacement parts was not due for a week, which left the town council with little room to bargain.

steps: An indirect question keeps statement order: subject before verb.

'The repair would take' satisfies both.

explanation.pattern: Indirect question: no inversion; after past reporting, shift tense.

items.passage: The largest expense in the county’s flood plan, a document that engineers revised in 2022 after two seasons of record rainfall and that the commissioners adopted unanimously, ______ the rebuilding of three bridges before the spring thaw, though widening the river channel comes a close second, according to the county engineer’s summary.

'Engineers', 'rainfall' and 'commissioners' are nearby distractors.
Present-tense context ('comes a close second') calls for 'is'.
explanation.why: 'Expense … is' matches the singular subject and present tense.
explanation.pattern: Find the true subject across a long appositive.

items.passage: The Orsley valley depends on a ring of eleven wells dug in the 1950s. 'Last year' is finished, so use the simple past.
'Was' is singular and past.
explanation.why: 'One ... was dry' is singular and past.
explanation.pattern: 'One of which' is singular; a finished time takes the simple past.

items.passage: The weaver Marit Soderquist spent three winters rebuilding the Aldermoor loom's warp frame from old photographs, a rusted bracket, and a diary that her grandmother had kept. When the foundation's grant, which covered materials and labor, was finally divided between the museum that owns the loom and ______, a dispute arose over who would hold the finished frame during the spring exhibitions.

explanation.why: 'Between the museum ... and her' uses the objective case after a preposition.
explanation.pattern: Both nouns after 'between' are objects, so any pronoun in the pair is objective.

items.passage: Residents of the Tamarack Street district have argued for years about who is to blame for the flooding. choices.text: would have been
choices.slip: 'Would' belongs in the result clause, not in the 'if' clause.

choices.text: had been

steps: The 'if' clause concerns something that did not happen in 1988, so it takes the past perfect.
The result clause ('would not be happening') is about the present; this is a mixed conditional.
'Had been built' completes the 'if' clause.
explanation.why: 'If ... had been built' with 'would not be happening' is the standard mixed conditional.
explanation.pattern: Unreal past condition: past perfect in the if-clause; would + base verb in the result.

items.passage: Glaciologists comparing records from polar stations depend on consistent depth readings. items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

require

A gerund subject is singular and the clue 'can shift' shows present tense.
The main verb must be finite: 'requires'.
explanation.why: 'Measuring ... requires' pairs a singular gerund subject with a finite present verb.
explanation.pattern: A gerund phrase is singular; plural nouns inside it do not change the verb.

items.passage: Archaeologists working in southern Mesopotamia were surprised by the condition of one find. steps: The subject is plural 'tablets'; 'that the survey team recovered' is a relative clause and 'team' is not the subject.
The tablets rested; 'lie' (rest) is intransitive, 'lay' (place) takes an object.
'For roughly four thousand years' up to now gives the present perfect: 'have lain'.
explanation.why: 'Tablets ... have lain' is plural, present perfect, and uses the intransitive verb.
explanation.pattern: Lie/lay: lie = rest (lain), lay = place (laid); then match the real subject.

items.passage: Questions about the Pendarvis Institute's research oversight have surfaced again. The antecedent is plural 'audits' and refers to things, so the relative pronoun is 'which' with a plural verb.
'Most of which were conducted' completes the clause.
explanation.why: 'Most of which were conducted' is a correct relative clause with a plural verb.
explanation.pattern: Quantifier + of + which/whom joins a clause; the verb agrees with the antecedent.

items.passage: Publishing historians still debate how scholarly books found wide audiences in the 1990s. items.passage: Bank archivists surveying old buildings often find that renovation has erased the original design. explanation.pattern: After 'the only one of', the relative clause verb is singular.

items.passage: Flood maps of the river basin show a striking imbalance among its watercourses. items.passage: Tenant groups often learn about lease terms only after a dispute begins, as one association did last year. ______ that the lease allowed the landlord to raise rent without notice, it would have asked for a revised contract before the tenants' association voted, but the clause appeared only in a footnote on page nineteen of a document that ran to forty pages.

items.passage: Water boards require regular proof that critical equipment works. items.passage: Conservation staff at the municipal library track how much of the rare collection has been stabilized. items.passage: Since 2018 the Corbel Strait port authority has levied a series of surcharges on container ships, and shippers have complained steadily. items.passage: Administrators at the Kestrel Hill clinic had assumed that pharmacy shortages came from late deliveries. items.passage: After the river overtopped its banks in March, regional planners met for three evenings but could not agree on a response, since each plan the staff drew up seemed to protect one district at the expense of another. items.passage: Last spring the Vellmont arts council announced that its festival, an event that organizers had held each July since 1994, would move to the fall. items.passage: The Skarrow ice field has drawn researchers for decades because it sits far from any town. items.passage: Routine inspections at the Tarnow dam last autumn turned up an unexpected problem. items.passage: The Eskwith Valley farmers' cooperative had warned in August that early frost could damage the apple crop, and the harvest report, released in November, confirmed it. explanation.why: 'As ... had predicted' uses a conjunction and the right tense.
explanation.pattern: As + clause; like + noun. Match the tense to the narrated past.

items.passage: Heritage groups across the region have long struggled to pay for upkeep. 'Own' is a state verb, so the simple present perfect 'has owned' is used, not the progressive.

items.passage: Until this year, only licensed processing plants could wholesale baked goods in the county, and small bakeries that wanted to supply cafes had to sell through a distributor. items.passage: Archivists at the Vantry Library have spent three decades re-examining texts whose authenticity was doubted. 'Since the 1990s' calls for the present perfect: 'has been authenticated'.

items.passage: Council crews have spent the spring digging up the eastern half of the district. Residents who live along Gresham Terrace, a street that flooded twice last winter, ______ the new drainage channels, which crews will finish in June, and several have already asked the council whether the work can start earlier.

In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition and takes a gerund: 'seeing'.
explanation.why: 'Residents ... look forward to seeing' is plural and uses a gerund.

items.passage: Divers who surveyed the intake tower last autumn reported that its concrete had begun to spall. The Dellmar reservoir was drained in November so that the engineers, who had found deep cracks in the tower during a September dive, ______ the foundation on dry ground before the spring melt refilled it, a job that the contractor had budgeted at six weeks.

items.passage: When a retired schoolteacher died in January, she left a gift to the city's library system with instructions about how it should be shared. The bequest, which the family's lawyers valued at 1.2 million dollars, ______ the four branch libraries in proportion to each branch's circulation, and the first payments reached the branches in March.

'Among' is used for three or more recipients; 'between' is for two.
explanation.why: 'Bequest ... was divided among' is singular and uses 'among' for four recipients.
explanation.pattern: Singular subject; between = two, among = three or more.

items.passage: Conservation biologists monitoring the Kirkholme wetland had long suspected that restoring its tidal flow would favor native species. The ratio of marsh sparrows to the invasive finches that nest along the drainage channels, which volunteers have counted at forty plots every spring, ______ to three to one in 2021, the year the floodgates were first opened, and the gap has kept widening since, as the most recent count showed.
items.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: has risen
choices.slip: A definite past year ('in 2021') cannot take the present perfect.

steps: The subject is 'ratio', singular; 'sparrows', 'finches' and 'plots' sit inside modifiers.
'In 2021, the year the floodgates were first opened' fixes a finished past time, so the simple past is needed, even though the gap keeps widening now.
'Rose' is singular-compatible and simple past.
explanation.why: 'Ratio ... rose ... in 2021' is singular and simple past.
explanation.pattern: Singular head through modifiers + definite past date means simple past, not present perfect.

items.passage: The authority's board had asked for an independent review after two years of deficits. The auditors who reviewed the Dravik Transit Authority's books concluded that its projected shortfall of nine million dollars could be closed neither by raising fares, a step the riders' council had already rejected twice, nor ______ because the contracts that fix service levels run through 2027 and cannot be reopened without penalties.

choices.slip: Same preposition, but a noun phrase does not match the gerund 'raising'.

choices.text: by trimming weekend service

steps: 'Neither ... nor' joins two elements that must have the same grammatical form.
The first element is 'by raising fares': preposition plus gerund phrase.
The second must repeat it: 'by trimming weekend service'.
explanation.why: 'By trimming weekend service' mirrors 'by raising fares'.
explanation.pattern: Neither/nor needs the same preposition and verb form on both sides.

items.passage: The Sedgmere aqueducts, built in the 1890s to carry spring meltwater to the lower town, have worried the ministry for years. 'Since March' with a continuing, unfinished effort calls for the present perfect progressive.
'Has now asked' confirms a present frame, so 'have been examining'.
explanation.why: 'Engineers ... have been examining ... since March' is plural and present perfect progressive.

items.passage: Landlords in the river district have argued for years that the city's flood rules fall unevenly on small property owners. items.passage: The tidal-turbine engineer Odalys Renn was a prodigy by any measure. items.passage: When the regional carrier added the island route in March, its crews had to learn a very different kind of airfield. 'Plotting their approaches by radar' fits.

items.passage: A state audit released last week reviewed how forty county governments handled the aftermath of a statewide revenue shortfall. items.passage: Enrollment planning at the college became unusually difficult last year. Not only the projected enrollment figures but also the two cost estimates that the registrar compiled for the dean ______ revised in the spring, after the county announced that its largest employer would close a plant that had supplied a quarter of the district's students, and trustees met in emergency session to review the new figures.

items.passage: The Aldwych Fellowship, which supports young researchers in marine biology, employs only six program officers for several hundred awardees. items.passage: Budget disputes at the city's parking authority have dragged on since the downtown garage was condemned in 2022. items.passage: Reporters pressed the transit director for details about the opening of the Lowmere extension, which the mayor had promised riders for the previous spring and had mentioned twice in public. items.passage: Growers in the Rushden valley, who supply most of the region's malting barley, had endured a difficult year. items.passage: In a study, volunteers rated a recorded lecture more highly when told that the speaker was a famous professor than when told that the speaker was a graduate student, though the recording was identical. This suggests that listeners' judgments of a lecture ______

choices.slip: The content was identical, yet the ratings differed.

choices.text: are most accurate when the speaker is famous.
choices.slip: The study shows ratings changed; it doesn't measure which rating was accurate.

choices.text: depend partly on beliefs about the speaker.
improve each time they hear the same recording.
choices.slip: Each volunteer's rating depended on the label, not on repeated listening.

steps: The recording was the same for everyone.
The only difference was who listeners thought the speaker was.
Ratings changed with that belief, so belief affects judgment.
explanation.why: Since only the stated identity of the speaker changed, that belief must have influenced the ratings.
explanation.pattern: In a study, find the one thing that differed between groups. The conclusion is about that thing.

items.passage: Linguist Dara Kemp notes that the island's two villages share almost all of their everyday vocabulary but use entirely different words for boats, nets, and fish. Since everyday words tend to be inherited, while the terms of a trade are often adopted along with the trade itself, Kemp reasons that the villagers ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: come from unrelated peoples who later borrowed everyday words from each other.
choices.slip: Everyday words 'tend to be inherited', so shared everyday words point to common origin, not borrowing.

choices.text: were already fishing long before the two villages became separate communities.
choices.slip: If so, they would have inherited the same fishing words.

choices.text: learned to fish from a single group of outsiders who visited both villages.
choices.slip: Learning from the same source would give both villages the same fishing terms.

choices.text: share a common origin but took up fishing separately, after they had divided.

steps: Shared everyday words + 'everyday words tend to be inherited' → the villages descend from one community.
Different fishing words + 'terms of a trade are adopted with the trade' → each village acquired fishing on its own.
So fishing came after the split.
explanation.why: Common everyday words point to shared ancestry; different fishing terms point to fishing being taken up independently.
explanation.pattern: Apply each general rule in the text to the matching fact, then combine the two results.

items.passage: A museum found that visitors stood longer in front of paintings with long wall labels than in front of those with short ones. Curator Bo Ferris cautioned against concluding that long labels hold attention on the art: cameras showed that the extra time went to reading and that visitors looked at the paintings themselves for about as long either way. Lengthening the labels, then, would probably ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: keep visitors at each painting longer without adding to the time they spend looking at it.
lead visitors to study each painting itself more closely than they do when its label is short.
choices.slip: Time spent looking at the paintings was 'about as long either way'.

choices.text: make no difference to how long visitors remain standing in front of each painting.
choices.slip: Visitors did stand longer where labels were long.

choices.text: shorten the time visitors spend at each painting, since reading would tire them.
choices.slip: Long labels went with longer, not shorter, stays.

steps: Long labels → more time standing at the painting.
But the extra time was spent reading the label.
Time looking at the painting itself didn't change.
So longer labels add standing time, not looking time.
explanation.why: The cameras separate two measures: total time (longer with long labels) and time looking at the art (unchanged).
explanation.pattern: Keep two similar measures apart. Here 'time in front of the painting' and 'time looking at the painting' behave differently.

items.passage: Economist Lila Brandt compared towns that raised parking fees with towns that did not. Shop revenue fell in the towns that raised fees, a result often cited as proof that fees drive shoppers away. But Brandt observes that towns tended to raise fees when their budgets were strained, and budgets are strained when the local economy is already slowing. The comparison, therefore, ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: indicates that the fees did not reduce revenue, since shops in those towns were losing sales already.
choices.slip: A slowdown could explain the fall, but that doesn't show the fees had no effect; the text supports doubt, not the opposite claim.

choices.text: leaves open whether the fees reduced revenue, since shops in those towns may have been losing sales already.
understates how far the fees reduced revenue, since the economies of those towns were already slowing.
choices.slip: A slowdown that was already lowering revenue would make the fees look more harmful, not less.

choices.text: shows that the fees reduced revenue only in those towns whose economies had already begun slowing.
choices.slip: Brandt has no fee-raising towns with healthy economies to compare, so 'only in those towns' can't be shown.

steps: Towns that raised fees were towns with strained budgets.
Strained budgets go with an economy that is 'already slowing'.
So shop revenue in those towns may have been heading down before the fees changed.
The comparison can't separate the effect of fees from the slowdown. It doesn't prove fees are harmless, either.
explanation.why: Because fee-raising towns were already slowing, the fall in revenue can't be pinned on the fees, and it can't be ruled out as their effect either.
explanation.pattern: A flawed comparison supports 'we can't tell', not the opposite claim. 'Did not reduce' goes as far beyond the evidence as 'did reduce'.

items.passage: The poet Sorrel Iyo dated each manuscript page, and scholars have used the dates to trace how her style developed. Analysis of her paper now shows that Iyo routinely recopied old poems onto fresh sheets, dating each page on the day of copying, and that she revised as she copied. The style of a poem on a page dated 1931, therefore, ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: must be assigned to some earlier year, since the date records only when Iyo copied the poem.
choices.slip: She 'revised as she copied', so parts of the poem may belong to 1931; and not every page is a recopy ('routinely', not always).

choices.text: can be assigned to 1931 with confidence, since Iyo dated each page on the day that she filled it.
choices.slip: The poem may have been composed years earlier and only copied in 1931.

choices.text: cannot be assigned wholly to 1931 or wholly to an earlier year without some further evidence.
may be assigned to a later year, since Iyo is known to have revised her poems after copying them.
choices.slip: The text says she revised while copying, and a page can't hold changes made after its date unless the text says so.

steps: The date on a page is the day she copied it, not the day she first wrote the poem.
So a page dated 1931 may hold a much older poem: the style can't be assumed to be that of 1931.
But she revised while copying, so some of what is on the page may be new in 1931: the style can't be assumed to be earlier, either.
Without more evidence, the poem's style can't be placed entirely in either period.
explanation.why: Recopying makes the poem possibly older than its date, and revising makes it possibly partly as new as its date, so neither assignment is safe.
explanation.pattern: When new evidence undermines one conclusion, don't jump to the opposite one. 'Must be earlier' overreaches as much as 'is 1931'.

items.passage: Economists studying remote work have often found that employees working from home report higher productivity than office workers. Yet a team led by labor economist Beatriz Anand noted that most such findings rest on workers' own estimates of their output. In her team's study of 3,100 customer-support employees at a large firm, productivity was instead measured by the number of cases each employee resolved per hour, as logged by the firm's ticketing system. Employees were randomly assigned to work from home or in the office for eight months. The home group resolved 4% more cases per hour on average than the office group, a smaller advantage than the 13% that home workers in a comparison survey had estimated for themselves. Anand's team also found, however, that among employees with less than a year at the firm, those assigned to work from home resolved fewer cases per hour than their office counterparts, while among employees with more than a year at the firm the reverse held. Anand suggests that the overall 4% advantage therefore ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: probably reflects workers' overestimates of their own output rather than any real difference, since home workers estimated a 13% advantage but only 4% was measured.
choices.slip: This follows from comparing the estimate with the measurement, not from the split by experience that 'therefore' refers to; it also leaves the newer employees' result unexplained.

choices.text: may be explained mainly by experience rather than workplace, since employees with more than a year at the firm resolved more cases whichever location they worked in.
choices.slip: Among experienced employees the home group resolved more cases than the office group, so location did matter; the effect also reversed for newer employees.

choices.text: likely understates how much working from home helps, since the firm's ticketing system may have logged cases from home workers less completely than from office workers.
choices.slip: Nothing in the text suggests the logging differed by location; random assignment and one system were used.

choices.text: may conceal a disadvantage for newer employees and therefore might not hold at a firm whose staff is mostly recent hires.

steps: Overall result: home group +4%.
But the effect splits: negative for newer employees, positive for those with more than a year.
An average can hide a subgroup that goes the other way. A firm with mostly newer staff could see a different overall effect.
So Anand would say the 4% may conceal a disadvantage for newer employees.
explanation.why: The 4% is an average of two opposite effects, so it may not hold where most employees are new.
explanation.pattern: When a subgroup result runs against the overall result, the overall number can't be assumed to hold for every group or every firm. Reject choices that overgeneralize or explain with facts the text doesn't give.

items.passage: Urban climatologist Lucía Ferreyra compared summer afternoon temperatures across 214 neighborhoods in a large city and found that neighborhoods with more than 30% tree canopy were on average 2.1°C cooler than those with less. Temperatures were read at 4 p.m. on the hottest day of each of three summers from sensors placed two meters above the ground along each neighborhood's main street, and canopy was measured from aerial images. She noted, however, that the high-canopy neighborhoods also tended to have the most parkland and the fewest paved parking lots, features that independently lower surface temperatures, and that canopy cover was highest in the neighborhoods developed earliest. Ferreyra cautions that her comparison therefore
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: shows that trees cool a neighborhood less than parkland does, since the high-canopy neighborhoods also had the most parkland and were the coolest.
choices.slip: Unsupported: the study never compared trees with parkland; it only notes they occur together.

choices.text: suggests that older neighborhoods are cooler mainly because they contain fewer paved parking lots than newer neighborhoods in the same city.
choices.slip: Attributes the whole difference to one feature; Ferreyra names several and does not rank them.

choices.text: does not separate the effect of trees from that of the other features, so it may overstate how much planting trees alone would cool a given neighborhood.
demonstrates that canopy cover has no effect on summer temperature once the amount of parkland in a neighborhood has been taken into account.
choices.slip: Overreaches: she never accounted for parkland, so she cannot show an effect vanishes.

steps: Result: more canopy, 2.1°C cooler.
Problem: canopy travels with parkland and fewer parking lots, which also cool.
So the 2.1°C can't be credited to trees alone; planting alone might do less.
explanation.why: Because other cooling features come with high canopy, the comparison cannot isolate trees and may overstate their effect.
explanation.pattern: A correlation with named confounds limits a causal claim; reject choices that rank the confounds or claim the effect is zero.

items.passage: Archaeologists at the Harrow Fen site found a distinctive style of incised pottery in two layers separated by a thin band of volcanic ash that has been dated by a separate method to about 3,900 years ago. Charcoal from the lowest layer in the sequence has been dated to roughly 4,300 years ago and charcoal from the highest layer to roughly 3,400 years ago, so the whole sequence spans about nine centuries. The style appears in the layer beneath the ash and in the layer immediately above it, where the site's earliest metal tools also appear. Metal tools, by contrast, appear at the site only in layers above the ash. The excavators are confident that the layers were laid down in an unbroken sequence. If they are correct, the pottery style
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: went out of use at the site once metal tools appeared there, since the style is found beneath the ash and metal tools are found above it.
choices.slip: The layer just above the ash holds both the style and the earliest metal tools, so the style did not stop when metal arrived.

choices.text: was already in use at the site before any metal tools appeared there, and was still in use when the first ones did.
must have been made by the people who first brought metal tools to the site, since both appear in layers close to the ash band.
choices.slip: Unsupported: nothing says who made either, and the style came first.

choices.text: was in use for at least several centuries, since a thin band of ash can be dated precisely and the style occurs on both sides of it.
choices.slip: A thin ash band says the layers are close in time, not how long the style lasted.

steps: Style appears below and above the ash.
Metal appears only above the ash.
Unbroken sequence: the layers below the ash are older, so the style predates metal.
The layer above the ash has the style too, so it continued.
explanation.why: Pottery beneath the ash predates the metal, and pottery above the ash shows the style continued.
explanation.pattern: Ordering puzzles: find which layers are older, then reject choices that read 'absent' or 'long' into evidence that only shows 'present'.

items.passage: A coastal town surveys visitors at its ferry terminal each August about their satisfaction with their stay. In a typical year about 80% of respondents rate their stay 'excellent.' The survey, run by the town's tourism office since 2009, is a one-page paper form handed out by staff at the terminal gate during the last week of the month, and its results have been cited in arguments for continued public funding of the ferry. Councilor Hamid Osei-Lindqvist points out that the survey is handed out only to passengers who are leaving by ferry; visitors who leave early by road, a group local hotels say is larger after rainy weeks, are never asked. Osei-Lindqvist argues that the 80% figure
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: is probably accurate, since it is based on a large number of responses collected at a single, busy location every year, and the figure has stayed close to 80% in each year that the survey has been run.
choices.slip: Ignores the point at issue: many responses from one group do not cure leaving out another.

choices.text: shows that visitors who leave by road are less satisfied with their stay than visitors who leave by ferry.
choices.slip: Unsupported: road visitors are never surveyed, so no comparison exists.

choices.text: would probably fall in a month with more rain, since rainy weather makes more visitors leave early and fewer of them take the ferry.
choices.slip: Goes beyond the text: it says more road leavers follow rainy weeks, not that satisfaction would fall in a rainy month.

choices.text: may overstate how satisfied visitors are overall, since the survey omits a group that could include a larger share of dissatisfied visitors.

steps: Survey reaches only ferry leavers.
Road leavers, who go early after rain, are excluded.
If those leavers are less happy, 80% is too high.
explanation.why: Leaving out early road leavers means the 80% might overstate satisfaction.
explanation.pattern: Selection problems: the flaw is who is missing; reject choices that claim the missing group's views or add predictions the text doesn't make.

items.passage: In a trial of a new asthma inhaler, 2,000 patients were randomly assigned to the new inhaler or to a standard one. Among patients using the standard inhaler, 20% had a severe attack during the year; among those using the new inhaler, 14% did. Both groups were seen at the clinic every three months, and an attack was counted only if it required emergency treatment or a hospital stay. A pharmaceutical newsletter reported that the new inhaler 'cut severe attacks by 30 percent.' Clinician Ruth Castellanos-Boyd objected that the figure, while accurate,
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: expresses the drop relative to the standard inhaler's rate, which could be mistaken for 30 fewer patients in every 100 having an attack when the difference was 6 in every 100.

exaggerates the benefit, since a difference between 20% and 14% in a trial of 2,000 patients is no larger than chance would produce, which would make the 30 percent figure unreliable even though patients were assigned at random.
choices.slip: Unsupported: the text gives no test of chance; accurate figures were reported.

choices.text: measures only the patients using the new inhaler, of whom 30% avoided an attack, and ignores the patients using the standard one, which is why Castellanos-Boyd considers the figure unusable.
choices.slip: Wrong arithmetic: the 14% attack rate means most new-inhaler patients avoided attacks.

choices.text: is correct only if the new inhaler is compared with no treatment at all, not with another inhaler already known to work.
choices.slip: Invents a condition: the 30% comes from the same two-group comparison.

steps: 20% to 14% is 6 percentage points.
6 out of 20 is 30%, a relative drop.
Readers may take '30 percent' as 30 per 100 patients, which overstates the absolute gain.
explanation.why: The 30% is a relative reduction, while the absolute difference is 6 patients in 100.
explanation.pattern: Relative versus absolute change: compute both (6 of 20 = 30%, but 20% - 14% = 6 points).

items.passage: Marine ecologist Dr. Sunniva Aberthaw trapped hermit crabs at a rocky site and recorded the sizes of the shells they occupied. Crabs in shells of the most common species, the banded whelk, were on average larger than crabs in shells of the thinner-walled moon snail, and Aberthaw found that 18 of 20 crabs offered a choice between the two kinds of empty shell, in a tank, chose the whelk. Yet in tide pools at the same site, where both shell types were readily available, nearly half the crabs lived in moon snail shells. Aberthaw concludes that the crabs' preference for whelk shells in the tank
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: does not by itself predict which shells crabs occupy in the wild, where factors other than preference may decide which empty shells a crab ends up in.
shows that crabs in tide pools choose moon snail shells deliberately, since nearly half of the crabs in the pools were found living in them.
choices.slip: Contradicts the tank result and invents deliberation; the text suggests other factors.

choices.text: shows that the crabs' preference for whelk shells is not real, since the crabs that were tested in the tank chose differently from the crabs living in the tide pools.
choices.slip: Overreaches: 18 of 20 crabs chose whelk, so the preference is real; Aberthaw says only that it does not by itself predict where crabs live.

choices.text: is stronger evidence of preference than the tide-pool data, since the tank trial controlled the number of shell choices that each crab was offered.
choices.slip: Not Aberthaw's conclusion; the question is what the preference predicts, not which data are stronger.

steps: Tank: 18 of 20 chose whelk.
Pools: nearly half live in moon snail shells.
So tank preference doesn't predict wild occupancy; other factors (availability, competition, size) may intervene.
explanation.why: The tank preference and the pool occupancy disagree, so preference alone doesn't predict where crabs live.
explanation.pattern: When lab preference and field behavior disagree, the safe inference is that the lab result does not transfer directly; reject choices that discard one data set or explain it with invented causes.

items.passage: Every manuscript in the Orlan collection that carries a water-stain was copied before 1500, since the monastery's roof was replaced in that year and the manuscripts were moved to a dry cellar. Archivist Casimir Fenwick found that the manuscript catalogued as O-47 has no water-stain. From these facts alone, it follows that O-47
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: was certainly copied after 1500.
choices.slip: A stain-free manuscript could still be older; the rule only runs from stains to date.

choices.text: was copied before 1500 and kept in the cellar.
choices.slip: Nothing says where it was kept.

choices.text: cannot be older than the monastery's new roof.
choices.slip: The text gives no such limit.

choices.text: might have been copied before 1500 or after it.

steps: Rule: stained implies copied before 1500.
O-47 is not stained.
Denying the 'if' part says nothing: stain-free manuscripts may be of any date.
explanation.why: The rule links stains to early dates but does not say early manuscripts are all stained, so O-47's date is open.
explanation.pattern: 'All A are B' does not tell you about things that are not A.

items.passage: Between 2010 and 2020, the number of public libraries in Tarn County fell from 31 to 24, while the number of books borrowed per library rose by 35%. Analyst Gideon Roark notes that the county's population grew only slightly over the same period. Based on this information, it is most likely that between 2010 and 2020
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the total number of books borrowed in the county rose by 35%.
choices.slip: Per-library borrowing rose 35%, but there are fewer libraries, so the total rose by less.

choices.text: the average library in the county lent more books than the average library had in 2010.
residents of the county began reading far more than they had before.
choices.slip: Borrowing per library says nothing directly about reading per person.

choices.text: library closures in Tarn County reduced the number of books available to borrow.
choices.slip: Books on hand are never mentioned.

steps: Libraries: 31 to 24.
Borrowing per library: up 35%.
So each remaining library handled more, while the total change is smaller than 35%.
explanation.why: A 35% rise per library means each remaining library carried more borrowing than before.
explanation.pattern: A per-unit rise and a falling count of units give a smaller rise in the total.

items.passage: Few letters written by tenant farmers in nineteenth-century Lorne survive. Historian Cecily Ardeen notes that nearly all of those that do survive were preserved in the archives of landlords' estates, and that most of them concern rent, repairs, or disputes over land. Based on this information, it is most likely that
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the surviving letters give a picture of tenant life weighted toward dealings with landlords.
landlords in Lorne destroyed most of the letters that tenants wrote about other subjects.
choices.slip: Nothing says landlords destroyed letters.

choices.text: tenant farmers in Lorne wrote more letters than the farmers of other regions did.
choices.slip: No comparison with other regions is given.

choices.text: tenant farmers in Lorne wrote mainly about rent and repairs in all of their correspondence.
choices.slip: The surviving sample may not match what tenants wrote overall.

steps: Surviving letters come from landlords' archives.
They mostly concern rent and land.
So the surviving record leans toward those topics.
explanation.why: Letters kept by landlords are likely to reflect tenants' dealings with landlords.
explanation.pattern: Ask how the evidence was preserved before treating it as a picture of the whole.

items.passage: In a study of a sound-based alarm for hospital patients, researchers found that nurses responded to the new alarm in an average of 22 seconds, compared with 35 seconds for the old alarm. However, the new alarm was installed only on the two wards with the fewest patients per nurse, while the old alarm remained on the other six wards. Based on this information, the results are best understood as
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: showing that the new alarm is faster on wards with few patients per nurse but no faster on wards with heavier workloads.
choices.slip: Nothing was tested on the heavier wards, so no claim about them follows.

choices.text: not establishing that the new alarm is faster, since the difference in response times may reflect the lighter workloads on the wards that received it.
ruling out any effect of the new alarm, since nurses on lightly staffed wards respond quickly to any alarm.
choices.slip: The text does not show that the alarm had no effect, only that its effect cannot be separated from workload.

choices.text: suggesting that the six wards with the old alarm would have averaged 22 seconds if they had received the new one.
choices.slip: The six wards have heavier workloads, so this prediction is not supported.

steps: New alarm only on the lightest-workload wards.
Faster responses could come from workload, not the alarm.
explanation.why: Because the wards differed in workload, the comparison cannot isolate the alarm's effect.
explanation.pattern: When groups differ in more than the treatment, the result cannot be credited to the treatment alone.

items.passage: Between 2022 and 2024, ridership on the Corvale city bus system rose by 12 percent, from 8.0 million to about 8.96 million trips a year. Over the same period, the system's annual fare revenue fell by 3 percent. Transit analyst Mireille Lagerfeld-Strand attributes this combination to a 2022 policy that made transfers between routes free and capped daily fares. She notes that no route was added or dropped, the price of a single ride was not changed, and the fleet and hours of service stayed the same throughout. Given these figures, her account implies that the average fare collected per trip ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: dropped by about 3 percent, the same amount as total revenue, since the price of a single ride was not changed.
choices.slip: Confuses total revenue with revenue per trip; trips rose too.

choices.text: declined by exactly 15 percent, the sum of the 12 percent rise in trips and the 3 percent drop in revenue.
choices.slip: Adding the two percentages is wrong; 0.97/1.12 is about 0.87.

choices.text: stayed roughly constant, because the increase in trips offset the fall in revenue that the capped daily fares caused.
choices.slip: If it stayed constant, revenue would have risen with trips.

choices.text: fell by more than 12 percent, because total revenue shrank while the number of trips grew by 12 percent.

steps: Revenue = trips x average fare.
Trips x1.12 and revenue x0.97 give average fare x0.97/1.12, about 0.87.
So average fare fell by about 13 percent, more than 12.
explanation.why: 0.97 divided by 1.12 is about 0.866, a drop of roughly 13 percent.
explanation.pattern: Percent changes in a product combine by multiplying, not adding.

items.passage: From 1960 to 1985, volunteers counted breeding pairs of the marsh-dwelling Verrick's warbler along a fixed 9-kilometer path by listening for its song at dawn. From 1990 to 2015, surveyors counted the same species along the same path but played a recording of the warbler's song at each stop and tallied every bird that approached, a method that draws in males that might otherwise stay silent. The average count was 38 pairs in the first period and 91 in the second. Weather and the length of the breeding season were similar in the two periods. Ornithologist Hester Quillon-Abbas, who cites both series, cautions that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: part of the rise from 38 to 91 pairs may reflect the new method's greater detection of birds, so the counts alone do not show how much the population grew.
population size must have more than doubled, because a method that draws in silent males cannot detect pairs that were never there.
choices.slip: Detection can differ from numbers; more detected does not mean more present.

choices.text: counts from the later period are unreliable because playback recordings can frighten warblers away from the path before surveyors tally them.
choices.slip: Invents a harm the text never mentions.

choices.text: only the earlier count is valid, since volunteers listening at dawn would have heard every pair that was present.
choices.slip: Silent males would have been missed, so it is not complete.

steps: The method changed between the two series.
The new method detects birds that stay silent.
So part of the rise could be better detection.
explanation.why: Because the later method finds birds the earlier one missed, the counts are not directly comparable.
explanation.pattern: When a measuring method changes, a trend may reflect the method, not the thing measured.

items.passage: A trial of the blood-pressure drug norvexin enrolled 1,200 adults aged 30 to 55 with no kidney disease. Patients taking the drug averaged a 9-point drop in systolic pressure after twelve weeks, compared with a 2-point drop among patients taking a placebo. Of those enrolled, 94 percent completed the twelve weeks, and the drug's makers have applied for approval for adults of all ages. Because the kidneys clear norvexin from the body, and kidney function usually declines with age, pharmacologist Wilhelmina Baptiste-Orr, who has studied how the body processes drugs for twenty years, states that the trial's results ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: demonstrate that the drug lowers blood pressure in adults over 70 by less than 9 points, since slower clearing would weaken its effect on the body.
choices.slip: Slower clearing would not obviously weaken the effect; nothing supports the direction.

choices.text: say little about how the drug would act in adults over 70, whose kidneys may clear it more slowly and who were not enrolled.
apply equally to every adult regardless of age, since the placebo group controlled for all differences between patients.
choices.slip: A placebo group does not extend the results to people outside the sample.

choices.text: prove that the drug is unsafe for adults over 70, because slower clearing would raise the drug's concentration in the blood.
choices.slip: Overreach: the trial reports nothing on safety for older adults.

steps: Trial included adults 30 to 55 only.
Clearance depends on kidneys, which change with age.
So results cannot be extended to over-70s without more evidence.
explanation.why: The sample excluded older adults and the mechanism differs with age, so the trial is silent on them.
explanation.pattern: Do not extend results beyond the sampled group when the relevant mechanism differs.

items.passage: The Pellwick Archive arranges donated papers in one of two ways. Everything acquired before 1990 is arranged by year. Everything acquired in 1990 or later is arranged by subject, unless the donor asked in writing for year order, in which case it is arranged by year. A donor's written request has no effect on papers acquired before 1990. The archive holds about 400 donated collections, and the acquisition records for some of the older ones were damaged in a flood. Cataloguer Petronela Szabo-Lindgren finds a bundle of letters arranged by year but cannot locate its acquisition record. She can therefore conclude that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: these letters were acquired before 1990, because the archive never allows donors to choose the arrangement of later papers.
choices.slip: Contradicts the stated exception for later donors.

choices.text: they were acquired in 1990 or later, because the archive normally arranges recent acquisitions by subject rather than by year.
choices.slip: A pre-1990 acquisition would also be arranged by year.

choices.text: either the letters were acquired before 1990 or their donor asked in writing for year order.
its donor asked in writing for year order, since the letters would otherwise have been arranged by subject.
choices.slip: Only holds if the letters came in 1990 or later.

steps: Year order arises two ways: pre-1990, or post-1990 with a written request.
The record is lost, so neither case can be ruled out.
Only the either-or conclusion is guaranteed.
explanation.why: Both routes produce year order, and nothing excludes either route.
explanation.pattern: When an outcome has two possible causes, only their disjunction is guaranteed.

items.passage: Dendrochronologist Aurelian Bexley-Moy dated a roof beam in the old Harlow tithe barn by matching its tree rings to a regional oak sequence. The barn stands on a farm in the north of the county and is thought to have been rebuilt at least once. The beam's final surviving ring formed in 1634. Its outer edge has been trimmed away, so an unknown number of rings is missing, and the sapwood, the pale outer layer that oak usually forms over its last 15 to 40 years of growth, is entirely gone. Bexley-Moy adds that timbers in such barns were sometimes reused from older buildings. From these observations it follows that the beam ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: was cut from a tree felled between 1649 and 1674, because the missing sapwood would have held between 15 and 40 rings of growth.
choices.slip: Overreach: more rings than the sapwood may also have been trimmed away.

choices.text: dates to 1634, the year of its final surviving ring, and was installed when the barn was first built.
choices.slip: Ignores the missing sapwood rings that formed after 1634.

choices.text: could have been felled no earlier than 1634, though the missing sapwood means that its felling date cannot be limited at all.
choices.slip: Misses the stronger limit: at least 15 more rings, so about 1649 or later.

choices.text: must have come from a tree felled no earlier than about 1649, because at least 15 more rings of sapwood must have formed after 1634.

steps: Last surviving ring: 1634.
All sapwood (15 to 40 rings) is missing, so at least 15 later rings existed.
Felled no earlier than about 1649; outer trimming means no upper bound.
explanation.why: The missing sapwood sets a floor of 1634 plus 15 years, and trimmed rings leave the ceiling open.
explanation.pattern: Missing evidence gives a firm bound on one side only.

items.passage: A clinic tracked 200 patients with seasonal flu, of whom 160 took the herbal supplement echinova and 40 did not. After ten days, 100 patients had recovered, and 80 of those 100 had taken the supplement. The clinic's records for the ten days were complete for every patient, and no patient took any other herbal remedy. A clinic newsletter, which goes to about 3,000 local readers, reported that 'most recovered patients took echinova.' Physician Davit Orlov-Maine replied that the newsletter's statement, though true, does not show that the supplement helped, because ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: recovery was equally common in both groups, at 50 percent among those who took the supplement and 50 percent among those who did not.
patients who took the supplement recovered at a rate of 80 percent, while those who did not recovered at only 20 percent.
choices.slip: Misreads shares of the recovered as recovery rates.

choices.text: only 100 of the 200 patients recovered, and a recovery rate of 50 percent is too low to show any benefit from the supplement.
choices.slip: A low overall rate does not show absence of benefit; comparison does.

choices.text: just 40 patients did not take the supplement, too few to be compared with the 160 who did, whatever their recovery rate.
choices.slip: Rates can be compared across unequal groups; the stronger point is that the rates are equal.

steps: Supplement group: 80 of 160 recovered = 50 percent.
No-supplement group: 20 of 40 recovered = 50 percent.
Equal rates, so most recovered took it only because most patients did.
explanation.why: Both groups recovered at 50 percent; 80 percent of the recovered took it only because 80 percent of patients did.
explanation.pattern: Compare rates within each group, not shares among the outcome.

items.passage: The Delmore Museum follows two rules about its east gallery. A work is displayed there only if it has been cleaned in the current year, and a work is cleaned in the current year only if it was sent to the conservation lab in the spring. Registrar Anselm Voss-Adeyemi reports that the painting Gull Study, which the museum bought in 1952 and has moved between storage rooms several times since, was never sent to the lab. From the two rules and the registrar's report, it follows that Gull Study ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: needed no cleaning this year because it hangs in the west gallery, which has no cleaning requirement for any work.
choices.slip: The west gallery is never mentioned; the cause is invented.

choices.text: could still be displayed in the east gallery this year if museum staff cleaned it themselves instead of the lab doing so.
choices.slip: Cleaning in the current year is allowed only after a lab visit.

choices.text: cannot be displayed in the east gallery this year, whatever other reasons the museum may have for keeping it elsewhere.
will be displayed in the east gallery after the spring, since every work sent to the lab is shown there.
choices.slip: Reverses the rule: lab visit is required, not sufficient.

steps: East gallery requires cleaning this year; cleaning requires a spring lab visit.
Gull Study had no lab visit, so no cleaning this year, so no east gallery display.
Only the third choice follows.
explanation.why: Two only-if rules chain: no lab visit rules out cleaning, which rules out the east gallery.
explanation.pattern: Chain 'only if' conditions and run them backwards: missing condition means missing outcome.

items.passage: A field kit for detecting arsenic in well water flags 90 percent of wells that contain unsafe levels, and it wrongly flags 5 percent of wells that are safe. In the Ketterman district, about 1 well in 1,000 has unsafe levels. Hydrologist Priyanka Lindahl-Osei has the kit applied to 100,000 wells chosen at random, and a district office sends a warning notice to every well the kit flags. Lindahl-Osei points out that, among the wells that receive a notice, ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: most are safe, because about 5,000 safe wells are wrongly flagged while only about 90 unsafe wells are correctly flagged.
nearly all are unsafe, because the kit correctly detects 90 percent of the wells that actually contain unsafe levels of arsenic.
choices.slip: Confuses detection rate with the share of flagged wells that are unsafe.

choices.text: about 5 percent are unsafe, because that is the share of safe wells that the kit wrongly flags in the district.
choices.slip: Mixes the false-flag rate with the share of unsafe flagged wells.

choices.text: roughly half are unsafe, because the kit's two error rates of 10 percent and 5 percent balance out in a large sample.
choices.slip: Error rates do not offset each other; the rare condition does the work.

steps: Of 100,000 wells, about 100 are unsafe and 99,900 are safe.
About 90 unsafe wells are flagged; about 5 percent of 99,900, roughly 5,000, safe wells are also flagged.
So most flagged wells are safe.
explanation.why: The flagged group contains roughly 5,000 safe wells and only 90 unsafe ones.
explanation.pattern: When a condition is rare, even a small false-alarm rate produces more false flags than true ones.

items.passage: A regional licensing board offers its boat-pilot exam in an easier morning session and a harder afternoon session. Between 2021 and 2024, the pass rate fell in each session: from 80 percent to 78 percent in the morning, and from 40 percent to 38 percent in the afternoon. Yet the board's overall pass rate rose from 60 percent to 66 percent. Analyst Evander Kowalski-Rhys, who notes that the exam's content and scoring rules did not change, concludes that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: grading was more lenient in 2024 than in 2021, since the overall pass rate rose between those two years.
choices.slip: Scoring rules did not change, and each session's rate fell.

choices.text: candidates in the afternoon session improved more than candidates in the morning session over the three years.
choices.slip: Both sessions fell by 2 points; neither improved.

choices.text: the overall pass rate must have been miscalculated, because it cannot rise when the pass rate falls in both sessions.
choices.slip: It can: the mix of candidates between sessions can change.

choices.text: a larger share of candidates sat the easier morning session in 2024 than in 2021.

steps: Overall rate = 38 + 0.40 x (morning share) in 2024 and 40 + 0.40 x (morning share) in 2021, in percent.
2021: 60 means a 50 percent morning share; 2024: 66 means about a 70 percent share.
More candidates in the easier session raises the overall rate.
explanation.why: Both pass rates fell, so the overall rise comes from more candidates taking the easier session.
explanation.pattern: Overall rates are weighted averages; a change in group mix can reverse the direction of the total.

items.passage: A monastery charter in the Orlow archive is undated, but it names three people who were living and holding office when it was issued: Abbot Hugh Tiernan, who held office from 1102 to 1125; Prior Anselm Vail, who held office from 1118 to 1140; and the cellarer Brother Osric, whose tenure ran from 1109 until his death in 1121. Historian Marguerite Dunstan-Achebe has no other evidence about the charter's date. The narrowest span of years in which the charter can have been issued is ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: 1102 to 1140, the span covered by all three tenures taken together.
choices.slip: The union of the tenures, not the overlap.

choices.text: 1118 to 1121, the years in which all three men held office at once.
1118 to 1125, the years in which both the abbot and the prior held office.
choices.slip: Ignores the cellarer, who died in 1121.

choices.text: 1109 to 1121, the years in which the cellarer held office.
choices.slip: Ignores that the prior was not yet in office before 1118.

steps: The charter must fall where all three tenures overlap.
The overlap starts when the prior arrives (1118) and ends when the cellarer dies (1121).
explanation.why: All three people held office only from 1118 to 1121.
explanation.pattern: Dates from several tenures: take the intersection, not the union.

items.passage: Across 18 countries, those where people eat more salt on average also have higher stroke rates. Epidemiologist Bartholomew Nakagawa-Lindqvist, who compiled the figures from national health surveys that used the same questionnaire in every country, observes that each country contributes a single average for salt intake and a single rate for strokes. He therefore cautions that the comparison ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: cannot show whether, within any one country, the people who eat the most salt are the ones who suffer strokes.
shows that salt has no effect on strokes within individual countries, since only national averages were compared.
choices.slip: Overreach: lack of individual data is not evidence of no effect.

choices.text: proves that national policies on salt, rather than what individuals eat, are what raise the stroke rates in these countries.
choices.slip: Invents a policy cause.

choices.text: is unreliable because averages for different countries cannot be compared, even when the surveys used the same methods.
choices.slip: The questionnaire was the same, so averages can be compared; the problem is what they cannot say about individuals.

steps: The data are country-level averages.
A pattern across groups need not hold for individuals inside the groups.
So the comparison is silent on who within a country has the strokes.
explanation.why: Group averages cannot tell which individuals within a country are affected.
explanation.pattern: Do not infer individual-level links from group-level patterns.

items.passage: The council of Quarrow Island surveyed 200 commuters about two proposed services.
