Of the 200, 130 said they would use the new ferry line and 90 said they would use the new bus line; every respondent answered both questions. Analyst Joaquim Mbatha-Frisk, working only from these totals, wants to know how many respondents said they would use both services. He can say that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: exactly 20 respondents would use both, since the two totals together exceed the number surveyed by 20.
choices.slip: Overlap is at least 20, not exactly 20.

choices.text: no more than 20 respondents would use both, since the two totals exceed the number surveyed by only 20.
choices.slip: Reverses the bound: 20 is the minimum.

choices.text: at least 20 respondents would use both, since the two totals together exceed the number surveyed by 20.
a minimum of 10 respondents would use both, since the shares of 65 percent and 45 percent total 110 percent.
choices.slip: Misconverts: 10 percent of 200 is 20, not 10.

steps: 130 + 90 = 220, which is 20 more than 200.
Those 20 extra counts must be people counted twice.
So at least 20 would use both; more is possible.
explanation.why: Counting 220 uses among 200 people forces at least 20 who use both.
explanation.pattern: Totals that exceed the sample set a minimum overlap, not an exact one.

items.passage: A university found that, among the 1,800 students it admitted last year, entrance-exam scores correlated only weakly with first-year grades. All of the admitted students had scored at least 1400 out of 1600, since the university admits no one with a lower score. Analyst Theodora Hallsworth-Nkemelu therefore concluded that the exam is of little use for predicting how well an applicant will do in college. Her colleague Emeric Torvaldsen-Ba replied that her conclusion goes beyond what the data allow, because ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: first-year grades are influenced by many factors besides exam scores, so a single predictor will always show only a weak relationship with grades in any group of students that one might study.
choices.slip: Overgeneralizes with 'always' and ignores the range problem.

choices.text: students who score above 1400 are likely to earn high grades whatever they do, so the weak relationship actually proves the exam works well as an admissions cutoff.
choices.slip: Claims more than the data show in the other direction.

choices.text: the students studied all scored within a narrow high range, so the data cannot show how well the exam predicts grades among applicants across the full range of scores.
only one year's admitted class was examined, so the relationship between scores and grades might be stronger in other years, which could be learned only by repeating the study.
choices.slip: Speculates about other years; misses the narrow score range.

steps: Everyone studied scored 1400 or above, a narrow band.
A relationship can look weak inside a narrow band and still be strong across all scores.
The choice naming the missing lower scores is the logical gap.
explanation.why: The sample excludes everyone below 1400, so it cannot say how the exam predicts across all applicants.
explanation.pattern: A weak link inside a restricted range does not show a weak link across the whole range.

items.passage: A weight-loss program enrolled 400 people in a 12-week course. Of these, 240 completed the course, and the program's brochure states that 80 percent of those who completed it lost at least 5 percent of their body weight. No weight data were collected from the 160 people who dropped out. Using only these figures, a reader can conclude that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: between 48 and 88 percent of everyone who enrolled lost at least 5 percent of body weight, depending on how the dropouts fared.
about 48 percent of everyone who enrolled lost at least 5 percent of their body weight, since only the 192 completers who lost weight can be counted.
choices.slip: Treats unmeasured dropouts as having lost nothing.

choices.text: about 80 percent of everyone who enrolled lost at least 5 percent of their body weight, since the completers' rate is the best estimate for all enrollees.
choices.slip: Assumes dropouts match completers, which is unsupported.

choices.text: between 48 and 80 percent of everyone who enrolled lost at least 5 percent of their body weight, since dropouts cannot have done better than completers.
choices.slip: Dropouts could have done better; the upper bound is 88.

steps: Completers who lost weight: 80% of 240 = 192, which is 48% of 400.
The 160 dropouts could be 0 to 160 more losers, giving up to 352, or 88%.
So the range is 48 to 88 percent.
explanation.why: Known losers set the floor and counting all dropouts as losers sets the ceiling.
explanation.pattern: When part of the group is unmeasured, state a range, not a single figure.

items.passage: In Harrow County, reported cases of a skin condition rose from 120 in 2022 to 310 in 2023. In 2023 the county opened free screening clinics, and the number of residents screened for the condition rose from about 2,000 in 2022 to about 9,500 in 2023. Based only on these figures, a health official can reasonably say that the rise in reported cases ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: shows that the condition became less common in the county, since the share of screened residents who had it fell from 6 percent to about 3 percent.
choices.slip: The screened groups differ, so the shares cannot show prevalence in the county.

choices.text: shows that the condition became far more common, since reported cases rose by 190, an increase of more than 150 percent in a single year.
choices.slip: Ignores that screening itself raises the count.

choices.text: suggests that the clinics found 190 cases that otherwise would have gone undetected, which is the exact number of new cases the condition produced in 2023.
choices.slip: The 190 mixes newly found old cases with any truly new ones.

choices.text: does not show that the condition became more common, since more residents were screened and the share of screened residents with the condition fell.

steps: Cases rose, but so did screening.
Share of screened with the condition: 120/2000 = 6%; 310/9500 is about 3%.
So the rise in counts is not evidence of a spread of the condition.
explanation.why: A larger screened population can raise counts even when the condition is no more common.
explanation.pattern: A rising count may reflect more detection, so compare rates and note what changed in measurement.

items.passage: A survey of 1,000 city residents asked whether each owned a bicycle. Residents under 30 made up 20 percent of respondents, and 70 percent of them owned a bicycle. Residents aged 30 to 59 made up 50 percent of respondents, and 30 percent of them owned one. Residents 60 and older made up the remaining 30 percent, and 50 percent of them owned one. Taken together, these figures indicate that the share of all respondents who owned a bicycle was ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: 50 percent, which is the plain average of the three age groups' ownership rates of 70, 30, and 50 percent.
choices.slip: Averages the rates without weighting by group size.

choices.text: 44 percent, because each age group's ownership rate counts in proportion to that group's share of all the respondents surveyed.
30 percent, because the 30-to-59 group is the largest and its ownership rate therefore sets the rate for all respondents.
choices.slip: Lets the largest group stand in for everyone.

choices.text: about 38 percent, which is the ownership rate among respondents aged 30 and older, the group that makes up most of the survey.
choices.slip: Leaves out the youngest group's 14 owners per 100 respondents.

steps: 14 + 15 + 15 = 44 percent of respondents.
explanation.why: Weighting each rate by its group's share gives 44 percent overall.
explanation.pattern: An overall rate is a weighted average, not a plain average, and not any one group's rate.

items.passage: The Tarn Island rail, a bird that had lost the ability to fly, was once found across the main island of Tarn and on two small offshore islets. Cats and rats, absent from Tarn until settlers arrived in 1890, spread across the main island within a decade but never reached the islets. By 1905 the rail had vanished from the main island, yet a census that year counted about 300 rails on the islets, a number close to earlier estimates. These facts best support the inference that the rail's disappearance from the main island ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: was more likely caused by the introduced predators than by a condition affecting the whole species, since the rail persisted where the predators did not.
resulted from its inability to fly, since a flightless bird cannot escape danger, and the islet rails survived only because they faced fewer dangers.
choices.slip: Flightlessness predates the decline and does not explain why islet rails persisted.

choices.text: shows that flightless birds cannot survive wherever mammals have been introduced, since the loss followed the arrival of cats and rats by only fifteen years.
choices.slip: Overgeneralizes from one case to all flightless birds.

choices.text: began before the settlers arrived, since the islet population stayed stable while the main island's rails were already in decline well before 1890.
choices.slip: Nothing in the text reports a decline before 1890.

steps: The decline occurred where cats and rats spread and not where they were absent.
A species-wide cause would have hit the islets too.
So the predators are the likelier cause.
explanation.why: Persistence on predator-free islets points to the predators, not a species-wide condition.
explanation.pattern: When a population survives where one factor is absent, that factor becomes the likelier cause.

items.passage: A zoologist weighed adult foxes from two valleys. Zoologists use body mass to ask whether two fox populations belong to the same subspecies. Each fox was weighed once during spring trapping, and all were adults of similar age. The 12 foxes from the Ketra valley ranged in weight from 3.1 to 4.8 kilograms, and the 9 foxes from the Pellan valley ranged from 4.2 to 5.9 kilograms. Based only on these measurements, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: every fox from the Pellan valley is heavier than every fox from the Ketra valley, since the heaviest fox weighed came from the Pellan valley.
choices.slip: The ranges overlap from 4.2 to 4.8 kilograms.

choices.text: the average Pellan fox weighs more than the average Ketra fox, since the Pellan range sits higher than the Ketra range overall.
choices.slip: Overlapping ranges do not fix the averages.

choices.text: a fox weighing more than 4.8 kilograms must be from Pellan, but a fox weighing less than 4.2 kilograms could be from either valley.
choices.slip: Below 4.2 kilograms, only Ketra foxes appear, so the second half is reversed.

choices.text: the lightest fox came from Ketra and the heaviest from Pellan, though a fox's weight alone does not always show its valley.

steps: Ketra spans 3.1-4.8 and Pellan spans 4.2-5.9, so they overlap between 4.2 and 4.8.
The extremes, 3.1 and 5.9, come from different valleys.
Within the overlap, weight cannot identify the valley.
explanation.why: The overall extremes differ by valley, but the overlapping band leaves some weights ambiguous.
explanation.pattern: Overlapping ranges allow statements about extremes but not about every individual or the averages.

items.passage: Ecologists surveying for a rare salamander use a method that detects the animal on any single visit with probability 0.7 when it is present and never reports it when it is absent. Visits are independent. At each of 15 ponds, surveyors visited three times and never detected a salamander. A careful reading of these results indicates that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: salamanders are absent from all 15 ponds, since a method that detects the animal 70 percent of the time would have found it on at least one of three visits.
choices.slip: Overstates: three misses are unlikely, not impossible.

choices.text: about 2.7 percent of the 15 ponds hold salamanders, since 2.7 percent is the chance that a present animal is missed on all three visits.
choices.slip: Confuses the miss chance at an occupied pond with the share of ponds occupied.

choices.text: at any pond, a failure to detect a salamander on three visits is only weak evidence of absence, since each single visit finds the animal 70 percent of the time.
choices.slip: Reverses it: three misses is strong, not weak, evidence.

choices.text: any pond that held salamanders would very probably have produced a detection, so the results make absence at each pond likely but not certain.

steps: Chance of missing a present animal on one visit is 0.3.
Three visits: 0.3 x 0.3 x 0.3 = 0.027.
So a pond with salamanders would show one about 97 percent of the time.
explanation.why: A 2.7 percent miss chance makes absence likely at each pond without making it certain.
explanation.pattern: Combine repeated independent chances before judging a negative result.

items.passage: Horticulturists grew identical tomato seedlings in soil amended with 0, 10, 20, 40, or 80 grams of compost per kilogram, with 30 seedlings per amount. Mean fruit mass per plant was 210 grams at 0, 290 at 10, 340 at 20, 330 at 40, and 250 at 80 grams of compost. Assume that mean fruit mass rises to a single peak as compost increases and then declines. Based on these results, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the amount of compost that gives the greatest mean fruit mass lies between 10 and 40 grams, though the data do not show where in that range.
20 grams is the amount of compost that gives the greatest mean fruit mass, since it produced the highest mean among the five amounts tested.
choices.slip: Only five amounts were tested; the true peak may fall between them.

choices.text: any amount of compost above 20 grams lowers mean fruit mass, since the means at 40 and 80 grams were both below the mean at 20 grams in this trial.
choices.slip: Only 40 and 80 grams were tested; amounts just above 20 may do better.

choices.text: compost at 80 grams harms the plants relative to unamended soil, since mean fruit mass at 80 grams was well below the peak.
choices.slip: Mean mass at 80 grams, 250, still exceeds 210 for no compost.

steps: Means rise to 340 at 20 and fall to 330 at 40 and 250 at 80.
With a single peak, the maximum is between the neighbors of the highest tested amount, 10 and 40.
The data cannot say where in that range.
explanation.why: With one peak and the highest mean at 20 grams, the maximum lies between 10 and 40.
explanation.pattern: A peak is located only to the interval between the tested neighbors.

items.passage: A district identified its 10 lowest-scoring schools in reading in 2022 and gave them a literacy program that year. In 2023, the average reading score at those 10 schools rose by 9 points; the average at the district's 120 other schools, which received no program, rose by 3 points. A school's average score varies somewhat from year to year for reasons unrelated to teaching, and schools with unusually low scores in one year tend to score closer to the district average the next. Based on this information, the program ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: caused the entire 9-point rise, since the lowest-scoring schools had the most room to improve and no other schools received the program.
choices.slip: Ignores the rise at other schools and the drift back toward average.

choices.text: had no effect, since scores at the schools without the program also rose, which indicates a district-wide trend rather than an effect of the program.
choices.slip: The program schools rose by more, so a zero effect is not shown either.

choices.text: may have contributed to the rise, but part of it could reflect low-scoring schools drifting back toward the average, so its effect is likely smaller than 9 points.
raised scores by exactly 6 points, the difference between the 9-point rise at the program schools and the 3-point rise at the other schools.
choices.slip: Treats the other schools as a fair comparison even though the program schools were chosen for low scores.

steps: Program schools were chosen for unusually low scores.
Such schools would tend to rise anyway.
So 9 points overstates the effect, but an effect is not ruled out.
explanation.why: Selection for low scores builds part of the rise into the result, so the effect is probably under 9 points but not zero.
explanation.pattern: Groups picked for extreme values will drift toward average without any treatment.

items.passage: Botanists at a seed bank use the term weedy for a plant that is both non-native to a region and able to spread into undisturbed habitat. In a survey of Marlin County, botanists examined 30 established non-native plants and 6 native plants. Twelve of the non-native plants had spread into undisturbed forest or grassland; the other 18 had stayed within gardens, roadsides, and plowed fields. All 6 native plants had spread into undisturbed habitat. Given these definitions and findings, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: none of the 18 non-native plants that stayed on disturbed ground can pose any harm to the native plants of the county.
choices.slip: The definition concerns spread and origin, not harm.

choices.text: the 12 non-native plants that spread into undisturbed habitat are weedy, while the 6 native plants that spread there are not, since they are not non-native.
the 6 native plants are weedy, since spreading into undisturbed habitat is the defining trait of a weedy plant.
choices.slip: Ignores the non-native requirement.

choices.text: all 30 non-native plants are weedy, since any plant that is non-native to a region has already spread beyond its original range.
choices.slip: Weedy also requires spread into undisturbed habitat, which 18 did not do.

steps: Weedy needs two conditions: non-native and spreading into undisturbed habitat.
Twelve non-natives meet both; the natives meet only the second.
explanation.why: Both conditions are met by the 12 non-native spreaders and by no native plant.
explanation.pattern: When a term needs two conditions, check each group against both.

items.passage: Labor economists note that the unemployment rate typically begins to fall only after total economic output has been rising for several months, because firms wait for sustained demand before hiring. In one country, output rose each month from March through August, and the unemployment rate, which had been steady for a year, was unchanged through August. A well-founded inference is that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the unchanged unemployment rate through August is consistent with the usual delay and does not show that the rise in output failed to create demand for workers.
output growth from March through August was too weak to affect hiring, since the unemployment rate did not fall during those months of rising output.
choices.slip: Reads the usual lag as a sign of weak growth.

choices.text: unemployment will begin to fall in September, since output has now risen for six consecutive months.
choices.slip: The text gives a typical delay of several months, not a date.

choices.text: firms in the country hired no workers from March through August, since the unemployment rate stayed the same during that period.
choices.slip: A steady rate allows hiring that matched departures and new job seekers.

steps: The usual pattern: output rises first, unemployment falls later.
Six months of rising output with no fall is within a normal delay.
explanation.why: A lagging indicator staying flat is expected and does not show that demand failed to appear.
explanation.pattern: Do not read a delayed indicator's silence as evidence of no change.

items.passage: A university's engineering school admitted 40 percent of its 5,000 applicants in 2020 and 45 percent of its 3,600 applicants in 2023. In both years, 60 percent of admitted students chose to enroll. Based on these figures, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: enrollment in 2023 was about 5 percent higher than in 2020, since the share of applicants admitted rose from 40 percent to 45 percent.
choices.slip: Treats a rise of five percentage points as a rise in enrollment.

choices.text: the same number of students enrolled in both years, since the share of admitted students who enrolled stayed at 60 percent.
choices.slip: A constant share does not mean a constant number.

choices.text: the drop in enrollment was caused entirely by the smaller pool of applicants, with no change in how selective the school was.
choices.slip: The admission rate also changed, so selectivity did change.

choices.text: fewer students enrolled in 2023 than in 2020, even though a larger share of applicants was admitted in 2023.

steps: 2023: 0.45 x 3,600 = 1,620 admitted, 972 enrolled.
Rate rose, count fell.
explanation.why: Enrollment fell from 1,200 to 972 even as the admission rate rose.
explanation.pattern: Compare counts by multiplying rates by their bases.

items.passage: A materials lab tested a polymer's stiffness at 20, 40, and 60 degrees Celsius and found that each 20-degree rise cut stiffness by roughly 10 percent, so the change per degree was about the same across the whole tested range. No tests were done at other temperatures. The lab now needs stiffness figures for 50 degrees and for 90 degrees. Based on these results, the lab can ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: treat 50 and 90 degrees alike, since stiffness fell at the same rate across the entire tested range and the trend should continue.
choices.slip: Treats a point beyond the tested range like one inside it.

choices.text: judge stiffness at 50 degrees fairly well, since 50 lies within the tested range, but cannot rely on the same rate at 90 degrees, which lies outside it.
estimate neither temperature, since stiffness was measured at only three temperatures and none of them was 50 or 90 degrees.
choices.slip: Too strict: 50 degrees lies between measured points on a steady trend.

choices.text: expect stiffness at 90 degrees to be about 25 percent below its value at 60 degrees, since the change per 20 degrees was constant.
choices.slip: Applies the observed rate beyond the tested range as if it were known.

steps: The trend is steady between 20 and 60 degrees.
50 lies between tested points; 90 lies outside the range.
explanation.why: Interpolation inside the tested range is reasonable; extrapolation past it is not supported.
explanation.pattern: Trends support estimates only within the range tested.

items.passage: In a germination trial of a desert shrub, none of 200 dishes kept below 10 degrees Celsius produced seedlings, whether the dishes were moist or dry. Of 200 dishes kept between 18 and 25 degrees, 140 were kept moist and 60 were kept dry. None of the 60 dry dishes produced seedlings; 130 of the 140 moist dishes did. A reasonable conclusion from these results is that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: warmth alone triggers germination, since 130 of the 200 dishes kept between 18 and 25 degrees produced seedlings, which is more than half of all the dishes in that temperature range.
choices.slip: The 60 warm dry dishes had no seedlings.

choices.text: moisture alone explains germination, since 130 of the 140 moist dishes in the warm range produced seedlings.
choices.slip: Moist dishes below 10 degrees also produced none.

choices.text: warmth and moisture both appear to be required, though they may not be sufficient, since some warm, moist dishes did not produce seedlings.
any warm, moist dish would produce seedlings, since 130 of the 140 such dishes in the trial did so.
choices.slip: 10 warm, moist dishes failed; no result is guaranteed.

steps: Cold dishes failed even when moist; warm dry dishes failed.
So both seem needed.
10 of 140 warm moist dishes failed, so something else matters too.
explanation.why: Failures when either factor is missing suggest both are necessary; failures when both are present show they may not suffice.
explanation.pattern: Find necessity from failures when a condition is absent and non-sufficiency from failures when all are present.

items.passage: A national health agency ranked 3,100 counties by their yearly rate of a rare kidney disease per 100,000 residents. The counties with the highest rates were mostly rural and sparsely populated, and so, surprisingly, were the counties with the lowest rates. A county of 800 residents will record zero cases in most years, and in a year with a single case it will show a rate of 125 per 100,000, whereas a county of 800,000 residents will show a rate close to the national average of about 3 per 100,000 year after year. The agency's data cover only a single year and contain no information about diet, occupation, or environment. Based on this information, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: living in a rural county lowers a person's risk of the disease, since the counties with the lowest rates in the ranking were also mostly rural counties.
choices.slip: Picks out one end of the ranking and ignores the other.

choices.text: rural counties near the top of the ranking contain more people with the disease than urban counties do, since their rates per 100,000 residents are higher.
choices.slip: A higher rate in a small county can come from very few cases; rates are not counts.

choices.text: a single case in a small county is good evidence of an environmental cause there, since it produces a rate far above the national average.
choices.slip: One case in a tiny county can occur by chance and gives a large rate.

choices.text: rural counties at both ends of the ranking could result from small populations alone, so the ranking does not show that rural residence raises risk.

steps: Highest and lowest rates are both mostly small rural counties.
Small populations make rates swing: one case gives 125 per 100,000, none gives zero.
So extremes at both ends can come from size alone, not rural residence.
explanation.why: Small populations produce extreme rates in both directions, so rural residence is not shown to matter.
explanation.pattern: Extreme values appear in small samples; do not read a cause into the extremes.

items.passage: A museum conservator is dating an undated merchant's letter. The letter describes the "new bridge at Ferrand's Landing" as open to wagons and mentions that the harbor master, Corbett, died "earlier this year." It is written on paper bearing a watermark used by a single mill, which operated from 1831 to 1858. Municipal records show that the bridge opened to wagons in 1842 and that Corbett died in March 1846. The conservator assumes that the writer was describing events already past, that "earlier this year" refers to the calendar year in which the letter was written, and that the paper was used soon after it was made. On this basis, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the letter was written in 1846, after Corbett's death, and the bridge and watermark clues are consistent with that date without narrowing it further.
the letter was written in 1842 or 1843, since the writer calls the bridge new and the bridge opened in 1842.
choices.slip: "New" is relative; Corbett's death, which came later, sets the year.

choices.text: the letter was written in 1846 or 1847, since a death in March could still be called recent the following year.
choices.slip: "Earlier this year" ties the letter to the calendar year of the death.

choices.text: the letter could have been written at any time from 1842 to 1858, since the bridge date and the watermark dates set only outer limits.
choices.slip: The reference to Corbett's death narrows the date to 1846.

steps: Bridge: letter after 1842. Watermark: letter within 1831-1858.
Corbett died in March 1846 and the letter says "earlier this year," so the year is 1846.
The other clues are consistent with 1846 and do not narrow it.
explanation.why: The year-specific phrase about Corbett fixes 1846; the other clues fit that year.
explanation.pattern: Use the most specific dated clue; broader clues only bracket the date.

items.passage: A city transit authority reported that the share of weekday riders paying by mobile app rose from 20 percent in 2021 to 35 percent in 2023. Over the same two years, total weekday ridership fell from 400,000 riders to 340,000 riders. Analysts at the authority were asked to describe how the number of weekday app riders changed, and a commentator noted that the change in the share, 15 percentage points, and the change in overall ridership, a drop of 15 percent, are easily confused with each other and with the change in the app's rider count. Based on these figures, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the number of weekday app riders rose by 15 percent, since the share of riders using the app rose by 15 percentage points.
choices.slip: Treats a change in percentage points as a percent change in riders.

choices.text: the number of weekday app riders rose by about 49 percent, although overall weekday ridership fell by 15 percent.
the number of weekday app riders rose by 75 percent, since the share of riders using the app rose from 20 percent to 35 percent.
choices.slip: Gives the relative change in share and ignores the fall in total ridership.

choices.text: the number of weekday app riders changed little, since the 15 percent fall in total ridership offset the rise in the share.
choices.slip: App riders went from 80,000 to 119,000; the fall in the total did not cancel the rise.

steps: 2021 app riders: 20 percent of 400,000 = 80,000.
2023 app riders: 35 percent of 340,000 = 119,000.
119,000 / 80,000 is about 1.49, a 49 percent rise, while total ridership fell 15 percent.
explanation.why: Compute counts from shares and totals: 80,000 rose to 119,000.
explanation.pattern: Percentage points, percent of a share, and counts are different quantities.

items.passage: A microbiologist grows a bacterial culture in nutrient broth and counts the cells at regular intervals. The count doubled between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m., from 5 million to 10 million cells per milliliter, and doubled again between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m. The broth can support at most 400 million cells per milliliter, because its nutrients run out beyond that point, and the culture is known to keep a constant doubling time of two hours until it approaches that limit. The microbiologist wants to know when the culture will reach the broth's limit if she does not add nutrients or remove cells, and she records the count at 6 p.m. as 20 million cells per milliliter. Based on this information, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the culture will still be far below the limit at 4 a.m., since its count has been rising by only 5 to 10 million cells in each two-hour period so far.
choices.slip: Treats the growth as adding a fixed amount, not doubling.

choices.text: the culture will reach the limit at about 2 a.m., since going from 20 million to 400 million cells per milliliter takes four more doublings.
choices.slip: Four doublings from 20 million reach 320 million, not 400 million.

choices.text: the culture will reach the limit between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m., since the count will be 320 million at 2 a.m. and another doubling would exceed it.
the culture will exceed the limit at 4 a.m., since the count will have doubled again and again to reach 640 million cells per milliliter by then.
choices.slip: The broth cannot support more than 400 million, so the count cannot reach 640 million.

steps: Count at 6 p.m. is 20 million and doubles every two hours.
8 p.m. 40, 10 p.m. 80, midnight 160, 2 a.m. 320 million.
The next doubling would pass 400 million, so the limit is reached between 2 and 4 a.m.
explanation.why: The count hits 320 million at 2 a.m., and the limit is reached before the next doubling finishes.
explanation.pattern: Exponential growth is capped by a stated limit; track doublings until the ceiling.

items.passage: Researchers at an occupational health institute measured the noise exposure of workers in a textile mill using small badge-style dosimeters clipped to collars, which record sound levels only up to 105 decibels; any louder sound is simply recorded as 105. Over a full shift, the badges worn by 20 weaving-room workers had a mean recorded level of 98 decibels, and 22 percent of all their readings sat at the 105 ceiling. Badges worn by 15 finishing-room workers recorded a mean of 91 decibels, with only 1 percent of readings at 105. The researchers want to know what the weaving room's true mean sound level was, and they note that the badges were calibrated correctly for sounds below the ceiling. From these data, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the weaving room's true mean level was about 98 decibels, since only 22 percent of readings were affected by the ceiling and the rest were recorded accurately.
choices.slip: Ignores that the capped 22 percent could have been far louder than 105.

choices.text: the weaving room's true mean level was below 98 decibels, since a badge that caps its readings at 105 would tend to overstate the sound levels.
choices.slip: A cap can only lower recorded values, so it understates, not overstates.

choices.text: the weaving room's true mean level was lower than the finishing room's, since the weaving badges were capped at 105 decibels and the finishing badges were not.
choices.slip: Both kinds of badge had the same cap; the finishing badges also hit it.

choices.text: the weaving room's true mean was at least 98 decibels and may have been higher, since the badges recorded nothing above 105.

steps: Readings above 105 are recorded as 105, so recorded values are never too high.
Therefore the recorded mean of 98 is a lower bound on the true mean.
How much higher cannot be told from capped data.
explanation.why: Capping can only understate, so 98 is a floor for the true mean.
explanation.pattern: Censored data give a bound, not an exact value.

items.passage: A toxicologist is testing river water for a pesticide whose concentration halves every 6 days. Her laboratory's instrument can detect the pesticide only at 4 micrograms per liter or higher; any lower concentration is reported as "not detected." A sample collected on day 0 measured 50 micrograms per liter. She wants to know whether a clean result on a later test would show that the pesticide is gone, and she plans to test the same stretch of river on days 18, 24, and 30. She assumes that no pesticide enters the river after day 0 and that the half-life stays constant. Based on these assumptions, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the first "not detected" result is expected on day 24, though about 3 micrograms per liter would remain, so it would not show the water is free of it.
the pesticide will have disappeared from the river by day 30, since by then its concentration will be below what the instrument can detect.
choices.slip: A reading below the limit does not mean the pesticide is gone; about 1.6 would remain.

choices.text: the pesticide will still be detected on day 24, since four half-lives leave a concentration that is a substantial fraction of the original 50 micrograms per liter.
choices.slip: Four half-lives leave 50/16, about 3.1, below the limit of 4.

choices.text: the first "not detected" result is expected on day 30, since the concentration reaches 4 micrograms per liter only after five half-lives.
choices.slip: Four micrograms is reached between days 18 and 24; it falls below by day 24.

steps: Day 6: 25, day 12: 12.5, day 18: 6.25, day 24: about 3.1, day 30: about 1.6.
The concentration drops below 4 by day 24, so day 24 is the first "not detected."
About 3 micrograms per liter remain, so "not detected" is not "absent."
explanation.why: Day 24 is the first test below the limit, yet pesticide remains.
explanation.pattern: Detection limits and half-lives: below the limit is not zero.

items.passage: A beverage company launched an advertising campaign for a cold-pressed juice at the start of April. Sales of the juice rose by about 4.0 percent per month from January through March, before the campaign, and by about 4.1 percent per month from April through June, after it began. Sales of the juice are known to rise every spring as the weather warms, and no other change was made to the product, its price, or the stores that carry it. The company's marketing director says the campaign explains the sales growth in April, May, and June, and the company's analysts were asked whether the figures bear that out. Based on these figures, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the campaign had no effect on the juice's sales at all, since monthly growth was nearly the same before and after it began.
choices.slip: Similar growth fails to show an effect; it does not show there was none.

choices.text: the campaign raised monthly growth by about 0.1 percentage point, which measures the true size of its effect on the juice's sales.
choices.slip: Seasonal spring growth could account for that tenth of a point.

choices.text: the figures do not show that the campaign increased sales, since sales were already rising at nearly that rate and rise every spring.
the campaign increased the juice's sales, since sales rose in every one of the months after it began.
choices.slip: Sales were already rising before it began.

steps: Growth before the campaign was 4.0 percent per month and after it was 4.1.
Spring growth is seasonal, so the rise would be expected anyway.
Nothing separates the campaign's effect from the existing trend.
explanation.why: The pre-existing trend and spring seasonality leave the campaign's effect indistinguishable.
explanation.pattern: Compare to the pre-existing trend before crediting an intervention.

items.passage: A seed bank can store at most 9,000 seed samples in its freezer. It currently holds 6,400 samples of wild species and 1,900 samples of crop varieties. A new policy requires that crop varieties make up at least 30 percent of all stored samples by the end of the year. The bank may add new samples, but it may not discard any wild samples and cannot exceed its freezer's capacity, and any samples added will be crop varieties. A staff member argues that since 30 percent of 9,000 is 2,700, the bank only needs 800 more crop samples. Based on these constraints, it follows that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the bank can meet the policy by adding 800 crop samples, since 30 percent of 9,000 is 2,700 and the bank now holds 1,900.
choices.slip: Ignores that the 6,400 wild samples fix the total above 9,000.

choices.text: the bank cannot meet the policy within its capacity, since the requirement would need at least 2,743 crop samples and a total above 9,000.
the bank can meet the policy by filling its remaining 700 spaces with crop samples, since 2,600 crop samples is about 30 percent of 9,000.
choices.slip: 2,600 of 9,000 is about 29 percent, short of the required 30.

choices.text: the bank could meet the policy if its capacity were raised to about 9,100 samples, since 2,700 crop samples would then be 30 percent of the total.
choices.slip: 2,700 of 9,100 is below 30 percent; it takes about 9,143.

steps: Wild samples stay at 6,400, so crop samples x must satisfy x >= 0.3(6,400 + x).
That gives x >= 2,743, so the total is at least 9,143.
The total exceeds the 9,000 capacity, so the policy cannot be met.
explanation.why: Needing 2,743 crop samples puts the total at 9,143, beyond capacity.
explanation.pattern: When one part is fixed, the share condition is solved on the total that includes the added part.

items.passage: In a model proposed by plant physiologist Cosmo Roukema-Dube, a seed of an alpine herb germinates as soon as its growth hormone level exceeds twice its germination inhibitor level. The hormone is produced only at temperatures above 10 degrees Celsius, at 1 unit per day, and is absent at the start. The inhibitor starts at 12 units. It does not change at temperatures above 5 degrees but halves every two weeks at temperatures below 5 degrees. Consider one seed kept at 12 degrees from the start and another held at 3 degrees for eight weeks and then moved to 12 degrees. The model assumes that temperature changes take effect immediately. According to the model, the second seed would ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: germinate during the cold period, because by the end of eight weeks its inhibitor level would have fallen well below its hormone level.
choices.slip: No hormone is produced at 3 degrees, so the hormone level stays at zero.

choices.text: germinate about 24 days after being moved to 12 degrees, exactly when the first seed would, since the cold period leaves its inhibitor unchanged.
choices.slip: The cold period does reduce the inhibitor.

choices.text: germinate about a day and a half after being moved to 12 degrees, over 22 days sooner than the seed kept at 12 degrees throughout.
germinate about 12 days after being moved to 12 degrees, half as long as the first seed, since eight weeks of cold would halve the inhibitor.
choices.slip: Eight weeks is four halvings, not one.

steps: First seed: inhibitor stays 12, so hormone must exceed 24 units: about 24 days.
Second seed in the cold: no hormone, so no germination, but inhibitor halves four times in eight weeks: 12 / 16 = 0.75 units.
After moving to 12 degrees, hormone must exceed 1.5 units: about 1.5 days.
Difference: about 22.5 days, 'more than 22 days sooner'.
explanation.why: Cold lowers the inhibitor to 0.75 units without any hormone being made, so warming triggers germination in about 1.5 days.
explanation.pattern: Apply a model's rules step by step to a new case; each condition (hormone only when warm, inhibitor decay only when cold) acts at a different time.

items.passage: A review of 41,000 hip-replacement surgeries found that patients operated on at hospitals performing more than 200 such surgeries a year had a complication rate of 3.1 percent, while patients at hospitals performing fewer than 50 a year had a rate of 5.6 percent. Health economist Matilde Ruggiero-Odu notes that the review, which covered 112 hospitals, adjusted for patients' age and overall health. She also notes, however, that patients and referring doctors often choose a hospital because of its reputation for good results, and that a hospital's reputation tends to improve as its results do. Ruggiero-Odu therefore cautions that the gap between the two groups of hospitals ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: may partly reflect hospitals with better results attracting more patients, so it does not by itself show that performing more surgeries lowers a hospital's complication rate.
is probably explained by differences in patients' age and overall health between the two groups, since those factors strongly affect complication rates.
choices.slip: The review already adjusted for age and health.

choices.text: likely understates the benefit of volume, since hospitals with the best reputations may also take on the most complicated cases, which would make their results look worse than they are.
choices.slip: Nothing in the text says reputation brings complicated cases; the caution concerns reputation following results.

choices.text: shows that choosing a hospital by reputation leads patients to better outcomes, since reputation reflects results, and so that patients should always choose the busiest hospital available.
choices.slip: This treats the cause as known; the text only says reputation tends to follow results.

steps: The gap: high-volume hospitals have fewer complications.
Reputation follows good results, and patients go where reputation is good; so good results may produce high volume.
That reverses the direction of the causal claim, so volume's effect isn't established.
Age and health were already adjusted for.
explanation.why: Good results may bring volume, so the gap doesn't prove volume lowers complications.
explanation.pattern: Reverse causation: when the outcome can drive the supposed cause, a correlation doesn't show the cause's effect.

items.passage: The Marwick Museum has three rules for lending an object. First, every borrower must guarantee climate-controlled display. Second, a conservator must have examined the object within the previous twelve months, except for objects in the museum's study collection, which are exempt from this requirement. Third, objects in the study collection may be lent only to registered institutions. Staff apply the rules in the order given, and there are no other exceptions. This season the museum lent a woven mantle to a private collector, who guaranteed climate-controlled display. The museum's records show that no conservator had examined the mantle in the previous twelve months. Based on these rules, it follows that the museum ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: followed its rules, because the collector guaranteed climate-controlled display and the mantle may belong to the study collection, which is exempt from examination.
choices.slip: Study-collection objects can't go to private collectors, so the exemption can't rescue the loan.

choices.text: followed its rules only if the mantle belongs to the study collection, which is exempt from the examination requirement that applies to other objects.
choices.slip: The study collection is also restricted to registered institutions.

choices.text: broke its rules if the mantle is in the study collection, but may have followed them if the mantle is not in that collection.
choices.slip: If the mantle isn't in the study collection, it needed an examination that it did not have.

choices.text: did not follow its rules, because the mantle either needed an examination it lacked or belongs to a collection that cannot be lent to private collectors.

steps: Case 1: mantle not in the study collection: it needed a conservator's examination and had none: rule broken.
Case 2: mantle in the study collection: exempt from examination, but may be lent only to registered institutions, and a private collector isn't one: rule broken.
Either way a rule was broken.
explanation.why: Both possibilities for the mantle's status lead to a broken rule.
explanation.pattern: Run a case analysis over every possibility; if every branch gives the same result, that result follows.

items.passage: To estimate the number of brook trout in a stream, ecologist Wilhelmina Adeyemi-Roux's team captured and tagged 300 trout and released them. Two weeks later the team netted 120 trout along the stream's whole 4-kilometer length, of which 18 carried tags. Because 15 percent of the second sample was tagged, the team reasoned that the 300 tagged trout were about 15 percent of the stream's trout, which gives an estimate of 2,000 trout. The team later found that the tagged trout had been handled roughly and afterward avoided the stretch of water where the nets were set. This finding suggests that the estimate of 2,000 trout ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: is probably too low, because tagged trout that avoided the nets were left out of the sample and so were not counted among the stream's trout.
choices.slip: Tagged trout still count in the stream; leaving them out of the sample lowers the tagged share, which raises the estimate.

choices.text: is probably too high, because a sample that underrepresents tagged trout makes the tagged share of the stream's trout look smaller than it is.
is probably accurate, because a sample of 120 trout is large enough that the share of tagged trout in it should match the share in the stream.
choices.slip: The sample is biased against tagged trout, so its size doesn't fix the problem.

choices.text: is probably too high, because tagging 300 trout removed them from the wild population, leaving fewer untagged trout than the estimate assumes.
choices.slip: Tagged trout were released; they stay in the stream.

steps: Estimate = 300 / (tagged share of sample).
If tagged trout avoid the nets, the sample's tagged share (15 percent) is lower than their true share in the stream.
A lower tagged share leads to a larger estimate, so 2,000 is probably too high.
A and D give the wrong reasoning or direction.
explanation.why: Undercounting tagged trout understates their true share, which inflates the population estimate.
explanation.pattern: Work out the direction of a bias through the formula: a smaller measured share gives a larger estimated total.

items.passage: Two polls of different random samples of 1,000 residents of Thornbury County, drawn by the same method and with similar age and income makeups, asked about a proposed bus lane. In the first poll, conducted by the county's planning office, 62 percent of respondents said they either strongly or somewhat support the bus lane. In the second poll, conducted by a local newspaper during the same week, 31 percent of respondents said they strongly support the bus lane. A columnist claims that the polls give contradictory pictures of residents' opinion, since one shows majority support and the other shows minority support. This claim overlooks that the results ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: are consistent, because the second poll counted only strong supporters of the lane and so would be expected to show a smaller share than the first.
indicate that exactly half of the residents who support the lane do so only weakly, since 31 percent is half of 62 percent.
choices.slip: The samples differ and the polls counted different things, so this precision is not justified.

choices.text: are inconsistent, because the planning office's poll was probably biased toward supporters, given that the newspaper's poll found a much lower share.
choices.slip: The polls measured different things, so the gap doesn't show bias.

choices.text: reflect a decline in support during the week, since the newspaper's poll found a lower share of supporters than the planning office's did.
choices.slip: Both polls were taken in the same week.

steps: Poll 1 counts strong plus somewhat supporters (62 percent); poll 2 counts only strong supporters (31 percent).
'Strong' is a subset of 'strong or somewhat', so its share must be smaller.
The two numbers aren't contradictory; the questions differ.
D invents a time change; C invents bias; B over-reads equal halves.
explanation.why: The polls counted different groups, so a smaller share in the second is expected.
explanation.pattern: Check what each statistic counts before calling results contradictory.

items.passage: A coffee shop raised the price of its drip coffee from $4.00 to $5.00 a cup. In the following month it sold 15 percent fewer cups of drip coffee than in the month before. The shop's cost of making each cup, including the cup and labor, is $3.60 and did not change. The owner, Tobias Nakamura-Ellery, is relieved that revenue from drip coffee did not fall, since he had feared that selling fewer cups would hurt the shop. No other prices at the shop changed that month, and its customers were otherwise unchanged. Based on these figures, the shop's monthly profit from drip coffee ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: fell by about 15 percent, since the shop sold 15 percent fewer cups.
choices.slip: Ignores that each cup now earns far more profit.

choices.text: rose by about 6 percent, the same as revenue, since the cost per cup did not change.
choices.slip: A fixed cost per cup makes profit change by more than revenue, not the same.

choices.text: rose to nearly three times its earlier level, even though revenue from drip coffee rose by only about 6 percent.
rose by about 25 percent, the same as the increase in price, since each cup still sold brought in a dollar more.
choices.slip: Fewer cups are sold, and the 25 percent rise is on price, not on profit.

steps: Revenue per original month: 1.25 x 0.85 = 1.0625, about 6 percent up.
Profit per cup rose from $0.40 to $1.40.
Profit: 1.40 x 0.85 = 1.19 against 0.40, about 2.98 times as large.
Profit rose to nearly three times its earlier level.
explanation.why: Profit per cup rises from $0.40 to $1.40, and with 15 percent fewer cups profit is almost three times its earlier size.
explanation.pattern: Profit is revenue minus costs: when the margin is thin, a price change moves profit far more than revenue.

items.passage: Climatologists comparing two forest sites, about 20 kilometers apart and at similar elevations, measured air temperature with different instruments. At the first site, thermometers of Type A recorded a mean summer temperature of 14.1 degrees Celsius. At the second site, thermometers of Type B recorded 13.9 degrees. In a calibration test in a controlled chamber, Type A thermometers were found to read 0.4 degrees too high on average, and Type B thermometers 0.3 degrees too low. Assuming the calibration results also apply to the field readings, the corrected means indicate that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: the first site was warmer than the second by about 0.2 degrees Celsius, as the raw readings show.
choices.slip: The raw readings are not corrected for the known errors.

choices.text: the second site was warmer than the first by about 0.5 degrees Celsius, reversing the order shown by the raw readings.
the second site was warmer than the first by about 0.2 degrees Celsius, since correcting the Type A readings alone reverses the order.
choices.slip: Type B readings also need correcting (upward by 0.3).

choices.text: the first site was warmer than the second by about 0.9 degrees Celsius, since the thermometer errors lie in opposite directions and so add to the raw gap.
choices.slip: The corrections are applied in the wrong directions.

steps: Type A reads high, so subtract 0.4: 14.1 - 0.4 = 13.7.
Type B reads low, so add 0.3: 13.9 + 0.3 = 14.2.
Second site is warmer by 0.5 degrees.
explanation.why: After correcting A downward and B upward, the second site is 14.2 against 13.7.
explanation.pattern: Correct each measurement for its own known bias, with the right sign, before comparing.

items.passage: Residents of Orrinsby tell of a flood generations ago that 'covered the church floor.' Geologist Prisca Dellacroix-Bamba reasons that water deep enough to cover a church floor would have left a layer of silt at least 2 centimeters thick across the church and the ground around it. Her team took nine soil cores in the village: six from the raised ground around the church, which stands 1.5 meters above the lowest part of the village, and three from the lowest part, near the river. Each of the three cores from the low ground held a silt layer about 5 centimeters thick. None of the six cores from around the church held any silt layer. These findings suggest that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: no flood of any size occurred in Orrinsby, since the silt layer expected after a flood is missing from six of the nine cores.
choices.slip: The silt in the three low-ground cores shows a flood did occur.

choices.text: the flood probably covered the church floor as residents say, since the silt layer in the low ground exceeds the 2 centimeters expected at the church.
choices.slip: The expected silt was for the church area, where none was found.

choices.text: the flood left silt only in the low ground because the church's raised ground had been cleaned after the flood, since churches are usually kept clean.
choices.slip: Nothing in the text supports this; it is an invented assumption.

choices.text: a flood did occur but probably did not reach the church floor, so the residents' account may exaggerate how far the water rose.

steps: A flood deep enough to reach the church floor would leave 2+ cm of silt around the church.
Silt exists in the low ground (so a flood happened), but none around the church (so water probably did not reach there).
So the account's claim about the church floor is probably exaggerated.
explanation.why: Silt on the low ground but none at the church means a flood occurred but probably stayed below the church.
explanation.pattern: Test a claim by the evidence it predicts; missing predicted evidence limits it, while present evidence elsewhere keeps the weaker claim.

items.passage: Each year, a bookstore chain's sales in December run about 25 percent higher than its sales in November because of holiday shopping. Last year, with sales in October close to the usual level for that month, the chain's December sales were 12 percent higher than its November sales. A regional manager, Clementine Okoro-Baptiste, said the increase showed that the chain's sales were healthy. An analyst responded that, compared with what December sales are usually like relative to November, the chain's December performance was actually ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: about 13 percent below the usual level, since the actual increase of 12 percent is 13 percent less than the usual 25 percent.
choices.slip: This subtracts percentages (13 points) instead of comparing ratios.

choices.text: about 12 percent above the usual level, since sales rose by that amount in a month when they usually rise.
choices.slip: It ignores that a 25 percent rise is the usual one.

choices.text: about 10 percent below the usual level, since sales reached 112 percent of November's when 125 percent would have been typical.
about as expected, because an increase of any size in December is consistent with ordinary holiday shopping.
choices.slip: The usual increase is a specific size, 25 percent.

steps: Typical December: 1.25 x November.
Actual December: 1.12 x November.
Ratio: 1.12 / 1.25 = 0.896, about 10 percent below the usual level.
Subtracting 25 - 12 = 13 compares percentage points, not the ratio.
explanation.why: 112 percent of November is about 90 percent of the usual 125 percent.
explanation.pattern: Compare against the expected benchmark with a ratio, not by subtracting percentage points.

items.passage: A medication has a half-life of six hours, meaning that the amount in a patient's body falls by half every six hours. It is effective only when at least 22 milligrams remain in the body. A patient takes an 80-milligram dose at 8 a.m. and another 80-milligram dose at 8 p.m. every day, beginning on Monday. The doctor wants the medication to remain effective throughout the day. Assume each dose enters the body immediately. Under this schedule, the amount of the medication in the patient's body ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: will fall below the effective level shortly before the first evening dose on Monday but will not fall below it before any later dose.
will fall below the effective level before every dose, because 80 milligrams is reduced to 20 milligrams in the 12 hours between doses.
choices.slip: Ignores the leftover medication from earlier doses.

choices.text: will never fall below the effective level, because each 80-milligram dose is added before the previous dose has fully left the body.
choices.slip: Before the first evening dose only 20 milligrams remain.

choices.text: will fall below the effective level before the first evening dose and again before the second morning dose, because only a quarter of each dose remains after twelve hours.
choices.slip: By Tuesday morning, 20 mg from the second dose plus 5 mg left from the first make 25 mg.

steps: Monday 8 p.m., before dose 2: 80 / 4 = 20 mg, below 22.
After dose 2: 100 mg. Tuesday 8 a.m. before dose 3: 100 / 4 = 25 mg, above 22.
Later pre-dose levels follow L = (L + 80) / 4, which approaches about 26.7 mg, always above 22.
explanation.why: Only the first pre-dose level (20 mg) is under 22 mg; carried-over medication keeps later levels above it.
explanation.pattern: With repeated doses, track the remainder carried from earlier doses rather than treating each dose alone.

items.passage: Agronomist Oswin Pellegrini-Sorrell tested nitrogen fertilizer on matched wheat plots at three doses. Plots receiving no nitrogen yielded 3.1 tonnes of wheat per hectare, plots receiving 60 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare yielded 4.6 tonnes, and plots receiving 120 kilograms per hectare yielded 5.4 tonnes. Each figure is the mean of 16 plots, and no plot received any other dose. These results indicate that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: yields would peak near 120 kilograms per hectare, since the gain from the second 60 kilograms was smaller than the gain from the first 60.
choices.slip: No dose above 120 kilograms was tested, so a peak can't be located.

choices.text: the second 60 kilograms raised yields less than the first 60 did, though the trial does not show yields at doses above 120 kilograms.
60 kilograms is the best dose, because the first 60 kilograms raised yields more per kilogram than the second 60 kilograms did.
choices.slip: Smaller gains per kilogram don't show that 60 is best; the extra yield may still be worth the extra fertilizer.

choices.text: doses above 120 kilograms would lower yields, because each added kilogram has raised yields by a smaller amount than the one before.
choices.slip: A shrinking gain does not show that yields fall; no higher dose was tested.

steps: Gains: 1.5 tonnes for the first 60 kg and 0.8 tonnes for the second 60 kg.
So the second step added less, but nothing was measured above 120 kg.
Claims about a peak, a best dose or a decline all go beyond the tested range.
explanation.why: The data show diminishing gains within the tested range and say nothing beyond it.
explanation.pattern: Describe the trend inside the data range; do not extrapolate beyond it.

items.passage: A professional society with 40 members offered two optional workshops. Records show that 28 members attended the budgeting workshop, that 22 attended the grant-writing workshop, and that at least 3 members attended neither. No member attended either workshop more than once. The secretary wants to report the largest number of members whom the records guarantee attended both workshops. Based on these records, the secretary can conclude that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: at least 10 members attended both workshops, because the two attendance counts total 50, which exceeds the society’s 40 members by 10.
choices.slip: True but not the strongest; it ignores the 3 members who attended neither.

choices.text: at least 13 members attended both workshops, because at most 37 members attended a workshop, and 28 + 22 - 37 = 13.
exactly 13 members attended both workshops, because the 3 members who attended neither leave 37 who attended at least one.
choices.slip: 'At least 3' attended neither, so 13 is only a minimum, not the exact number.

choices.text: at least 6 members attended both workshops, because 28 attended budgeting and only 22 attended grant writing.
choices.slip: The difference 28 - 22 is not the overlap bound; it ignores how many attended at least one workshop.

steps: At least 3 members attended neither, so at most 40 - 3 = 37 attended at least one workshop.
Overlap = 28 + 22 - (number attending at least one) >= 50 - 37 = 13.
Because the number attending neither could exceed 3, the overlap could be larger; 13 is the guaranteed minimum.
explanation.why: At most 37 attended some workshop, so at least 28 + 22 - 37 = 13 attended both.
explanation.pattern: Guaranteed overlap comes from the union actually attended, not from total membership.

items.passage: A weather station's temperature logger cannot record values above 45 degrees Celsius: on any day when the air gets hotter, the logger stores 45. The station's records show that the number of days stored as 45 rose from 3 in 2005 to 11 in 2015, and that the average of the daily high readings rose by 0.6 degrees over those ten years. A climatologist wants to say what these records show about the hottest days. They show that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: at least 8 more days in 2015 than in 2005 reached 45 degrees or higher, but the records cannot show how much hotter those days were.
the hottest day in 2015 was exactly 45 degrees, the same as in 2005, because the logger stored the same maximum value in both years.
choices.slip: The logger stores 45 for any hotter day, so the real maximum may have been higher in either year.

choices.text: the hottest days became about 8 degrees hotter, since 8 more days were stored at the maximum value in 2015 than in 2005.
choices.slip: Eight more capped days is a count of days, not degrees.

choices.text: the true average daily high rose by less than 0.6 degrees, since the logger's ceiling prevents it from recording the full heat of the hottest days.
choices.slip: A ceiling hides the hottest values and pushes the recorded average down, so the true rise could be larger, not smaller.

steps: Days stored as 45 are days that reached 45 or higher: 3 in 2005 and 11 in 2015.
The difference is 8 days.
How far above 45 any day went is not recorded.
explanation.why: The cap tells us the count of days at or above 45, not their size.
explanation.pattern: A measurement ceiling hides how large the top values were.

items.passage: At Ardenne Academy, the mean score on the district reading exam rose from 70.0 last year to 73.0 this year. Students who had attended a preschool program had a mean score of 80 in both years, and students who had not attended one had a mean score of 66 in both years. School officials credit the rise to new reading instruction. The groups' unchanged means suggest, however, that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: preschool attendance caused the rise, because students who attended preschool scored 14 points higher than students who did not attend one.
choices.slip: The gap between groups doesn't show that preschool caused anything, and it doesn't explain the change between years.

choices.text: the new instruction raised each student's score by about 3 points, the amount by which the school mean rose.
choices.slip: Neither group's mean rose, so no group gained 3 points on average.

choices.text: the rise in the school mean reflects a larger share of preschool students this year, not higher scores within either group.
the school mean should not have changed at all, since neither group's mean changed between the two years.
choices.slip: The school mean is a weighted average and moves when the group shares move.

steps: Both group means stayed fixed (80 and 66).
The school mean is a blend of them, so it can rise only if the share of the higher-scoring group (preschool) grew.
Weights: about 29 percent preschool last year, 50 percent this year.
explanation.why: The overall mean can rise with both group means fixed only if the higher-scoring group grew as a share.
explanation.pattern: An overall average can change purely because group proportions change.

items.passage: Soil scientist Hamid Roquefort-Aina tested whether spreading wood-chip mulch increases the carbon stored in orchard soil. Her team measured carbon in 24 mulched plots and 24 unmulched plots at the start and again after 2 years, finding 1.80 percent carbon in both groups at the start and 1.84 percent in mulched plots versus 1.83 percent in unmulched plots at the end. Wood chips decompose slowly, and earlier studies indicate that the carbon they add to soil typically becomes measurable only after about 4 years. Given this, the two-year results suggest that ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: mulch does not raise soil carbon, since the mulched plots ended only 0.01 percentage points above the unmulched plots after two years.
choices.slip: A null result in a period shorter than the expected delay can't show no effect.

choices.text: mulch raises soil carbon only after 4 years, since carbon in the mulched plots was measurable at that point in the study.
choices.slip: No measurement at 4 years was made, so the claim isn't supported.

choices.text: mulch raised soil carbon modestly, since the mulched plots gained 0.04 percentage points while the unmulched plots gained only 0.03.
choices.slip: A 0.01-point difference at an unreliable early stage is not evidence of a modest effect.

choices.text: the trial ended before mulch could be expected to show an effect, so it cannot show whether mulch raises soil carbon.

steps: Mulch's carbon is expected to appear after about 4 years.
The trial lasted 2, so a small or absent difference is expected either way.
It therefore says little about the longer-term effect.
explanation.why: The trial's two years are shorter than the roughly four-year delay before any effect should show.
explanation.pattern: A null result is weak evidence if the study ended before the expected effect could appear.

items.passage: A food company's panel of 20 tasters compared snack bars in pairs. When shown bars A and B, 14 tasters preferred A. When shown bars B and C, 13 tasters preferred B. Each taster made both comparisons, but bars A and C were never compared directly. A manager concludes that most of the 20 tasters would prefer A to C. The panel's results suggest that this conclusion ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: is not guaranteed, since at least 7 tasters must prefer A to C but as many as 13 could prefer C.
follows from the panel's results, because a majority of tasters preferred A to B and a majority of tasters preferred B to C.
choices.slip: Majority preferences need not be transitive across a group.

choices.text: must be false, since no more than 7 of the 20 tasters can prefer A to C, according to the panel's pairwise results.
choices.slip: 7 is the minimum, not the maximum, number who prefer A to C.

choices.text: must be true, because A's margin over B (8 tasters) was wider than B's margin over C (6 tasters) in the panel's results.
choices.slip: Comparing margins doesn't fix how tasters would rank A against C.

steps: At least 14 + 13 - 20 = 7 tasters preferred A to B and B to C, so they prefer A to C.
The other 13 could still prefer C to A (for example, 7 ranking C, A, B and 6 ranking B, C, A).
So a majority for A over C is possible but not guaranteed.
explanation.why: Overlap forces only 7 tasters to prefer A to C; the other 13 could prefer C.
explanation.pattern: Majority preferences across pairs need not chain into a majority preference for the third pair.

items.passage: Lake Ormond receives 10 tonnes of phosphorus each year from farm runoff, and the lake loses about 5 tonnes a year through its outflow and through burial in sediment. After a new farming rule took effect, the annual runoff dropped by 20 percent, while the lake's yearly loss stayed the same. In the years after the rule took effect, the total amount of phosphorus in the lake probably ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: decreased each year by about 20 percent, since the runoff entering the lake was reduced by that percentage.
choices.slip: The cut applies to the yearly input, not to the lake's total phosphorus.

choices.text: continued to rise at the same pace as before, since the lake's rate of loss did not change.
choices.slip: The net gain went from 5 tonnes a year to 3, so the pace slowed.

choices.text: continued to rise, but more slowly than before, since 8 tonnes entered each year while only about 5 tonnes left.
began to fall within a few years, since a cut in runoff is followed by a delayed drop in the lake's phosphorus.
choices.slip: Input of 8 tonnes still exceeds the 5 tonnes removed, so there is no net fall.

steps: Before: 10 in, 5 out, net +5 per year.
After: 8 in, 5 out, net +3 per year.
Total phosphorus still rises, just more slowly.
explanation.why: As long as inputs exceed removal, the lake's total keeps rising even after inputs are cut.
explanation.pattern: Cutting a flow doesn't reduce a stock until the inflow falls below the outflow.

items.passage: A weight-loss program enrolled 200 adults. After 12 weeks, 120 of them had completed the program, and these completers had lost an average of 7.5 kilograms. The other 80 enrollees left before week 12. At a weigh-in at week 6, which all 200 attended, the 80 who later left had lost an average of 2 kilograms, compared with 4 kilograms for those who stayed. The program advertises that participants lose an average of 7.5 kilograms. The data suggest that this figure ______
items.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: describes the average loss of all 200 enrollees accurately, since the completers were a majority of those who enrolled.
choices.slip: Being a majority doesn't make completers representative; the leavers did worse.

choices.text: probably overstates the average loss for all enrollees, since those who left had lost less than those who stayed.
equals about 4.5 kilograms across all 200 enrollees, since the 80 who left can be counted as having lost no weight.
choices.slip: The leavers had lost 2 kilograms by week 6, so counting them at zero is wrong.

choices.text: probably understates the average loss across all enrollees, since participants who left the program early also lost weight by week 6.
choices.slip: Leavers lost less than stayers, so including them pulls the average down, not up.

steps: The advertised figure averages only the 120 completers.
At week 6 the leavers were losing less (2 vs 4 kg), so they would drag the all-enrollee average down.
So 7.5 kg likely overstates the typical enrollee's loss.
explanation.why: The people who dropped out were the ones losing less weight, so the completers' average overstates the typical result.
explanation.pattern: An average over completers overstates results when those who drop out do worse.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The town of Eastmere has two footbridges over its river.
• The Willow Bridge was built in 1911; the Copper Bridge was built in 1958.
• Both bridges are made of steel.
• The Willow Bridge is 40 meters long; the Copper Bridge is 65 meters long.
• Both were designed by engineer Hanne Roos.
items.question: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two bridges. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: The Willow Bridge was built in 1911, while the Copper Bridge, the town's newer footbridge, was not built until 1958, nearly fifty years later.
choices.slip: This points out a difference (their dates), not a similarity.

choices.text: At 65 meters, the Copper Bridge is longer than the 40-meter Willow Bridge.
choices.slip: This points out a difference (their lengths).

choices.text: Engineer Hanne Roos designed the Willow Bridge in 1911.
choices.slip: This is about one bridge only, so it can't show a similarity.

choices.text: The Willow Bridge and the Copper Bridge, both made of steel, were designed by the same engineer, Hanne Roos.

steps: A similarity needs both bridges and something they share.
Shared facts in the notes: both are steel, and both were designed by Hanne Roos.
Only one choice mentions both bridges and what they have in common.
explanation.why: It names both bridges and two things they share: steel and the same engineer.
explanation.pattern: For 'similarity', the choice must mention both things and a shared feature; for 'difference', both things and a contrast.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ecologist Petra Hale ran a one-season study in the Brannock community garden.
• She wanted to find out whether planting marigolds near tomato plants reduces damage from pests.
• She planted marigolds next to half of the garden's tomato rows.
• Rows with marigolds had 30% fewer damaged leaves than rows without them.
items.question: The student wants to present the aim of Hale's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Hale set out to learn whether planting marigolds near tomato plants reduces pest damage.
In Hale's study, tomato rows with marigolds had 30% fewer damaged leaves.
choices.slip: This is the result, not the aim.

choices.text: Hale planted marigolds next to half of the tomato rows in the Brannock community garden and left the other half of the rows without them.
choices.slip: This is the method, not the aim.

choices.text: The Brannock community garden grows tomatoes.
choices.slip: This is background; it says nothing about what the study set out to learn.

steps: A study's aim is what the researcher wanted to find out.
The second note states it: whether marigolds near tomatoes reduce pest damage.
explanation.why: It states what Hale set out to learn, which is the study's aim.
explanation.pattern: Keep aim (what they wanted to know), method (what they did) and result (what they found) apart; the goal names one.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Researchers at the Kestrel Point Marine Station tested a rope made from kelp fibers.
• They wanted to know whether kelp rope could replace nylon rope on small fishing boats.
• In the tests, kelp rope held 85% as much weight as nylon rope.
• Kelp rope broke down in seawater within two years; nylon rope did not.
items.question: The student wants to present a result of the tests. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: The researchers wanted to know whether kelp rope could replace nylon rope on small fishing boats.
choices.slip: This is the purpose of the tests, not a result.

choices.text: In the tests, the kelp-fiber rope held 85% as much weight as nylon rope.
The tests of kelp rope were carried out at the Kestrel Point Marine Station.
choices.slip: This says where the tests took place, not what they found.

choices.text: In the tests, kelp-fiber rope proved stronger than nylon rope.
choices.slip: This misstates the result: kelp rope held less weight (85%) than nylon.
