steps: The results are the third and fourth notes.
One choice reports the 85% figure correctly.
Another sounds like a result but reverses it: the kelp rope was weaker, not stronger.
explanation.why: It reports one of the test results exactly as the notes give it.
explanation.pattern: A result-sounding choice can still be wrong: check every claim against the notes word for word.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Historian Ruth Calloway studied how residents of Halden got news in the 1880s.
• She read 400 letters written by Halden residents that are kept in the town archive.
• She counted how often the letters mentioned newspapers, church notices and word of mouth.
• Word of mouth was mentioned most often.
• Calloway suggests Halden's two newspapers reached fewer people than historians had assumed.
items.question: The student wants to describe the methods Calloway used. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Calloway wanted to learn how residents of Halden got their news in the 1880s.
choices.slip: This is the aim of the study, not how it was done.

choices.text: Calloway found that the letters written by Halden residents in the 1880s mentioned word of mouth more often than newspapers or church notices.
choices.slip: This is a finding, not a method.

choices.text: Calloway read 400 residents' letters held in the town archive and counted how often each source of news was mentioned.
Calloway's work suggests Halden's newspapers reached fewer people than historians had assumed.
choices.slip: This is her conclusion, not her method.

steps: Methods are what the researcher did: what she examined and how.
The second and third notes describe that: reading 400 letters and counting mentions of each news source.
The other choices give the aim, a finding and the conclusion, all accurate but not methods.
explanation.why: It describes what Calloway actually did: read the letters and count the mentions.
explanation.pattern: Every wrong choice here is true. The test is fit to the goal: label each choice aim, method, finding or conclusion.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Tanager Street community garden waters its plots with rain collected in barrels.
• The Lark Hill community garden waters its plots with city water.
• Tanager Street pays nothing for water; Lark Hill pays about $340 per season.
• Tanager Street has 40 plots; Lark Hill has 25 plots.
items.question: The student wants to contrast the two gardens' water costs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: The Tanager Street garden, which collects rain in barrels, has 40 plots, while the Lark Hill garden, which uses city water, has only 25 plots.
choices.slip: This contrasts the gardens' sizes, not their water costs.

choices.text: Both gardens provide water for the vegetables grown in their plots.
choices.slip: This is a similarity, and it leaves out cost.

choices.text: The Tanager Street garden spends about $340 a season on water, while the Lark Hill garden pays nothing.
choices.slip: This reverses the facts: Lark Hill is the garden that pays $340.

choices.text: Unlike the Lark Hill garden, which pays about $340 a season for city water, the Tanager Street garden pays nothing because it collects rain.

steps: The goal needs both gardens and their water costs.
Lark Hill pays about $340 per season; Tanager Street pays nothing.
One choice states this correctly; another states the same contrast with the gardens swapped.
explanation.why: It contrasts the right feature (water cost) with the facts the right way around.
explanation.pattern: For a contrast, check three things: both items are named, the right feature is compared, and the facts aren't swapped.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Volunteers in Westbury have counted local birds every winter since 1979.
• The first count, in 1979, had 9 volunteers, who recorded 41 species.
• The 2023 count had 212 volunteers.
• In 2023, volunteers counted 18,400 birds of 96 species.
items.question: The student wants to emphasize how much the bird count has grown since it began. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: The Westbury bird count began in 1979 with 9 volunteers recording 41 species; in 2023, 212 volunteers recorded 96 species.
In 2023, 212 Westbury volunteers took part in the winter bird count and recorded 18,400 birds belonging to 96 different species.
choices.slip: This describes only 2023, so it can't show growth since the start.

choices.text: The first Westbury bird count, held in the winter of 1979, was carried out by just 9 volunteers, who recorded 41 species.
choices.slip: This gives only the starting point (1979), with nothing from later to show growth.

choices.text: The Westbury bird count recorded more species when it began in 1979 than it did in 2023, when 212 volunteers took part.
choices.slip: This is false: 41 species in 1979 and 96 in 2023.

steps: Growth needs a 'then' and a 'now'.
The notes give both: 1979 (9 volunteers, 41 species) and 2023 (212 volunteers, 96 species).
Only one choice puts both years side by side.
explanation.why: It sets the first count against the latest one, which is what shows the growth.
explanation.pattern: 'Emphasize growth or change' needs two points in time. Impressive numbers from one year alone don't do it.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2015, engineer Oren Malik surveyed the Hollis Reservoir.
• Malik estimated that the reservoir lost about 2.0 million cubic meters of water per year.
• He concluded that most of the loss was caused by evaporation.
• In 2022, hydrologist Ada Brenner placed sensors along the reservoir's dam.
• Brenner measured the yearly loss at about 2.1 million cubic meters.
• Her sensors showed that seepage under the dam caused about 60% of the loss and evaporation about 40%.
items.question: The student wants to emphasize how Brenner's findings challenge Malik's conclusion. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Malik concluded in 2015 that evaporation caused most of the Hollis Reservoir's water loss; Brenner's 2022 sensors measured the yearly loss at about 2.1 million cubic meters.
choices.slip: Gives both studies but contrasts only the amounts, which nearly agree; Malik's conclusion was about the cause of the loss.

choices.text: Malik concluded that evaporation caused most of the reservoir's water loss, but Brenner's sensors showed that seepage under the dam accounts for about 60% of it.
Brenner's sensors, placed along the dam in 2022, showed that seepage caused about 60% of the reservoir's water loss and evaporation about 40%.
choices.slip: Accurate, but it never mentions Malik's conclusion, so it doesn't show a challenge to it.

choices.text: Malik's 2015 estimate of about 2.0 million cubic meters of yearly loss is close to Brenner's 2022 measurement of 2.1 million, so the two studies largely agree on the amount.
choices.slip: Stresses agreement on the size of the loss, not a challenge to the cause.

steps: Malik's conclusion (third note) is about the cause of the loss: mostly evaporation.
Brenner's sensors found the main cause was seepage (about 60%), which contradicts that conclusion.
The tempting choice A is also phrased as a contrast, but it compares the yearly amounts, which nearly match (2.0 vs 2.1 million), and it is not about Malik's conclusion at all.
explanation.why: Only B sets Brenner's finding about the cause (mostly seepage) against Malik's conclusion about the cause (mostly evaporation).
explanation.pattern: 'Challenge the conclusion' means: find what the conclusion was about, then find the finding that contradicts that same point. Contrast wording on a different point is a trap.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hydrologist Cecilia Oyelowo-Marsh studies how fog contributes to the water supply of coastal hills.
• In 2021 she installed mesh nets on a ridge to collect fog droplets.
• Over twelve months, the nets collected an average of 4 liters of water per square meter per day.
• The collected water was used to irrigate 300 young oak seedlings.
• Seedling survival was 78% with net-collected water.
• Seedlings on the same ridge that were not irrigated had a survival rate of 41%.
items.question: The student wants to present the study's method and main result to an audience unfamiliar with the topic. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Hydrologist Cecilia Oyelowo-Marsh installed mesh nets on a coastal ridge in 2021, and over twelve months the nets collected an average of 4 liters of water per square meter per day.
choices.slip: Gives the method and a measurement but not the seedling result.

choices.text: Cecilia Oyelowo-Marsh irrigated 300 oak seedlings on a coastal ridge with fog water collected by mesh nets; 78% survived, compared with 41% of seedlings that were not irrigated.
Seedlings irrigated with net-collected fog water survived at 78% on the ridge where Oyelowo-Marsh worked, compared with 41% for seedlings on that ridge that received no irrigation.
choices.slip: Gives the result but not the purpose or the method, which a newcomer needs.

choices.text: Oyelowo-Marsh's nets collected an average of 4 liters of water per square meter per day for a year, and the water was used to irrigate 300 oak seedlings, of which 78% survived.
choices.slip: Leaves out the comparison with the 41% survival of unirrigated seedlings, so the result has no baseline.

steps: Audience: unfamiliar, so give purpose, method and result.
Method: nets, 300 seedlings.
Result: 78% versus 41%.
explanation.why: It states the purpose, the method, and the main result with the right comparison.
explanation.pattern: Match the choice to the goal's parts (method + result); reject choices missing a part or blending figures.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Fennimore Quartet premiered Merle Iversen's String Quartet No. 2 in 1962.
• Critics at the time called the piece 'relentlessly dissonant.'
• The Hartwell Ensemble recorded the same quartet in 1998.
• Reviews of the 1998 recording described the music as 'warm' and 'lyrical.'
• The 1998 recording used slower tempos in all four movements.
• Iversen's score contains no tempo markings.
items.question: The student wants to emphasize how the reception of the quartet changed between 1962 and 1998. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Merle Iversen's String Quartet No. 2, premiered by the Fennimore Quartet in 1962, was recorded by the Hartwell Ensemble in 1998 at slower tempos in all four movements.
choices.slip: Lists events and tempos but says nothing about how the piece was received.

Others drop the finding, the adjusted result, or overclaim.
explanation.why: Only the key states the finding and the adjusted size.
explanation.pattern: Finding-with-confound goals need both the raw result and the adjusted one.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A gene bank keeps seed samples from many varieties of a crop in cold storage.
• The Ludlow gene bank holds seeds from about 9,000 varieties of barley.
• Seeds are dried to 5 percent moisture and kept at minus 18 degrees Celsius.
• Many barley varieties once grown by farmers are no longer planted anywhere.
• Some stored varieties resist drought, a trait breeders can cross into modern crops.
• The Ludlow bank was founded in 1974.
items.question: The student wants to explain to readers unfamiliar with gene banks what one does and why that matters for plant breeding. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: A gene bank stores seed samples of many crop varieties in cold storage, preserving traits such as drought resistance that breeders can cross into modern crops even when no farmer plants those varieties anymore.

The Ludlow gene bank holds about 9,000 barley varieties, dried to 5 percent moisture and kept at minus 18 degrees Celsius, conditions that preserve the seeds so that each variety can be grown again later.
choices.slip: Describes storage conditions; never says why it matters for plant breeding.

choices.text: Because many barley varieties are no longer planted anywhere, the Ludlow gene bank, founded in 1974, keeps samples of about 9,000 of them in cold storage for future use by growers.
choices.slip: Explains why the bank exists but not the value to breeding.

choices.text: Breeders can cross traits such as drought resistance from older barley varieties into modern crops, which is why the Ludlow bank, founded in 1974, is valued by those who develop new crops.
choices.slip: Gives the breeding value but never explains what a gene bank does for readers unfamiliar with one.

steps: Goal: say what a gene bank does and why that matters for plant breeding.
The key defines the bank (seed samples in cold storage) and links stored traits to breeders.
The others give only one half, or details about the Ludlow bank.
explanation.why: The key covers both halves of the goal.
explanation.pattern: Define-and-justify goals need the definition and the consequence.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sea otters in Kellan Sound were hunted nearly out of existence by 1900.
• Otters eat sea urchins.
• With fewer otters, urchin density rose from 2 to 40 per square meter in surveyed plots.
• Urchins graze on kelp holdfasts, and kelp cover dropped by more than 80 percent.
• Fish that shelter in kelp also declined.
• Otters were reintroduced in 1977, and kelp began to recover.
items.question: The student wants to explain how the loss of otters led to the loss of kelp. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Otters were hunted nearly out of existence in Kellan Sound by 1900, and kelp cover in the sound later dropped by more than 80 percent from its earlier level.
choices.slip: Places the two events side by side without the urchin link.

choices.text: Urchin density rose from 2 to 40 per square meter and kelp cover fell by more than 80 percent, which in turn caused the decline of the fish that shelter in kelp beds.
choices.slip: Leaves out otters and extends the chain to fish.

choices.text: Because otters eat urchins, their near-disappearance let urchin density rise from 2 to 40 per square meter, and urchins grazed kelp holdfasts until kelp cover fell by over 80 percent.
Otters eat urchins and urchins graze kelp holdfasts, so the reintroduction of otters in 1977 allowed kelp to begin recovering across the plots that had been grazed bare.
choices.slip: Gives the mechanism but for recovery, not loss.

steps: Goal: otters lost -> kelp lost.
Chain: fewer otters, more urchins, grazed kelp.
Key is the only one that states each link.
explanation.why: The key names the intermediate step (urchins).
explanation.pattern: Mechanism goals need each link in the chain.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lab culture testing of well water costs $45 per sample and takes 48 hours.
• A field test strip costs $4 per sample and gives a result in 10 minutes.
• Culture testing identifies the species of bacteria; strips detect only whether coliform bacteria are present.
• The county must screen 600 wells within a 10-week summer window.
• The county's lab can process at most 40 cultures per week.
• In a 2022 trial, strips agreed with culture results 92 percent of the time.
items.question: The student wants to explain why the lab's limited weekly capacity, rather than cost, makes culture testing impractical for the county's summer screening. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Culture testing costs $45 per sample against $4 for a strip, so screening all 600 wells with cultures would cost about $27,000 rather than about $2,400 with strips.
choices.slip: Argues from cost, which the goal sets aside.

choices.text: Strips detect only whether coliform bacteria are present, while cultures identify the species, so cultures give the county more information about the safety of each well it screens.
choices.slip: Argues for cultures on information, not capacity.

choices.text: Strips agreed with culture results 92 percent of the time in a 2022 trial, so they are reliable enough to use for screening wells across the county in a single summer.
choices.slip: Argues from accuracy, not capacity.

choices.text: At 40 cultures a week, the county's lab could finish only 400 of the 600 wells in the 10-week window, so strips, which give results in 10 minutes, are the practical choice.

steps: Goal: capacity, not cost.
Key alone applies the capacity limit to the window.
explanation.why: Only the key uses capacity and the window.
explanation.pattern: Constraint goals need the specific limit and the requirement it fails.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A potter's first firing, the bisque, is done at about 950 degrees Celsius.
• Bisque firing drives water out of the clay while leaving it porous enough to absorb glaze.
• The glaze firing is done at about 1,200 degrees Celsius.
• Glaze contains silica, which melts into a glassy coating at roughly 1,100 degrees or above.
• Potters apply glaze by dipping bisque-fired pieces into a liquid mixture.
• A kiln of this type takes about 12 hours to heat.
items.question: The student wants to explain why the glaze firing must be hotter than the bisque firing. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: The bisque firing at 950 degrees drives water out of the clay but leaves it porous enough to absorb glaze, which is why potters dip bisque pieces before the 1,200-degree firing begins.
choices.slip: Explains why bisque comes first, not why the second firing is hotter.

choices.text: Silica in glaze melts into a glassy coating only at roughly 1,100 degrees or above, so the second firing at 1,200 degrees must exceed the 950-degree bisque firing, which only drives out water.
The glaze firing, at about 1,200 degrees, is hotter than the bisque firing at 950 degrees, and the kiln of this type needs about 12 hours to heat before either firing.
choices.slip: States that it is hotter but gives no reason.

choices.text: Potters dip bisque pieces into a liquid mixture containing silica, which melts at roughly 1,100 degrees, so glaze must be applied to the porous clay before the second firing.
choices.slip: Explains the order of application, not the temperature.

steps: Goal: reason for the higher temperature.
Silica melts at 1,100 or above; bisque at 950 would not melt it.
Only the key gives that reason.
explanation.why: The melting point of silica is the reason.
explanation.pattern: Why-goals need the cause, not just the comparison.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Between 2015 and 2023, the number of daily cyclists on Camlet Avenue rose from 1,200 to 3,000.
• Over the same period the city's population rose from 410,000 to 451,000, an increase of 10 percent.
• The city added 22 kilometers of protected bike lanes in 2019.
• Cyclists on Camlet Avenue are counted on weekdays in May.
• Cycling's share of commuter trips citywide was 5 percent in 2023.
• Camlet Avenue was resurfaced in 2017.
items.question: The student wants to argue that the rise in cycling on Camlet Avenue reflects more than population growth. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Daily cyclists on Camlet Avenue rose 150 percent between 2015 and 2023, from 1,200 to 3,000, while the city's population rose only 10 percent.
Daily cyclists on Camlet Avenue rose by 1,800 between 2015 and 2023, a period that included the addition of 22 kilometers of protected bike lanes in 2019.
choices.slip: Gives an absolute rise and a possible cause but no comparison with population.

choices.text: The city's population rose 10 percent between 2015 and 2023, from 410,000 to 451,000, a period in which cyclists were counted on weekdays in May.
choices.slip: Gives the population change but not the cycling change.

choices.text: Cycling accounted for 5 percent of commuter trips citywide in 2023, while the city's population grew by about 41,000 residents.
choices.slip: Gives a share and a population change but no comparison of growth.

steps: Goal: show growth beyond population.
150 percent vs 10 percent.
Key puts the two growth rates side by side.
explanation.why: The comparison of rates is what shows more than population growth.
explanation.pattern: Beyond-baseline goals need growth rates side by side.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A trial on a 40-hectare farm applied nitrogen at 60, 120 and 180 kilograms per hectare.
• Wheat yields were 5.8, 7.1 and 7.0 tonnes per hectare, respectively.
• Wheat takes up nitrogen only until its grain heads fill; uptake in the trial leveled off near 120 kilograms per hectare.
• Soil tests showed that unused nitrogen at the 180 rate washed below the root zone after heavy rain.
• Rainfall in the 2023 season was above average.
• The wheat was sown in October.
items.question: The student wants to explain why extra nitrogen above 120 kilograms per hectare could not raise yield, including what became of the surplus. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: Yields rose from 5.8 tonnes at 60 kilograms per hectare to 7.1 tonnes at 120 kilograms, then slipped slightly to 7.0 tonnes at the highest rate of 180 kilograms.
choices.slip: Describes the pattern without explaining it.

choices.text: Wheat takes up nitrogen only until its grain heads fill, and uptake in the trial leveled off near 120 kilograms per hectare, where yield had already reached 7.1 tonnes.
choices.slip: Gives the cap but not what became of the surplus.

choices.text: Wheat's nitrogen uptake leveled off near 120 kilograms per hectare, so the surplus at 180 went unused and washed below the root zone after heavy rain, leaving yield at 7.0 tonnes.
Unused nitrogen at the 180 rate washed below the root zone after heavy rain, in a season when rainfall was above average on the 40-hectare farm where the trial was run.
choices.slip: Gives the fate of the surplus but not why it went unused.

steps: Goal: why no gain and where the surplus went.
Uptake cap explains no gain; runoff explains the surplus.
Key joins both.
explanation.why: Both halves of the goal appear only in the key.
explanation.pattern: Two-part explanation goals need both parts in one choice.

items.passage: For decades, historians assumed that the stone walls on Corran Island were built by farmers in the 1700s. In 2019, however, archaeologist Teo Brandt dated charcoal found beneath one wall to roughly 900 years earlier. Brandt's finding suggests that the walls were the work of a much older community.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It states the conclusion that Brandt's 2019 finding went on to support.
choices.slip: Brandt's finding goes against the first sentence ('however').

choices.text: It presents a long-held view that the text goes on to question.
It identifies a debate among historians that Brandt set out to settle.
choices.slip: Historians 'assumed' one thing; no disagreement among them is described.

choices.text: It offers background on the method that Brandt later used on the walls.
choices.slip: The dating method (charcoal) appears only in the second sentence.

steps: Sentence 1 gives what historians 'assumed' for decades.
'However' in sentence 2 introduces evidence against it.
Sentence 3 draws the new conclusion.
So sentence 1 sets up the old view that is then challenged.
explanation.why: The first sentence states the earlier assumption; Brandt's dating then undercuts it.
explanation.pattern: 'For decades … assumed' followed by 'however' is a common pattern: old view, then a challenge to it.

items.passage: Mr. Asher wound the shop's forty clocks every morning, though no customer had come in for a month. "A clock that stops," he told his granddaughter, "has given up." She noticed that he looked at the door each time he said it.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.text: To explain the steps involved in winding an old clock
choices.slip: The text says he winds the clocks but gives no steps.

choices.text: To show that the granddaughter wants to leave the shop
choices.slip: She only observes him; nothing shows what she wants.

choices.text: To describe why customers stopped visiting the shop
choices.slip: The lack of customers is stated, but no cause is given.

choices.text: To suggest that a man's routine expresses his hope

steps: He winds forty clocks daily even with no customers.
He says a stopped clock 'has given up'.
He looks at the door as he says it, linking the clocks to the customers he is waiting for.
So the routine stands for his refusal to give up on the shop.
explanation.why: The details (daily winding, the remark, the glance at the door) point to a man who keeps hoping customers will return.
explanation.pattern: In fiction, the purpose is often what the details reveal about a character, not the literal actions.

items.passage: Engineers testing a new road surface in Halden first laid a short strip of it on a quiet side street. After a winter of frost left the strip uncracked, they repaved a busy avenue with the same material. The avenue has now gone three years without a single repair.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It describes a small trial, then a wider use of the material, then the outcome.
It describes a new material, then compares it with an older one, then recommends it.
choices.slip: No older material is mentioned, and nothing is recommended.

choices.text: It reports a result, then describes the test behind it, then questions that test.
choices.slip: The test comes first, and no one questions it.

choices.text: It describes a setback in a trial, then a change of method, then the final outcome.
choices.slip: The strip survived the winter uncracked; there was no setback.

steps: Sentence 1: a short test strip.
Sentence 2: the test succeeds, so the material is used on a busy avenue.
Sentence 3: the result after three years.
explanation.why: The text moves from test, to larger use, to result.
explanation.pattern: For structure questions, label each sentence in two or three words, then match the labels to a choice in order.

items.passage: Studies of urban gardens often report that gardeners eat more vegetables than their neighbors do. It is tempting to conclude that gardening changes diets. Yet sociologist Runa Kessel notes that people who already favor vegetables may simply be likelier to take up gardening. To separate the two possibilities, she tracked households' diets for a year before any of them were offered a plot.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It rejects as inaccurate the reports mentioned in the first sentence.
choices.slip: Kessel doesn't dispute that gardeners eat more vegetables; she questions why.

choices.text: It states the result that Kessel's year of tracking produced.
choices.slip: No result is given; the last sentence only describes how the study was set up.

choices.text: It offers a rival explanation that Kessel's study is designed to test.
It provides evidence that taking up gardening changes what people eat.
choices.slip: It suggests the reverse: diet may lead to gardening.

steps: Sentence 1: the pattern (gardeners eat more vegetables).
Sentence 2: the tempting explanation (gardening changes diet).
Sentence 3, 'Yet': a second explanation (vegetable eaters choose gardening).
Sentence 4: a study built 'to separate the two possibilities'.
explanation.why: The third sentence gives a rival explanation of the same pattern, and the study that follows is meant to tell the two apart.
explanation.pattern: Separate a finding from its explanation. A sentence can accept the finding while offering a different cause.

items.passage: The discovery of a fossil forest beneath the Pell glacier has been widely reported as proof that the region was once warm. Paleobotanist Imre Dalca does not dispute that reading, but he considers it the less interesting one. The trees' growth rings, he points out, are unusually even, implying that seasons at the site differed far less than they do anywhere at that latitude today.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.text: To argue that a widely reported reading of a recent discovery is mistaken
choices.slip: Dalca 'does not dispute that reading'; he adds to it.

choices.text: To present a researcher's view that a discovery reveals more than has been reported
To explain how growth rings are used to find the age of fossil trees
choices.slip: The rings are used here to learn about seasons, not the trees' age.

choices.text: To describe how a fossil forest came to be found under a glacier
choices.slip: The text doesn't say how the forest was discovered.

steps: Sentence 1: the common reading (the region was once warm).
Sentence 2: Dalca accepts it but finds it 'the less interesting one'.
Sentence 3: what he finds more interesting (evidence of mild seasons).
So the text presents his view that the find reveals something further.
explanation.why: Dalca accepts the reported reading and points to an additional, more striking implication.
explanation.pattern: Watch verbs of stance: 'does not dispute' means agreement, so a choice saying the view is 'mistaken' is wrong.

items.passage: Translator Mirela Voss has called her English version of the novel Salt Roads "unfaithful on purpose." Reviewers who quote the phrase as a confession are not wrong that the translation strays: whole idioms in it have no source in the original. But the original's narrator speaks a coastal dialect with no English counterpart, and a word-for-word rendering would have left her sounding merely formal. Voss's invented idiom abandons the novel's words to preserve what they do.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It concedes the fact behind a reading of Voss's phrase, a reading the text then disputes.
It endorses the reviewers' view that Voss's phrase admits a failing in her translation.
choices.slip: 'But' turns against the confession reading: the text goes on to show the departures were needed, not a failing.

choices.text: It corrects the reviewers' mistaken belief that the translation departs from the original.
choices.slip: The sentence says the reviewers 'are not wrong that the translation strays'.

choices.text: It shows that Voss's phrase was an apology for the idioms she was unable to translate.
choices.slip: The rest of the text presents her choices as deliberate and successful, not as something to apologize for.

steps: Sentence 1: Voss calls her translation 'unfaithful on purpose'.
Sentence 2: reviewers read this as a confession. The text grants one thing: they 'are not wrong that the translation strays'.
'But' (sentence 3) turns: a literal version would have lost the narrator's voice.
Sentence 4: so straying was the way to stay true to the novel. The 'confession' reading is rejected, though its facts were granted.
explanation.why: The second sentence admits that the translation does depart from the original, then the text argues that this is no confession of failure.
explanation.pattern: 'Are not wrong that …' concedes a fact. Watch for a 'But' that then rejects the conclusion drawn from it.

items.passage:
The following text is from Walt Whitman's 1868 poem "A Noiseless Patient Spider."

A noiseless patient spider,
I mark'd where on a little promontory it stood isolated,
Mark'd how to explore the vacant vast surrounding,
It launch'd forth filament, filament, filament, out of itself,
Ever unreeling them, ever tirelessly speeding them.

And you O my soul where you stand,
Surrounded, detached, in measureless oceans of space,
Ceaselessly musing, venturing, throwing, seeking the spheres to connect them,
Till the bridge you will need be form'd, till the ductile anchor hold,
Till the gossamer thread you fling catch somewhere, O my soul.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: The speaker describes a spider's effort to reach outward, then turns to the soul, which the speaker says is better equipped than the spider to complete the connection it seeks.
choices.slip: The poem never says the soul is better equipped; the soul is shown doing the same thing, still hoping the thread will 'catch somewhere'.

choices.text: The speaker describes a spider's effort to reach outward, then asks whether the soul will find, as the spider has, a place where its threads finally hold.
choices.slip: The spider's threads are never said to have held; the poem shows it still 'ever unreeling' them. The hope of a catch belongs to the soul.

choices.text: The speaker describes a spider's solitary effort to reach outward, then turns to the soul, whose isolation and search for connection resemble the spider's.
The speaker presents a spider's behavior as puzzling, then offers the soul's search for connection as the explanation for that behavior.
choices.slip: The speaker never calls the spider puzzling; the spider is the image and the soul is what the image is applied to.

steps: First stanza: the speaker 'mark'd' a spider on a promontory, sending out filaments into empty space.
Second stanza begins 'And you O my soul': the speaker turns to address the soul.
The soul is also 'surrounded, detached' and keeps flinging out threads hoping one will 'catch'. The stanzas mirror each other.
So the structure is an image followed by an address that draws the parallel.
explanation.why: The first stanza describes the spider; the second turns to the soul and shows it doing the same thing in the same kind of isolation.
explanation.pattern: For a poem, say in one line what each stanza does. When the second stanza uses the same words as the first ('surrounded', 'filament', 'fling'), it is applying the image, not contrasting it.

items.passage:
The following text is from Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1892 short story "The Yellow Wallpaper." The narrator and her husband, John, have taken a house for the summer.

John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage.
John is practical in the extreme. He has no patience with faith, an intense horror of superstition, and he scoffs openly at any talk of things not to be felt and seen and put down in figures.
John is a physician, and perhaps—(I would not say it to a living soul, of course, but this is dead paper and a great relief to my mind)—perhaps that is one reason I do not get well faster.
You see, he does not believe I am sick!
And what can one do?
If a physician of high standing, and one's own husband, assures friends and relatives that there is really nothing the matter with one but temporary nervous depression—a slight hysterical tendency—what is one to do?
My brother is also a physician, and also of high standing, and he says the same thing.
So I take phosphates or phosphites—whichever it is, and tonics, and journeys, and air, and exercise, and am absolutely forbidden to "work" until I am well again.
Personally, I disagree with their ideas.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence beginning "John is a physician" in the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It acknowledges that John's medical training gives him a legitimate reason to doubt that she is seriously ill, though she regrets that he does.
choices.slip: She never calls his doubt legitimate; she says he 'scoffs' at what can't be put in figures and ends by disagreeing with him.

choices.text: It qualifies the narrator's complaint about John by suggesting that his profession makes him unusually cautious about her health.
choices.slip: He is not cautious about her health: 'he does not believe I am sick'.

choices.text: It suggests that the narrator blames John's profession for the gentleness of a treatment that she finds too undemanding for her condition.
choices.slip: She objects that the treatment forbids the work she wants, not that it is too gentle.

choices.text: It reveals a private suspicion, voiced only in writing, that her husband's professional confidence may be part of what keeps her unwell.

steps: Just before: John 'scoffs' at anything that can't be 'put down in figures'. That sets up his skepticism.
The sentence in question adds that he is a physician and that 'perhaps' this is why she isn't getting better. She adds that she 'would not say it to a living soul', so it's private.
The next sentences show why: he doesn't believe she is sick and neither does her brother.
So it brings out a doubt she can only write down, about the effect of her husband's confidence.
explanation.why: The parenthesis ('I would not say it to a living soul') and 'perhaps that is one reason' mark a doubt she keeps private, which the following sentences back up.
explanation.pattern: For a sentence-function question, look at what the sentence adds to what came before and how the next lines use it. Hedges ('perhaps') and asides show how the narrator regards what she says.

items.passage: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived. . . . I wanted to live deep and suck out all the marrow of life, to live so sturdily and Spartan-like as to put to rout all that was not life, to cut a broad swath and shave close, to drive life into a corner, and reduce it to its lowest terms, and, if it proved to be mean, why then to get the whole and genuine meanness of it, and publish its meanness to the world; or if it were sublime, to know it by experience, and be able to give a true account of it in my next excursion. For most men, it appears to me, are in a strange uncertainty about it, whether it is of the devil or of God, and have somewhat hastily concluded that it is the chief end of man here to 'glorify God and enjoy him forever.'
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It contrasts the narrator's willingness to test life by direct experience with other people's readiness to accept a conclusion about it without having tested it.
It admits that the narrator shares the general uncertainty about whether life is of the devil or of God and has been unable to resolve it.
choices.slip: Misreads 'most men': the narrator separates himself from them and plans to find out.

choices.text: It explains why the narrator expects his time in the woods to prove that life is sublime rather than mean.
choices.slip: The narrator says he will accept whichever he finds; he predicts neither.

choices.text: It criticizes the narrator's own earlier haste in settling on a view of life before having enough experience to support it.
choices.slip: The 'haste' (somewhat hastily) is attributed to most men, not to the narrator.

steps: Sentences 1-2: the narrator's purpose, to test life and report either way.
Last sentence: 'most men' are uncertain, yet 'somewhat hastily' have decided.
The sentence sets other people's hasty conclusion against his plan to find out.
explanation.why: It sets the speaker's open, experiential approach against the quick conclusions of others.
explanation.pattern: For a sentence-function question, find who 'they' are in the last sentence and how it relates to the speaker's stated plan.

items.passage: It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us. These laws, taken in the largest sense, being Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance which is almost implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and direct action of the external conditions of life, and from use and disuse; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved forms. Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death, the most exalted object which we are capable of conceiving, namely, the production of the higher animals, directly follows. There is grandeur in this view of life.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence (beginning 'Thus, from the war of nature') in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It qualifies the preceding list by naming a condition under which the laws fail to operate, a condition that the closing sentence then removes.
choices.slip: Nothing in the sentence limits the laws; it states what 'directly follows' from them.

choices.text: It restates the scene in the first sentence in more abstract terms, before the laws that explain the scene have been named.
choices.slip: The laws have already been named in the second sentence; this sentence concerns their outcome.

choices.text: It draws out a consequence of the laws just listed, which the author calls the most exalted object conceivable and which prepares the closing judgment of grandeur.
It admits that the process described is harsh and argues that this harshness is a reason to doubt that the process has any grandeur.
choices.slip: The harshness is stated, but the final sentence draws the opposite conclusion: 'There is grandeur in this view of life.'

steps: Sentence 2 lists the laws.
Sentence 3 says that from the war of nature, famine and death, the production of the higher animals 'directly follows': a consequence of the laws.
Sentence 4 judges the whole view grand.
explanation.why: The sentence states the outcome the laws produce and sets up the closing evaluation.
explanation.pattern: Function-of-a-sentence questions: locate the sentence's neighbors, say what comes before and after it, and reject choices that reverse their order or add a move (a limit, a restatement, a doubt) that is not there.

items.passage: Textile conservator Ayesha Brandvold has spent eleven years studying a fragment of a seventh-century tapestry, the Lindholm Hanging, whose red dyes were assumed to be entirely plant-derived. That assumption was reasonable: no insect-derived pigments had previously been identified in textiles from the region and period, and madder, a plant, was the standard red. But chemical analysis by Brandvold's team has detected a compound characteristic of an insect-derived dye in the Hanging's red threads. The finding does not show how the dye reached the weavers, and Brandvold says she will not speculate until threads from similar tapestries have been tested.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It casts doubt on the team's chemical analysis by noting that it was carried out on a single fragment of the tapestry.
choices.slip: The sentence concedes what the analysis does not show (how the dye arrived), not a flaw in the analysis; the fragment is not mentioned as a limit.

choices.text: It limits what the team's finding establishes by noting a question it leaves open and reporting Brandvold's caution about it.
It reports a second finding that confirms the red dye came from an insect species native to the region where the tapestry was made.
choices.slip: No second finding is reported; the sentence says what is not known.

choices.text: It argues that the dye must have been imported, since no insect-derived pigments had been identified in the region's textiles.
choices.slip: Brandvold says she will not speculate about how the dye arrived.

steps: Sentence 3: the team detected an insect-derived compound.
Last sentence: the finding 'does not show how the dye reached the weavers', and Brandvold will not speculate until similar tapestries are tested.
So it marks a limit of the finding and Brandvold's caution.
explanation.why: It names a question the finding leaves open and reports the author's refusal to speculate.
explanation.pattern: A final sentence that begins by limiting a finding ('does not show') usually marks scope; reject choices that invent a flaw, a new result, or the speculation the text declines to make.

items.passage: Translators often face words with no neat equivalent. The Finnish word 'sisu', for example, names a stubborn courage that persists after hope has gone, and renderings such as 'grit' or 'guts' keep only part of it. Translator Mirabel Quint has argued that such words should usually be left in the original and glossed once, since any single English word forces the reader to take one meaning and drop the rest.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.text: To argue that English has fewer words for courage than Finnish does
choices.slip: Not claimed: one example is not a comparison of vocabularies.

choices.text: To criticize translators who render 'sisu' as 'grit' or 'guts'
choices.slip: The renderings are used as an illustration; Quint is not said to criticize anyone.

choices.text: To present a translator's advice on hard-to-translate words and illustrate it with an example
To explain the history of how the Finnish word 'sisu' entered other languages
choices.slip: The text says nothing of its history.

steps: Opens with a general problem.
Gives 'sisu' as an example.
Reports Quint's recommendation and its reason.
explanation.why: The example supports Quint's recommendation, which is the point of the text.
explanation.pattern: Identify what the example is for: it illustrates the claim that follows, it is not the topic itself.

items.passage: Few dispute that the Karrow Canal cut shipping costs in the decade after it opened. Economic historian Winifred Penhallow does not deny this, but she points out that the canal's backers measured costs only for goods that passed through its locks. Goods that moved on parallel rail lines, whose costs rose, were left out. Once those are counted, she argues, the canal's net effect on regional costs was close to zero.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text?

choices.text: It accepts the earlier claim while introducing the point on which Penhallow disagrees.
It supplies a statistic that proves the claim made in the first sentence.
choices.slip: No statistic is given and the sentence qualifies rather than proves.

choices.text: It identifies a flaw in Penhallow's own method of counting costs.
choices.slip: The flaw it points to is in the backers' counting, not Penhallow's.

choices.text: It summarizes the conclusion that Penhallow reaches at the end.
choices.slip: The conclusion comes in the final sentence, not here.

steps: Sentence 1: the common view.
Sentence 2: Penhallow does not deny it, but...
Her real objection follows.
explanation.why: 'Does not deny this, but' concedes the claim and turns to the objection.
explanation.pattern: A concession sentence ('does not deny... but') agrees in part and sets up the disagreement.

items.passage: Urban planners often cite the principle that streets should be as narrow as safety allows, since narrow streets slow cars and keep neighborhoods walkable. Yet the principle has exceptions. In the Tavernier district, planners narrowed a main road to eight meters in 2016, expecting traffic to calm; instead, delivery trucks began double-parking, buses were delayed by as much as ten minutes, and cyclists reported more near-collisions. Planner Rafaela Linwood, who reviewed the project, concluded that narrow streets work in old towns because they carry few vehicles, and that the principle should be applied only where traffic volumes are low.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.text: To argue that planners should widen streets in districts where traffic has been slowed by earlier projects.
choices.slip: Linwood's conclusion limits the principle; it does not recommend widening streets.

choices.text: To use a specific project to show that a widely cited planning principle depends on conditions that do not always hold.
To recount how a district's road-narrowing project was designed, built, and paid for.
choices.slip: The text reports the project's results, not its design or cost.

choices.text: To criticize planners for ignoring the opinions of cyclists and bus passengers before acting.
choices.slip: No claim about ignoring opinions is made.

steps: States a common principle.
Says it has exceptions and gives a case.
Ends with a condition under which it holds.
explanation.why: The case and Linwood's conclusion show that the principle holds only under certain conditions.
explanation.pattern: The main purpose is the point the example is used to make.

items.passage: In the 1970s, nutrition researchers assumed that people who ate more fish would develop heart disease less often, because fish oils lower certain fats in the blood. Large trials later gave mixed results: some found a protective effect, while others found none. Epidemiologist Beatrix Holloway suggested that the trials disagreed because they enrolled different kinds of people. In trials of patients who already had heart disease, fish oil appeared to help; in trials of healthy adults, it did not. If she is right, the question is not whether fish oil protects the heart but whose heart it protects.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It reframes the debate by naming the question that Holloway's explanation makes central.
It summarizes the findings of the large trials described earlier in the text.
choices.slip: The sentence draws a conclusion from Holloway's idea; it does not restate the trials.

choices.text: It rejects Holloway's explanation in favor of the researchers' original assumption.
choices.slip: It builds on Holloway's explanation.

choices.text: It introduces a new trial that contradicts the mixed results described earlier.
choices.slip: No new trial is mentioned.

steps: Assumption, mixed trials, Holloway's explanation.
Last sentence: if she is right, the real question changes.
explanation.why: The last sentence says what the debate should now be about, given Holloway's explanation.
explanation.pattern: Ask what job a final sentence does: summary, rebuttal, new evidence, or reframing.

items.passage: For decades, scholars explained the collapse of the Bronze Age city of Tell Verran as the result of invasion, pointing to a thick layer of ash that covers its palace. Recent analysis complicates that account. Radiocarbon dates from the ash layer span nearly a century, which is far too long for a single burning, and the ash contains the remains of stored grain, suggesting that the fires were set deliberately in storehouses. Archaeologist Ilse Bergmann-Cole proposes that the city was abandoned slowly during a long drought and that its storehouses were burned by residents as they left, to deny the grain to anyone who might follow.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It describes a long-standing explanation, defends it against recent evidence, and concludes that it should be kept.
choices.slip: Recent evidence is used to revise the explanation, not to defend it.

choices.text: It introduces a long-standing explanation, offers new evidence in its favor, and proposes extending it to other sites.
choices.slip: The new evidence complicates the explanation rather than supporting it.

choices.text: It presents a new explanation, compares it with an older one, and concludes that the two cannot be reconciled.
choices.slip: The older explanation comes first and the new account replaces it.

choices.text: It presents a long-standing explanation, introduces evidence that complicates it, and proposes a revision.

steps: Sentence 1: the old explanation (invasion).
Sentences 2-3: evidence that complicates it.
Last sentence: Bergmann-Cole's revised account.
explanation.why: The text moves from the old view to complicating evidence to a new proposal.
explanation.pattern: Describe structure by what each part does, not by its topic.

items.passage: Economist Calista Ferreira-Nwosu argues that minimum-staffing laws for hospital nurses improve patient outcomes. In her analysis of 41 hospitals, those in states with such laws reported fewer deaths after surgery than hospitals in states without them. One might conclude that the laws themselves are responsible. But Ferreira-Nwosu notes that states adopting the laws tended to be those whose hospitals already employed more nurses per bed, so the comparison may reflect staffing levels that existed before any law was passed. She therefore compares each hospital with its own record from before the laws took effect, a design that, she says, isolates the laws' effect more cleanly.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence ("One might conclude...") in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It states an inference that the first comparison seems to support, which the next sentence then qualifies by raising a competing explanation.
It summarizes Ferreira-Nwosu's own conclusion, which the rest of the text supports by describing further hospitals in states that have passed such laws.
choices.slip: The inference is one she goes on to question, and no further hospitals are described.

choices.text: It introduces an objection from critics of staffing laws, which Ferreira-Nwosu answers by showing that hospitals with more nurses report fewer deaths.
choices.slip: No critics are mentioned, and the nurse-count point is her own caution, not an answer to an objection.

choices.text: It presents a claim that Ferreira-Nwosu rejects outright by showing that the hospitals compared were chosen because they reported unusually few deaths after surgery.
choices.slip: She does not say the hospitals were chosen for their results, and she does not reject the idea outright.

steps: Sentence 2: hospitals with laws had fewer deaths.
Sentence 3: an inference that seems natural.
Sentence 4 ('But'): states with laws already had more nurses, a rival explanation.
explanation.why: The sentence voices the tempting conclusion that the next sentence puts in doubt.
explanation.pattern: A sentence that begins 'One might conclude' is usually a view the author will complicate; check what 'But' does next.

items.passage: Many musicologists hold that the metronome, invented in the 1810s, transformed how composers thought about tempo. Marks printed in scores of the following decades seem to bear this out: tempos are specified with a precision that earlier scores lack. Yet the composer Anselmina Craddock, whose letters survive, abandoned her metronome marks within a year, complaining that performers treated them as rules rather than as guides. Her case does not refute the view that the device changed notation, but it suggests that changes in what was printed need not reflect changes in how composers wanted music played.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It outlines a widely held view, supports it with examples from composers' letters, and concludes that the view applies to every composer of the period.
choices.slip: The letters are used against part of the view, and no claim is made about every composer.

choices.text: It states a common view, cites apparent support, and then offers a case that separates one part of the view from another.
It reports a disagreement among musicologists, traces it to a difference in the evidence consulted, and proposes a method for deciding which side is correct.
choices.slip: The musicologists share one view; no competing camp or method is described.

choices.text: It describes a technological invention, explains why composers resisted it, and argues that performers rather than composers were responsible for changes in notation.
choices.slip: Craddock is one composer who dropped the marks; the text does not say composers resisted the invention or blame performers for notation changes.

steps: Sentences 1-2: the view and its apparent support.
Sentence 3: Craddock's case.
Sentence 4: the case does not refute the notation claim but undermines an inference about intentions.
explanation.why: The text states a view, shows apparent support, and then uses one case to split the view into a claim that stands and one that does not.
explanation.pattern: Describe structure by what each part does to the claim that came before it.

items.passage: Ecologist Mireille Tovar-Quist describes the fungal networks of forest soil as a kind of marketplace: trees deliver sugars to fungi in exchange for phosphorus, and each side gives more to partners that give more in return. The comparison captures how reciprocal trade can stabilize cooperation without any central authority directing it. But Tovar-Quist stresses that it fails in one respect. Markets involve parties who choose among many trading partners and who can walk away from a poor deal, whereas a seedling's roots are often colonized by whichever fungus happens to be nearby, and the seedling may be unable to switch. Where that is so, she argues, the network behaves less like a market than like a dependency.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.text: To argue that fungal networks should be studied as economic systems because trees and fungi respond to incentives much as traders do.
choices.slip: The text limits the market comparison rather than recommending it as a research approach.

choices.text: To compare two competing analogies for fungal networks and conclude that the dependency account explains seedlings' behavior better than the market account does.
choices.slip: The market and the dependency are not presented as rival accounts to be weighed in general; the second describes where the first fails.

choices.text: To explain a common analogy for a biological relationship and to identify a condition under which the analogy becomes misleading.
To show that cooperation between trees and fungi is unstable without a central authority and that seedlings therefore cannot benefit from fungal partners.
choices.slip: The text says reciprocity can stabilize cooperation without a central authority, and it does not say seedlings gain nothing.

steps: Sentences 1-2: the market analogy and what it explains.
Sentences 3-5: where the analogy fails (seedlings may be unable to switch partners).
explanation.why: The text presents an analogy and then marks the case where it stops working.
explanation.pattern: Main-purpose answers must cover both halves of a two-part text; reject choices that keep only one half or reverse the author's stance.

items.passage: Mattias had kept the lighthouse log for thirty years in the same blue ink, and he kept it even after an automated beacon made the log unnecessary. Each evening he wrote the weather, the tide, and the number of vessels passing; each morning he locked the book in a drawer without reading it. When his niece Linnet offered to take the books to a museum, he told her that nobody would want them, since nothing in them was out of the ordinary. Yet he had never let a day pass blank, and when a storm cut the power for a week he wrote the entries by candlelight, in letters a little larger than usual.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It explains why the automated beacon made the log unnecessary by describing how storms affect the island's power supply.
choices.slip: The beacon is mentioned only in the first sentence, and the storm detail is about Mattias's habit.

choices.text: It contradicts Mattias's claim that the log contains nothing unusual by showing that the storm was the most severe of his career.
choices.slip: Nothing says the storm was exceptional, and the entries concern his behavior, not the weather.

choices.text: It suggests that Mattias hoped a museum would accept the books and therefore wrote the entries more legibly than before.
choices.slip: Mattias told his niece nobody would want the books; the sentence shows care, not hope for a museum.

choices.text: It shows through a concrete detail that Mattias values the log more than his dismissive remark to his niece suggests.

steps: Mattias tells Linnet the log is worthless.
Yet he never skipped a day and wrote even by candlelight, a little larger than usual.
explanation.why: The final detail shows care for the log that his words deny.
explanation.pattern: When a character says one thing and a detail shows another, the detail's function is to reveal the true attitude.

items.passage: Shopkeepers often oppose bike lanes, fearing that removing parking will cost them customers. In a survey of 1,200 shoppers on one commercial street, urban planner Zainab Okonjo-Pryce found that 62 percent had arrived on foot, by bike, or by transit, though shopkeepers on that street had estimated the figure at about 20 percent. She does not conclude that bike lanes help business; her data come from a single street and cannot show how shoppers would behave if parking were removed. Her point is narrower: decisions about the street should rest on how customers actually arrive rather than on how shopkeepers assume they do.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It gives evidence that the shopkeepers' belief rests on a mistaken estimate, without by itself showing that the policy they oppose is beneficial.
It demonstrates that bike lanes increase retail sales by comparing the share of customers who arrive on foot or by bike with the shopkeepers' estimate.
choices.slip: The survey says nothing about sales, and the next sentence denies that bike lanes were shown to help.

choices.text: It supports Okonjo-Pryce's claim that parking is unnecessary on retail streets by showing that most customers on one street did not drive.
choices.slip: She makes no such claim; she says the data cannot show what would happen if parking were removed.

choices.text: It reports a limitation of the survey, namely that the shopkeepers' estimates were collected on only one commercial street.
choices.slip: The limitation concerns the data's scope and appears in the third sentence; the second sentence reports the results.

steps: Sentence 2: 62 percent arrived without a car; shopkeepers guessed 20 percent.
Sentence 3: this does not show bike lanes help business.
explanation.why: The statistic corrects the shopkeepers' estimate, and the next sentence keeps it from being read as proof of the policy.
explanation.pattern: Ask what the evidence does and what the author says it does not do.

items.passage: On the day the river was diverted, the engineer Corliss Venkataraman reportedly spent the morning counting herons from the bank. The anecdote is often retold as proof of her sentimentality, but her field notebooks suggest a different reading. The counts, taken at the same stretch each year since 1952, form the only continuous record of the heron population before the dam, and the counts of that last morning were entered in the same columns as all the others, with the same abbreviations and no remark. Far from a farewell, the entry reads as a measurement made so that the loss, if it came, could later be quantified.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It confirms the common interpretation of the anecdote by pointing to notebook entries that show how deeply Venkataraman cared about the herons.
choices.slip: The sentence says the notebooks suggest a different reading from the common one.

choices.text: It offers a different reading of the opening anecdote, which the rest of the text supports with evidence from her notebooks.
It shifts from a story about Venkataraman to a general account of how engineers should record changes in wildlife caused by dams.
choices.slip: The text stays on Venkataraman's notebooks and offers no general rule for engineers.

choices.text: It questions the accuracy of the anecdote by suggesting that Venkataraman did not actually count herons on the morning the river was diverted.
choices.slip: The notebooks show that she did count that morning; the dispute is about what the counting meant.

steps: Sentence 1: the anecdote.
Sentence 2: the usual reading (sentimental) and a different reading from the notebooks.
Rest: notebook evidence for the different reading.
explanation.why: The sentence sets the common reading against the notebooks' reading, and the rest develops the latter.
explanation.pattern: Look for 'often... but' as a signal that the sentence introduces a revised view.

items.passage: For decades, ornithologists explained the autumn departure of warblers from northern forests by falling temperature. The theory predicts that a cold snap should trigger departure, and in several studies it did. But in a 2019 experiment, captive warblers kept at a constant warm temperature still became restless at nearly the same date as wild birds, and the restlessness faded at the same date in spring. The result does not show that temperature plays no part: wild birds that met a sudden freeze left a few days earlier than those that did not. It indicates instead that an internal calendar sets the season of departure while temperature adjusts the timing within it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It presents a long-standing explanation, reports an experiment that overturns it, and proposes an unrelated account in which temperature plays no part.
choices.slip: The text says temperature still adjusts the timing, so the original factor is not discarded.

choices.text: It describes two competing explanations, reports an experiment that favors the newer one, and concludes that the older one should be abandoned.
choices.slip: Only one explanation is described at first, and the conclusion keeps part of it.

choices.text: It presents an accepted explanation, reports an experiment that complicates it, and revises the account while keeping part of it.
It reports an experiment, explains why its results conflict with earlier field studies, and calls for further tests on captive birds.
choices.slip: The text reconciles the experiment with the field evidence and does not call for more captive tests.

steps: Sentences 1-2: temperature theory, with support.
Sentences 3-4: captive-bird experiment complicates it.
Last two sentences: temperature still matters; a calendar sets the season.
explanation.why: The text moves from an old explanation to an experiment that complicates it to a revision that keeps temperature in a supporting role.
explanation.pattern: Track what each part does to the opening claim: supports, complicates, revises.

items.passage: When Ines Vantongeren sold the family orchard, she kept the ladder. It stood against the wall of her new apartment, too tall for any room, still marked with the green that had flaked from the barn, and visitors assumed it was a joke she had stopped explaining. She never used it to reach anything. In the evenings she would sometimes rest a hand on a rung, the way one steadies a horse, and look out at the street, where no tree taller than a lamppost had been allowed to grow.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the ladder in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It represents the life Vantongeren gave up, something she keeps near her without using it or explaining it.
It serves as a comic detail showing that Vantongeren can treat the sale of the orchard lightly in front of her visitors.
choices.slip: The text says visitors assume it is a joke, but her gesture in the evenings shows she does not treat it as one.

choices.text: It signals a practical plan to return to orchard work once she has saved enough money from the sale.
choices.slip: Nothing in the text suggests a plan; she never uses the ladder.

choices.text: It becomes a source of conflict with visitors who misunderstand it, a tension the evening scene develops.
choices.slip: The visitors' assumption is only a passing detail, and no conflict is developed.

steps: The ladder is kept, unused, and visitors misread it.
She touches it as one steadies a horse.
The street has no tall trees: the orchard is lost.
explanation.why: The ladder stands for the lost orchard life, kept as a presence rather than a tool.
explanation.pattern: Ask what an object does emotionally across the whole passage, not only what it looks like.

items.passage: Transport planners generally expect that placing a toll on a bridge reduces the traffic it carries. A widely cited exception is the Pellmoor Strait bridge, where traffic rose in the year after a toll was introduced. But the toll coincided with the closing of the ferry that had been the bridge's only competitor, and when ferry passengers are set aside, the picture changes: among the bridge's original users, car traffic fell by about 6 percent, much as the general expectation predicts.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It states a general expectation, introduces an exception, and concludes that the expectation holds only where drivers have no alternative route.
choices.slip: The text does not limit the expectation to such conditions; it says the exception is explained by a ferry closing.

choices.text: It introduces a widely cited exception, questions the quality of the data behind it, and concludes that no toll has ever raised traffic.
choices.slip: The text accepts the traffic figures and explains them; it makes no claim about every toll.

choices.text: It states a general expectation, offers a case that confirms it, and then offers a second case that confirms it by a different route.
choices.slip: Only one case is discussed, and it first appears to contradict the expectation.

choices.text: It states an expectation, presents an apparent exception, and shows that a separate change explains the exception.

steps: General expectation: tolls reduce traffic.
Exception: traffic rose at one bridge.
Ferry closing explains it; original users fell 6 percent.
explanation.why: The apparent exception disappears once the ferry closing is accounted for, so the expectation stands.
explanation.pattern: Notice when a counterexample is introduced only to be explained within the original rule.

items.passage: The art historian Wenzel Obradovic once dismissed the painter's late landscapes as 'rehearsals for a performance never given,' pointing to their loose edges and unfinished skies. The phrase has stuck, and with it the assumption that the canvases were abandoned. Yet the painter's account books record each of them as sold, several to the same patron, who hung them unframed in a corridor for thirty years. Whatever the pictures were rehearsals for, they were evidently not mistaken for failures by the one person who paid to live with them.
items.question: Which choice best describes how the text uses Obradovic's phrase?

choices.text: It quotes the phrase to praise Obradovic's perceptiveness before extending his argument with details about the painter's patron.
choices.slip: The text does not endorse the phrase; it casts doubt on the assumption it fostered.

choices.text: It quotes the phrase as a widely repeated judgment and then offers evidence that complicates the assumption the phrase encouraged.
It quotes the phrase as one example of the vivid language critics have used for unfinished works in general.
choices.slip: The phrase is tied to this painter's landscapes, not used as an example of a general habit.

choices.text: It quotes the phrase to open a dispute over whether the paintings were sold, which the account books settle in the critic's favor.
choices.slip: The account books show the paintings were sold, which works against the assumption of abandonment.

steps: Phrase quoted and said to have stuck.
Account books show sales and a patron who displayed them.
This complicates the assumption of abandonment.
explanation.why: The phrase is presented as influential and then complicated by evidence of sale and display.
explanation.pattern: Notice whether a quotation is endorsed, mocked, or tested by the rest of the text.

items.passage: Ecologists call a species 'keystone' when its removal changes its community far more than its numbers would predict. The criterion is deliberately not abundance: wolves are scarce compared with the elk they hunt, and the fig trees of some tropical forests make up a small part of the canopy. Yet when wolves were absent from one park, elk browsing thinned the streamside willows, and when fig trees failed in a dry year, fruit-eating birds and monkeys across the forest declined the following season. In each case the species mattered through a role its neighbors could not easily fill, rather than through its share of the living mass.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It defines a term, gives two cases that fit it, and then argues that the term should be extended to the most abundant species.
choices.slip: The text argues the opposite: abundance is not the criterion.

choices.text: It contrasts two kinds of species, gives one case of each, and concludes that rarity is the most reliable sign of influence.
choices.slip: Both cases are of keystone species, and rarity is not offered as a sign of influence.

choices.text: It defines a term, rules out a likely criterion for applying it, and then gives two cases in which the defining feature appears.
It defines a term, criticizes ecologists who rely on abundance, and proposes a new criterion based on removal experiments.
choices.slip: The text does not criticize ecologists; the criterion it states is part of the definition.

steps: Definition of keystone.
Abundance is not the criterion.
Two cases show removal effects out of proportion to numbers.
explanation.why: The text defines, excludes abundance as a test, and illustrates with wolves and fig trees.
explanation.pattern: Map each sentence to a job: define, exclude, illustrate.

items.passage: At first, astronomers explained the faint dimming of a distant star as the passage of a single large planet. When the dips proved irregular, varying from 15 to 22 percent over successive weeks, they proposed a swarm of comets. That account in turn gave way when spectra showed none of the gas that comets shed. The current favorite, a ring of dust unevenly spread around the star, fits both the irregular depth of the dips and the absence of gas, although it is hard to see how such a ring could survive for long, and observers have not ruled out a fourth explanation.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It compares three explanations by their predictions and concludes that the dust ring is the only one consistent with the evidence.
choices.slip: The text says a fourth explanation has not been ruled out, so no explanation is declared the only one.

choices.text: It traces successive explanations of a phenomenon, noting what displaced each, and ends by saying the latest remains uncertain.
It describes a phenomenon and argues that an early explanation was abandoned too soon in favor of a more complicated one.
choices.slip: The text does not argue that the planet or comet explanations deserved to be kept.

choices.text: It contrasts older observing methods with newer ones to show why the preferred explanation of the dimming has changed.
choices.slip: The text cites new observations, not a contrast between methods.

steps: Planet, then comets, then dust ring.
Each replaced after a specific observation.
Last explanation has problems and alternatives remain.
explanation.why: The text is a sequence of replaced explanations ending in an uncertain current one.
explanation.pattern: Look at the order of sentences and the reason given for each change.

items.passage: Why did the town library, unlike others in the region, see more visitors after it began charging a small annual fee? The obvious reading is that residents valued the library more once they had paid for it. But the fee was introduced alongside a new weekend schedule, and branch records show that nearly all of the increase fell on Saturdays and Sundays, when attendance had previously been close to zero. The question, in other words, assumes that the fee did something; the evidence suggests it may have done nothing at all.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It poses a question whose underlying assumption the rest of the text examines and finds weak.
It poses a question that the rest of the text answers by identifying the value residents placed on paid access.
choices.slip: The text rejects this reading rather than supplying it.

choices.text: It states a puzzle that the text resolves by showing that weekday attendance rose after the fee was introduced.
choices.slip: Records show the rise was on weekends, not weekdays.

choices.text: It introduces a general claim about fees and libraries that the text goes on to illustrate with branch records.
choices.slip: The first sentence is a question about one library and is not a general claim.

steps: Sentence 1 asks why the fee raised visits.
The rest shows the rise came with weekend hours.
So the question's assumption is doubtful.
explanation.why: The question presupposes that the fee caused the rise; the text then undermines that presupposition.
explanation.pattern: Notice when a question's wording contains an assumption the text goes on to test.

items.passage: The house on Tarn Lane had been empty for a year before the new tenants came, and for that year the neighbors had spoken of it in the lowered voices people keep for the sick. When the moving van finally arrived, nobody went out to watch. Instead, curtains were drawn back an inch, and over the following days, as lights appeared one by one in the upstairs windows, the lowered voices rose, gradually, to something like the ordinary pitch of the street, as though the house had been forgiven for something.
